World.title: What to know: US court hearing held for alleged Lockerbie bombmaker
World.content:
Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi is the third person charged in the downing of Pan Am Flight 103.

Share What to know: US court hearing held for alleged Lockerbie bombmaker on social media

A United States judge has scheduled a hearing in Washington, DC, to discuss the case against a former Libyan intelligence official accused of participating in the 1988 Lockerbie bombing, an attack on a commercial aeroplane that killed everyone on board.

The case concerns Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi, who reportedly worked for Libya’s external security organisation at the time of the bombing.

Federal prosecutors have accused Mas’ud of delivering the bomb that was later loaded onto Pan Am Flight 103, which exploded over Lockerbie, Scotland, on December 21, 1988.

His trial is expected to be the first held in the US for the Lockerbie bombing. Hundreds of people, many of them Americans, were killed in the explosion.

A court hearing is currently scheduled for Tuesday, but the trial has long been delayed.

Jury selection was set to begin last week. But US District Judge Dabney Friedrich unexpectedly postponed the trial, citing the discovery of new evidence. The delay is designed to give Mas’ud’s defence team time to review the new material.

It is yet another stunning development in a saga that has witnessed countless twists and turns. Here’s what you need to know:

What is this case about?

The US has accused Mas’ud of making the bomb that downed a Pan American Airways plane bound for New York City.



Just over half an hour after it took off from London’s Heathrow airport, the flight exploded, killing all 259 people on board, including passengers and crew.

The plane was 9.45km (31,000 feet) over Scotland when the bomb went off, and the wreckage tumbled onto the town of Lockerbie, destroying an entire city block and killing 11 people on the ground.

The death toll included citizens of 21 countries, including 190 Americans and 43 from the United Kingdom. The passengers included 35 students from New York’s Syracuse University who were returning from a semester abroad.

Nearly four decades later, the bombing remains the deadliest “terrorist” attack in UK history.

What is the new evidence?

Judge Friedrich did not specify the nature of the newly discovered evidence.

According to The Associated Press news agency, Mas’ud’s lawyers said federal prosecutors disclosed the new evidence to them days before jury selection was scheduled to begin.

They added that “constitutional and ethical obligations require the defense to investigate this development”.

What is Mas’ud charged with?

The possible identity of the Lockerbie bombmaker has remained a mystery for years, but US prosecutors have accused Mas’ud of taking part in making and planting the explosive.

Mas’ud, now in his mid-70s, is charged with two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted.

He has denied building the bomb and pleaded not guilty to the charges.

US officials charged Mas’ud on December 21, 2020 – nearly 32 years to the day after the bombing. He was arrested two years later.

What do prosecutors say happened?

According to US prosecutors, Mas’ud worked for the Libyan intelligence service from approximately 1973 to 2011, rising to the rank of colonel.

The US government alleges that Mas’ud and others carried out the bombing at the direction of then-Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was ousted and killed during the country’s civil war in 2011.

Prosecutors say Mas’ud flew from Libya to Malta with a bomb concealed in a Samsonite suitcase. Upon meeting his co-conspirators, he allegedly set the bomb’s timer to go off 11 hours later.

From there, Mas’ud is accused of handing the bomb to a co-conspirator, who placed the suitcase on an airport conveyor belt, before returning to the Libyan capital, Tripoli.

What other cases have occurred?

Two other suspected Libyan intelligence agents, Abd al-Basit al-Magrahi and Al-Amin Khalifa Fahimah, were tried by a panel of Scottish judges in the Netherlands in 2000.



The court acquitted Fahimah and convicted al-Magrahi in 2001, sentencing him to life imprisonment.

Al-Magrahi was released on compassionate grounds in 2009 and died in Libya in 2012. Fahimah died on August 25 this year. US prosecutors believe they met Mas’ud in Malta to plant the bomb.

Why has it taken so long for this case to be tried?

The Lockerbie bombing has been the subject of a joint Scottish-US investigation since December 1988.

Mas’ud has been in US custody since 2022. He was originally due to stand trial in May 2025.

That date was set aside following a joint request from the prosecution and defence, who cited the complexity of the case and Mas’ud’s ill health.

The trial was scheduled for this past April, but was called off again after Mas’ud’s legal team asked for more time to prepare.

When could the trial start?

Judge Friedrich has agreed that the trial’s start date should be pushed back. It is now expected that the trial may not start until next year.

World.title: Far-right Israeli Minister Ben-Gvir and settlers storm Al-Aqsa Mosque

NewsFeed Far-right Israeli Minister Ben-Gvir and settlers storm Al-Aqsa Mosque

World.title: Israel’s Ben-Gvir storms Al-Aqsa mosque in occupied East Jerusalem
World.content:
The far-right Israeli national security minister entered Islam’s third-holiest site alongside settlers and under the protection of Israeli occupation forces.

Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem, performing prayers and appearing to call for a Jewish temple to be located on the site.

With the protection of Israeli occupation forces, Ben-Gvir entered the compound on Monday, accompanied by several rabbis, settlers and security personnel, and declared plans to alter the historical status quo of Islam’s third-holiest site. The far-right politician has performed such provocative antics several times.

Ben-Gvir performed Talmudic prayers and rituals in the eastern section of the mosque’s courtyards, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

As part of the status quo arrangement in place since 1967, performing prayers is not allowed for non-Muslims, although Jewish people are permitted to visit the compound.

“When I was 14 years old, prayer was forbidden, and anyone who murmured was arrested. Today we see redemption. It is very moving to be with you today, and you are right, we must blow the shofar and bring the prayer incantations, and there must be a temple… a temple… a temple… but little by little”, Ben-Gvir said during the incursion, according to Al Jazeera Arabic’s Elias Karram.

“I am very moved… and you say that we must bring the prayer incantations and blow the shofar [ram’s horn],” the national security minister remarked.

The leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, has stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound several times since taking office in 2022, drawing widespread condemnation.



A regular advocate of ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from the territories occupied by Israel, Ben-Gvir is part of a growing settler movement that wants to take over the compound and build a Jewish synagogue in place of the Muslim holy site.

This latest incursion comes as tens of thousands of Jews have participated in recent days in Yom Kippur prayers, which last for a full month at the Western Wall, also known as the Wailing Wall, preceding Jewish holidays in September.

The Jerusalem governorate condemned the incursion, describing it as a dangerous escalation and a flagrant violation of the mosque’s existing historical and legal status, as well as an attempt to impose new realities at the site and alter its Islamic identity, according to Wafa.

Since 2003, Israeli police have allowed settlers to make daily incursions into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, except on Fridays and Saturdays.

Israel often imposes restrictions on Palestinian worshippers. They prevented Eid al-Fitr prayers at Al-Aqsa this year, allowing only 10,000 Palestinians from the occupied West Bank, home to 3.3 million people, into one of Islam’s holiest sites for the first Friday prayers of Ramadan.

World.title: Top US general says no plans to send troops to polls for November elections
World.content:
Remarks come in response to concerns from Democrats that military could be used to interfere in elections.

Share Top US general says no plans to send troops to polls for November elections on social media

The chairman of the United States Joint Chiefs of Staff, the country’s highest ranking military officer, has assured an opposition lawmaker that there are no plans to deploy troops to polling places during elections on November 3.

“The Joint Force has no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections,” General Dan Caine said in the letter obtained on Monday by The Associated Press news agency. “Likewise, the Joint Force has no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material.”

Caine’s letter was addressed to Democratic US Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who recently asked Caine and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to confirm they won’t send troops to the polls. Caine, who advises Hegseth and President Donald Trump on military matters, also wrote: “I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections.”

Anxiety among Democrats that the Trump administration could try to meddle in the midterm elections has grown, particularly after the president deployed federal agents in Democratic-led states over the objections of local leaders. He said they were needed for immigration enforcement and due to crime and protests.

Slotkin told the AP earlier in August that Trump has been laying the groundwork to claim November’s elections will have been stolen. She noted that Trump contemplated using the military to seize voting machines after his loss in 2020 to President Joe Biden and has deployed the National Guard to cities against the wishes of Democratic leaders. He also deployed active-duty Marines to Los Angeles during his immigration crackdown in 2025.



Federal law prohibits the deployment of armed federal forces to election locations unless “necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States”. If any element of the military were to get involved, it would likely be the National Guard under state control.

“The nonpartisan tradition of military service and the constitutional guardrails that prevent our military from becoming a domestic police force for one political party are essential to maintaining our democracy,” Slotkin said in a news release this month announcing her letters to US military officials. “Thus, our nation’s senior-most defense and security leaders are the final failsafe for our democracy.”

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles denied in a Vanity Fair interview last year that Trump would use the military to suppress voting in the midterms.

Sonja Thrasher, Slotkin’s press secretary, said Hegseth has not replied to the letter asking him to confirm troops won’t be deployed to the polls in November.

Slotkin had asked for a response by last Thursday.

In 2020, General Mark Milley, then-chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, responded to a similar letter from Slotkin, then a member of the US House of Representatives.

“I believe deeply in the principle of an apolitical U.S. military,” Milley wrote. “In the event of a dispute over some aspect of the elections, by law U.S. courts and the U.S. Congress are required to resolve any disputes, not the U.S. military.”

World.title: Nepal rescuers blast hillside in search of hydropower workers as families wait anxiously
World.content:
The families of more than 600 workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels along Nepal's Trishuli River are clinging to hope their loved ones can be found alive.

Rescuers continued battling to reach them on Monday, using explosives to blast into the hillside before pumping air into the Trishuli-3A site - fearing a critical window to reach survivors is closing.

"I wish we could find him. I wish he would come home," Anushila Bhandari, wife of Aurus Bhandari, a 33-year-old engineer missing on a project site, told BBC Nepali.

It comes as the death toll from the flood disaster on the Nepal-Tibet border reached 939, according to the country's disaster management authority.

The agency also revised its estimate of the number of missing to 3,925, of whom 592 are foreign nationals.

Roughly one in seven missing people are believed to be workers at the hydropower plants. Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.

The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved.

World.title: US and Iran trade strikes for first time in weeks
World.content:
Iran and the US have traded strikes after American forces attacked two rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

The first known US strikes on Iran since late July killed two people and injured two others, according to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which vowed "response and punishment".

US Central Command (Centcom) said it took "limited, precise action" after observing Iran preparing to "launch rockets and deploy sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz", according to its spokesperson.

Iran said it had struck US military bases in Jordan in response, with Jordan's army saying it had intercepted eight missiles early on Monday morning.

Iran's state TV also said the Iranian army had targeted an air base in the UAE with drones.

However, the UAE's Ministry of Defence denied the reports that Al-Minhad Air Base had been targeted as "unfounded". The UAE did confirm it shot down a drone.

The US strike is the first known attack on Iran since President Donald Trump paused a renewed military campaign in late July.

Larak Island is just offshore from the key port of Bandar Abbas and sits right on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global shipping. Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel through before the war began.

Since the conflict began in February, the strait has effectively been closed, causing wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets.

Iran is currently demanding that tanker traffic pass by Larak Island for checks and reportedly forcing vessels to pay $2m (Â£1.5m) to cross.

Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, said earlier that the attack on Larak was carried out by drones.

World.title: Man arrested after Swiss rave shooting that killed woman
World.content:
A 43-year-old Swiss man has been arrested following a shooting at a rave in Switzerland in which a woman was killed.

Italian 22-year-old Maria Spinelli was killed and several others injured at a techno rave being held at a horse racing track in Aarau, a town about 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich on Sunday.

The shooting initiated a nearly 24-hour manhunt before Aarau cantonal police confirmed they apprehended the suspect shortly before 01:00 local time on Monday (23:00 GMT on Sunday).

"The investigation into the exact sequence of events, the background and the possible motive is currently under way," police said in a statement. "At this time, it is assumed that the perpetrator acted alone."

Police first received a report of shots fired at the Schachen race track at about 02:30 local time on Sunday.

Spinelli died at the scene, while four men and a woman, aged between 24 and 27, were taken to hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe".

An eyewitness told Swiss news outlet Blick that he had "suddenly heard the gunshots" minutes after the music stopped, initially believing they were fireworks.

He said he was told to hide by a man and a woman, the latter of whom was shot.

Organisers had expected 3,500 people to attend. Aarau, home to approximately 23,000 people, is less than 40km from the border with Germany, where local media reported police were supporting Swiss forces.

The arrest marks a quick progression in the police investigation - on Sunday afternoon, the force in Aarau said it had no leads on the perpetrator and was unsure whether it was one person or several.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni previously said she was confident Swiss authorities would "shed full light on what happened and find anyone responsible".

Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement that it was sending officials to Zurich "to closely follow the investigation".

Switzerland has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe, although violent shootings are rare and tighter controls were introduced in recent years.

The last major shooting occurred in 2001, when 14 members of the parliament and local government of Zug, near Lucerne, were killed by a gunman who then took his own life.

World.title: 'She slipped out of my hand' - children missing after ferry sinks off northern Cyprus
World.content:
Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her grasp and disappear as the ferry they were travelling on capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing eight people.

Her daughter Miray and six-year-old son Memhet Asaf are among 20 people still missing after the vessel sunk while en route to Turkey from the coastal town of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus.

She and her husband Hayri survived, and like many other families are waiting for news of their loved ones back in port as rescuers continue to search.

"She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Bicer told reporters through tears.

Bicer said a suitcase fell on top of her, which forced her daughter from her grip. She managed to grab hold of her daughter's foot, but her shoes were coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel and she slipped through her hands.

"It was slippery everywhere. It was like oil. She slipped out of my hand," she recalled.

The family was returning to Turkey after a holiday on the Mediterranean island.

"We couldn't intervene, we lost our children," Hayri Bicer said. "Two of my three children are gone. We left them. We are leaving them on this island as we go."

The vessel had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members. Nineteen passengers are currently being treated in hospitals in northern Cyprus, local authorities say.

The eight crew members, including the ship's captain, and one other man were formally arrested on Monday. They will be detained for three days, while warrants have been issued for several other people.

The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 (09:30 GMT), en route to the town of Tasucu in Turkey.

It had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday but its journey was delayed due to severe storms hitting the island. The seas were still rough on Sunday.

Some eyewitness accounts say the double-hulled ferry jolted violently before slamming onto the sea surface, with part of its bow bursting open on impact.

Ãnal Ãstel, prime minister of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized.

While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he said.

World.title: US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case
World.content:
The celebrity lawyers hired to represent US musician D4vd in his upcoming murder trial have withdrawn from the case.

The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has been appointed a public defender to mount his defence against the charge of murdering Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, whose remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to his address.

Burke, 21, pleaded not guilty to the murder charges in a Los Angeles court on Monday.

A judge determined last month that he will stand trial for murder. Prosecutors have alleged he stabbed the teen after years of sexual abuse before dismembering her body.

World.title: US Supreme Court clears way for Trump to keep building White House ballroom
World.content:
The US Supreme Court has ruled that construction of a $400m (Â£297m) ballroom at the White House can go ahead, handing a win to President Donald Trump.

In a 5-4 ruling, the justices granted the Trump administration's emergency request, blocking lower court rulings that would have halted construction of an above-ground portion of the project.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation filed the legal challenge, arguing that the president did not have unilateral authority to proceed with construction.

Trump demolished the historic East Wing of the executive residence last autumn to begin building the ballroom.

On Friday, the high court had temporarily allowed construction of the White House ballroom to move forward.

Chief Justice John Roberts issued a stay, allowing the ballroom project, which includes a military complex, to continue while the high court considered the lawsuit aiming to halt it entirely.

On Monday, it was Roberts, a conservative, who sided with the three dissenting liberal justices to write that "construction is likely unlawful".

The dissenting justices said that Congress "has explicitly prohibited" the construction of any building or structure on federal grounds in the capital "without express authority of Congress".

They added that the legislative branch had "not passed any law resembling 'express authority' for the Executive's construction of it".

In the unsigned order, the five judges who cleared the way for construction said the Trump administration had established that it was likely to succeed in arguing that it would "suffer irreparable harm without a stay, and that the balance of equities tips in its favor".

"Beginning with the merits, the government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks standing to challenge the East Wing project," they wrote.

Trump has long argued that the White House needs a larger events space, and more recently, that it was important for his security.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation argued that construction was causing irreversible damage to a historical landmark.

World.title: Dolly Parton laid to rest alongside husband in Nashville
World.content:
Dolly Parton has been laid to rest, the music legend's great-niece has said.

The singer had a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, following her death earlier in the week at the age of 80.

She has been placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city.

Lainey Parton posted an emotional tribute, external a day after the burial, saying: "It still doesn't feel real that she's gone. I'm going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there."

World.title: Ex-congressman George Santos banned from betting platform for life
World.content:
Prediction-market operator Kalshi has permanently barred former US congressman George Santos from trading on its platform.

The company alleged that Santos, who was expelled from Congress following a series of fraud and identity-theft charges, placed bets in February related to his own attendance at US President Donald Trump's State of the Union address, according to a notice of disciplinary action.

Kalshi said its compliance team concluded his activity showed signs of insider dealing, prompting the lifetime ban. It said it was acting independently without waiting for external enforcement action.

Santos on X thanked Kalshi for the ban and said "Let's see how much longer you guys are around for".

The BBC has contacted Santos for comment.

In 2025, Trump ordered the release of Santos, who had been sentenced to a seven-year prison term for wire fraud and identity theft. He had served three months.

In July, Santos agreed to pay $35,000 to settle a federal investigation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission into his State of the Union trades.

Kalshi, alleging Santos used non-public information to place bets, issued a penalty of $71,356 (Â£38,000).

The disciplinary moves come at a moment when prediction markets â which allow users to wager on outcomes ranging from elections to economic indicators â are facing heightened scrutiny.

Both Kalshi and rival Polymarket have reported an uptick in unusual trading patterns, forcing platforms to strengthen monitoring systems and respond more aggressively to potential misconduct.

Kalshi said Santos's case was referred to federal authorities earlier this summer after internal systems flagged suspicious behaviour linked to his account.

The company said the case centered on his trades in a market tied to whether he would attend Trump's address â an event he could directly influence.

Its compliance team found he placed a series of sizeable bets between 2 and 25 February, some of which were based on false or misleading public statements about his plans, according to the company.

His comments moved contract prices, and he ultimately earned $17,839.57 from the trades.

Santos has denied wrongdoing in various matters but has admitted to stealing identities of nearly a dozen people, including next of kin. He pleaded guilty to wire fraud and aggravated identity theft and served three months in prison before Trump commuted his sentence last year.

He embellished much about his biography in the run-up to his election to Congress in 2022. The former lawmaker was only the sixth in US history to be expelled from Congress.

The Kalshi episode underscores the growing compliance burden facing prediction markets as they attract more users and move closer to mainstream products. Regulators have signalled that platforms will be expected to meet higher standards as the industry matures, particularly when political or economic events are involved.

World.title: Gunmen invade Anambra community, kill two
World.content:
Gunmen, suspected to be cultists, have killed two persons at separate locations in Awka, the Anambra State capital.

The incident, PREMIUM TIMES gathered, occurred on Sunday within the Amaenyi Area and S.M. Okeke Street, both in Awka.

Residents told this newspaper that although several persons were shot during the encounter, two persons have been confirmed dead as of Sunday night.

One of the persons killed during the attack was identified as Isaac Nwosu, an elderly man.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

A resident, who asked not to be named for fear of attack, said the gunmen were believed to be members of Aye, a dreaded cult group.

The resident said that although Mr Nwosu was not a cultist, the attackers were said to have targeted one of his sons, named Chinedu, who is reportedly a member of Vikings, another cult group.

Police speak

The police in Anambra State confirmed the development in a statement on Monday.

In the statement, the police spokesperson in the state, Tochukwu Ikenga, said the police command condemned the deadly attack.

Mr Ikenga, a superintendent of police, confirmed that two persons, including Mr Nwosu, were killed during the attack, but did not state that cultists carried it out.

“The Command has consequently intensified the ongoing manhunt for the perpetrators and is calling for the support and cooperation of members of the public to assist in bringing the suspects to justice,” he said.

The spokesperson narrated that police operatives immediately stormed Awka upon receiving information that gunmen had attacked and killed two persons in the area.

Upon arrival at the scenes, the operatives recovered the bodies of the victims along Capital City Road, Amaenyi, and S.M. Okeke Street, Amaikwo, Awka, respectively.

“The victims were taken to a hospital, where they were subsequently confirmed dead by medical personnel.

“While one of the victims is yet to be identified, the second victim has been identified as Isaac Nwosu, male, also known as ‘Azia,’” he stated.

“The operatives also recovered from the scene the sum of ₦7,550, one Moniepoint ATM card and a pair of slippers.”

Police commissioner reacts

Mr Ikenga said the Commissioner of Police in Anambra State, Nnanna Ama, condemned the deadly attack, describing the killings as “unacceptable and a direct affront to the peace and security of the state.”

Mr Ama directed that the case be transferred to the State Criminal Investigation Department, Awka, for discreet and comprehensive investigation.

The commissioner also ordered operatives to intensify patrols, surveillance and intelligence gathering across Awka and adjoining areas.

The police chief called on community leaders, residents, motorists, business owners and other members of the public who may have witnessed the incidents or have information regarding the suspects, their movements or the vehicle used in the attacks to come forward and assist the police.

“Such information will be treated with utmost confidentiality,” he assured.

He reiterated the Command’s readiness to partner with the community, which he said remains critical to effective policing.

World.title: 2027: NDC accuses INEC of replacing party’s candidates with ‘unknown persons’
World.content:
The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has accused the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) of “systematically removing” the party’s nominated candidates for the 2027 general elections, and replacing them with “strange names” unknown to the party.

The NDC’s National Chairman, Moses Zuwoghe, disclosed this in a statement posted on the party’s official X handle on Sunday.

Giving an instance of the replacement, Mr Zuwoghe said INEC published a list of the NDC Anambra State House of Assembly candidate that “reads like a deliberate plot to sabotage the NDC ahead of the general elections and cause dissatisfaction among its millions of supporters.”

“The NDC, totally condemns the action of the INEC and its officials over the uploading and publication of unauthorised names in various constituencies, principally in the Anambra State House of Assembly, home state of our presidential candidate, Peter Obi, where 10 names unknown to the party; names not authorised by the party; names not sent by the party to INEC, in accordance with the law, have now been uploaded and published as candidates of the party,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The national chairman asked the electoral commission to urgently investigate the matter and unravel the circumstances surrounding the decision.

The official said the investigation should also be extended to other constituencies nationwide where the NDC had observed a pattern of fencing out “authentic candidates of the party INEC-chosen imposters.”

“We, as a party, are also carrying out our own independent investigation, the preliminary findings of which are already pointing to the complicity of INEC officials foisting names purporting to be our candidates, but who are not from us, and using the uploading process as tool of blackmail and intimidation against the party, and getting those names to be uploaded and published, for whatever purpose or ulterior motive,” he said.

Mr Zuwoghe listed some of the individuals allegedly smuggled into the NDC list of candidates, including Umennaaijiego Jude Ezenwa (Onitsha South I), Akpotue Obinna Chibuike (Onitsha South II), Nwankwo Chiemerie (Orumba North), Maduagwu Eric K. (Anaocha I), and Ngoebisi Obinna (Idemili North).

Others are Isintume Charles (Njikoka), Nwachukwu Nonso (Nnewi South), Okeke Ifeanyi Akunne (Nnewi South II), Nnonyelu Samson (Ayamelum), and Azotani Chuks Francis (Dunukofia).

How the names were uploaded without NDC approval

Mr Zuwoghe stressed that he and the NDC leadership never uploaded those names on the INEC portal.

“What happened was that after the conclusion of our primaries and the appeal process which is also a part and parcel of the primaries and candidates nomination process, the stakeholders from Anambra working with the party leadership, representatives of our presidential candidate, and the appeals panel, which is the tradition of our party, produced a final list of candidates, a list which was signed off on by all.

“However, when that final list was uploaded to the INEC portal, using the code given to us by the electoral commission, the INEC officials who are in complete control of the backend of the portal kept nine of the names on ‘pending’ status.

“Their claim was that their system already had those names, which they said were submitted by their officials who monitored the NDC primaries on the field,” he narrated.

The national chairman expressed surprise that the commission remained adamant despite the NDC formally appealing against the uploading of the individuals, as they were not part of the party’s leadership.

“To further confirm that there was a predetermined effort on the part of INEC to impose the said nine candidates on the party, and embarrass both NDC and Mr Peter Obi, INEC went behind the NDC to collect the Form EC-9 directly from the candidates, bypassing the party, and uploading the same.

“It then went ahead to publish the controversial names as authentic candidates of the party,” the official said.

‘This is unacceptable’

Mr Zuwoghe said the development was unacceptable and stressed that the INEC’s action “runs against the grain of the Electoral Act and INEC’s own guidelines.”

The national chairman argued that, rather than uploading “fictitious names,” INEC could have left the NDC’s space for the list of candidates blank if the commission believed that the party’s submitted list of candidates did not tally with those its monitoring teams supplied.

“At the very worst, NEC could have left us with no candidates for those positions if they knew they were unwilling to engage us in addressing any perceived anomaly,” he said.

‘Opposition parties probably on target’

Mr Zuwoghe frowned at the pattern of alleged deliberate effort by INEC to prevent political parties from uploading their rightful candidates while “criminally handpicking candidates for parties and instigating a crisis of confidence and internal disharmony within the said parties.”

The national chairman suggested that the opposition parties appear to be targeted by the electoral commission.

He vowed that the NDC would take legal action against INEC to ensure that what they termed “mischief” was reversed.

“Even as we move to approach the court of competent jurisdiction to seek redress and restore our authentic candidates, the general public and our millions of supporters should note that these are not our candidates,” he said of the disowned candidates uploaded by INEC.

INEC denies wrongdoing

When contacted on Monday, INEC spokesperson Mohammed Haruna denied the NDC’s allegations.

Mr Haruna explained that the electoral commission uploaded only a copy of the NDC’s list of candidates, which was signed at the party’s primaries by both the party’s representatives and the commission’s officials who monitored the primaries.

The INEC spokesperson further said that, in line with its guidelines, the commission trained a representative of the NDC, like representatives of other parties, who would have access to upload the party’s nominated candidates’ list to the electoral body’s portal.

“When (representatives of the parties) try to upload (the list of candidates), if it is different from what was originally uploaded, it will not come to our system.

“So, they should ask their secretariat about the list of candidates they want to upload, whether it is different from what has already been uploaded based on results received from the party’s primaries by our monitors,” he said.

“The results that they signed by themselves (NDC) and our monitors immediately after the primaries are over are what we upload to our portal.”

Mr Haruna said even a mix-up or misspelling of names in the original list could lead to the portal rejecting the upload of such names as candidates.

“If they have their own internal mechanism, maybe an appeal to change a candidate, they have to tell us that this has happened.

“But if, without telling us, they want to change it, it will not even come to our system. It is not possible to even change it (from their end),” he said.

World.title: Police fire tear gas at pensioners protesting arrears at Lagos House
World.content:
Police officers in Lagos State on Monday fired teargas at pensioners who gathered at the Lagos House in Ikeja to protest unpaid pension increases, wage awards and other outstanding benefits.

According to Vanguard newspaper, the retirees, drawn from the Nigeria Union of Pensioners (NUP) and the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS), had gone to the government premises to press the Lagos State Government to implement the increases and settle the arrears they said had accumulated.

The situation became tense after police officers deployed teargas, sending some of the protesters away from the premises.

The action came on the date the retirees had earlier set as a deadline for the government to address their grievances.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The pensioners had warned that they would stage a larger demonstration on 31 August

if the state failed to act, particularly on the pension enhancement and wage award.

Their demand for an increase also has a policy dimension. The National Pension Commission (PenCom) had previously asked the Lagos Government to extend periodic pension increases granted to retirees under the Defined Benefit Scheme to those under the CPS.

The disagreement has persisted despite the state’s assurances on pension payments.

The Lagos State Pension Commission (LASPEC), responding to complaints from retirees in an earlier report, said the government had paid N168 billion to about 48,000 pensioners.

READ ALSO: FRCN pensioners resolve to join naked protest

The retirees, however, have continued to complain about unpaid increases and other benefits, saying delays have put many of them under financial strain as living costs rise.

Monday’s protest at Lagos House has now added a new dimension to the dispute, with the pensioners questioning the decision to use teargas to disperse them.

The Lagos State Government and the police had not issued a statement on the incident as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: Umohette celebrates 20th career win, hails Anthony Joshua, Itauma
World.content:
Akwa Ibom-born boxer Enobong “The Nigerian Gentleman” Umohette has secured the 20th victory of his professional career after defeating former WBL heavyweight champion Fidel “Infierno” Munoz by unanimous decision.

Umohette successfully defended his UBC South American regional title in an eight-round bout held at the Santa Marta Sports Complex in Colombia on the penultimate weekend.

According to a report by the sports correspondent of Santa Marta Heraldo, Munoz was not only a Colombian native and hometown favourite but also a vastly experienced professional with more than 80 fights, including 35 knockout victories.

The bout was described as tactical, with the highly mobile Munoz attempting to use lateral movement to outmanoeuvre Umohette.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, Umohette frustrated his opponent by controlling the centre of the ring, steadily applying pressure, cutting off the former champion’s escape routes and landing clean punches consistently.

All three judges scored the fight in Umohette’s favour, handing him a unanimous decision victory.

The win extended Umohette’s current run to 11 consecutive victories.

Umohette thanked God, his family, promoter Erik Fleming, co-promoter Monte Ekott, boxing fans and his supporters in Nigeria and the United States for backing his comeback journey.

United boxers

He also congratulated fellow Nigerian heavyweight champion Anthony Joshua on his recent knockout victory over Albanian fighter Kristen Prenga in the second round.

Umohette said Joshua overcame significant adversity in the bout, rising from two knockdowns before stopping Prenga. He also praised Joshua’s resilience in returning to the ring after the death of close associates in a fatal car crash last year.

The crash nearly claimed Joshua’s life and left him with significant physical and emotional trauma.

Umohette also congratulated and commended Moses Itauma, the 21-year-old European-born boxer and fellow Akwa Ibom indigene, following his IBF world title fight against highly decorated Croatian heavyweight Filip Hrgovic.

He said Itauma displayed the qualities that had accelerated his rise to world-title contention at such a young age.

According to Umohette, Itauma was on the verge of achieving a feat last accomplished by Mike Tyson 40 years ago and deserved the highest praise for reaching such heights early in his career.

READ ALSO: Anthony Joshua records stunning knockout victory over Kristian Prenga

He described Itauma as the future of heavyweight boxing and expressed confidence that the young boxer would recover from the defeat and eventually win a world heavyweight title.

Reacting to Umohette’s victory, his promoter, Fleming, said the bout was an important test of the boxer’s durability at the championship level.

Speaking from California, Fleming said it was necessary to reassess Umohette’s ability to compete over eight-, 10- and 12-round distances without becoming desperate to secure a knockout.

Umohette last completed an eight-round bout in Mexico in 2023 and subsequently won seven consecutive fights by knockout.

Fleming also praised the professionalism of the Santa Marta boxing commission, noting that Umohette secured a unanimous decision against a hometown favourite in front of his home crowd.

He said discussions would soon begin over a possible bout between Umohette and Labinot Xhoxhaj, the current European heavyweight champion.

Umohette’s professional record now stands at 20 wins and three losses.

World.title: A leadership lesson for Nigeria from Dolly Parton, By Dakuku Peterside
World.content:
Dolly Parton has never governed a state, controlled a public budget, or commanded the machinery of government. Yet her life offers Nigeria a timely lesson: leadership is measured not by the grandeur of office, the length of a convoy or the volume of publicity, but by the durable good created for others.

Parton built global fame through music, entertainment, and business. She could have treated success as private property. Instead, she converted influence into service — supporting literacy, medical research, disaster relief, education, hospitals, and community programmes. Her example is not an invitation for Nigerian leaders to imitate an American celebrity. It is a reminder of a universal principle: influence is stewardship.

Nigeria does not lack influential people. It has presidents, governors, ministers, legislators, regulators, traditional rulers, business leaders, religious figures, and celebrities. What it too often lacks is the disciplined conversion of influence into trusted public value.

Parton’s Imagination Library captures this distinction. Launched in 1995 as a local literacy initiative, it became an international programme that has distributed hundreds of millions of free books to children. Its significance lies not merely in generosity, but in institutional design. She did not simply give books on a celebrated occasion; she created a system capable of delivering them repeatedly.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

During the COVID-19 pandemic, she donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Centre, supporting early research connected with the development of Moderna’s vaccine. The principle was straightforward: identify a public problem, commit resources, and support a practical solution.

Nigeria’s leadership deficit often begins where this sense of stewardship ends. Public office is too frequently approached as privileged access to contracts, appointments, protection, and personal accumulation. Political loyalty can outweigh competence; public resources are captured by private networks; and institutions are bent around the interests of those who temporarily control them.

The consequences are not abstract. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2023 national corruption survey found that 27 per cent of Nigerians who had contact with public officials paid a bribe during the preceding year. Although this was slightly lower than the 29 per cent recorded in 2019, cash bribes paid to public officials were estimated at approximately ₦721 billion in 2023.

Behind that figure are millions of humiliating encounters: a motorist compelled to pay at a checkpoint, a trader charged unofficially for a permit, a patient denied attention without inducement or a jobseeker expected to purchase an opportunity. When influence becomes a private commodity, citizens pay in money, dignity, and lost opportunity.

The deeper lesson from Parton’s philanthropy is that leadership must build institutions, not merely monuments. A ceremonial donation generates applause for a day; a credible literacy programme changes lives for decades. A ribbon-cutting attracts cameras; a transparent procurement system, a reliable hospital, or a professionally managed scholarship scheme continues to serve after the officeholder has departed.

Nigeria’s governance culture remains excessively attached to visible projects and individual personalities. Administrations arrive, rename inherited programmes, abandon unfinished projects, remove experienced officials, and announce new beginnings. Continuity is sacrificed to political ownership. Public institutions become temporary estates rather than enduring national assets.

The claim that most public institutions lack effective, public-facing systems for disclosing how they use public resources is not my conjecture. The evidence is clear. The 2025 Transparency and Integrity Index (TII) found alarmingly weak transparency and accountability across Nigerian public institutions. Of the 517 MDAs assessed, only six scored above the 50% benchmark, while the vast majority fell in the “red zone.” Nine MDAs scored zero.

The message is clear: institutions entrusted with public resources are falling seriously short on disclosure, accountability, and public-facing integrity. The picture is even more disturbing at the level closest to citizens. The Nigerian Local Government Integrity Index reported that 85 per cent of the country’s 774 local governments fell within the “very high” or “critical” risk categories, reflecting opacity, weak enforcement, and poor service delivery.

For citizens, institutional failure has a physical address. It is the primary healthcare centre without medicine, the community road rendered impassable by rain, the refuse left uncollected, the market without sanitation and the local council whose budget cannot be meaningfully examined. An institution is not strengthened because a new building bears a leader’s name. It is strengthened when rules work, professionals are protected, resources are accounted for and services reach the public consistently.

Nigeria’s preference for monuments over institutions is reinforced by a political culture that rewards what can be photographed. The remodelled Abuja City Gate, presented as a symbol of renewal, identity and national pride, illustrates the attraction of ceremonial achievements. A capital city should maintain attractive landmarks. But ceremonial visibility must not be confused with institutional progress.

The meaningful questions are less glamorous: Was the project cost publicly disclosed? Was procurement transparent? Is there a credible maintenance plan? What measurable improvement did it bring to the administration of the city? A monument may embody national aspiration, but without transparency and sustainable management, its symbolism can exceed its public value.

Institution-building rarely produces immediate spectacle. Transparent planning approvals, audited asset registers, responsive complaint systems, enforceable service standards, and competitive procurement do not always offer dramatic commissioning ceremonies. Yet these are the achievements that make government dependable.

Crisis provides an even sterner test. Nigeria regularly confronts floods, insecurity, displacement, food inflation, unemployment, and public-health emergencies. The official response often follows a familiar script: visits to affected communities, sympathetic speeches, high-level committees, promises of intervention and relief that arrives late — or not at all.

The 2022 floods exposed this gap between appearance and impact. Homes, farms, and infrastructure were destroyed, communities displaced and vulnerable households pushed deeper into hardship. A subsequent recovery assessment found that 80.4 per cent of surveyed households considered external flood-response and recovery services unhelpful.

That finding should trouble every level of government. Emergency leadership is not measured by the number of officials photographed in flooded communities. It is measured by whether warnings were acted upon; whether evacuation routes and shelters were prepared; and whether food, medicine, sanitation, compensation, and reconstruction reached affected families in time. Sympathy without an effective response is public relations, not leadership.

The removal of the petrol subsidy in 2023 presented a different but equally consequential test. There were defensible fiscal arguments for reform, including the enormous cost and questionable sustainability of subsidy spending. But economic logic does not erase human pain. Transportation, food, and energy costs increased almost immediately, while credible cushioning measures remained distant from the daily experience of many citizens.

A people-centred transition would have preceded sacrifice with preparation: a clear explanation of the policy, transparent accounting of the savings, targeted income support, dependable mass transportation, wage protection, food security measures, and safeguards for vulnerable households. Good leadership does not merely take tough decisions. It equips people to withstand their consequences.

This is where proximity matters. Parton’s working-class background did not remain a convenient detail in her biography; it informed the causes she supported. Nigeria’s governing class, by contrast, often appears insulated from the conditions under which most citizens live.

A citizen who spends hours navigating a broken road struggles to make sense of the sirens and convoys of officials who have failed to repair it. A family unable to afford treatment cannot easily trust leaders who routinely seek healthcare abroad while public hospitals deteriorate. Calls for citizens to “endure,” “sacrifice,” or “be patient” sound hollow when sacrifice flows in only one direction.

This distance is also democratic. Many Nigerians have little direct contact with elected representatives outside campaign periods. Leaders who enter communities to solicit votes may become inaccessible once elected. Major taxes, subsidy reforms, infrastructure choices, and budgetary priorities are frequently announced without meaningful consultation, accessible data, or functioning feedback mechanisms. Citizens become an audience for government decisions rather than partners in governance.

Humility offers a necessary corrective. Roads, hospitals, schools, and security services are not personal gifts from officeholders. They are public obligations financed by taxes, national revenue, borrowing and the work of civil servants and contractors. A governor who commissions a school has not bestowed private generosity upon the people; the governor has performed a constitutional duty.

Yet publicly funded projects are routinely personalised through oversized portraits, self-congratulatory publicity and naming practices that portray ordinary responsibilities as exceptional acts of benevolence. Institutional credit is displaced by personal glorification. The state becomes indistinguishable from the officeholder.

Humility also requires openness to scrutiny. Nigeria’s Constitution requires public officers to declare their assets upon assuming office, periodically while serving and at the end of their tenure. Yet concerns persist about compliance and the limited accessibility of declarations. When leaders resist disclosure or treat questions from journalists, citizens, legislatures, and civil-society organisations as hostility, they undermine the accountability that gives democratic office legitimacy.

Dolly Parton’s lesson is therefore not really about celebrity or philanthropy. It is about the moral purpose of influence. Leadership should leave behind stronger institutions, better-prepared communities, more educated children, greater public trust, and citizens who feel respected rather than exploited.

Nigeria will not be transformed by speeches, monuments, or ceremonies alone. It will change when those entrusted with power treat office as service, public resources as a sacred trust, crisis as a call to practical action and achievement as an invitation to humility. The true legacy of leadership is not how prominently a leader’s name is displayed, but how well the people continue to live when that leader is gone.

Dakuku Peterside is the author of Leading in a Storm and Beneath the Surface.

World.title: Aston Villa sign Imuran as Nigeria defender eyes bigger stage
World.content:
Rofiat Imuran’s limited role with the Super Falcons has not stopped the Nigerian defender from taking another major step in her club career, with Aston Villa confirming her signing ahead of the 2026/27 season.

The 22-year-old full-back joins the English club after establishing herself in the domestic game with London City Lionesses, earning a move to a Villa side that is continuing to strengthen under manager Natalia Arroyo.

Aston Villa announced the signing over the weekend, subject to visa approval, making Imuran the club’s ninth addition of the summer transfer window.

While her opportunities with Nigeria have been restricted in recent years, Imuran has remained part of the national team setup.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

She made her senior international debut in 2022 and was included in Nigeria’s squads for the 2023 FIFA Women’s World Cup and the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco.

At the most recent WAFCON tournament in Morocco, Imuran was largely a substitute and made only one appearance, coming off the bench in Nigeria’s 1-0 victory over Zambia.

Her club career, however, has followed a different trajectory.

Imuran began her senior career in France with Stade de Reims, where she made 27 league appearances and scored seven goals over two seasons.

She moved to England in 2024 to join London City Lionesses, where her performances have helped her earn another opportunity in the Women’s Super League with Aston Villa.

The move gives Imuran a fresh platform to compete at a higher level and potentially strengthen her claim for increased involvement with the Super Falcons.

“I’m very excited to be here, and I want to achieve a lot of things,” Imuran said after completing the move.

“It’s a big club with a lot of history, and it has big ambitions, and I want to be part of it.”

Right qualities

Marisa Ewers, the club’s director of Women’s Football, said Imuran’s qualities suited the style Arroyo is seeking to implement.

“Rofiat is an exciting young defender who already has good experience in English football and at the international level.

“She brings pace, energy and quality to our defensive options, and we believe her attributes are a really good fit for how Natalia wants the team to play.”

Ewers also highlighted the club’s ambition to strengthen its links with African football.

“As a club, we have ambitions to build stronger connections across Africa and continue to identify and develop exciting talent from the continent. Rofiat’s arrival is another positive step in that direction.

“We’re delighted to welcome her to Aston Villa and look forward to seeing her continue to develop with us.”

Villa ended their announcement with a message to its new signing: “Welcome to the Villa family, Rofiat!💜”

World.title: APGA sweeps Anambra LG polls, wins 21 chairmanship seats
World.content:
The All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) has won all 21 chairmanship and 326 councillorship seats in the 29 August Local Government elections held in Anambra State.

Declaring the results on Sunday, the Chairman of Anambra State Independent Electoral Commission (ANSIEC), Genevieve Osakwe, said the election was free, fair, and credible.

She also said the election was conducted peacefully in accordance with the state electoral laws and guidelines.

Mrs Osakwe said APGA fielded candidates for various positions across the 21 Local Government Areas (LGAs), while the Young Progressives Party (YPP) fielded a chairmanship candidate only in Anambra East.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

She said APGA won in 20 LGAs through a “Yes or No” voting pattern, having produced sole candidates, while in Anambra East, APGA polled 50,169 votes to defeat YPP, which scored 1,658 votes.

“I hereby declare the APGA candidates winners after polling the majority of votes for all the positions.

“I reaffirm the declaration of councillorship results already declared at the local government levels and append the commission’s approval to the outcome of the elections,” she said.

The ANSIEC chairman congratulated the winners and urged them to serve with a high sense of responsibility.

She also appealed to candidates who lost the election to accept the outcome in the spirit of democratic competition.

Mrs Osakwe commended voters, political parties, security agencies, civil society organisations, ANSIEC personnel, and the media for their support in conducting the election.

“The electoral process also provides lawful avenues for challenging any results, where legitimate grounds exist,” she added.

Winners

The elected chairpersons and the LGAs were Kingsley Ezeagu (Aguata), Ifeanyi Chinwzee (Anambra East), Tony Obierika (Anambra West), Paulinus Okafor (Anaocha), ThankGod Anago (Awka North) and Chinedu Okafor (Awka South).

Others were Mgbechi Igwebuike (Ayamelum), Clement Ozumba (Dunukofia), Ifeanyi Onuchukwu (Ekwusigo), Stanley Nkwoka (Idemili North), Oluchukwu Ilogbenam (Idemili South), Anayo Orjiakor (Ihiala) and Ikechukwu Okakpu (Njikoka).

Also elected were Echezona Anazodo (Nnewi North), Chinedu Ezeogidi (Nnewi South), Nnamdi Ifejika (Ogbaru), Chukwuemelie Ibekwe (Onitsha North), and Okechukwu Mofunanya (Onitsha South).

Others were Casmir Nwafor (Orumba North), Shedrack Azubuike (Orumba South) and Igbem Elochukwu (Oyi).

However, the YPP candidate, Sunday Nnabuife, alleged that his agents and party members were barred at gunpoint from entering the polling units or monitoring the process on Saturday.

The YPP spokesperson in Anambra East LGA, Charles Ifediora, accused the ruling APGA of using the Agunechemba Security operative to harass and intimidate the party’s members and agents.

(NAN)

World.title: “The Bako of Zereshé”: Building a world beyond the ordinary
World.content:
Dexter Loko has crafted an Afro-inspired work that is as intellectually engaging as it is entertaining, inviting readers to reflect on themes of identity, courage, and the burdens of power. If you enjoyed Nnedi Okorafor’s dynamic characters in “Akata Witch” and “The Nsibidi Scripts” series, or Tomi Adeyemi’s vivid imagery in “Children of Blood and Bone” and the “Legacy of Orisha” trilogy, or if you’re simply looking for more African-inspired fantasy, then this is a book well worth picking up.

Book Title: The Bako of Zereshé

Author: Dexter Loko

Publisher: GrandTouch Press

Year of Publication: 2026

The Bako of Zereshé is the second novel by Nigerian-Irish author, Dexter Loko. It follows the story of Jeremy Fletcher, a disillusioned 22-year-old BBC reporter of British descent who finds himself displaced in the enchanted land of Zereshé, Nigeria’s secret thirty-seventh state. There, he befriends Asha, the Prime Minister’s daughter; Shani, Asha’s wary best friend; and Chudi, a kind-hearted outcast shunned for his lack of magical abilities. As Jeremy is plunged deeper into Zereshé’s magical world, where he is an unwelcome foreigner, he becomes entangled in an age-old battle between good and evil. Amidst political tensions, intrigue, and fragile loyalties, Jeremy must not only confront the external forces of corruption and destruction, but also his own personal demons of cynicism, grief, self-doubt, and a suppressed capacity for faith. Together with his newly found friends, where alliances are tried and tested, they must attempt to avert an impending disaster that threatens not only Zereshé but the world at large. Will they succeed in changing the course of fate, or will Zereshé’s dreaded fear finally come to pass?

The story is narrated from a third-person limited point of view, closely following the experiences of the protagonist, Jeremy Fletcher.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Chudi didn’t answer. He just smiled. Then Jeremy saw it. Shells. Enormous shells floating on the river. Not just shells. They were turtles. Giant turtles. Each one was roughly the size of a small ferry.”

From the quotation above, if one aspect of the novel deserves particular praise, it is its world-building, a feat that truly earns Loko his well-deserved accolades. From grandiose landscapes featuring towering mountains, shimmering lakes, and lush greenery to the fictional creatures (Kitas and Grocupines) that inhabit them, such elements continually remind the reader that they have stepped into a world beyond the ordinary. Complementing this immersive setting is the distinctive technology employed by the Zereshéan civilisation, further enriching the novel’s imaginative landscape.

Additionally, Loko’s handling of contrasting themes is especially noteworthy. By weaving together recurring literary oppositions — good and evil, tradition and modernity, theism and atheism, native and foreigner, purist and reformist, strong and weak, powerful and powerless among others — he creates thematic depth and invites readers to engage with complex and often competing worldviews.

Having praised the novel’s many strengths, it is only fair to acknowledge that it is not without its flaws. While the characters are engaging and enjoyable, they rarely develop beyond their initial archetypes, limiting the depth of their characterisation.

Another aspect that momentarily disrupts the reader’s immersion is the novel’s inconsistent use of real-world pop culture references. Consider the following excerpt:

“…Mudiaga told him the words in Avani. They translate loosely to the English words – Watermelon Sugar High”.

At one point, Asha’s household password, ‘Watermelon Sugar High’, appears to reference the well-known Harry Styles song, “Watermelon Sugar”, suggesting that elements of contemporary pop culture exist within the novel’s universe. Yet, elsewhere, this occurs:

“Jeremy perked up, ‘The cuffs are like kryptonite and Superman!’ …’Who is Superman?’ Chudi asked”.

Jeremy’s friends are unfamiliar with Superman, one of the most recognisable figures in global pop culture. While this discrepancy may have an in-universe explanation, the novel offers none, making the contrast feel somewhat jarring. As a result, this inconsistency, though minor, risks pulling readers out of the fictional world, however briefly, by raising questions about the boundaries of the novel’s shared cultural landscape. This is not to suggest that the novel is riddled with logical inconsistencies; this is the only such occurrence in the book.

Overall, The Bako of Zereshé is a novel that succeeds far more than it stumbles. Dexter Loko has crafted an Afro-inspired work that is as intellectually engaging as it is entertaining, inviting readers to reflect on themes of identity, courage, and the burdens of power. If you enjoyed Nnedi Okorafor’s dynamic characters in Akata Witch and The Nsibidi Scripts series, or Tomi Adeyemi’s vivid imagery in Children of Blood and Bone and the Legacy of Orisha trilogy, or if you’re simply looking for more African-inspired fantasy, then this is a book well worth picking up.

Glory Folami writes from Lagos.
