On the afternoon of July 25, the Greek-owned supertanker Kiku docked at Qatar’s Mesaieed oil export terminal, a massive, 30-berth port on the country’s west coast, 25 miles south of Doha.

Four days later, loaded with crude oil, the Kiku passed through the Strait of Hormuz. The Very Large Crude Carrier – one of the largest oil tanker classes, stretching over 1,000 feet – maintained a steady pace of 13 knots across the Persian Gulf, near its top speed.

Then, on July 31, shortly after 2 pm just off the coast of Dubai, the Kiku vanished.

The vessel had switched off its AIS transponder, a marine radio device that broadcasts a ship’s identity, speed, course and position. To tracking services that monitor worldwide maritime traffic, it was as if the Kiku simply disappeared.

Suddenly, at 10 am on August 1, the Kiku’s signal reappeared – on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz.

It was part of the oil industry’s latest tactic – “dark,” US-military-escorted nighttime transits across the strait. The aim: Avoid Iranian drone attacks – like the one that struck the Kiku a month earlier, but failed to explode.

Aided by the US Navy, Saudi, Kuwaiti, Qatari and Emirati oil companies have chartered oil tankers to turn their transponders off and shuttle oil out of the Persian Gulf, through the Strait of Hormuz, to the Gulf of Oman, where they offload their crude to waiting tankers owned by their customers and then head back through the strait.

That has taken the costly burden of insurance risk and physical danger of Iranian attacks away from commercial shippers and placed it on the US government and the oil producers themselves.

It has become an effective strategy, according to the US Department of Energy, which says oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has averaged between 8 million and 9 million barrels per day. That’s a meaningful amount of crude – roughly double what Wall Street oil analysts and shipping trackers like Kpler, using transponder data, would suggest.

The clandestine transits have changed the game for the Middle Eastern oil industry.

CNN has observed more than a dozen ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman over two days, with tankers moving on to destinations such as China, Taiwan, South Korea, the Philippines, Vietnam and Thailand.

It’s a dangerous and expensive gambit that offers some temporary relief to the oil market. But with permanent solutions – a negotiated end to the war and lasting plan for the strait – remaining elusive, this workaround buys time.

Dark transits

The increase in dark transits like the Kiku’s recent journey comes at a crucial time for the energy market.

The war, lasting far longer than many had imagined, has disrupted a fifth of the world’s oil supply for six months but reached an inflection point in recent weeks: Billions of oil and fuel barrels in commercial stockpiles have vanished. US emergency reserves haven’t been this small since the early 1980s. China’s reliance on its massive oil inventory – a key factor in preventing $150 oil – won’t last forever. And bond market investors and voters are running out of patience with high prices.

Facing a nightmare scenario, Middle Eastern oil producers starting using their new strategy over the past several weeks. It’s not a perfect solution – the strait is famously narrow, just 23 miles wide. There aren’t many places to hide, and radar can still spot a ship even with its transponder off. Two ships belonging to the UAE were attacked this week.

But more than 80% of liquids transits through the Strait of Hormuz over the past two weeks have taken the Omani route – a UN-authorized shipping channel that Iran vehemently opposes – or have been “dark” transits that likely took the Omani route, according to Kpler, which tracks ships using transponders and satellite data. Because of the regional conflict, some tracking data has been subject to GPS jamming, which can make it difficult to make assessments.

Like many ships using this new tactic, the Kiku reappeared a day after its transponder turned off while anchored near the Emirati port city of Fujairah. After its transponder started pinging again, the Kiku anchored alongside another Greek supertanker, the Nave Electron, which had arrived in the Gulf of Oman a day earlier.

Satellite imagery from August 7, 2026 shows the Kiku and Nave Electron conducting a ship-to-ship transfer off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, shortly after the Kiku transited the strait with its AIS transponder disabled. The vessels are among several others engaged in similar transfers nearby. European Union Copernicus Sentinel-2

The two ships stayed together for a week in a ship-to-ship oil transfer. When they finally separated on August 8, the Nave Electron exited the Gulf, loaded with oil, headed toward the Arabian sea on route to Ningbo, China.

The Kiku stayed put off the coast of Fujairah until around August 14, when it went dark once again. The next day, just before 4 pm, its signal reemerged in the Persian Gulf, heading back toward Qatar.

Flipping the script

The escorted dark transits are the latest example of Middle Eastern oil producers increasing the amount of oil that they can export to customers around the world, flipping the script on Iran.

Most notably, Saudi Arabia has rerouted about 5 million barrels of oil per day that would have been destined for awaiting oil tankers in the Persian Gulf. Instead, that oil has traveled through its East-West pipeline to its port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. Middle Eastern oil producers have rerouted another 2 million barrels per day around the Strait of Hormuz.

Production has ramped up around the world to compensate, too. Brazil, Guyana and Venezuela have combined to add more than 1 million barrels per day of extra production. The United States has added hundreds of thousands more barrels daily to the market.

Pumpjacks operate in Midland, Texas, US, on Sunday, Aug. 16, 2026. Kaylee Greenlee/Bloomberg/Getty Images

And far less coordinated (or militarily protected) dark transits have been taking place for months.

On the other side of the equation, the United States has released 400 million barrels of emergency oil, vastly drawing down its stockpiles in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. China, too, has relied heavily on its own massive oil stockpiles, while simultaneously drastically reducing its crude imports. Global demand has also shrunk significantly with rising prices, helping to balance the oil market and get oil to the customers who need it.

The market keeps finding a way. It has proven far more complex and significantly more flexible than even the most knowledgeable experts anticipated when the war started.

A temporary solution

Radar and satellite imagery of the Strait of Hormuz paints a picture transponder data can’t see. For example, in August 14 satellite photos, rows of dots appear arcing around the coast of Oman through the strait of Hormuz. But those dots don’t align with ship-tracking data from the same day and time. The “dots” went dark.

On August 7, two Greek-owned tankers appeared next to one another in the Gulf of Oman on transponder data. Satellite images show the Nissos Kythnos, a shuttle tanker that had made a dark strait run, lined up next to the Front Otra. On August 14, the Front Otra was detected in the Arabian Sea on route to Taiwan. The Nissos Kythios was back in the Persian Gulf.

But it can’t last this way forever.

Oil inventories have been depleted by as much as 1.9 billion barrels during the course of the war. If the market reaches equilibrium, those will need to be filled to prevent the next crisis. If it doesn’t, those stockpiles will eventually be drained so low that they can no longer be relied on to meet the world’s oil demand, reaching a tipping point where the only solution is to raise oil prices significantly to choke off even more demand.

A similar problem has already emerged in the fuel market: Three of the world’s four refining hubs are in severe distress.

The Iran war has damaged refineries in the Middle East and slowed the export of fuel out of that region.

Russia, another major source of fuel, has been knocked offline by another war, the conflict with Ukraine. Refineries in Russia have been targeted by Ukrainian drones and Moscow, facing a fuel shortage at home, has cut off its exports.

Black smoke rises from the refinery where a fire broke out following a strike as firefighting efforts continue in Moscow on June 18, 2026. Sefa Karacan/Anadolu/Getty Images

China, seeking to avoid fuel shortages of its own, is limiting its own refined fuel exports. That’s critical because China is normally a major fuel exporter.

That leaves US refineries along the Gulf Coast shouldering the burden of global demand. But US refineries can’t run all-out forever.

Gas, and especially diesel and jet fuel, are in such high demand with such little refining capacity to make it, that prices have soared – well beyond what crude oil prices would suggest they should be.

President Donald Trump had successfully jawboned oil prices lower for months by promising a looming breakthrough in negotiations. His plan has recently changed, though: America’s new strategy is to strangle Iran, unleashing a “crushing economic operation” by means of a prolonged naval blockade of Iran’s ports.

That has sent oil prices creeping higher for weeks, edging closer to $100 a barrel.

With the two countries locked in an intractable quagmire of a war, the battle over control of the strait has kept oil – especially gas, diesel and jet fuel – at uncomfortably high prices for consumers, boosting inflation and shrinking their disposable income.

But the market’s impressive ability to at least partially work its way around the conflict has also prevented prices from surging as astronomically high as the world’s largest-ever oil supply shock would suggest.

CNN’s Sarah El Sirgany and Farida Elsebai contributed to this report.

Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated what percentage of ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has transited around the coast of Oman. More than 80% of traffic has either transited around Oman or has been dark and not able to be reliably tracked, according to Kpler. This story has also been updated to clarify the size of VLCC tankers.

World.title: Eight officials suspended after probe into Pakistan hospital fire that killed 14 newborns
World.content:
Islamabad AP —

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday ordered the suspension of eight officials and directed that criminal proceedings be initiated against those found responsible for a fire that killed 14 newborns at an Islamabad hospital, his office said.

Sharif issued the orders after an investigative committee headed by retired senior civil servant Shahid Khan presented its interim report on Wednesday’s fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, or PIMS, his office said in a statement.

The fire was confined to a third-floor nursery but officials said it spread so quickly that staff were able to rescue only one baby from among the 15 being cared for there.

The inquiry found that the nursery had no fire alarm or sprinkler system and that the hospital lacked detailed procedures and training for responding to fires and other emergencies, the statement said.

The fire has intensified public anger, prompting grieving families and civil society groups to demand accountability.

“Those guilty of criminal negligence deserve no leniency,” Sharif was quoted as saying.

He ordered departmental and criminal proceedings against those identified by the committee.

The eight included the hospital’s executive director, two joint executive directors, the head of the neonatal department, two other doctors, the hospital’s assistant director for security and the head of the Capital Development Authority’s emergency services.

Sharif also approved action against a company responsible for hospital security and its officials.

The government also already announced compensation of 5 million rupees (about $18,000) for each bereaved family.

The statement said the interim inquiry found that supervisory staff were not on duty when the fire began. Two nurses, a female security guard and a house officer were in the ward.

Emergency services were not called until six minutes after the fire started, and the first emergency responders arrived 15 minutes after receiving the call, the statement said.

Investigators found that only two subsections of the hospital’s 13 standard operating procedures referred to fires or other emergencies.

About two minutes of surveillance video of the nursery fire was shown during Saturday’s meeting. The footage was not immediately released.

The interim report said a nurse risked her life to save a baby before the flames spread through the ward. Sharif approved a recommendation that she receive the Sitara-i-Khidmat, a state award recognizing public service.

The deaths have prompted broader reviews of fire-safety measures at hospitals across Pakistan. The government in Punjab, the country’s most populous province, this week ordered an immediate review of fire-safety systems, firefighting equipment and emergency-response facilities at hospitals.

Sharif earlier dismissed Health Secretary Aslam Ghauri, the Health Ministry’s highest-ranking civil servant, after the blaze.

The fire was among Pakistan’s deadliest recent tragedies involving children. In June, 14 schoolchildren were killed when the roof of a tutoring center under construction collapsed in the eastern city of Lahore.

World.title: How Tim Cook made Apple one of the world’s most valuable companies
World.content:
When Tim Cook became Apple’s CEO in August 2011, he had big shoes to fill. His predecessor, Steve Jobs, was widely considered one of the world’s greatest innovators.

Now, 15 years later, Cook has catapulted the company to stratospheric heights by forging his own path. His successor, hardware engineering chief John Ternus, has a very different act to follow on September 1. Cook will be remembered for making the iPhone feel essential to everything from buying a coffee to listening to music, hitting the gym or paying a credit card bill. That’s all thanks to the web services and accessories Cook pioneered over the past decade.

Apple’s stock has soared by more than 2,000% during his time at the helm. The company also briefly reached a $5 trillion market capitalization in July, the second company to ever reach that milestone.

“(Cook) managed to scale the iPhone to a level that no one would have thought was likely or possible over that period of time,” said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School who wrote a case study on Apple and Tim Cook.

Then-Apple CEO Steve Jobs, right, and Tim Cook, then the company’s COO, speak at Apple’s headquarters in Cupertino, California, on July 16, 2010. Kimberly White/Corbis/Getty Images Cook shows off the new iPhone 6 and the Apple Watch on September 9, 2014, in Cupertino, California. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Cook presents the new iPhone 11 on September 10, 2019. Stephen Lam/Reuters Apple CEO Tim Cook (C) takes a selfie with customers at an Apple Store on November 3, 2017 in Palo Alto, California. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

But getting there wasn’t just about making smart product decisions. It also involved navigating political relationships across the US and China – both of which are critical to Apple’s operations and its massive iPhone empire – at a time when relations have been tense between the two nations.

Cook is just as much “a statesman” as he was a CEO, according to Gene Munster, managing partner at tech investment firm Deepwater Asset Management who’s been following Apple since 2004.

Cook came into the CEO role with expertise in operations and supply chain management. But it was his mild-mannered approach, swift decisions and knack for negotiation that helped keep the iPhone machine running smoothly despite geopolitical challenges, experts say.

Ron Johnson, who oversaw Apple’s retail operations from 2000 to 2011, described Cook – then the company’s chief operating officer – as “intelligent” and “strategic” during weekly team meetings with Jobs and Apple’s executive team.

In pictures: Apple CEO Tim Cook 35 photos Apple CEO Tim Cook poses for a portrait at Apple’s global headquarters in Cupertino, California in 2016. Andrew Burton/The Washington Post/Getty Images

“He was perhaps the most thoughtful of the executive team members,” Johnson told CNN. “He would always listen first and speak when he had something to add.”

Under his leadership, Apple made a decision that helped it dodge the Trump administration’s sky-high tariffs. Under pressure to build its phones in America, the company instead promised to invest $600 billion to expand its US operations, including producing critical iPhone parts stateside.

Even during Trump’s first term, the president said Cook was one of the few leaders who personally called him.

“In terms of CEOs that Trump has come to respect, Tim Cook would be very high on the list,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and a former White House advisor.

Cook pushed the company to diversify some production away from China while still appealing to Chinese consumers and leadership, which Munster said is a rare feat.

“I don’t know how you do that,” he said. “I don’t know if that dynamic makes sense.”

Still, the Covid pandemic and Trump’s tariffs illustrated how Apple’s reliance on China could be a problem. That’s just one of the hurdles that Ternus inherits.

An Apple store in Beijing, China, on September 19, 2025. Cook pushed the company to diversify some production away from China while still appealing to Chinese consumers and leadership. Maxim Shemetov/Reuters

There’s also the tense relationship with regulators in Europe, Apple’s second-largest market; the company was forced to make changes to how it runs the App Store in the region. Apple’s revamped version of Siri won’t launch in Europe because of the European Union’s rules.

Then there’s AI. The company increasingly faces pressure to catch up, especially after its last major product – the Vision Pro – didn’t live up to expectations. Meanwhile, an ongoing shortage of memory chips due to the AI race has forced Apple and other companies to raise product prices.

But Cook gave Ternus some advice during one of his last earnings calls as CEO: focus on making products that “enrich” the lives of customers.

“If you keep focusing on that and make your decisions around that, it will produce a great business,” he said in April. “And we’ll be able to build more products and do it all over again.”

World.title: A date to remember: The Abu Dhabi ice cream maker turning palm trees into soft serve
World.content:
By the time night falls and the last few customers trickle out of an ice cream parlor tucked behind Abu Dhabi’s Zayed Port, it may seem as though the day’s work is done. But for Amira Al Dosari, it’s just beginning.

Her shift starts in the kitchen at 9 p.m., where she spends up to three hours prepping, churning, and tasting 12 different bases before they are transformed into unique batches of premium soft serve.

By morning, a dozen flavors are ready to be served at Al Dosari’s shop, Ice Station — many featuring ingredients that come from an unusual

source: the date palm.

The date palm tree is a symbol of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and the dates that grow in bunches on it are one of the country’s most important agricultural exports.

Globally, nearly 11 million metric tons of dates were produced in 2024. Middle Eastern and North African countries, such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt led the way, with the UAE ranking in the top 10, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization.

Al Dosari, 53, didn’t intend to showcase dates when she founded the store in 2023. That changed after she took ice cream-making courses around the world and saw how reliant many recipes were on ready-made mixes, preservatives, and artificial flavorings. What concerned her most, however, was the high sugar content.

“I was thinking about what the future could be for (children) who eat a lot of sugar when they are that young. How would that affect their body?” she told CNN.

Ice Station’s mission is to make ice cream free of artificial ingredients. Ice Station

That led her to begin experimenting with kholas rotab — the softest, ripest stage of the kholas variety of date. Its natural sweetness inspired her to rework the original recipe she had opened Ice Station with, this time without adding any sugar.

Al Dosari acknowledges that dates are also high in sugar. But, as a whole fruit, they contain dietary fiber that can slow the absorption of those sugars, unlike refined cane sugar. For her, what matters is that the sweetness comes naturally from the fleshy, dark fruit itself.

“The main thing in soft serve is the sugar. It gives it its creamy texture,” she said. Creating soft serve without added sugar “was the challenge.”

Roots to trunk

After countless attempts and 15 broken machines from her experimentation, Al Dosari created a rotab-flavored ice cream. But she later came to realize that the date palm tree, from its roots to its trunk, could provide ingredients for her ice creams — inspiring 145 flavors over the last three years.

One such flavor is her matcha. Instead of using the Japanese green tea powder, Al Dosari uses date palm leaves, which she says achieve the same flavor profile and vivid green hue. It’s known as “safcha” and it’s a timely substitution: as the world’s appetite for the tea grows, the craze has put mounting pressure on Japan’s supply.

“Every single person in my family is like, ‘matcha, matcha, matcha!’ I said, ‘Okay, but matcha has caffeine, so let’s go for something similar, but with no caffeine.”

Her daughter, Ghalia Al Mazrouei, a sustainability consultant, helped her find a use for the many seeds left over from using dates, brewing them into a caffeine-free coffee. They also pour the drink over a mound of ice cream and brand it an “affogato,” after the Italian dessert of ice cream drowned in espresso.

“We know that the entire plant is quite safe for consumption, so it was just more about how we could present this in a way that is enjoyable for everyone?” Al Mazrouei said.

Ice Station’s matcha is made from palm fronds. Ice Station

Al Dosari has found culinary uses for the palm’s pollen, creating an entire flavor from it. She uses date molasses to help sweeten her ice creams and discovered that different date varieties can produce different tastes, like that of banana.

But the date palm is hardly her only source of inspiration. Ice Station’s menu has boasted a revolving door of international flavors over the years, from Costa Rican pineapple to ube, the purple sweet potato native to the Philippines. Al Dosari has even swirled savory variations, including smoked salmon with cream cheese, caviar with vanilla, and parmesan with white truffle.

“I have so many (ideas),” she said, laughing. She is currently inventing her 448th flavor.

Frozen heritage

For the founder, her date-laden scoops, however, are about more than innovative flavors; they are a way of turning a traditional ingredient into one of cultural relevancy and regional identity. “All Gulf countries share the same heritage: the palms,” she said.

The date palm can flourish in the arid conditions of the Gulf, where its fruit has sustained communities for centuries and become a symbol of hospitality and generosity. In 2019, UNESCO recognized its significance by adding the date palm to its Intangible Cultural Heritage List.

Al Dosari continues to extend that heritage in a frozen-form, reimagining traditional Emirati desserts like “khabisa,” a fragrant mix of roasted flour, ghee and spices, and “rahash,” a sesame-based confection, which she says are a hit with both locals and tourists alike.

Dates, and the date palm, are an important part of Gulf nations’ heritage. Ice Station

She has opened a second branch of Ice Station, but launching her product internationally, has proven difficult. While Ice Station has showcased its flavors at events abroad, including in Uzbekistan and Egypt, and received global franchise enquiries, Al Dosari worries about compromising quality by scaling up.

For now, she continues to churn out soft serve with a larger mission: to encourage people to eat more natural ice cream and put Abu Dhabi on the map for premium soft serve, while reminding customers of the legacy they are consuming.

“Food is almost like an international language,” Al Mazrouei said. “You don’t need to have a complete understanding with someone to connect through food.”

World.title: Shanghai Professor hails Chinese President’s visit to Egypt as “historic”, discusses relations in exclusive interview
World.content:
A professor at the Middle East Studies Institute at Shanghai International Studies University, Ding Long, called Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Cairo “historic” – marking the first such visit in a decade.

In this exclusive interview, he added that relations between Cairo and Beijing are at their best – noting a rise in the volume of trade exchange – and discussed further opportunities to boost ties between both nations.

Interview transcript:

How do you view Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt and the relationship between Cairo and Beijing?

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit, undertaken at the invitation of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, comes at a historic juncture coinciding with the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two nations.

It represents a milestone of exceptional significance—measured not merely by its bilateral importance, but by its role as a practical declaration that Sino-Egyptian relations are “at their best,” as officially described by the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

It stands as a leading model of solidarity and mutually beneficial cooperation among Global South nations; furthermore, under the strategic leadership of Presidents al-Sisi and Xi, the relationship evolved into a “comprehensive strategic partnership”—announced in 2014—and has continued to deepen to the point where both countries now speak of “building a China-Egypt community with a shared future in the new era.”

President Xi Jinping’s visit to Cairo serves to crown a long-standing journey and transform the 70th-anniversary milestone from a mere celebratory occasion into a launchpad for a “new golden decade.”

Preliminary indications suggest the visit’s agenda will extend beyond a joint statement to include the signing of agreements covering e-commerce, the green economy, healthcare, digital transformation, and local currency financing. This signifies a shift in cooperation from “heavy infrastructure”—such as ports and towers—to “superstructure” elements, including cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and regional supply chains.

The strategic value of this visit lies in three key points:

First, it affirms that the Sino-Egyptian relationship is not subject to changes in Western administrations or pressures from traditional blocs; rather, it is grounded in respect for sovereignty and non-interference—a fact that explains its stability amidst regional volatility.

Second, it transforms the “Global South” from mere political rhetoric into operational mechanisms—ranging from currency swaps and special economic zones to an Egyptian satellite built by Egyptian hands.

Third, it offers an alternative model for international cooperation based on “building together” rather than “building for others,” on technology transfer rather than monopolization, and on financing conditioned by development rather than political dictates.

Do you believe the 70th-anniversary celebrations mark the beginning of a new phase of cooperation?

Seventy years after the initial mutual diplomatic recognition, Egypt and China are no longer merely two nations exchanging ambassadors – they have become pillars in reshaping the economic order of Eurasia and Africa.

This visit to Cairo is but one step in a long journey—yet it is a step that embodies decades of trust, billions of dollars in trade, thousands of jobs, and even a satellite orbiting Earth named “EgyptSat-2,” built through the joint efforts of Egyptian and Chinese hands.

This is precisely why the 70th anniversary signifies not the end of a chapter, but the beginning of a broader vision: a vision of a community with a shared future between two civilizations—bound not by geography, but by the will to forge the future using the tools of the future.

In the last decade alone, the Chinese and Egyptian presidents have met thirteen times.

President Sisi visited China seven times between 2015 and 2025, participating twice in the Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation.

Engagement has not been limited to the summit level but has extended to reciprocal visits by prime ministers, parliamentary speakers, and foreign ministers, thereby establishing a mechanism for high-level political coordination.

In multilateral forums, a consistent stance of mutual respect for core interests has prevailed: China steadfastly supports Egypt’s independent decision-making and its sovereignty over its territory and waters, while Egypt upholds the One-China principle, regards Taiwan as an integral part of Chinese territory, and opposes any foreign interference in China’s internal affairs.

What about economic cooperation between the two countries?

In terms of the economy and development, the achievements realized since 2013 alone suffice to demonstrate that the relationship has moved beyond the stage of “good neighborliness” to that of “structural integration.”

Bilateral trade volume rose from US$10.21 billion in 2013 to $20.79 billion in 2025—a historic record—while China has remained Egypt’s largest trading partner for fourteen consecutive years.

China is also the primary supplier of intermediate goods, accounting for 66 percent of such imports; these are processed locally in Egypt before being exported to third-party markets.

To address the trade imbalance, a Chinese policy granting full duty-free access to products from 53 African nations came into effect in May 2026.

This includes Egypt, which benefited from a 100 percent exemption on customs duties—free of caps or political conditions—a move that immediately resulted in a 117 percent surge in Egyptian exports to China in February 2026 compared to the same month the previous year.

In the investment sector, statistics indicate that by the end of 2025, there were over 2,860 registered Chinese companies operating in Egypt, with a cumulative investment stock of approximately $9 billion—concentrated in manufacturing, mining, and services—alongside new Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows totaling $93.03 million in 2024 alone.

The China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone in Ain Sokhna stands out as a key hub for industrial cooperation; following a decade of expansion, its developed area has exceeded 10 square kilometers, attracting around 200 Chinese and international enterprises with actual investments surpassing $3.8 billion.

It achieved cumulative sales exceeding $6.6 billion, created over 10,000 direct jobs, and contributed approximately $310 million in taxes to the Egyptian treasury.

Furthermore, in July 2025, both parties signed an agreement to allocate an additional 2.86 square kilometers as a western expansion zone, paving the way for new projects in renewable energy, automotive manufacturing, chemicals, and textiles.

These figures cannot be viewed in isolation from the major projects that have transformed Egypt’s infrastructure landscape.

In the New Administrative Capital, China State Construction Engineering Corporation (CSCEC) executed the Central Business District (CBD) project—featuring the 385.8-meter Iconic Tower, the tallest in Africa—with the structure’s completion marked in 2021.

Meanwhile, on the North Coast, the “New Alamein” residential complex features soaring high-rises, establishing it as the continent’s tallest integrated concrete residential complex.

In the transport sector, the “CREC-AVIC International” consortium completed the first and second phases of the 10th of Ramadan City electric train—Africa’s first electric railway line—which entered service in 2022, reducing travel time between Old Cairo and the New Administrative Capital.

In the space sector, China launched the Egyptian satellite “EgyptSat 2” in December 2023 under the management of a joint Egyptian-Chinese team, making Egypt the first African nation to possess full domestic capabilities for satellite assembly and testing.

In 2024, Egypt’s government data and cloud computing center became operational using Chinese technologies, followed by the inauguration of the first Chinese public cloud node in Cairo, which hosts over 200 Egyptian companies.

Do you believe that cooperation between the two countries is growing and evolving with Egypt’s accession to the BRICS bloc?

Egypt’s accession to BRICS in 2024 has placed Sino-Egyptian relations within a broader framework of South-South cooperation, particularly in navigating global trade volatility and restoring balance to international economic governance.

China’s Belt and Road Initiative complements “Egypt Vision 2030” across key sectors such as renewable energy, digitization, modern agriculture, and sustainable transport.

For instance, Chinese companies participated in the development of the Benban Solar Park—one of the world’s largest solar farms—while wind energy projects have been implemented in Sohag and the Red Sea region.

Additionally, the “Obelisk” solar energy project, featuring battery storage capabilities sufficient to power approximately 1.6 million households, entered service in 2026.

In the electric vehicle sector, Chinese brands have initiated local assembly operations and established vocational training centers in collaboration with Egyptian institutes; meanwhile, academies affiliated with Chinese companies have trained over 60,000 Egyptian personnel in information and communication technology.

This engagement extends to the human dimension as well: prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, the annual number of Chinese tourists visiting Egypt exceeded 300,000, and direct flights between Beijing and Cairo resumed in 2025.

Furthermore, the number of Egyptian students at Chinese universities has surpassed 3,000, alongside a steady stream of technical, agricultural, and medical training delegations.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, China was the first country to dispatch urgent medical aid to Egypt in March 2020.

This was followed by shipments of the Sinopharm vaccine, facilitated by a local production partnership in Cairo. All of this redefines the “brotherhood” between the two nations—not merely as a slogan, but as an interconnected network of material and knowledge-based interests.

World.title: PM: Africa faces unprecedented challenges, calls for comprehensive action
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly affirmed that the African continent faces unprecedented challenges and ongoing conflicts requiring urgent, comprehensive action to address root causes, primarily poverty, climate change impacts, water scarcity, rising terrorism, and transnational organized crime, urging joint work to advance AU and regional economic community mechanisms.

The remarks came during Madboly’s address, on behalf of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, at the extraordinary AU summit on conflict prevention and resolution mechanisms in Luanda, attended by Angolan President João Lourenço, Burundian President and AU Chairperson Évariste Ndayishimiye, AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, and African leaders.

At the outset, the Prime Minister conveyed President Sisi’s greetings and wishes for summit outcomes that fulfill African aspirations for peace, security, and development.

He expressed gratitude to President João Lourenço for hosting the crucial summit amid complex continental challenges and commended President Évariste Ndayishimiye’s continental leadership, reaffirming Egypt’s support for the Burundian chairmanship.

Highlighting President Sisi’s leadership of the AU post-conflict reconstruction and development portfolio, Madbouly stressed that post-conflict reconstruction is a fundamental pillar for continental peace and security, complementing conflict resolution efforts.

Madbouly noted that the 20th anniversary of the AU Post-Conflict Reconstruction and Development Policy serves as an opportunity to review progress and turn policies into concrete programs tailored to national needs.

He added that post-conflict priorities must focus on rehabilitating critical infrastructure, building capable state institutions, generating jobs, and reintegrating affected populations, particularly women and youth.

Madbouly urged the AU Commission to continue supporting the Cairo-based AU Centre for Post-Conflict Reconstruction and Development, and commended the establishment of the PSC sub-committee of experts, which held its inaugural meeting under Egypt’s chairmanship in February 2026.

He also voiced Egypt’s support for AU Peace and Security Council reforms to rectify historical imbalances by granting North Africa a third seat to ensure equitable geographic representation.

Madbouly concluded by saying Egypt looks forward to hosting the 8th AU Mid-Year Coordination Meeting in New Alamein on October 4, 2026, and invited leaders and business executives to the first Alamein-Africa Business Forum on October 2-4 to advance integration and sustainable development.

World.title: Egypt ranks among world’s leading fertilizer producers, exporters
World.content:
Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem said Egypt has established itself as a major global producer and exporter of fertilizers, supported by a strong industrial base, reliable energy supplies, and abundant natural resources, particularly phosphate, that are essential to fertilizer production.

Hashem said the fertilizer industry has benefited from significant government support in recent years, as global crises and regional geopolitical tensions disrupted fertilizer production in a number of countries.

He attributed the resilience of Egypt’s fertilizer industry to stable energy supplies, which allowed plants to maintain uninterrupted production, meet domestic demand and expand exports.

The Minister also pointed to rising European demand for Egyptian fertilizers in recent years, following the shutdown of a number of European fertilizer plants amid global energy crises. He said the stability of Egyptian production has strengthened the competitiveness of locally produced fertilizers and reinforced Egypt’s position in international markets.

Hashem also described sugar as a strategic commodity because of its direct bearing on food security and market stability. He said the ministry is working to increase domestic production and improve manufacturing efficiency with the aim of achieving self-sufficiency in sugar while expanding exports.

The Minister made the remarks during a visit to Suez Governorate, where he inspected a fertilizer plant and a sugar refinery in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, accompanied by Suez Governor Hany Rashad.

World.title: Sports Minister congratulates Modern Pentathlon body on world championship win
World.content:
Minister of Youth and Sports Gohar Nabil congratulated on Sunday, August 30, 2026, the Egyptian Modern Pentathlon Federation’s Board of Directors, headed by Sherif al-Erian, as well as the national team’s athletes.

He also congratulated the team’s technical, administrative and medical staff on Egypt’s strong performance at the Modern Pentathlon World Championships in China.

Egyptian athletes won four medals at the championships, including three silver and one bronze.

Nabil also congratulated rising star Farida Khalil after she won silver in the women’s individual event.

Khalil also helped Egypt’s women’s team, alongside Jana Attia and Janna al-Gendy, secure silver in the team event.

The Minister congratulated men’s team members Moataz Mohamed, Mohannad Shaaban and Mohamed al Ashqar after they won silver in the team event.

He also congratulated Zeina Amer and Jana Attia after the duo secured bronze in the women’s relay event.

Nabil praised the efforts of the Egyptian Modern Pentathlon Federation and its support for the country’s athletes, saying these efforts have helped establish Egypt among the sport’s leading nations internationally.

World.title: Liberia: UMC Bishop Declares Africa “New Epicenter Of Faith” At Thanksgiving Service In Monrovia
World.content:
Monrovia, August 30, 2026 – The preacher at the Thanksgiving Service in Monrovia ahead of 2026 Africa College of Bishops Meeting has called on the global church to “enlarge its tent” and prepare for unprecedented growth, declaring Africa the new epicenter of Christianity.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The service, held at the historic First United Methodist Church and hosted by the Liberia Episcopal Area, set the pace for the opening of the 2026 Africa College of Bishops Meeting. At the Thanksgiving Service, Bishops, clergies, and lay leaders from across the continent and the U.S. gathered under the theme drawn from Isaiah 54:2: “Enlarge the place of your tent.”

Delivering the sermon, Bishop L. Jonathan Holston of the Alabama-West Florida Episcopal Area of the United States Southeastern Jurisdiction, cautioned the congregation that God is demanding “a new way of stretching and a new way of doing things.”

“We are witnessing a monumental shift in the landscape of global Christianity. Africa is emerging as a new epicenter of the faith,” Bishop Holston declared.

“This is a season of spiritual preparation and transition. While the center of influence has shifted, it brings with it a sacred responsibility: To develop leaders; to engage our communities and to make room for what God is doing next.”

A Call To Expand And Lead Courageously

Preaching from Isaiah 54:2, Bishop Holston urged Methodists and the Christian community to move beyond their comfort zones and traditional thinking.

“God is calling us to expand – spiritually and structurally. True progress is not about changing titles. It’s about changing hearts. To fulfill this divine mandate, we must: Love boldly. Serve joyfully. Lead courageously.”

He challenged the church to reach “people you have never seen before, and speak to people you have never spoken to before,” including younger generations and those divided by politics.

“It’s time to stretch beyond rigid traditions and political divisions. It’s time to create space for God to work through us,” Bishop Holston stated, adding: “The world needs our witness. God is calling us forward, not backward. This is the moment to go.”

The Bishop acknowledged current challenges confronting the world maintained that no situation should ever deter Christians from advancing further.

“We are living in a time of political uncertainty and inflation, but we must be ready to go forth. Do not hold back.”

“Do not be afraid. The most impactful work of the Church is still ahead of us. This is a word of expansion. Prepare yourself. Enlarge your capacity. Welcome the larger, more inclusive future God is bringing,” the renowned US-based Methodist Church Bishop added.

The service was climaxed with prayers for the bishops, the Liberia Episcopal Area, and for the United Methodist Church worldwide as well as Christians across the globe.

Liberia Hosts Continental Gathering

The Thanksgiving Service served as both worship and preparation for the week-long Africa College of Bishops Meeting hosted by the Liberia Episcopal Area. The meeting, which will be hosted at the Farmington Hotel Town in Unification Town, Margibi County, will focus on leadership development, evangelism strategies, and the church’s role in addressing social issues across Africa.

“Do not be afraid. The most impactful work of the Church is still ahead of us. This is a word of expansion. Prepare yourself. Enlarge your capacity. Welcome the larger, more inclusive future God is bringing.”

The service concluded with prayers for the bishops, the Liberia Episcopal Area, and for the United Methodist Church worldwide.

World.title: Jackson F. Doe Hospital Expansion Signals Liberia’s Push to Decentralize Specialized Healthcare
World.content:
TAPPITA, Nimba County — The Government of Liberia is advancing plans to expand specialized healthcare services outside Monrovia with a major upgrade of the Jackson F. Doe Memorial Regional Referral Hospital in Tappita, Nimba County.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The government has dedicated newly constructed housing for healthcare workers and broken ground for a new emergency room, intensive care unit (ICU), and three additional duplexes for hospital staff.

The projects form part of an ambitious plan to transform Jackson F. Doe into a major regional referral center and, eventually, Liberia’s second national referral hospital.

Speaking at the ceremony over the weekend, Deputy Minister for Fiscal Affairs Anthony G. Myers, who represented Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung and Finance Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, said the investment demonstrates the government’s commitment to extending critical public services beyond Monrovia.

“Strengthening healthcare infrastructure outside Monrovia is fundamental to inclusive national development,” Myers said, noting that Jackson F. Doe Hospital has been designated a priority Public Sector Investment Program (PSIP) project.

US$44.4 Million Invested Since 2010

According to Myers, Jackson F. Doe Hospital was incorporated into Liberia’s national budget in 2010, and the government has since invested approximately US$44.4 million in the facility.

Of that amount, about US$3.9 million was allocated during the 2026 fiscal year, he said.

Myers warned, however, that additional resources will be required as the hospital’s catchment area expands and improved road connectivity makes Tappita more accessible to patients from Nimba and neighboring counties.

Focus on Emergency and Critical Care

A major component of the latest expansion is the construction of a new emergency room and intensive care unit, facilities expected to strengthen the hospital’s capacity to treat life-threatening illnesses, severe injuries and other medical emergencies.

Myers said the investment is about more than constructing physical infrastructure.

“When a patient arrives with a life-threatening condition, the quality and speed of emergency care can determine the outcome,” he said.

The government expects improved emergency and specialist services at Jackson F. Doe to reduce pressure on referral hospitals in Monrovia by allowing more patients from southeastern and central Liberia to access advanced treatment closer to home.

Staff Housing Targets Retention Challenges

The staff housing component is intended to address another persistent challenge facing regional healthcare facilities: the recruitment and retention of qualified health professionals.

Myers said adequate accommodation for doctors, nurses, specialists and other healthcare workers is critical to retaining skilled personnel and ensuring continuity of services at the hospital.

He also commended the hospital’s financial management, noting that its 2025 budget execution rate exceeded the health sector average of 97 percent.

However, he acknowledged growing pressure on health financing as some external sources of funding decline.

Myers said the government is responding by reallocating resources within the national budget to protect essential health services.

Part of Boakai’s ARREST Agenda

The Jackson F. Doe expansion is being implemented under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development and is listed as a priority PSIP project.

For a country where advanced medical services remain heavily concentrated in Monrovia, the expansion could represent a significant step toward decentralizing healthcare and bringing specialized treatment closer to patients in the counties.

The government says the investment is part of a broader, long-term strategy to strengthen Liberia’s national referral system and expand access to specialized and life-saving medical care outside the capital.

Myers Honored in Nimba

During the visit, chiefs and elders of Nimba District Six honored Deputy Minister Myers for what they described as his contribution to the development of the region.

The ceremony brought together Nimba County Senator Nya D. Twayen Jr.; Nimba District Six Representative Dorwohn Twain Gleekia; Deputy Health Minister for Research, Policy and Monitoring & Evaluation Atty. Malayah Tamba Chieyoe; Deputy Director General for Administration at the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority Stephen R. Johnson; hospital administrators; and local government officials.

World.title: Liberia: Cummings Demands Speedy, Fair Trial for Howard-Taylor, Accuses Government of ‘Selective Justice’
World.content:
Monrovia – Political Leader of the Alternative National Congress, Alexander Benedict Cummings, has called on the Government of Liberia to ensure a speedy and fair trial for former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, who remains incarcerated at the Monrovia Central Prison over allegations linked to the country’s ongoing narcotics investigation.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Cummings made the call Sunday after visiting Howard-Taylor at the prison, commonly known as “South Beach,” where she is being held in connection with the drug case.

Speaking to reporters after the visit, Cummings accused the government of applying justice selectively and warned that Liberia risks becoming a “narco-state” if authorities fail to prosecute all individuals implicated in the narcotics trade, regardless of their political status.

Cummings said his visit was personal but acknowledged that it carried a broader political message.

“I came this afternoon to visit the former Vice President, Jewel Howard-Taylor. The former Vice President is a friend; I call her my ‘small sister.’ I came to empathize with her and check on her circumstantial situation,” he said.

Cummings declined to disclose details of his private conversation with Howard-Taylor but said she feels aggrieved and maintains that authorities do not have sufficient evidence against her.

“That conversation was private between her and me. She obviously feels aggrieved. She feels they have no evidence, etc., but I will say no more than this,” he said.

Cummings Calls for Speedy Justice

The ANC political leader outlined what he described as key principles that should guide the government’s handling of the narcotics investigation, with a speedy trial among his principal demands.

“One is, of course, the legal piece of it: the innocent are presumed innocent until proven guilty. There is a presumption of innocence, and the evidence should be followed wherever it leads,” Cummings said.

“But justice needs to be speedy. It needs to be speedy, and justice should not be selective. It appears that justice is being selectively prescribed,” he added.

Cummings said Liberia’s narcotics problem has become increasingly serious under the current administration and called for the prosecution and arrest of all persons implicated in the drug trade.

“This narcotic issue is a serious problem for our country. Our country appears to be becoming a narco-state, and it is happening now under this government’s watch,” he said.

“We want to see prosecution. We want to see arrests of current officials because it is happening now.”

Demands Independent Investigation

Cummings also renewed his call for an independent investigation into the narcotics allegations, citing comments attributed to the Inspector General of Police that senior government officials were allegedly implicated.

“The Inspector General of Police, in his press conference, said there were big shots, big heads in this government who were implicated. We want to know who they are because otherwise the process seems unjust. It seems selective,” Cummings said.

He argued that an independent process would help establish the facts and ensure that the law is applied equally to current and former officials.

ANC Vows to Keep Pressure on Government

Cummings said the ANC would continue to hold the government accountable beyond the ongoing narcotics investigation, citing corruption, injustice and other governance concerns.

“The next step of the party is to keep reminding the government of ills in society, including corruption, injustices, violence and drugs,” he said.

“We want this narco-state situation to be curtailed. We want the government to go after corruption. You know, we wrote a letter on this whole Foya construction in Lofa. We haven’t gotten a response. We will be speaking on that again.”

Cummings also confirmed that he had followed through on an earlier commitment to engage international partners over Liberia’s narcotics crisis.

“I said I would speak to international partners to get involved, and I did do that. I just hope this government does the right thing. It’s not about taking sides here or there. It’s about following the evidence, but applying it to everybody,” he said.

While expressing sympathy for Howard-Taylor, Cummings stopped short of declaring her innocent, instead insisting that the government should present whatever evidence it has against her.

“It is not my impression that the person, the woman I know, will be involved in what is being alleged. But again, let’s see the evidence. That’s why they need to do it quickly, speedily, and provide whatever evidence they have,” he said.

The ANC said it will continue to demand speedy trials and justice for everyone incarcerated in connection with the narcotics investigation, including the former Vice President.

World.title: Liberia: Nimba Elders Back Boakai’s Drug Fight, Warn Illicit Drugs Threaten Liberia’s Future
World.content:
Monrovia — The Nimba Council of Elders has thrown its support behind the government’s ongoing crackdown on illicit drugs, commending President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and his administration for what it described as the political will and determination to confront the growing drug menace in Liberia.

In a press release dated August 21, the Council said the government should remain resolute in detecting illegal drug activities, holding perpetrators accountable and ensuring that the law takes its course, regardless of the status or influence of those involved.

The Elders acknowledged that no government can completely prevent individuals with criminal intentions from attempting to smuggle illegal substances into the country, but said the true test of leadership lies in the willingness to uncover such activities and prosecute those responsible.

The Council urged the government to pursue the fight against illicit drugs “without fear or favor,” regardless of political affiliation, social status, influence or personal connections.

“Drugs know no tribe, political party, religion or social status. Their consequences reach every community, destroy the lives of our young people, weaken families and threaten the future of our nation,” the Council stated.

The statement comes amid heightened national concern over Liberia’s escalating drug crisis and recent major narcotics seizures that have triggered calls for stronger law enforcement and accountability.

The Nimba elders also stressed that the responsibility for combating illicit drugs cannot rest solely with the government.

They called on traditional and religious leaders, parents, young people, civil society organizations, communities and citizens across Liberia to actively participate in efforts to prevent drug abuse and trafficking.

“As elders, we have a responsibility not only to the present generation but also to those yet unborn. We must not leave to our children a country overwhelmed by a problem we had the opportunity and responsibility to confront,” the Council emphasized.

The Council further called for stronger measures in drug prevention, law enforcement, prosecution, treatment and rehabilitation, arguing that a comprehensive national response is needed to effectively address the problem.

The Elders reaffirmed their support for what they described as every lawful and genuine effort to combat illicit drugs, while urging all Liberians to unite behind efforts aimed at protecting young people and safeguarding the country’s future.

World.title: Liberia: What a Secretly Recorded ‘Gift’ Call – and the Koffa Precedent – Mean for the Case against Jewel Howard Taylor
World.content:
Liberian law is openly hostile to secret recordings. A Monrovia courtroom let one in anyway earlier this year, in the Capitol arson case against former Speaker J. Fonati Koffa, and the Supreme Court declined to stop it. That precedent may now matter more than any statute when Jewel Howard-Taylor’s lawyers try to keep a wiretapped “gift” call out of evidence.

By Rodney D. Sieh | [email protected]

Monrovia — Every account of how Jewel Howard-Taylor came to be arrested runs through the same piece of evidence: a phone call, recorded by a cooperating informant, in which Sheikh Bassirou Kante told the former Vice President that the “investors” she had met in Dubai had sent her a “gift.” It is the closest thing the government has to a smoking gun. It is also, under Liberian law, exactly the kind of evidence that is not supposed to reach a jury easily.

A Legal Framework Built to Keep Secret Recordings Out

Liberia’s constitutional and statutory framework treats secretly recorded conversations with open suspicion, not casual acceptance. Articles 16 and 17 of the Liberian Constitution protect citizens’ privacy and personal property, which Liberian courts have read as attaching a strong expectation of privacy to private conversations. Title 26, Article 19.1 of the Penal Code goes further, classifying unauthorized eavesdropping, the hidden installation of recording devices in private places, or the interception of non-public communications without consent as a first-degree misdemeanor. Taken together, the framework creates what defense lawyers in Liberia have long relied on: an exclusionary tendency, in which recordings obtained illegally, or in violation of a reasonable expectation of privacy, face a real risk of being thrown out before a case ever reaches trial.

The Koffa Precedent

That is the legal backdrop against which Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie made a very different call earlier this year. In the high-profile Capitol arson trial against former House Speaker J. Fonati Koffa and several co-defendants, prosecutors sought to introduce secret audio recordings allegedly extracted from a defendant’s phone. The defense objected on nearly every ground available to it: the recordings were inaudible, unauthenticated, possibly generated or altered by artificial intelligence, and unsupported by any documented chain of custody linking what was played in court to what had been recovered from the phone.

Judge Willie admitted the recordings anyway — provisionally. His reasoning drew a distinction that is likely to matter a great deal in the Taylor case: admissibility is not the same thing as credibility. Under Liberia’s evidentiary standards as he applied them, material can be admitted so long as it is “potentially relevant,” leaving it to the jury to weigh its quality and decide how much, if anything, it deserves to be believed. In the same ruling, Willie denied a defense request to have the audio transcribed into text, insisting the original recordings stand as the primary evidence — meaning jurors would have to rely entirely on what they could make out, in a case where observers described the audio quality as extremely poor and muffled. When the defense tried to halt the proceedings entirely and have the evidence suppressed at the Supreme Court, the justices instead issued a ruling that left Willie’s jurisdiction over the case, and his evidentiary rulings within it, intact. Legal observers and commentators have since accused the Court of ducking a direct constitutional question rather than resolving it — criticism that has followed the ruling into the court of public opinion even as it stands, for now, as binding precedent.

What This Means for the Recording Against Howard-Taylor

Applied to the case against Jewel Howard-Taylor, the Koffa precedent cuts in a specific, predictable direction. If “potentially relevant” is the bar for provisional admission, the Kante recording almost certainly clears it — a recorded reference to a “gift” tied to a Dubai meeting prosecutors say she took part in is relevant on its face, whatever else may be wrong with how it was obtained or preserved. That suggests Taylor’s lawyers are unlikely to succeed in keeping the recording out of the case entirely through a pretrial suppression motion, at least not on the strength of Liberia’s exclusionary tendency alone. The Supreme Court’s unwillingness to intervene in Koffa’s case, even amid public criticism, signals an appellate posture that gives trial judges wide latitude on exactly this kind of evidentiary call.

There is, however, a legal wrinkle in the Taylor case that did not exist in quite the same form in Koffa’s. Kante was not a third party secretly recording two other people’s private conversation — he was, according to this newspaper’s prior reporting, wired by investigators and a direct participant in the call with Taylor himself. Whether Liberian law treats a recording made by a cooperating, consenting participant in a conversation the same way it treats a recording secretly extracted from a third party’s phone is a genuinely open question, and one this newspaper has not seen definitively resolved in Liberian case law. Taylor’s defense may well argue the two situations are legally distinct; prosecutors will almost certainly argue the Koffa precedent applies regardless of who held the recording device.

Admissible Doesn’t Mean Believed

Assuming the recording is provisionally admitted, legal experts say, former Speaker Koffa’s trial offers a preview of where the real battle will move next: not whether jurors hear the recording, but what they are allowed to conclude from it. Expect Taylor’s lawyers to challenge the recording on precisely the grounds Koffa’s defense raised — audio quality, authentication, whether the copy played in court can be reliably tied to an unaltered original, and whether a proper chain of custody exists connecting Kante’s phone to whatever investigators ultimately presented to prosecutors. Expect, too, a fight over transcription. If Judge Willie’s approach holds as the template, a Liberian court may again require jurors to parse a poor-quality recording with their own ears rather than a clean transcript — a dynamic that can cut either way, since ambiguous audio can just as easily create reasonable doubt as it can suggest a cover-up.

None of this determines Howard-Taylor’s guilt or innocence, and FrontPageAfrica does not offer it as a prediction of the case’s outcome. What Koffa’s trial establishes is narrower but still significant: in Liberia’s current judicial climate, a secretly or covertly obtained recording is unlikely to be excluded outright simply because the Constitution and the Penal Code disfavor it in principle. The more realistic battleground, as it was for Koffa, is credibility — and that is a fight that plays out in front of a jury, not in a pretrial motion to suppress.

World.title: African Civil Society Leaders Say the Global Aid System Is Broken; 200 Gather in Accra This Week to Create a New Africa-Led Model
World.content:
Summary:

200 civil society leaders, funders, policymakers and others from almost 30 countries will gather in Ghana this week to design a new African-led approach to development.

They say the existing model, designed by non-Africans in capitals of Europe and America, has failed to understand the communities where they work, fueling dependence, and failing to deliver lasting impact.

The debate has particular significance for Liberia, where critics say billions of dollars of development aid has fueled corruption and dependency and had limited impact.

By Tetee Gebro, gender and health correspondent with New Narratives



In the four years to 2023 the European Union spent $16 million to boost the systems that would keep Liberians safe from gender-based violence. But in 2026 FrontPage Africa/New Narratives found a completely broken legal system in which victims had little chance of accessing justice. The head of the sexual and gender-based violence unit conceded just two perpetrators had been convicted in six years.

The outcome came as little surprise to a growing movement of people in the development sector. They have condemned an aid system designed largely in Western capitals and where the people who understand a problem best are rarely the people trusted to define it.

A major conference in Accra this week will bring together more than 200 African civil society organizations, including from Liberia, with plans to change that. Organizers say the answer is not simply more foreign aid. They want Africans themselves—from governments to communities—to have greater power to determine development priorities and how money is used.

“Let’s shift away from those of us who want to control communities to a situation where communities are in the driving seat,” said Charles Kojo Vandyck, of the West Africa Civil Society Institute, organizers of the Africa at the Center convening, in an interview.

Charles Kojo Vandyck of West Africa Civil Society Institute in promotional material for the Africa at the Center Convening of African civil society leaders in Acca this week.

The idea for the Convening grew out of a WACSI project called RINGO — Reimagining the INGO — launched in 2021. More than 95 civil society leaders, funders and organizations were given one instruction: stop writing reports about what is broken and build something that works instead.

Jimm Chick Fomunjong and Gideon Ahenkorah of the West Africa Civil Society Institute, WACSI, described the assumption buried inside that system in a soon to be released opinion piece.

“The form is only the smallest expression of a much larger architecture: who controls resources, who sets the terms on which they move, and who gets to decide what counts as a legitimate priority,” the pair write. “The scale of what these prototypes are responding to is difficult to overstate, and African institutions have spent years documenting it themselves.

Africa received $74 billion in official aid in 2023. In the same year, according to the Mo Ibrahim Foundation, the continent lost an estimated $90 billion to illicit financial flows, largely through trade mis-invoicing and tax avoidance. It paid a further $103 billion servicing external debt in 2024.

At the International Monetary Fund, where decisions of consequence require an 85 percent majority, the 46 nations of sub-Saharan Africa, a region with a combined economy larger than India’s, shared just two seats on the 24 member executive board until 2024. A third was added only after a decade of advocacy. Africa’s collective vote today stands at roughly 5 per cent. None of these figures, taken together, simply describe a system that malfunctioned. They point instead to an architecture in which the rules governing money, risk and decision-making have too often been set elsewhere, with African countries carrying consequences without possessing an equivalent share of power over the system itself.”

Organizers want the Accra gathering to advance three broad goals: an African-led development financing system, development in which communities are in the driving seat, and stronger institutions that work for Africa. The conference will also showcase practical approaches already being tested rather than simply producing speeches about problems in the existing system.

One model already being tested is what the organization calls a “reverse call for proposals.” Traditionally, donors determine what they want to fund, issue a call for proposals and African organizations compete for the money. Under the reverse model, communities identify their own development priorities, develop proposals and then invite donors to apply to support them.

In a first-ever “reverse call for proposals” Nyankanga community in Zambia issued their own call for proposals, demanding international organizations show them how they can meet their requirements.

The approach has already been tested in the Nyankanga community in Zambia. Working with the Zambian Governance Foundation, community members identified their own development priorities and issued a proposal. Potential partners applied and the community assessed the applications and selected Plan International Zambia.

When Plan arrived with its normal due-diligence requirements, Vandyck said the community turned the process around. Community members first asked Plan to provide its annual reports, explain where it had previously invested in Zambia and demonstrate that it would remain committed to the community.

“You do not send the call, we send the call,” the community told Plan, according to Vandyck.

The amount involved, about $17,000, was small. But Fomunjong and Ahenkorah wrote that the reversal it represents is much bigger than the dollar figure suggests. The Zambian Governance Foundation has since repeated the process in nine more communities. Groups in Malawi and Ghana are testing early versions of the same approach.

Critics of existing aid model say Liberia has more to gain from a new approach than most

In Liberia the failure of the existing development model has been acute. Critics say billions of dollars spent in the country since 2003 has little to show for it with half the population in poverty and extreme poverty rising.

Wonderful Logan is on the frontline. In 2022 she heard good news that free mosquito nets were being handed out across Liberia. The Ministry of Health had received millions in funding from the $5 billion annual donor pool known as the Global Fund to supply nets to people in five counties. So she waited for her net.

“I didn’t receive any,” Logan said. “I got children, I got grandchildren.”

She ended up spending her own money to buy a net instead. Since then, she has watched some of the nets that were supposed to protect families end up somewhere else entirely — used for fishing, draped over chicken coops, or cut into pieces and sold in the market.

“I don’t really see mosquito nets in people’s houses,” Logan said. “I see it in the marketplaces.”

The Global Fund touts its success in mosquito net distribution, but a fraud investigation raised questions about the numbers in Liberia.

Nets, medicines and other supplies that are meant to be free are routinely stolen and reappear in markets to be bought by the very people they were intended for. Even if they are not stolen, Logan says most of her friends don’t believe the nets work to prevent malaria. Some believe misinformation that they constrain their spirits from leaving their bodies while they sleep.It’s difficult to trust data showing malaria incidence has decreased in Liberia. The 2022 Malaria Indicator Survey found that half the population had access to an insecticide-treated net in their household. Half of children under five and 53 percent of pregnant women — the people malaria threatens most — slept under a net the night before the survey.

But a 2022 investigation by its Office of the Inspector General found systemic fraud. Investigators found problems with 91 percent of expenditures reviewed, totaling $1.1 million – citing fraudulent vehicle contracts, inflated bills and almost no internal controls. For 75 percent of field activities checked, they couldn’t confirm programs had even happened. The Malaria Indicator Survey was one of the activities undertaken with Fund money.

It is exactly the kind of failure Charles Kojo Vandyck, WACSI’s head of capacity building, says has to end on both sides. Secretive decision making without clear explanations, reporting and community buy-in leaves communities powerless to hold leaders accountable.

“There’s very little attention on when the funds are disbursed and where the funds actually go,” Vandyck said.

Vandyck says that African ownership and greater transparency with populations will ensure greater accountability. He said citizens and civil society organizations must follow public money and hold governments accountable for how it is actually spent. The Africa at the Centre gathering comes at a pivotal moment. Foreign aid is being cut while African governments and civil society organizations are increasingly questioning a decades-old development model. Ghana turned down a new health funding agreement with the US Trump administration this year after officials decided the data-sharing terms it demanded cost more than the funding was worth. Zimbabwe had already rejected a similar deal. Kenya’s version of the same fight is now in its own courts.

Organizers of the Accra conference, running from September 1 to 3, say the gathering will produce a formal commitment to build what they call an African-owned architecture for development — one with African priorities, African resources and African agency at its center.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project.

World.title: 800,000 Liberians Likely Have Kidney Disease. Most Won’t Survive It
World.content:
A nurse at the John F. Kennedy–Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Dialysis Centre attends to patients in the renal care unit, where dialysis treatment is provided to individuals living with kidney disease. Source: John F. Kennedy Hospital facebook video

Summary:

At least 800,00 Liberians have kidney disease according to experts. Doctors say most kidney failure in this country is preventable and can be detected early with a simple urine test, but most Liberians do not know; Many damage their kidneys by overmedicating with common painkillers.

Health officials say most Liberians diagnosed with kidney failure do not survive, and preventable diseases and weak screening are driving more people toward the same fate.

Liberia’s only public dialysis center opened in 2022 as a national breakthrough, but four years later, it cannot keep up with the number of patients who need it.

By Augusta S. Lafalay, senior reporter with New Narratives

In 2021 Anthony Gbeh had never heard the word “dialysis”. Today, it has become the center of his life. The 45-year-old goes to the country’s only dialysis center here at John F. Kennedy hospital, every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, spending about 12 hours a week connected to the machine that cleans toxins and waste from his blood, because his own kidneys no longer can.

The family scrambles to find the $US300 he needs to pay for it every week. The illness cost Gbeh his teaching job at the University of Liberia and left him dependent on his sister-in-law. The financial strain has shattered the family. Most have distanced themselves from him.

Gbeh also begs for money. He has no choice.

“It is either you beg to survive, or you die,” he says.

Chronic kidney disease is often called a silent killer because it can destroy the kidneys for years before a person feels anything is wrong. By the time symptoms appear — swelling, fatigue, high blood pressure, foamy urine — the damage is advanced. No one knows exactly how many Liberians have kidney disease, because the country has never done a nationwide count. But researchers looking at the West Africa region have found that about 1 in every 6 to 8 adults has some form of kidney disease. The World Health Organization has cited a figure of 13.9 percent for Africa in articles on Liberia. That would be nearly 800,000 people in Liberia living with the condition, many without knowing it.

Liberia carries a double burden. It is seeing more diabetes and high blood pressure — the two leading causes of kidney failure worldwide – but with far less public information on how to prevent or control them. Layered on top are causes more specific to this region: malaria, HIV, hepatitis B and C, sickle cell disease, and the widespread use of herbal remedies and painkillers that can quietly poison the kidneys.

Gbeh is an example. He originally thought he had malaria. He became weak and tired and could barely get out of bed. Doctors at Fidelity Hospital, in Sinkor, where he lived, said it was typhoid. Gbeh moved from clinic to clinic as his legs swelled and his blood pressure climbed, until doctors finally found the real problem: his kidneys were failing.

Doctors determined that what caused his kidney failure was uncontrolled high blood pressure.

That is the cause in almost all cases in Liberia. Uncontrolled high blood pressure, infection and diabetes, in that order, are the biggest factors.

Doctors also warn that some medicines can damage the kidneys, particularly when they are taken excessively or for long periods without medical supervision. These include common non-steroidal anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and indomethacin. Long-term daily use of paracetamol has also been linked to kidney damage.

Some traditional or herbal preparations whose ingredients may be unknown, as well as medicines containing aristolochic acid, which can be found in some traditional Chinese medicines, can also be a cause according to specialists at JFK.

Prednisolone, a steroid often taken without medical supervision for conditions such as joint or knee pain, can also contribute indirectly to kidney problems by raising blood pressure and blood sugar.

They warn its yet another result of Liberia’s unregulated pharmaceutical industry where Liberians can buy any medicine without a prescription and without any knowledge of the damage they may be causing.

The tragedy, said experts, is that most kidney failure in Liberia is preventable.

“The commonest cause is ignorance,” said Dr. Ejikeme Arodiwe, a Nigerian consultant physician at JFK. Liberia has no kidney specialists though several are now being trained. “People don’t go for routine medical checkups. They come when the disease is already advanced.”

Health experts say Liberia urgently needs its own study to know the real numbers. And an awareness campaign to save lives.

Doctors at John F. Kennedy said people’s best defense is prevention: routine blood pressure and urine checks that can catch trouble years before kidneys fail. Until that kind of screening reaches ordinary Liberians, doctors warn, more families will learn about kidney disease only after it has already taken hold, and will be left, like Gbeh negotiating between staying alive and staying afloat.

“If they remember one thing,” Dr. Arodiwe, said, “it should be prevention.”

“Kidney is life,” Dr. Comfort Nyenetu Cooper, administrator of the dialysis center warned. “Take care of your kidney, take care of yourself.”

Gbeh is one of those who use the dialysis center now. When ten dialysis machines arrived here in 2022 for the opening of the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Dialysis Center, many people thought wrongly that kidney disease could now be treated and even cured.

But doctors warn that it is a dangerous misconception. Dialysis machines act in place of kidneys, filtering the body’s blood when the kidneys can no longer do so. They keep people alive, but they are not a cure.
