Right now almost all patients here are eventually handed a death sentence not because medicine failed them, but because the cost of staying alive is more than an ordinary Liberian family can bear. Many eventually receive a transplanted kidney from a family member, or deceased donor. In Liberia that is not available. In developed countries with health insurance costs can be reduced. The burden of keeping people alive is carried by families.

Many families eventually have no choice but to give up.

Staff here suffer as they watch patients die unnecessarily. Dr. Arodiwe is treating one patient whose family could not afford treatment. Ultimately they decided as a family that they could not continue.

“We lost that patient this morning,” he said sadly.

Dr. Arodiwe described another man who kept a strict three-times-a-week schedule in his first year, then slipped to once a week, then to “occasionally,” as the cost wore down his family’s savings. “You can now see he started going down,” Dr. Arodiwe said. “He looks sicker. He looks weaker.”

Even when patients can afford it, the unit cannot keep up with demand. It now runs three shifts a day on eleven machines about 300-400 dialysis sessions monthly, according to Dr. Cooper. It is far more than the unit was designed to handle when it opened.

Patients line up as early as 2 a.m. to secure a place in the day’s first shift. When the unit is full, some are turned away and sent home to wait for another day. Gbeh said two of the center’s machines were out of service when conducted the interview.

“The hospital suffers daily,” Dr. Cooper said, describing a facility that spends far more on imported, single-use dialysis supplies — bloodlines, dialyzers, concentrate — than it recovers in patient payments each.

Dr. Cooper said ignorance about the disease remains as dangerous as the disease itself. “What you do not know, you cannot prevent,” she said.

Many patients, she said, only discover their kidneys are failing after being treated for something else entirely, often the very high blood pressure or diabetes that caused the damage in the first place.

New Narratives made a written request for the Ministry of Health’s response to issues raised in this story to Augustus Walker, communications director of the ministry’s communications office. As of publication, the ministry had not responded.

The strain of kidney failure is placing intolerable strains on families

Momolu Kormah, a restaurant operator in his 20s, was diagnosed with kidney failure in 2023. He became one of the few Liberians who have received a kidney transplant.

The possibility of a transplant came through an unexpected network of friends. Kormah, who had lost both parents and was known in his community from his days as a dancer, turned to Facebook for help. He posted about his illness; friends shared the appeal and formed a group to raise money for him. An interview arranged through that effort eventually led to someone offering to sponsor his trip to India and pay the US$70,000 costs for the transplant.

The kidney came from his younger brother, Ahmed, who volunteered to donate. People have two kidneys and can live long healthy lives with only one. Kormah said doctors in India explained that transplantation would mean taking medication for the rest of his life, following dietary restrictions and undergoing regular medical monitoring. The hospital also screened both him and his brother before the operation, including blood-type and kidney-compatibility testing.



India faces a serious illegal kidney trade problem, fueled by scarce legal supply—only about one in 300 kidney patients get a donated organ. While law limits donation to close relatives or approved cases, brokers routinely fake documents and even DNA results to bypass this. A major 2024–2025 India-Bangladesh trafficking investigation revealed that transplant tourists often receive kidneys from poor, indebted people recruited through deception or coercion, including migrants from Bangladesh. Recipients pay around as much $26,000, but donors see only $2,500–$4,000, with brokers and corrupt officials pocketing the rest.

The hospital required Kormah to provide documents including a family tree, bank statement and authorization from the Liberian government because of concerns he and his brother may have been involved in fraud.

The transplant was performed at Marengo Asia Hospital in Gurugram. Kormah remained under observation for about two months before returning to Liberia.

But once he got home Kormah’s struggle didn’t end. Transplant patients must take anti-rejection drugs for life. Konneh said some of his drugs were not available in Liberia and had to be sent from India. He spent about US$400 a month on the medications.

Friends and relatives sometimes contributed, but delays in getting the medicines from India added another problem. Eventually, he could no longer afford them.

“Having HIV is better than kidney failure,” he said. If you take HIV medication you will live a healthy life. But with kidney failure, the medicines just keep you barely alive.

In 2026 Konneh’s luck ran out. He became one of the one in five people in whom the transplant is rejected in the first five years. He was forced to return to dialysis at John F. Kennedy Medical Center.

Momolu Kromah at the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Dialysis Center after receiving dialysis recently.

Since then his life has since been a misery. He walks this journey with a grim brigade of the almost-dead. He watched recently as a fellow patient, robbed of his belongings and money on his way to an early-morning session, grew weaker and died making the same trip weeks later.

“If somebody like me who is doing dialysis, being stronger, more stable than me can pass away (die), what more can I do?” Kromah said.

Doctors urge better screening, early diagnosis and awareness raising. Kidney specialists at JFK were eager to make clear that a few steps could save people from ending up here. Liberia is treating kidney failure at the final stage, when the cost is highest, and survival depends on money instead of catching the disease early when a simple test and a change in habits could still save a life.

A dialysis patient running their three- to four-hour session on the machine at the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Center at the John F. Kennedy Memorial Hospital. Source: Smith Online Television

Dr. Arodiwe said there are warning signs every Liberian should take seriously, especially anyone who already has high blood pressure or diabetes:

Passing little or no urine, or noticing urine that foams like soup which is a sign of protein leaking from damaged kidneys.

Swelling in the face or body, especially noticeable first thing in the morning.

A test that can catch the disease early is simple and inexpensive. A basic urine test that takes under five minutes, alongside a blood pressure check. Both are available at most Liberian clinics, but neither is routinely offered unless a patient specifically asks. Dr. Arodiwe would like to see that change.

“Any patient that comes to any health facility, even for something else, must have the person’s blood pressure checked,” Dr. Arodiwe said. “It’s very easy to check pressure. A lot of people with high blood pressure could be picked up just by that simple policy.”

Liberia’s severely stretched health budget has just 1.2 million for every Liberian. That is now facing even greater strain due to cuts in international donor funding. A national health insurance scheme seems very far off. But experts say a public health campaign would be a low-cost solution that could go a long way.

Gbeh says that would have helped him. “If I had known more about this disease earlier, I would have paid closer attention to my health.”

This report is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” project. Funding was provided by the Swedish embassy in Liberia, which had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Follow The Law on The Books, Then Ask What the Tape Actually Proves
World.content:
Liberia’s Constitution and Penal Code already say what should happen to a secretly recorded conversation. A precedent set in one courtroom this year should not quietly rewrite that law. And even if a judge lets Liberians hear the recording against Jewel Howard-Taylor, the harder question — the one this newspaper thinks matters — is whether the words on it come anywhere close to proving nine felony charges.

SOMEWHERE BETWEEN A COURTROOM in Monrovia and the front pages of this newspaper, a subtle but important shift has been happening Liberians have started talking about the recording at the center of the Howard-Taylor case as though the only question worth asking is whether a judge will let jurors hear it. That is the wrong question, or at least an incomplete one. Liberia already has an answer, in writing, for how secretly recorded conversations are supposed to be treated. Articles 16 and 17 of the Constitution protect the privacy of citizens and their communications. Title 26, Article 19.1 of the Penal Code makes unauthorized eavesdropping and the covert interception of non-public communications a first-degree misdemeanor. That is not ambiguous language open to a judge’s mood on a given morning. It is the law, passed by the people entitled to write it, and it deserves to be applied with the same rigor in this case that it would be applied to anyone else’s private phone call.

WE UNDERSTAND WHY a different standard has crept into the conversation. Earlier this year, in the Capitol arson case against former Speaker J. Fonati Koffa, a judge provisionally admitted a secret recording over serious defense objections, reasoning that evidence need only be “potentially relevant” to reach a jury, with credibility left for jurors to sort out later. The Supreme Court, asked to intervene, declined to disturb that ruling.

WHATEVER THE LEGAL reasoning behind it, and whatever criticism it has attracted since, this newspaper does not believe that one ruling in one case should now function as an unwritten amendment to the Constitution and the Penal Code. A precedent is not a statute. If Liberia’s courts believe the exclusionary standard written into Articles 16, 17 and Title 26 no longer reflects how justice should work in an age of cell phones and cooperating witnesses, that is a conversation for the Legislature, argued in the open, not a quiet drift accomplished one provisional ruling at a time.



SO, OUR FIRST REQUEST of the court hearing the case against Jewel Howard-Taylor is the simplest one: read the law as it is written before reaching for how another judge read it in a different case, with a different recording, under different facts. If the recording of Sheikh Bassirou Kante’s call was obtained in a way the Constitution and the Penal Code were specifically written to prohibit, that fact should carry real weight in whether it is admitted at all — not get waved through because a precedent exists that makes waving it through easier. But suppose the recording is admitted, cleanly and lawfully, exactly as the government hopes. Even then, this newspaper believes Liberians are being asked to skip past the more important question in their rush to litigate the legal technicalities.

WHAT, PRECISELY, does the recording say? By every account made public so far, it amounts to a single sentence: that the “investors” Howard-Taylor met in Dubai had sent her a “gift.” That is a suggestive sentence. It is not, on its own, a confession to illicit drug trafficking, importation, exportation, conspiracy, facilitation, solicitation, money laundering or abuse of office — the nine separate charges she is now facing. A gift can be an investment. A gift can be a courtesy. A gift can be exactly what prosecutors allege it to be. The recording alone does not tell us which, and neither, as far as the public record shows, does anything else that has been made public about this case.

THIS IS THE STANDARD we would ask any court to hold any defendant to, and we ask it here without any interest in shielding a former Vice President from accountability she may, in the end, deserve. The question that should drive this case forward is not whether a recording exists, or even whether a judge lets it into evidence. It is whether the actual words on that recording, combined with whatever else the state can lawfully produce, add up to proof of the specific crimes charged — proof strong enough to survive a defense that will contest every word of it, exactly as Koffa’s defense contested the tape used against him. If the facts support the charges, Liberians deserve to see that case made plainly, evidence to element, count by count. If they do not yet support all nine counts, Liberians deserve to hear that too, rather than watch a single ambiguous word carry the weight of an entire prosecution.

LIBERIA HAS SPENT this whole summer learning, the hard way, what happens when the government announces conclusions before the evidence is ready to support them.



THE COUNTRY CANNOT afford to make that mistake again, this time in a courtroom the entire region is watching. Follow the law on secret recordings as it is written. Then ask, honestly and specifically, whether what was said on that recording proves what the charge sheet claims. Everything else is noise.

World.title: North Chief hails HH leadership
World.content:
Chief Mwamba of the Mambwe people of Mbala district has expressed optimism that President Hakainde Hichilema’s administration will continue to roll-out development, following his re-election in the August 13, general elections.

The traditional leader says he remains hopeful that the government will accelerate development in Mbala district, particularly in the road sector.

Chief Mwamba cited the road leading to the Zombe border, as well as the road connecting Kawimbe through Mwamba chiefdom to Kaka, as some of the developmental projects that need urgent attention.

He said improved road infrastructure will boost economic activities and make it easier for people in the area to access markets and essential services.

Chief Mwamba said this in an interview with the media in Mbala today.

“Improved roads will not only enhance connectivity, but will also open up opportunities for our people to participate more actively in economic activities,” Chief Mwamba said.

The traditional leader has also appealed to UPND Member of Parliament for Saise, Remmy Sikazwe, to help facilitate the completion of his palace.

World.title: Serenje Chief calls for illegal mining end
World.content:
Senior Chief Muchinda of the Lala people of Serenje district has called on the government to curb illegal mining in the area, which he says endangers the lives of the youths in his chiefdom.

Chief Muchinda notes that illegal mining activities pose a threat, saying those engaged, continue to conduct mining activities without taking safety precautions.

The traditional leader made these remarks when Serenje District Commissioner Ellen Miselo, who is on a familiarisation tour of the district, paid a courtesy call on him.

He explained that illegal mining activities have become prevalent in his area, with young people being employed without proper Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), thereby endangering their lives.

“We need to work together to fight illegal mining to safeguard the lives of our children. We need to deal with criminals, illegal miners and those selling land illegally, in order to preserve our land,” he said.

And Senior Chief Muchinda said most mining companies operating in his area are doing so illegally, stating that they are not undertaking Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) programmes in the chiefdom.

He urged the government to regulate the working conditions of mine workers and ensure that they are provided with the necessary protective and working equipment.

Meanwhile, Serenje District Commissioner Ellen Mibenge commended the traditional leader for preserving trees in his chiefdom and assured him of the government’s support in fostering development in the district.

She said her office will ensure that investors comply with the law so that local people will benefit from their investments.

World.title: UPND petitions parley seats in Muchinga
World.content:
The United Party for National Development (UPND) has petitioned for two parliamentary seats in the Chinsali High Court in Muchinga Province.

The seats are the Chinsali Central seat in Chinsali District where UPND candidate, Christopher Chiponde has petitioned the election of Chanda Mwansa of the National Restoration Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP).

The other is the Shiwangandu seat in Shiwangandu district where a UPND supporter and voter, Victor Beleshi has petitioned the election of Stephen Kampyongo of the NRPUP.

According to records obtained by the media at the Chinsali High Court, Mr Chiponde is seeking the court to nullify the results of the parliamentary election.

Mr Chiponde said the election was marred with shockingly widespread illegalities and violence against persons and property.

He cited other grounds to warrant the nullification of the results as alleged intimidation, corruption, procedural breaches and other misconduct during the election that declared Mr Mwansa.

The petitioner further alleged that there was widespread non- compliance with the provisions of the Electoral Process Act no. 35 of 2016 stating that this affected the outcome of the elections.

Mr Chiponde has further cited Mr Mwansa who was declared winner as the first respondent, while the Electoral Commission of Zambia as the second respondent.

And in Shiwang’andu Constituency, Victor Beleshi a voter who is also a member of the United Party for National Development (UPND) has petitioned for the parliamentary seat.

The Petitioner is seeking recourse against the respondent Stephen Kampyongo Member of Parliament elect in Shiwangandu Constituency and wants the results be declared null and void.

Mr Beleshi stated that NRPUP members at various polling stations were allowed to vote for more than two people and spent long periods of time inside the polling stations.

The other grounds have been cited are that at some polling stations, the respondent and his agents were giving money to the electorates and evidence abounds in this area.

The NRPUP scooped both the Chinsali Central seat and the Shiwangandu parliamentary seat during the August 13th general election.

NRPUP candidate Chanda Mwansa obtained 11254 votes against Christopher Chiponde of the UPND who got 4430 votes.

In the Shiwangandu, Stephen Kampyongo got 11,536 votes against Robert Kapeya of the UPND who got 9941 votes.

Both seats were petitioned on Friday, August 28th, 2026.

World.title: We’ll be back for the title – Mwila
World.content:
ZESCO Ndola Girls Head Coach Florence Mwila has described Saturday’s 2-1 defeat to Mamelodi Sundowns in the CAF Women’s Champions League COSAFA Qualifier final as “not part of the plan” but says her team will return stronger.

It was déjà vu for the Zambian champions, who were losing finalists for the second year running after conceding a controversial late penalty in Botswana.

“I think we started on a very slow note, but the positive thing is that the girls pushed, equalized,” Mwila said.

“Obviously they were so much under pressure, so we conceded that penalty which really put us down,” she said.

Despite the heartbreak, Mwila said there were positives to take from the tournament. ZESCO topped Group A with 9 points from 3 wins and beat *Silver Strikers 2-1 to reach the final.

“We have picked up positives from here like the commitment and the fighting spirit from the players, “she said.

“We have a task to defend the championship back home. We will improve in the grey areas as a team so that when we come back we will come back for the title.”

With the win, Mamelodi Sundowns will represent the COSAFA region at the CAF Women’s Champions League continental finals.

World.title: Government calls for stronger HAI surveillance
World.content:
Government has called for stronger and sustainable Healthcare-Associated Infections (HAIs) surveillance systems across Africa to improve patient safety and strengthen the fight against antimicrobial resistance.

Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary for Technical Services, Kennedy Lishimpi, says healthcare-associated infection surveillance should be integrated into routine national surveillance and quality of care systems, rather than remain a stand-alone activity dependent on external support.

Dr Lishimpi was speaking in Lusaka today, when he officiated at the Multi-Country Training of Trainers on Healthcare-Associated Infection Surveillance (HAIs), which has brought together national Infection Prevention and Control and Antimicrobial Resistance focal persons, from 13 African Union Member States.

He said reliable surveillance is critical in helping health facilities identify priority infections, detect outbreaks early, determine the organisms involved and link laboratory and clinical data to appropriate infection prevention and control measures.

“Healthcare-associated infections are not merely statistics,” Dr. Lishimpi said, noting that such infections can delay patient recovery, increase risks to newborns and health workers as well as impose additional costs on families and health systems.

He said the surveillance of HAIs is also central to addressing antimicrobial resistance because infections acquired during healthcare often result in additional or prolonged antimicrobial treatment, while resistant organisms make infections more difficult and costly to manage.

He called for the cascading of training to subnational and facility levels and the regular analysis and sharing of surveillance data with health workers and managers to support decision-making.

Dr Lishimpi said sustainable HAIs surveillance requires trained personnel, reliable laboratories, appropriate digital and paper-based tools, adequate water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure as well as domestic financing.

He also stressed the importance of regional collaboration and peer learning in helping African countries adopt common standards and strengthen their surveillance systems.

He disclosed that the World Health Organisation estimates that about 15 in every 100 patients in acute-care hospitals in low and middle-income countries acquire at least one healthcare-associated infection.

And Africa CDC Director General Jean Kaseya in a speech read for him by Africa CDC Regional Director Peter Kumpalume, called for stronger measures to prevent hospital-acquired infections.

Dr Kaseya Africa CDC said HAIs are among the most frequent adverse events occurring in hospitals, with a significant proportion being preventable through stronger infection prevention and control systems.

He noted that HAIs not only put patients at risk but also place an additional burden on health systems through increased hospital bed occupancy, medicine use and pressure on doctors, nurses and laboratory personnel.

He also said infection prevention and control should be institutionalised as a permanent component of clinical care.

Dr Kaseya reaffirmed Africa CDCs commitment to supporting member states in strengthening infection prevention and control.

World.title: Ministry of Green Economy hands over vehicles to Eastern Province
World.content:
The Ministry of Green Economy and Environment has handed over five vehicles worth k6.1 million to the Eastern Province Jurisdictional Sustainable Landscape Programme to strengthen field operations aimed at reducing carbon emissions and deforestation.

Ministry of Green Economy and Environment Permanent Secretary, Douty Chibamba said the vehicles will enhance monitoring, reporting, data collection and verification of emission reductions across the 15 districts covered by the programme.

Dr Chibamba noted that reliable transport is critical to the success of the programme, particularly in reaching communities in remote areas where sustainable forest management, climate-smart agriculture and energy-efficient cooking initiatives are being implemented.

He said the Eastern Province Jurisdictional Sustainable Landscape Programme is targeting the generation of approximately 20 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent by 2030 through interventions aimed at reducing deforestation and forest degradation while promoting sustainable land management.

Dr Chibamba said the five vehicles were procured through the United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS) at a cost of about 321,000 United States dollars, equivalent to approximately

6.1 million kwacha.

He said one of the vehicles will be allocated to the Zambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA), while the others will support implementation of the programme in Eastern Province.

World Bank Group Agriculture Economist Michael Kabwe said the Bank remains committed to supporting Zambia’s efforts to strengthen forest management and promote climate-smart agriculture.

Mr Kabwe said the bank is pleased to support the Ministry of Green Economy and Environment in implementing activities under the Jurisdictional Sustainable Landscape Project in Eastern Province.

Zambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA) Director for Human Resource and Administration, Sipho Sinkala, said the vehicles will provide critical logistical support to technical teams conducting field activities under the jurisdictional Sustainable Landscape Programme.

Kitwe’s Nkana Golf Club have won the 2026 Zambia Golf Union (ZGU) National Quadrangular Tournament after edging three other regional representatives at the Lusaka Golf Club.

Nkana ended with 74 points, 11 better than their closest competitor, Bonanza Golf Club.

2024 champions, Mazabuka Golf Club, emerged third with 45 points while defending champions Nchanga finished last with just 34 points.

Bhagoo called for unity in the sport saying harmony is key to growing the sport.

“There will always be differences of opinion. That is natural in any organization. What is important is how we deal with those differences and its better through dialogue, understanding, cooperation and respect, rather than allowing them to divide us,” Bhagoo said.

Bhagoo pledged ZGU’s commitment to developing golf across the country by strengthening clubs and creating opportunities for the next generation of golfers.

Meanwhile, Nkana’s elite amateur golfer Dominic Musonda won the Johnnie Walker Uganda Amateur Open title with a nine-under-par 279, three shots better than fellow Zambian Gilbert Chalwe, who finished second.

Another Zambian, Musamba Kapoma Jnr, finished fifth.

“Their success is a wonderful example of what can be achieved through discipline, dedication and hard work. They have set a high standard and shown our young golfers what is possible,” Bhagoo said.

World.title: Niger: Russia Helped Foil Coup in Niger - - Official
World.content:
In a viral video interview, Viktor Voropaïev, Russian ambassador to Niger, said the Nigerien government requested its assistance in quelling the mutiny which lasted for hours between 28 and 29 August.

Russia says it helped the military regime in Niger Republic repel a coup.

In a viral video interview, Viktor Voropaïev, Russian ambassador to Niger, said the Nigerien government requested its assistance in quelling the mutiny, which lasted for hours between 28 and 29 August.

"The rebels who organised these demonstrations have been neutralised, particularly thanks to the intervention of Africa Corps military personnel from the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation," Sahel Alert quoted Mr Voropaïev as saying.



PREMIUM TIMES reported that mutinous soldiers abandoned their frontline positions to stage a fight with presidential elite forces in what analysts described as an attempt to oust the military junta in the francophone country.

The fighting disrupted state broadcast services in Niger.

The mutineers besieged Diori Hamani International Airport, Air Base 101 and attempted to breach the perimeter of the presidential palace including key positions around the airport.

The rebellious soldiers, according to analysts, were frustrated by worsening insecurity and the regime's unfair treatment of frontline troops.

After hours of fighting and gaining ground, the mutineers were suppressed by a joint air-ground offensive launched by Nigerien elite forces and the Russian-backed Africa Corp.

Subsequently, the regime announced that it remained in control, although the head of the junta, Abdourahamane Tchiani, was yet to make any public appearance or comment.

By Sunday morning, footage of captured mutineers started showing on the internet with reports that some of them were killed.

Since it cut ties with France, its former colonial power, Niger has shifted its focus to Moscow as a strategic partner. According to reports, about 300 Russian troops are on the ground in Niger.

The Eurasian country is gaining influence in Sahelian states where military authorities have seized power.

In April, it helped the Malian government repel what could have been a more devastating jihadi attack in Bamako. Its recent intervention in Niger, analysts argue, will further boost its popularity in Africa.

The Sahel region continues to witness terror attacks by Islamic State and al-Qaeda affiliates.

The recent uprising in Niger could open a window of terror, some analysts warned, arguing that those positions abandoned by the mutineers are prone to be infiltrated by jihadists.

Many countries including junta-led Mali and Burkina Faso, with which the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) was formed, have stood in solidarity with the Niger.

World.title: Kenya: Consumers Warn of Milk Price Squeeze As Formal Supply Falls
World.content:
Nairobi — Kenyan consumers are facing renewed pressure on milk prices after formal-sector milk deliveries declined in June, with the Consumers Federation of Kenya (COFEK) calling for urgent government measures to prevent further shortages and price increases.

Data from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) shows that milk intake by processors and other formal-sector players fell by 5 percent to 84.44 million litres in June 2026, from 88.89 million litres in May.

The June intake was also 6.4 percent lower than the 90.24 million litres recorded in the same month last year, pointing to growing pressure on the formal dairy supply chain.



COFEK Secretary-General Stephen Mutoro said the figures should prompt the government to provide a clear picture of what is happening in the dairy sector, particularly as consumers begin to experience higher prices and intermittent shortages.

"Consumers are entitled to a clear, evidence-based account of the true state of the sector."

The federation said the situation is already being felt in Nairobi, where some retailers have started rationing milk purchases while prices of fresh milk have risen.

At Waithaka Dairy Centre, for example, the federation said the price of a liter of fresh milk had increased from Sh70 to Sh80. It also reported intermittent shortages of branded packaged milk in supermarkets.

The squeeze is being compounded by difficulties facing smallholder farmers, who account for about 80 percent of Kenya's milk supply, according to COFEK.

The federation said farmers in some areas are reporting daily yields falling from between seven and nine litres per cow to four to five litres, as delayed rains weaken pasture availability.

Commercial feed costs have also risen by about 45 percent, increasing the cost of maintaining dairy herds.

The Kenya Dairy Board has previously raised concerns that some farmers could leave dairy production altogether, including by selling cows they can no longer afford to feed.

COFEK, however, argues that the current pressure is not solely a weather-related problem, pointing to weaknesses in how the country managed the milk surplus recorded last year.

The federation says milk powder from the 2025 surplus was not incorporated into strategic food reserves as anticipated, leaving the market with limited buffers as production came under pressure.

Formal milk intake between January and June stood at 513.32 million litres, broadly unchanged from 516.34 million litres in the corresponding period of 2025.

However, the monthly figures have been volatile, with intake falling to 74.43 million litres in February before recovering in subsequent months.

Close 

COFEK is now demanding that the Agriculture Ministry publish a recovery plan within seven days, including monthly milk-intake targets and emergency fodder and feed support for affected dairy-producing counties.

It is also calling on the Kenya Dairy Board to account for the 2025 milk surplus and disclose the status of milk powder reserves.

The federation wants the National Treasury to remove import duty and VAT on key dairy-feed ingredients, including yellow maize and soya, arguing that lower feed costs would help farmers remain in production.

"The priority now should be to protect both the farmer who produces the milk and the consumer who buys it."

COFEK is further urging the government to strengthen retail price monitoring and provide fortnightly updates on milk intake, prices and reserves until supply conditions stabilize.

The demands come as the dairy sector navigates the competing pressures of maintaining viable farm-gate prices for producers while keeping milk affordable for households.

World.title: Algeria: Algeria Sends Fighter Jets to Niger After a Failed Military Coup
World.content:
Niamey — Four Su-30 fighter jets, accompanied by an Il-76 transport aircraft and an Il-78 aerial tanker, have been deployed by Algeria to Air Base 101, adjacent to Diori Hamani International Airport in Niamey, following the military uprising that broke out last weekend. This is the first overseas deployment of the Algerian military and demonstrates the importance Algiers attaches to the situation in its southern neighbor. This is probably the most significant geopolitical development to emerge from the attempted uprising in Niger.

The direct intervention by the Algerian military, which does not appear to have taken part in suppressing the revolt, was preceded several days ago by the donation to the Nigerien armed forces of four helicopters, along with ammunition, spare parts, maintenance equipment and logistical support.

The uprising by several special forces units, deployed in the fight against jihadist groups in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions, broke out during the night of August 28-29, when residents heard gunfire and explosions coming from several sensitive areas of the capital: in the city center, around the Presidency of the Republic, near the headquarters of Niger's Radio and Television network, and close to Air Base 101.

The Italian military mission is stationed at the latter facility, making it the last contingent of Western troops still present in Niger following the withdrawal of French, US and German forces.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

During the day on August 29, Nigerien authorities said they had regained control of the situation and restored calm in the capital. Confirming the military junta's statements, an official ceremony was held the following day, Sunday, August 30, at Air Base 101 to mark the arrival of the Algerian Air Force contingent.

According to a statement from Algeria's Ministry of National Defence, the aircraft were deployed to Niger at the request of the Nigerien authorities. The mission is intended to support the Nigerien armed forces in the face of what the authorities described as an "attempt to destabilize" the State.

This year, the airport and Air Base 101 in Niamey have been targeted on three occasions: on January 29, in an attack claimed by the Islamic State in the Sahel (see Fides, 30/1/2026); on June 18, in another attack attributed to JNIM (see Fides, 19/6/2026); and now, on August 29, by rebel soldiers.

The attempted uprising was also thwarted with the assistance of members of the Africa Corps, the Russian force operating under the Ministry of Defence in Moscow, which replaced Wagner mercenaries. Air Base 101 hosts both the Africa Corps contingent and the joint headquarters of the unified force of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), comprising Niger, Burkina Faso and Mali.

Algeria has resumed relations with Mali following tensions in recent years (see Fides, 8/4/2025). Relations had already deteriorated since 2023-2024, particularly after Mali withdrew from the 2015 Algiers Agreement, which had been mediated by Algeria with armed groups in the north.

Close 

Mali has also accused Algiers of supporting or providing refuge to certain armed groups.

The Algerian military deployment at the heart of the AES joint headquarters could therefore also mark a turning point in relations between Bamako and Algiers.

World.title: Matthew Berry details how he reported Tom Brady signing with Tampa Bay while drunk at a bar with team official
World.content:
Do you remember who first reported that Tom Brady would join the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2020?

Matthew Berry thought about the question for a brief moment before remembering. "Oh, I believe it was me," he told OutKick.

For context, Brady announced his departure from the New England Patriots weeks before signing with Tampa Bay. At the time, his rumored destinations included the Los Angeles Chargers, Las Vegas Raiders and Indianapolis Colts. No one had mentioned the Buccaneers.

MATTHEW BERRY DISCUSSES WHETHER HE'D HIRE DIANNA RUSSINI FOR HIS BUDDING FANTASY FOOTBALL EMPIRE

Then, after the NFL Combine, Berry wrote in his annual rumors column that he would bet on Brady heading to Tampa. He told OutKick he was quite confident about his prediction at the time.

"I won’t give away my source, but I will tell you how I came across the information. I was at the NFL Combine, and it was about 2 a.m., and I was in a bar. I met somebody who worked for the Buccaneers organization," he explained.

"We were drinking for an hour and were hammered. This particular person tells me, ‘I think we have a shot at Brady.’ And I’m like, ‘No, you don’t.’"

Berry added: "And this person tells me, ‘No, man. We worked him out. We’ve had conversations with him. We think it’s down to us and, I think he said, the Raiders. He goes, Gisele wants a South Florida team to make it easier for her to get home, to fly out of a Florida airport."

As they continued drinking, Berry realized the person was, in fact, serious.

"The more he talked, the more convinced this person sounded. I thought, ‘Well, okay.’ These are things that I hear drunk in a bar."

MATTHEW BERRY HAS HAD TALKS WITH ESPN ABOUT A RETURN, FOLLOWING PAT MCAFEE MODEL

As I mentioned to Berry during the conversation, I remember reading his report and asking an NFL insider about it. The insider said they had not heard that. Fans and media were also skeptical that a fantasy football guru, rather than a traditional insider, would have the correct information about one of the biggest transactions in NFL history.

Later that night, the insider texted me back: "Berry is onto something."

Brady eventually signed with Tampa Bay and led the Buccaneers to a Super Bowl victory in his first season there.

The takeaway is obvious. For those who want to break major NFL stories, the real information is not obtained at journalism school, but while drunk in a bar at 2 a.m.

Berry appreciated that we asked him about the scoop. "No one has ever brought that up before. Thank you."

A ferry carrying 267 passengers and crew capsized off the northern coast of Cyprus, leaving at least eight people dead and 20 others missing as search efforts continued Monday.

The vessel was traveling from Kyrenia in northern Cyprus to the Turkish port of Tasucu when it began taking on water shortly after leaving port Sunday, according to Reuters.

Survivors were rescued from the water and from the overturned ferry as nearby vessels and coast guard crews responded, Reuters reported.

CRUISES THROWN INTO CHAOS AS DROUGHT STRANDS SHIPS, LEAVES PASSENGERS SCRAMBLING

"She was saying, 'Don't let go,'" Bicer told Reuters. "And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go."

A suitcase fell on Bicer during the chaos, causing her to lose her grip on the girl.

She managed to grab her daughter's foot, but said oil from the vessel made the area slippery and the child slipped away.

World.title: Kansas City Chiefs may have ruined Jack Pyburn's plan to make big money at LSU  by giving him a job in the NFL
World.content:
Folks who track such things last week were estimating that Jack Pyburn could make around $1 million in 2026 if he was cut by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and allowed to return to college at LSU. Except, well, the Kansas City Chiefs had other plans.

The Chiefs on Monday afternoon claimed the linebacker off waivers from the Bucs, per the NFL waiver wire.

That means Pyburn's NFL career continues as a member of the Chiefs' 53-man roster.

NCAA CREATED THIS MESS, NOW LSU SET TO MAKE DAE’QUAN WRIGHT COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S FIRST NFL RETURNEE

It also means Pyburn is seemingly headed for a pay cut by being in the NFL rather than back in college.

Yes, crazy world.

Pyburn's rookie salary is scheduled to be $885,000. And that is less than the $1 million he was expected to make in college.

So we have reached the critical juncture where the NIL rules and countless court filings and rulings on eligibility have turned college football into something of a financial competitor for the NFL in the case of some players.

MATT RHULE SOUNDS ALARM ON NFL RETURNEES, $45 MILLION ROSTERS AND COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S PAYROLL PROBLEM

It's been that way before.

There have been examples where quarterbacks forego their final years in college and the sizeable pay they might have earned in that season, and go to the NFL to take a financial shave.

But that's quarterbacks.

Stars.

And it is their choice to start what promises to be a lucrative career longterm.

Jack Pyburn?

He was not drafted in April coming out of LSU. He played only one season there after playing at the University of Florida in 2023 and 2024.

Pyburn played in 12 games with 11 starts at LSU and collected 52 tackles with 2 sacks and 5.5 tackles for loss. That's nice.

But that doesn't scream $1 million nice.

NCAA WINS TENTH CIRCUIT 'STAY', BUT FACES MORE ELIGIBILITY LAWSUITS FROM 2022 CLASS ATHLETES IN CHAOTIC TIME

And how did we get here?

Pyburn was part of a lawsuit filed by more than 30 athletes in Louisiana that won a temporary restraining order allowing them to play in college in the 2026 academic year.

Pyburn and other players meeting certain criteria who signed with or were drafted by NFL teams were allowed to return to school as long as they could terminate their pro contracts and repay any pro earnings.

Pyburn was reportedly ready to do that with the Bucs because they were expected to cut him – as they eventually did. They had guaranteed him $115,000, including a $15,000 signing bonus.

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

But now that contract is not terminated. It and the rights to Pyburn belong to the Chiefs.

Pyburn, by the way, reportedly informed LSU that he is withdrawing his name from the ongoing eligibility lawsuit and will remain in the NFL – not that the Chiefs gave him a choice, really.

World.title: Tips for your fantasy football draft: How to build a winning team without overthinking it
World.content:
It's that time of year again. You've read the rankings, listened to the podcasts, watched some preseason football and probably done at least one mock draft that completely fell apart by the fifth round (or you literally stopped paying attention after round three).

You've got a strategy, and you're ready for your actual fantasy football draft.

So, naturally, the guy in your league who hasn't done a second of research and shows up 10 minutes late asking, "Wait, Mike Evans is on the 49ers now?" is probably going to win the championship.

That's fantasy football.

There are hundreds, probably thousands, of fantasy football analysts on the internet, and many of them are very good at what they do. They'll tell you which running backs are undervalued, which rookie wide receivers are about to break out and which quarterback is being drafted three rounds too early.

TIME TO FACE FACTS: FANTASY FOOTBALL PUNISHMENTS HAVE OFFICIALLY JUMPED THE SHARK IN 2026

Find an analyst whose opinion you trust. Better yet, find a few.

That's not what we're doing here.

Instead, I want to talk about general fantasy football draft strategy. I've been playing fantasy football for a long time, in a lot of different leagues with a lot of different people, and there are certain mistakes that people make over and over again.

Avoiding a few of them won't guarantee you a championship. Nothing will.

But it certainly won't hurt.

Know the rules of your fantasy football league

Let's start with the most obvious one, because it's also one that people routinely screw up: know the rules.

Sounds simple, right?

Well, is your league full PPR, half-PPR or standard scoring? How many wide receivers start? How many flex spots are there? Is it a one-quarterback league or superflex? Are passing touchdowns worth four points or six? Do you get bonuses for long touchdowns or 100-yard games?

How many bench spots does everyone have? How does the waiver/free agency system work after the draft?

All of that matters.

A player can have significantly more value in one scoring system than another. A league that starts three wide receivers and a flex puts a lot more pressure on wide receiver depth than one that starts two receivers. Superflex leagues push quarterbacks way up the board.

So before you start obsessing over whether Player A should be ranked 37th or 41st, make sure you understand the game you're actually playing.

And that includes roster rules.

I've seen people get halfway through a draft before realizing the league adjusted the roster spots between seasons. I've seen people draft like they're playing standard scoring when receptions are worth a full point.

Don't be that person.

This is especially important if you're playing in multiple leagues. If the setup is different enough, an elite draft in one league might be a last-place roster in another.

Honestly, just knowing the rules probably puts you ahead of at least one player in your league (but likely more than one).

Who are your opponents?

This is one of the most important parts of fantasy football drafting, and I don't think people talk about it nearly enough.

Who are you playing against?

There's a huge difference between a casual home league and a league filled with people who spend all summer studying fantasy football.

Maybe you're in a league with 11 friends you've known since college. Three of them are really into fantasy football. Five pay attention once the calendar flips to September but not one day sooner. One guy still thinks it's 2022.

Then there's Derek, who forgot the draft was today. Side note: definitely don't be this guy. There's nothing worse than those frantic phone calls to first locate "Derek" and then, if unsuccessful, calls to find a last-minute fill-in.

Home leagues are a completely different environment from a competitive league where nearly everyone understands Average Draft Position (ADP), knows the depth charts and has already done 50 drafts. If that's your league, I'm not sure why you're reading my fantasy football advice in the first place.

In a casual league, good players tend to fall further. There's often no reason to reach aggressively for someone just because you like him. There's a decent chance your league mates aren't even looking at the same players you are.

Sharper leagues are different. Sleepers aren't really sleepers when everyone knows about them. A player you think is going to last another round might have six other people waiting to draft him.

You also need to know the specific people in your league.

Home leagues develop personalities over time. One guy always takes a quarterback early. Another drafts rookies like he's waiting for his shot to be an actual NFL GM (it's not going to happen, Kevin). Someone else has to get at least three players from his favorite team every year.

Pay attention.

NFL COACHES AND EXECUTIVES SAY PATRICK MAHOMES IS NO LONGER THE BEST QUARTERBACK IN THE NFL

I live in Connecticut, and I've made this same point about NCAA Tournament pools. Filling out a bracket against a bunch of UConn fans is different because you already know UConn is probably going to be more popular in that pool than it would be nationally.

Fantasy football works the same way.

Drafting with a room full of Eagles fans? Philadelphia players probably aren't slipping very far.

And after 10 or 15 years in the same home league, you probably know your friends' bad habits better than they do. In fact, they probably don't even realize their own bad habits. Now is the time to use that information against them.

Know where your fantasy football draft is being held

Are you drafting on ESPN? Yahoo? Sleeper? CBS? NFL?

Or are you sitting in someone's garage with a giant draft board and a stack of stickers?

Those are not the same drafts.

Every fantasy platform has its own rankings and its own ADP. And whether people realize it or not, those rankings sitting on the screen have a huge influence on who gets drafted when.

A player ranked near the top of the available list is going to attract attention.

Maybe you're using rankings from an analyst who has a certain wide receiver ranked 45th overall. Great. But your league is drafting on a site where that player typically goes around No. 70.

Why take him at 45?

You might be right about the player. But the entire point is to get him as late as you reasonably can.

That's why you need to check the site you're actually using. A player you have to grab in the sixth round on ESPN might still be sitting there in the eighth on Yahoo.

And that's before you even get to live drafts.

There isn't one universal list controlling the room when you're sitting around a table. One person has a printout from ESPN. Another has rankings from some fantasy analyst he follows. Someone is drafting off his phone.

Then there's the guy who bought a fantasy magazine in an airport six weeks ago (this guy usually falls into the "Mike Evans plays for who?!" category).

Good luck figuring out what he's going to do.

Those drafts can get weird quickly, which is part of what makes them fun.

Rankings and ADP aren't the same thing

This ties directly into the previous point.

Rankings are your opinion, or somebody else's opinion, of how players should be valued. ADP tells you where people are actually taking them.

You need to know both because that's how you're going to find value.

Let's say you absolutely love a player and have him ranked 50th overall. His ADP is around 80.

You have pick No. 52.

Taking him there isn't necessarily wrong if you believe he's worth the pick.

But what if you also select again at No. 69 (nice) and there's a very good chance he's still going to be available?

Now you've got a decision to make.

Fantasy football isn't just about identifying good players. It's also about figuring out how long you can afford to wait before somebody else takes them.

Of course, ADP isn't some magical law that everyone has to follow. Players get picked ahead of ADP all the time, and sometimes that's the right move.

Same thing with rankings.

There isn't nearly enough certainty in fantasy football to pretend that the player ranked 42nd is definitely better than the player ranked 49th. They're probably pretty close.

That's why tiers can be useful.

You might have six wide receivers that you view almost identically who are all still available. Meanwhile, there's one running back left before you see a significant drop at the position.

That matters a lot more than whether WR18 is technically ranked three spots ahead of RB17.

Don't panic because everyone else is drafting one position

It happens in almost every fantasy draft.

Three quarterbacks go in quick succession.

Then someone takes another one.

Suddenly, a person who had absolutely no intention of drafting a quarterback starts thinking, "Oh no, I need to get one."

Do you?

Maybe. But it's also possible four people just helped you by taking quarterbacks while good players at other positions sat there.

Obviously, you can't completely ignore a run. If the last quarterback you really like is sitting there and six have already gone, you might have to pull the trigger.

But that's different from getting nervous because the room suddenly decided now is the time to grab QB1.

There are drafts where jumping into the run makes sense. There are others where I'm perfectly happy watching everyone else do it and taking whatever good players they're leaving for me.

This is called "board texture" if you're really into fantasy football, and I promise that's the last time I'm going to use a nerdy term like that.

You're building a fantasy roster, not completing a checklist

There's something satisfying about looking at your fantasy team during the draft and seeing every starting position filled.

Quarterback? Got one.

Running backs? Done.

Wide receivers? Check.

Tight end? Taken care of.

Defense and kicker? Yep, got them, too.

Great.

Nobody gives you bonus points for that.

Your goal isn't to be the first person in the league with a complete Week 1 starting lineup. You're trying to build a roster for an entire season.

Maybe there's a tight end you like, but there are four others you'd be perfectly happy drafting later. Meanwhile, a running back you had ranked much higher than the rest of the board is still available even though you already have two running backs.

I'm probably taking RB3 and dealing with tight end later.

Obviously, this has limits. You can't completely ignore roster construction and just draft 14 running backs because they're the highest-ranked player every time you're on the clock.

But I see people pass on good players all the time because they don't like seeing an empty spot next to "TE" or "QB" on the draft screen.

Don't turn every sleeper into a reach

Everyone loves sleepers.

It's one of the best parts of fantasy football, and if you Google "fantasy football sleepers" you'll probably get 10,000 results. Why? Every analyst writes those articles because they know how many people are looking for that exact analysis.

There's no better feeling than taking the guy no one in your league has even heard of and having him post a 1,000-yard, 10 TD season. Now you get to talk about what a football expert you are (but you're still not getting that GM gig, Kevin).

The problem is that fantasy players sometimes get so excited about finding sleepers that they destroy the entire point of finding them.

A player isn't much of a bargain if you draft him four rounds ahead of where anyone else was going to take him.

Now, there's nothing wrong with reaching sometimes. In fact, you have to do it.

Fantasy drafts don't let you select whenever you want. Maybe you pick 65th and don't pick again until 88th. There's a player with an ADP around 78 whom you really want.

Take him.

Waiting around for some perfect ADP value is a good way to watch the guy picking three spots behind you draft all the players you wanted.

But taking someone 15 picks early because you know he won't make it back to you is different from taking someone 50 picks early because you watched two preseason highlights and fell in love.

And, yes, maybe you really did find the next superstar.

I'd still rather draft him later if I can.

Be ready for your fantasy football draft to go completely sideways

You can do 100 mock drafts before your real draft (but you shouldn't, because this is a major waste of time).

It won't matter.

Someone is going to take a player 25 picks earlier than expected. A player you've never seen fall past the fifth round is going to be sitting there in the seventh. You're going to have three players queued up for your next pick and watch all three come off the board right before you're on the clock.

Welcome to fantasy football.

This is why I never go into a draft thinking things like, "I'm definitely taking two running backs with my first two picks."

Maybe that's how it works out.

Then again, maybe the second round comes around and a receiver you never expected to see is sitting there.

Same with waiting for a quarterback, taking an elite tight end early or any other draft strategy you decided on before the first team was even on the clock.

Having a plan is smart. Just don't spend the entire draft trying to force the board to match the mock draft you did Tuesday night.

Most importantly, fantasy football is supposed to be fun

I saved this one for last because I think people sometimes forget it.

Fantasy football is supposed to be fun.

Yes, we all want to win. Winning is a lot more fun than losing. And everything written above is designed to help you make better decisions during your draft.

But you're also going to spend the next four months rooting for these players.

You'll watch a random Monday Night Football game between two teams you don't care about because you need 11 points from your wide receiver (I'm looking at you, Falcons at Saints in Week 4). You'll spend Sunday afternoon checking your phone to see whether your running back got credit for a reception (c'mon, that wasn't a lateral; he definitely threw it forward!)

You're going to care about these guys.

So, if there's a player you really like, and you want him on your fantasy team, take him.

Maybe it's your favorite player. Maybe you just really want to root for the guy this season. That's good enough for me. Take him.

Does that mean you should take someone with a 10th-round ADP in the third round because you really like him?

Probably not.

But we're talking about fantasy football here, not managing your 401(k) (unless you're in a league where you're playing for the value of someone's 401(k), but again, you're probably not taking advice from me if that's the case).

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

So pick a player a little earlier than ADP if you really want him. Who cares if some fantasy expert has another guy ranked two spots higher?

Do your homework. Understand the room you're drafting in and try not to light value on fire for no reason.

After that, get some players you actually like.

You might even win the league. If you do, don't forget to tell everyone how good you are at fantasy football.

And if you don't, blame injuries and bad luck.

That's what everyone else does.

World.title: Dad of third-grade girl in Massachusetts allegedly barged in on by trans student in bathroom calls for action
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Massachusetts father of a third-grade girl who says his daughter was subjected to a disturbing bathroom incident involving a transgender classmate is not backing down from his fight with the school district.

Luis Rivera, whose daughter attends Rochester Memorial School, has hired attorney Sam Whiting of the Massachusetts Liberty Legal Center after filing a federal Title IX complaint against the Old Rochester Regional School District in May.

A letter filed by Whiting on Rivera’s behalf alleges that Rivera’s 9-year-old daughter was the victim of sex-based harassment after a transgender female classmate, who was born male, entered her bathroom stall. The letter also alleges that the student had previously watched female students use the bathroom, which Rivera and his attorney argue invaded their privacy and undermined their dignity.

Rivera and his wife, Kerri, along with other parents, have repeatedly contacted Rochester Memorial School Principal Heidi Letendre about the transgender student’s use of the girls’ bathroom, according to the letter.

WASHINGTON MOTHER SAYS SHE FOUND ADULT MALE SHOWERING IN WOMEN'S LOCKER ROOM DURING CHILDREN'S SWIM MEET

"On numerous occasions, during this actual event, we reached out multiple times. And we were told by the principal that no boy is supposed to be in the bathroom. Then somewhere along the line, they changed their story," Rivera told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital reached out to Letendre for comment.

Rivera said he has attended every school committee meeting since the incident, joining other community members in pushing the district to change its bathroom policy.

He also said he and his wife have decided to remove their daughter from the school for the upcoming school year. His daughter wrote a letter to President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump asking for help with the situation.

"I feel scared to use the girls' bathroom," she wrote.

WASHINGTON MOTHER PULLS CHILDREN FROM SCHOOL AFTER PRIDE LESSON SHOWN IN MUSIC CLASS WITHOUT NOTICE

The dispute centers not only on the alleged incident involving Rivera’s daughter but also on the district’s interpretation of state and federal anti-discrimination laws, Whiting said.

Massachusetts law prohibits discrimination against students based on protected characteristics, including gender identity, and bars schools from excluding students from "the advantages, privileges and courses of study" they offer.

The Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education also says transgender students should have access to school facilities, including bathrooms, consistent with their gender identity.

For now, however, the Old Rochester Regional School District does not appear to have plans to change its policy regarding transgender students.

In a message to parents, Superintendent Michael Nelson said that, following a Title IX investigation, school staff and district administrators acted in compliance with the law. The decision, he said, was made by an independent decision maker following the complaint brought forward by the Rochester Memorial School parent.

TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS WOKE SCHOOLS ACCUSED OF HIDING STUDENTS' GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

In a written statement, Nelson said the district is bound by the Massachusetts laws.

"Additionally, our schools adhere to the policies and procedures of the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education," he said.

"... We believe that we are bound by law and state education policy and that age-appropriate handling of student matters in a public school setting is best left to the professional educators who know how to do their jobs correctly and effectively," he said.

He also noted that during this process, his educators and administrators have been subject to "innumerable explicit, angry and threatening communications," directly and indirectly through social media.

Fox News Digital reached out directly to Nelson.

Whiting said he and the parents involved are particularly disappointed by the superintendent’s response, which he claims downplayed the seriousness of the incident.

According to Whiting, the response amounted to, "Oh, these things just happen between 9-year-olds… sometimes bathroom doors are unlocked and these things happen."

PORTLAND PARENT BANNED FROM SCHOOL EVENTS AFTER OPPOSING GENDER IDENTITY ASSIGNMENT FILES LAWSUIT

Whiting said he hopes the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights will investigate the complaint.

"Ultimately, we hope they will find that the school district is in violation of Title IX and will refer the case to the Department of Justice for enforcement," he said. "School districts who violate Title IX can be at risk of losing their federal funds… We’re always hopeful they’ll do the right thing, but if they don’t, our plan is to try to get this in front of the proper authorities at the federal level."

Rivera said the lack of what he considers meaningful action from the district has left him with no choice but to escalate the matter.

"They haven’t taken any remedial action. And so that’s why we feel like we have to kind of bring this up to the higher authorities and the federal government," Rivera said. "There’s no transparency. There’s no accountability. It’s just they’re running around free, and they’re violating these girls’ privacy rights, because what happened to my daughter should have never happened if the policies were put into place."

"And I have to deal with her emotional trauma behind this," Rivera added.

World.title: Vance unloads on El-Sayed after Usha swipe with brutal warning: 'Way out of your league'

Vice President JD Vance urged Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed during a rally on Monday to focus on substantive policy issues instead of attacking his wife.

"I actually think that the people of Michigan think it's kind of weird when you talk about another guy's wife," Vance said at a metro Detroit rally organized by MAGA Inc., a super PAC aligned with the president.

"I think the people of Michigan would like you to talk about the public policy ideas …I think the people of Michigan would like you to talk about how you're going to protect auto workers when you're supporting every single policy that has undercut the wages and jobs of Michigan auto workers your entire life in public service."

EL-SAYED UNDER FIRE ONLINE AFTER TAKING AIM AT USHA VANCE, FEMALE TRUMP AIDE IN WEEKEND SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

"But whatever you want to talk about, Abdul, keep my wife's name the hell out of your mouth because she's way out of your league," the vice president added.

Vance's quip was in response to El-Sayed saying "do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no" after the vice president suggested that Sharia law would have been an alien concept to his grandfather.

Critics said the post appeared to take aim at Usha Vance’s Indian heritage. El-Sayed later said his point was that Vance seemed to be suggesting some people are "more American" than others because their families have been in the country longer, noting that Vance’s own in-laws are immigrants.

"If you’re a rural White American living in Michigan, just remember El-Sayed believes you’re a racist," conservative commentator Ryan Girdusky said in response to the Democratic hopeful’s statement.

SECOND LADY USHA VANCE FIRES BACK AT POINTED JAB FROM DEMOCRATIC SENATE NOMINEE ABDUL EL-SAYED

Earlier in his speech, Vance accused El-Sayed of undercutting his support for working people by taking liberal positions on immigration issues.

"We're here to talk about protecting Michigan truck drivers, but also protecting the safety of every single person who drives on the road with a semi truck, which is all of us," Vance said. "Here's the crazy thing. Just a few years ago, Abdul El-Sayed said that we need to make sure that illegal aliens have driver's licenses in this country. He would love to undercut the wages of American truckers."

TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATING 75 TRUCK DRIVER SCHOOLS FOR FRAUD, HELPING NON-CITIZENS GET LICENSES

In 2018, El-Sayed expressed support for allowing illegal immigrants to obtain standard driver's licenses, though he did not specifically push for those in the country illegally to receive the commercial driver's licenses necessary to operate long-haul trucks.

While Vance and El-Sayed differ in their approaches to immigration, the two both agree, in principle, that tariffs should be used to benefit American industry.

World.title: Supreme Court allows Trump to move forward with White House ballroom construction
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday handed a win to President Donald Trump by allowing him to move forward indefinitely with the construction of his new White House ballroom.

The court, divided 5-4, granted an emergency request filed by the Trump administration, blocking lower court rulings that would have put the aboveground portion of the project on hold. This followed an interim decision along similar lines issued by Chief Justice John Roberts on Aug. 21.

The legal challenge was brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which argued that the president did not have unilateral authority to proceed with construction.

In the unsigned ruling, the court said that the trust likely does not have legal standing to bring the underlying lawsuit. The court did not reach any conclusion on whether Trump has authority to carry out construction without congressional approval.

“Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government’s East Wing project. We conclude only that, based on the submissions before us, the government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks ... standing to challenge the project in federal court,” the court said.

Roberts ultimately joined the court’s three liberal justices in dissent.

“Construction of the ballroom has proceeded apace for the better part of a year. That construction is likely unlawful,” Roberts wrote.

Marine One with President Donald Trump passes over construction on the new White House ballroom, Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, seen from the Washington Monument in Washington. Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP

The trust’s claim for standing hinges on a declaration made by member Alison Hoagland, a preservationist who lives in Washington and serves on the organization’s board of trustees.

Hoagland regularly walks by the White House, adding that she would “suffer both professional and personal injuries, including to my aesthetic, cultural and historical interests, if a ballroom of the proposed form and scale were constructed.”

The Supreme Court majority concluded the court had never found legal standing in such a situation before.

“To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury,” the court said.

Roberts said he would have found that Hoagland did have standing, noting that as a historic preservationist, she can be “aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys.”

The administration has said in court filings that construction was 65% complete as of Aug. 24, with a 250-person crew working 20 hours a day, seven days a week. The White House has said the $400 million project will be funded entirely by private donations, an assertion that has been widely disputed. Secret Service funds have already been directed to cover some of the project’s security enhancements.

The overall plan includes an extensive underground component, including secure locations and medical facilities that the administration has argued are needed for security.

A federal judge had ruled in favor of the trust, saying that while the underground construction could move forward, the ballroom itself could not be built while litigation continued.

On Aug. 7, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld that decision.

The trust argued that the government had no authority to build the ballroom under a federal law that requires the “express authority of Congress” to build on federal land in Washington, D.C.

But the Trump administration countered that other provisions of federal law allow the president to undertake improvements on the White House grounds.

World.title: Bootleg ‘Spider-Man’ swings into Russian cinemas despite Hollywood boycott
World.content:
So cinemas illegally obtain digital cinema packages — the standard industry format used to screen films — through third-party distributors and copy them, Aliev said, adding that the owners coordinate a release date among themselves.

Moviegoers buy a ticket to see what is known as a short film under what is known as a “prescreening service,” he said. But while this is what is recorded on the receipt, in reality, “I’ll be watching ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day,’ or ‘Batman,’” Aliev added.

Sony Pictures did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment.

And authorities appear more than willing to look the other way on the screenings, including those of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.”

Russia’s Ministry of Culture did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment on the seeming unwillingness to prosecute cinema owners. But earlier this week, Elena Drapeko, the deputy chair of the culture committee in Russia’s Duma, or parliament, called for law enforcement to act against what she called an “illegal business activity.”

Nonetheless, 18 seconds of the song “Monopoly” by Russian singer Monetochka appears to have been cut out of the copies of the movie being shown in her homeland.

The outspoken critic of the war in Ukraine was labeled a “foreign agent” by Russian authorities in 2023 after leaving the country for Lithuania the previous year. She said in an Instagram post that she “hadn’t expected anything else,” but she found the song’s removal “painful and sad.”

A "Spider-Man" fan meeting at the Kinograd cinema in St. Petersburg this month. Andrei Bok / SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

However, fans dressed in Spider-Man costumes posted videos of themselves with the song playing in the background on social media.

That was only after many were left livid when the movie’s Aug. 6 release date was delayed by three weeks by the distributors of “The Last Warrior: Kolobok,” according to Cinemaplex, a Russian website devoted to the movie industry.

The move prompted a huge online backlash, and authorities were hunting for people who sent death threats on social media to Anton Maslov, the director of the film, which is based on one of the country’s most popular fairy tales, about a piece of bread that comes alive, according to the influential Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti, or “Beware of News” in English.

“It’s a symbolic conflict between a release, heavily funded by the state, about all things Russian, and a major foreign release, heavily funded by a foreign company,” Aliev said, adding that the audience felt “deprived of choice.”

Ordinary moviegoers would have been hit “pretty hard” by the order from above, he said.

Among them, Maria, a mixed-media collage artist from the city of St. Petersburg, who said she watched old “Spider-Man” movies until the new one came out. The delay, she said, was like sitting at a table where “everyone is eating cake” and you are forced to “eat a bowl of crackers” instead.

World.title: The House returns with a short to-do list: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur explains why the House may not be doing much more legislating ahead of the midterms. Plus, Henry J. Gomez digs into Republicans’ anxiety in the Ohio Senate race.

— Adam Wollner

Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.

The House returns with a short to-do list

Analysis by Sahil Kapur

The House reconvened this afternoon after a five-week recess with one main item on the legislative agenda: preventing a government shutdown at the end of September.

As early as tomorrow, House Republican leaders plan to hold a vote on a Senate-passed bill to continue existing funds on autopilot through Dec. 11, buying time for lawmakers to get through the Nov. 3 midterm elections to hammer out a funding deal for the new fiscal year.

It will come up under “suspension of the rules,” meaning it’ll be fast-tracked to the floor and require a two-thirds majority. After the Senate passed it 90-6 in early August, that’s a reasonably safe bet — at least unless President Donald Trump swoops in with last-minute demands.

Beyond that, it’s a thin agenda. And there are no major deadlines or program expirations until after the elections.

There are some resolutions on deck. One would censure Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., as recommended by the Ethics Committee after it found that he “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.” Another two are contempt resolutions regarding witnesses in the investigation of then-Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, D-Fla.

The House is poised to go back on recess next week and return for three weeks starting Sept. 14. But without much to do — and a wafer-thin majority for Republicans — speculation has grown on Capitol Hill that the chamber will depart for two months after this week and return after the elections. Without a doubt, plenty of incumbents would prefer to go home and campaign.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., sidestepped the question when asked this afternoon whether the House is going to return in mid-September.

“You’ve all seen the schedule. That’s what’s on the schedule,” Johnson told reporters on Capitol Hill. “The first thing is we’ve got to make sure the government is funded and we don’t have another Democrat shutdown.”

The House’s schedule has been famously fluid all year. The Senate, meanwhile, is still expected to return Sept. 14 and process presidential nominations and judicial appointments.

Apart from a full-year government funding package, other legislative agenda items like reauthorizing FISA Section 702, the National Defense Authorization Act and finishing a potential Russia-Iran sanctions bill could, in theory, wait till the lame-duck session in November and December.

When Congress has the luxury of waiting, it often does.

When asked about the potential change in schedule, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said: “We’re focused on doing the business of the American people at all times.”

Brennan Leach contributed.

Republican concerns mount as Sen. Jon Husted navigates a tricky race in Ohio

By Henry J. Gomez

MASSILLON, Ohio — When Sen. Jon Husted filed his most recent campaign finance report in July, the Ohio Republican boasted a war chest of more than $6 million. But the cash is not for Husted’s battle with Democrat Sherrod Brown in what is expected to be one of the year’s most expensive Senate races. Rather, it is the remaining balance in an account that Husted established years ago to fund his long-held ambition of being governor.

The fact that the money is parked there is among a list of worries that have cropped up around Husted this summer as he runs to keep the seat he was appointed to after JD Vance won the vice presidency. The National Republican Senatorial Committee, for example, warned this month that the politically fraught issue of data centers for artificial intelligence companies could doom Husted.

Meanwhile, in conversations with NBC News, seven Republicans who are closely following the race and are experienced in Ohio campaigns expressed varying levels of anxiety about the effort that Husted is waging.

These people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly assess the race, pointed in part to a difficult climate for GOP candidates hamstrung by President Donald Trump’s unpopular war with Iran, a related rise in gas prices and broader affordability concerns. They also complained about Husted’s message in response to these challenges and what they view as a struggle to defend himself against attacks.

“He’s been getting thrashed,” a GOP operative working to preserve the party’s Senate majority said of Husted. “And his negatives are spiking.”
