Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Samba do Trabalhador with Moacyr Luz Monday is Rio’s great samba day, and its warmest institution is Samba do Trabalhador. For two decades, Moacyr Luz and friends have played a roots-samba roda every Monday at the Renascença Clube in Andaraí, an all-ages, joyful, unpretentious afternoon-into-evening affair. Doors at 4:30 pm; buy ahead on Sympla, get there early for a good spot, and settle in.

Tonight at a Glance —Samba do Trabalhador · Andaraí Moacyr Luz’s two-decade Monday roda at the Renascença, doors 4:30 pm. —Pedra do Sal · Saúde The flagship free roda in the old port, at its Monday best from around 7 pm. —Choro da Esquina · Flamengo An open choro circle that has kept Monday evenings musical for eleven years, from 7 pm. —CCBB Rio · Centro Open today (it closes Tuesdays), with “Vik Muniz: A Olho Nu”. Free, timed tickets. —Quiet elsewhere: Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, Bip Bip, TribOz and Trapiche Gamboa are all closed on a Monday.

Tonight, Monday 31 August 2026, Rio closes the month on its best-kept secret: Monday is the city’s great samba night. Two institutions carry it — Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador up in Andaraí, and the flagship free roda at the Pedra do Sal in the old port, which is at its biggest and best on a Monday. Add an open choro circle in Flamengo and CCBB in the centre, and the quietest day of the week turns out to be one of the most rewarding.

What’s On Tonight

Samba do Trabalhador — Renascença Clube — Rua Barão de São Francisco 54, Andaraí. Moacyr Luz’s “workers’ samba” has run on Mondays for two decades — a roots-samba roda born for musicians who only had Mondays off, and now one of the most beloved regular events in the city. The house opens at 4:30 pm and the group plays several sets across the late afternoon and evening, to a mixed, devoted, all-ages crowd. Tickets are R$40 (US$8) half-price and R$80 (US$15) full through Sympla — buy ahead, and arrive near the opening for a spot.

The Pedra do Sal, at its Monday best — Largo João da Baiana, Saúde. The free open-air roda on the historic stone steps in the old port — the birthplace of Carioca samba — runs Friday through Monday, and Monday is one of its two biggest nights. Musicians set up at the foot of the hill, the crowd fills the largo, and beer flows from the bars around it, from around 7 pm. Free, cash-based for drinks, and one of the essential Rio experiences.

Choro da Esquina, Flamengo’s open Monday circle — Flamengo. While the samba houses rest, this open choro roda keeps Monday musical: instrumentalists gather in a circle, listeners ring them, and the repertoire runs through the classic choros. Running for eleven years, it plays Mondays from 7 to 10 pm; the week’s corner is announced on Instagram. Free and open — musicians can sit in, listeners just keep their voices low.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Late afternoon (4:30 pm) — Samba do Trabalhador opens in Andaraí, an early, all-evening affair.

Early evening (6–7 pm) — The Vik Muniz show at CCBB before it closes, or dinner near the port.

Main event (7 pm onward) — The Pedra do Sal roda gets going and fills through the evening.

Choro (7 pm) — Choro da Esquina in Flamengo, an open circle in the square.

Getting home — Rideshare door-to-door; Andaraí and the port both quieten quickly once the music stops.

Scenes & Sounds

Roots samba — The night’s heart: Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador, a two-decade Monday institution in Andaraí. Where: Renascença Clube (Andaraí).

Street samba — The free Pedra do Sal roda in the port, at its Monday flagship best. Where: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde.

Choro — Choro da Esquina keeps Mondays musical with its open circle in Flamengo. Where: Flamengo (corner announced weekly on Instagram).

Culture — CCBB is open with the Vik Muniz show; a rare Monday option in the centre. Where: CCBB (Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro).

Closed tonight — Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, Bip Bip, TribOz and Trapiche Gamboa all rest on a Monday and reopen midweek. Where: back from Wednesday (Trapiche Tuesday; Bip Bip’s roda is Tuesday).

Pick Your Night

An institution: Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí — the pick of the night.

Free and essential: The Pedra do Sal roda in the port, at its Monday best.

Choro in the square: Choro da Esquina in Flamengo, from 7 pm — free and open.

Culture first: The Vik Muniz show at CCBB before it closes.

Quiet: Most of Lapa is closed — Monday is a night for the samba, not the strip.

Where to Go

Samba do Trabalhador — Renascença Clube, Andaraí Moacyr Luz’s legendary Monday roda, a two-decade institution of roots samba in a Zona Norte social club, drawing a mixed, devoted crowd. Tonight: Moacyr Luz and the Samba do Trabalhador, several sets across the late afternoon and evening. Doors 4:30 pm. Best time: Get there near the 4:30 pm opening for a spot; it fills up. Cost: R$40 (US$8) half-price, R$80 (US$15) full, via Sympla. Buy ahead. All ages. Address: Rua Barão de São Francisco 54, Andaraí Tickets: sympla.com.br Getting there: Rideshare is easiest to Andaraí, in the Zona Norte. Arrange your ride home too. Good to know: An early, all-evening affair — very different in rhythm from a late Lapa night.

Pedra do Sal — Saúde (Pequena África) The stone steps in the old port where Carioca samba was born — a free, open-air largo with a loose, street-party energy, and its flagship roda on Mondays. Tonight: The Monday roda — open-air samba from around 7 pm into the night. Best time: Monday is the flagship (with Friday); get there early for the atmosphere before the crush. Cost: Free to attend. Drinks from bars and vendors on a cash basis — carry small bills. Address: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde Getting there: VLT to the port, or metro Uruguaiana and a short walk/ride. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Wear comfortable shoes and keep an eye on your belongings in the crowd.

Choro da Esquina — Flamengo An open choro circle that has kept Monday evenings musical in Flamengo for eleven years — instrumentalists of every level sit in, and listeners ring the circle for the classic repertoire. Tonight: The open Monday roda, from 7 pm to around 10 pm. Best time: Arrive near 7 pm to catch the circle at full strength. Cost: Free — an open roda. Bring cash for drinks from the bars nearby. Address: Flamengo — the week’s corner is announced on Instagram. Instagram: @choro_da_esquina_oficial Getting there: Metro Flamengo or Largo do Machado, then a short walk. Rideshare home. Good to know: It is about the music — keep voices low near the circle.

CCBB Rio — Centro The Banco do Brasil’s grand cultural centre in a neoclassical landmark — free, high-quality exhibitions, and open on Mondays. Tonight: “Vik Muniz: A Olho Nu” and other shows. Open until 8 pm; last entry around 7 pm. Best time: Wednesday to Monday, 9 am to 8 pm. Closed Tuesdays. Cost: Free, but reserve timed tickets online in advance. Café on site. Address: Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro Website: ccbb.com.br/rio-de-janeiro Getting there: Metro Uruguaiana or Carioca, short walk. A short ride to the port afterwards. Good to know: A calm early-evening stop before the Pedra do Sal roda nearby.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Andaraí / Zona Norte: A residential northern district, home to the Renascença Clube and Samba do Trabalhador. Rideshare in and out.

Centro / Saúde / Gamboa: The old port and the cradle of samba — the Pedra do Sal is its Monday heart. Alive for the roda, quiet otherwise, so travel by car.

Lapa: Dark on a Monday — Carioca da Gema, Rio Scenarium and the rest all rest. The strip comes back midweek.

Flamengo: Residential South Zone district where Choro da Esquina holds its open Monday circle. Metro Flamengo or Largo do Machado, rideshare home.

Santa Teresa: Bohemian hilltop of cobbled lanes and artist bars. A relaxed early dinner; rideshare up and down.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

A quiet Monday — the big queer parties run Thursday to Sunday, so tonight is low-key. The Samba do Trabalhador and the Pedra do Sal roda are both mixed, welcoming, everyone-together kinds of night.

Everyday-friendly spaces — Tonight’s rodas and the choro circle are relaxed and open to all.

Money & How Paying Works Tickets: Samba do Trabalhador sells through Sympla — R$40 (US$8) half-price, R$80 (US$15) full. Buy ahead. Free at the largo: Pedra do Sal is free to attend; drinks are cash-based from bars and vendors. Carry about R$150 (US$30) in small notes. Choro: Choro da Esquina is a free, open roda — bring cash for drinks from the bars around the square. Tipping: 10% is usually added to the bill as ‘serviço’. Check before adding more.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: MetrôRio runs roughly 5 am to midnight Monday to Saturday. Check the last-train time for your line before you rely on it.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and the safest way home from Andaraí and the port late at night. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

Andaraí: Residential and off the tourist track — rideshare directly to and from the club.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets, and keep it away in the largo crowd. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

The port at night: Lively at the largo, quiet around it — book a car door-to-door rather than walking to find one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Monday such a big samba night in Rio?

Tradition — Monday was historically the musicians’ day off, so the rodas grew up around it. Samba do Trabalhador (the “workers’ samba”) and the Pedra do Sal’s Monday gathering are both institutions, making Monday one of the best samba nights of the week.

Samba do Trabalhador or Pedra do Sal?

Samba do Trabalhador is an earlier, ticketed, seated-ish afternoon-into-evening affair in a Zona Norte club; the Pedra do Sal is a free, open-air, standing street roda in the port that gets going later. They start at different times, so the ambitious can catch some of both.

I’ve just landed at GIG (Galeão) tonight. Where should I go?

If it’s still early, Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí is about a 20–30 minute rideshare from Galeão; later, head to the Pedra do Sal in the port. Take a rideshare door-to-door and carry some cash.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

Not at all. The music does the work and the crowds are welcoming. A smile, a cold beer, and cash for the drinks are all you need.

Sources: Samba do Trabalhador (official), Visit Rio (Pedra do Sal), Choro da Esquina (official), ccbb.com.br

World.title: Honduras in Washington’s Sights: Energy, Gas, AI and Data Centres
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

HONDURAS · INVESTMENT

Key Facts —The visit: Senior US trade official Thomas Hardy spent three days in Honduras and met President Nasry Asfura. —The target list: Washington is looking at energy reform, natural gas, data centres and artificial intelligence. —The promise: Hardy said Honduras can become a regional leader for energy if its power law passes. —The catch: Everything is conditioned on an energy reform that Congress has yet to approve. —Already running: US funds are committed to the interoceanic corridor and the ports of Puerto Cortés and San Lorenzo. —What comes next: The US agency will now study what generation and transmission projects it can fund.

Washington has put Honduras energy, natural gas, artificial intelligence and data centres on its investment map. The message came from Thomas R. Hardy, a senior US trade official, after three days in Tegucigalpa.

Who came to Tegucigalpa, and why it matters

Thomas R. Hardy is deputy director and director of operations at the United States Trade and Development Agency, known as the USTDA. It is the agency that funds the early, risky stages of infrastructure abroad.

Hardy spent three days in Honduras last week. He met President Nasry Asfura at the presidential house and sat down with the energy ministry, the state power company and the private sector.

He also met the governments and banks already circling the country. His talks included Japan, South Korea, Spain, the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and the Central American Bank for Economic Integration.

The political framing was explicit. Hardy said President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio want closer economic cooperation with allies in the hemisphere, and Honduras is one of them.

“A regional leader for energy”

The headline quote belongs to Hardy himself. If the energy law passes, he told El Heraldo, Honduras “can be a regional leader for energy”.

The logic runs through gas. The United States is a leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, and Hardy said his agency has 30 years of experience with gas terminal projects.

The vision is a Honduras that imports US gas, generates power and exports electricity to its neighbours. The agency has done similar work in other countries.

But the condition is the reform. Investors need a stable power market, Hardy said, and that includes a state operator that does not lose money on every megawatt it sells.

That operator is the Empresa Nacional de Energía Eléctrica, the state utility known as the ENEE. Its chronic losses are the core problem the liberalisation bill is meant to fix.

Hardy stressed that Honduras energy reform is what unlocks everything else. New generation, transmission lines and gas pipelines all wait on it.

From power lines to data centres

The interesting part for foreign investors is what comes after the electricity. Hardy linked power directly to manufacturing, artificial intelligence and data centres.

His argument is a chain. Reliable electricity brings industry, and industry-grade electricity brings the digital infrastructure that Central America lacks.

Data centres are famously hungry for power, which is why the Honduras energy question comes first. Nobody builds a server farm behind an unstable grid.

Hardy said his agency will now work out what it can fund. Studies with the ENEE, the ministry and private firms are the next step after his departure.

The corridor that is already funded

Unlike the energy plans, the interoceanic corridor is already moving. The USTDA and the State Department have committed funds to it.

The corridor links Puerto Cortés on the Caribbean with San Lorenzo on the Pacific. Ports, dry docks, roads and possibly rail would move cargo between the two oceans.

The first US investments are going into both ports to measure their capacity. The goal is to know what to buy and build next.

Asfura signed the corridor agreement in Washington in March. Hardy said the president’s growth vision is what brought him back to Honduras now.

Honduras already qualifies for USTDA feasibility studies, technical assistance and pilot projects. The agency’s condition is simple: an environment where US companies want to do business.

What this means for expats and investors

For foreign residents, cheaper and steadier power is the tangible prize. Blackouts and high tariffs have shaped daily life and business costs for years.

For investors, the signal is that Washington is doing early-stage risk work. That is the phase before banks and builders arrive.

The open question is political. The energy bill must pass Congress, and the ENEE’s finances must survive contact with liberalisation.

Watch two dates in practice. The first is the vote on the energy law; the second is the first funded study out of Puerto Cortés or San Lorenzo.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the United States targeting in Honduras? Washington is looking at energy reform, electricity generation and transmission, natural gas, data centres and artificial intelligence. The interoceanic corridor between Puerto Cortés and San Lorenzo is already funded. Who said Honduras can be a regional leader for energy? Thomas R. Hardy, deputy director and operations chief of the US Trade and Development Agency. He made the remark to El Heraldo after a three-day visit and a meeting with President Nasry Asfura. Why is Honduras energy reform essential for investment? Investors need a stable power market where the state utility does not lose money on every megawatt. The ENEE’s losses are the core problem the liberalisation bill is meant to fix. What is the USTDA? The US Trade and Development Agency funds feasibility studies, technical assistance and pilot projects abroad. It takes the early-stage risk so that private companies and lenders can follow. Does Honduras already qualify for US funding? Yes, Hardy said Honduras meets the agency’s conditions. The requirement is an environment where US companies want to invest and do business.

World.title: Fintechs and Digital Banks in Brazil 2026: Market Guide
World.content:
Brazil: Fintech

Key Facts —Nubank. The São Paulo-based digital bank serves 139 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia (Q2 2026), including nearly 118 million in Brazil. It reported net income of US$2.9 billion for 2025 and a record US$1.1 billion in Q2 2026 alone, per its NYSE filings. —Pix. Brazil’s instant-payment system processed 79.8 billion transactions in 2025, moving R$35.4 trillion (about US$6.8 trillion, at the August 31, 2026 rate of R$5.18 per dollar), and has run at roughly 6 billion transactions per month in early 2026, per the Central Bank (BCB). More than 170 million Brazilians — about 80% of the population — use Pix. —Concentration. Brazil’s five largest banks (Itaú, Bradesco, Banco do Brasil, Caixa, Santander) still control roughly 80% of total banking assets, per BCB data. Fintechs have gained share in payments and consumer credit but not in commercial lending. —Open Banking. Phase 4 of Brazil’s Open Banking framework, mandating payment initiation services, took effect in August 2025. As of June 2026, 148 institutions are registered as data transmitters, per BCB’s Open Finance registry. —Credit. Total household credit in Brazil reached R$3.1 trillion (about US$600 billion) in June 2026, with delinquency rates (over 90 days) at 3.4% — down from 4.7% in 2023 but still above the 2019 pre-pandemic level of 2.8%.

Brazil’s fintech sector has produced Latin America’s most successful digital bank and the world’s most widely adopted instant-payment system — but the old banking oligopoly still controls the economy’s commanding heights.

Brazilian consumers have shifted en masse to app-based banking and instant payments. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA)

Nubank: The Benchmark and Its Limits

Nubank’s trajectory from a purple credit card startup in 2013 to a 139-million-customer digital bank listed on the NYSE is the defining story of Brazilian fintech. The company, founded by Colombian-born David Vélez with Brazilian partners Cristina Junqueira and Edward Wible, has been profitable since 2023 and reported net income of US$2.9 billion for 2025 — and a record US$1.1 billion in Q2 2026 alone, its first billion-dollar quarter. In August 2026 it launched its full bank in Mexico, where it already has 16 million customers, and is adding a full banking license to its Brazilian operation.

The business model is straightforward: acquire customers cheaply through digital marketing, cross-sell credit cards and personal loans, and monetize float on deposits. Nubank’s customer acquisition cost is estimated at US$5–8 per account, compared to US$30–50 for traditional banks opening branches. The key metric is engagement: Nubank reports a monthly activity rate of 83.5% — and over 86% in Brazil — a figure that drives cross-selling efficiency.

The limits are equally real. Nubank’s loan book is heavily concentrated in unsecured consumer credit — credit cards and personal loans. Its 90-day non-performing loan ratio was 6.9% in Q2 2026, up from 6.5% in the previous quarter and above the industry average — a level the company says reflects its deliberate expansion into riskier credit segments. The bank has been more cautious than some competitors in expanding into mortgage lending or small-business credit, segments that require more capital and longer-dated risk assessment.

Pix: The Public Infrastructure That Changed Everything

If Nubank is the headline, Pix is the infrastructure. Launched by the Central Bank in November 2020, Brazil’s instant-payment system allows real-time transfers between any registered account — bank, fintech, or payment institution — 24 hours a day, with no fees for individuals. The adoption curve has been steeper than any financial innovation in Brazilian history.

In 2025, Pix processed 79.8 billion transactions with a total value of R$35.4 trillion (about US$6.8 trillion), according to BCB data — growth of 26% in transaction count and 34% in value over 2024 — and the system has continued to run at roughly 6 billion transactions a month in early 2026. More than 170 million individuals, about 80% of Brazil’s population, are registered Pix users, and the system has largely displaced cash for small transactions in urban areas.

The impact on fintechs has been mixed. On one hand, Pix leveled the playing field: a customer of a small digital wallet can pay a Nubank user instantly, removing one of the traditional banks’ advantages in interbank transfers. On the other hand, Pix commoditized payments. Fintechs can no longer charge for P2P transfers, and merchant fees on Pix average a fraction of the 1.5–2.5% charged on credit card transactions. The winners are merchants and consumers; the losers are payment processors whose revenue depended on transfer fees.

The B3 stock exchange in São Paulo. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY)

The Oligopoly: Why Traditional Banks Still Win

Despite the fintech buzz, Brazil’s banking sector remains extraordinarily concentrated. The five largest institutions — Itaú Unibanco, Bradesco, Banco do Brasil, Caixa Econômica Federal, and Santander Brasil — still control roughly 80% of total banking assets, per BCB data. That concentration has declined only marginally in recent years, despite the fintech boom.

The reason is structural. Large corporates and high-net-worth individuals — the most profitable segments — still prefer traditional banks for complex lending, treasury services, and international operations. Itaú’s wholesale banking division alone generates tens of billions of reais in annual revenue. Mortgages, which represent the largest household liability class, are dominated by Caixa Econômica Federal, a state-owned bank that holds the majority of the housing finance market through the SFH system.

The traditional banks have also fought back digitally: Itaú, Bradesco, and Banco do Brasil each claim tens of millions of active app users. These are not startups experimenting with product-market fit — they are incumbent institutions with existing balance sheets, regulatory relationships, and corporate client networks that fintechs cannot easily replicate.

Open Banking and the Regulatory Shift

The Central Bank’s Open Banking initiative, launched in 2021 and rebranded as “Open Finance,” is the most consequential regulatory change in Brazilian retail banking since the Plano Real. The framework requires financial institutions to share customer data (with consent) and to allow third-party providers to initiate payments and offer credit products using bank infrastructure.

Phase 4, which mandated payment initiation services, took effect in August 2025. As of June 2026, 148 institutions are registered as data transmitters in the BCB’s Open Finance registry, including all major banks and most large fintechs. The practical effect is that a Nubank customer can now view their Bradesco account balance inside the Nubank app, and a small fintech can initiate a payment from a customer’s Itaú account without the customer leaving the fintech’s interface.

The long-term goal, according to the Central Bank, is to transform banking from a relationship-based model to a data-based model. The risk is data concentration: the largest fintechs, with the most users and the best algorithms, could end up with more customer insight than the banks themselves. Regulatory attention has already shifted to data privacy and algorithmic discrimination, with the National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) issuing guidelines in March 2026 that restrict how fintechs can use shared credit data.

Credit, Delinquency, and the Consumer Debt Cycle

Brazil’s household credit market is both large and expensive. Total outstanding credit reached R$3.1 trillion (about US$600 billion) in June 2026, equivalent to roughly 48% of GDP. The average interest rate on non-directed consumer credit was 32.6% per year in July 2026, according to BCB’s monthly credit survey. Directed credit — subsidized mortgages and agribusiness loans — carries lower rates (8–10%) but is restricted to specific purposes and borrower profiles.

Fintechs have expanded access to credit for borrowers previously excluded by traditional banks’ risk models. The trade-off is price: fintech personal loans typically charge 4–8% per month (60–150% annualized), well above bank rates. The justification is that fintechs serve a riskier population — gig workers, informal entrepreneurs, and young adults without credit history — that traditional banks refuse to lend to at any price.

Delinquency rates have stabilized but remain elevated. The 90-day non-performing loan ratio was 3.4% in June 2026, down from a post-pandemic peak of 4.7% in 2023 but above the 2.8% recorded in 2019. Fintech portfolios show higher delinquency than traditional banks: Nu Holdings reported a 6.9% 90-day NPL ratio in Q2 2026, and Inter and C6 Bank have also run above-industry-average delinquency, per their disclosures. Whether these rates are sustainable depends on Brazil’s employment trajectory and the Central Bank’s monetary policy cycle. With the Selic rate at 14.0% in August 2026 — after four consecutive cuts from the 15% peak reached in 2025 — borrowing costs are easing, but they remain high by international standards.

What Comes Next for Brazil’s Fintech Market

For a foreign reader, Brazil’s fintech landscape offers two lessons. First, regulatory infrastructure matters more than startup culture: Pix succeeded because the Central Bank mandated interoperability and subsidized the infrastructure. Second, market share in payments does not translate automatically to profitability in lending: Nubank’s path to profit required years of scale-building and careful risk selection.

The next phase of competition will focus on three areas: small-business banking, where fintechs like Stone and Mercado Pago are challenging Itaú and Bradesco; wealth management, where digital brokers such as XP and Avenue are democratizing access to US equities; and embedded finance, where non-financial platforms (delivery apps, ride-hailing, e-commerce) are integrating lending and insurance into their core products.

The oligopoly is not dead — Itaú and Bradesco will remain dominant in corporate and high-net-worth banking for years. But the retail battlefield has shifted. The Brazilian consumer now expects free instant payments, a fully digital account opening process, and credit decisions in minutes rather than days. That expectation, more than any single company’s market share, is the lasting legacy of the fintech wave.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Pix and how does it work?

Pix is Brazil’s instant-payment system operated by the Central Bank. It allows real-time, fee-free transfers between any registered accounts 24/7 using a phone number, email, or QR code. It processed 79.8 billion transactions in 2025 and roughly 6 billion per month in early 2026.

Is Nubank profitable?

Yes. Nubank has been profitable since 2023, reported net income of US$2.9 billion for 2025, and earned a record US$1.1 billion in Q2 2026. It serves 139 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia.

Do traditional Brazilian banks still dominate?

Yes. The five largest banks (Itaú, Bradesco, Banco do Brasil, Caixa, Santander) control roughly 80% of total banking assets. Fintechs have gained ground in payments and consumer credit but not in commercial lending or mortgages.

World.title: Costa Rica Expansion and Rebuild of the Limón Airport
World.content:
Costa Rica plans to invest about $40 million to rebuild and expand Limón Airport, with the long-term goal of bringing international flights directly to the Caribbean. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) said the project will include a new passenger terminal, improvements to the runway and additional facilities needed to handle larger commercial aircraft.

The government hopes the upgraded airport could eventually receive nonstop flights from cities such as Miami and Mexico City. However, no airline has announced plans to operate either route. The first stage calls for construction of a new terminal in a different part of the airport. The existing building is vulnerable to flooding during heavy rain, one of several problems that have limited the airport’s growth.

Other planned work includes fire and security facilities, fuel infrastructure, improved access roads, parking and protection from the nearby sea. The government also plans to build a separate parking area for private and commercial aircraft. A later phase would repair and extend the runway by about 600 meters, or nearly 2,000 feet. Officials say the longer runway would allow the airport to receive smaller international passenger jets.

The airport currently has a short runway and limited facilities. Although it is officially classified as an international airport, it mainly serves small domestic and regional aircraft. Most travelers visiting Puerto Viejo, Cahuita, Tortuguero and other Caribbean destinations arrive through Juan Santamaría International Airport near San José but they must then travel several hours by road or take a domestic flight.

Direct international service to Limón could shorten those trips and help bring more visitors and investment to Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast. It could also benefit hotels, tour companies, restaurants and transportation businesses across the province. Still, rebuilding an airport does not guarantee that airlines will use it. Carriers normally consider passenger demand, operating costs, immigration and customs services, aircraft requirements and the profitability of a route before beginning service.

MOPT Minister Efraím Zeledón said the government wants the airport to accommodate narrow-body commercial aircraft. He mentioned Miami and Mexico City as examples of destinations that could become possible after the improvements. No U.S. or Mexican airline has announced Limón service, and the government has not identified any carrier currently negotiating a route.

Once the state completes the initial improvements, officials are considering offering Limón Airport to a private operator as part of the same contract as Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia. Liberia’s airport already operates under a private concession and receives scheduled flights from the United States, Canada and other international markets. Its current concession expires in 2030.

By combining Liberia and Limón in one contract, the government believes it could make the smaller Caribbean airport more attractive to private investors. No possible operator has been named and the latest government estimate says bidding for parts of the Limón project could begin in 2027 but that does not necessarily mean major construction will begin that year.

Earlier this year, officials said the main expansion might not start until 2029 because technical studies and a final airport master plan were still needed. Studies of tides, waves and wind have since been completed, but the government has not released a firm construction schedule.

The airport project forms part of a larger plan to increase investment in Limón. The government is also supporting a proposed marina and cruise terminal that could bring hotels, shops, restaurants and other tourism businesses to the city’s waterfront. For now, you should not expect any immediate changes. The airport still needs detailed designs, bidding, construction and airline commitments before international passenger service can become a reality.

World.title: Costa Rica’s OIJ Invests in Israeli Technology to Unlock Seized Phones
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) is investing heavily in technology capable of unlocking and getting information from cellphones seized during criminal investigations, as police increasingly confront cases in which critical evidence is stored behind passwords and encryption.

The agency has purchased Cellebrite Inseyets, an Israeli-developed digital forensics system used by law enforcement agencies to access and analyze data from mobile devices. Public procurement records show that the OIJ made two purchases related to the technology in September 2025 totaling nearly $700,000. Another contract worth $382,700 was being processed in August 2026.

The purchases include software licenses as well as powerful computers, storage systems and equipment used to connect different phones and SIM cards. For investigators, the basic purpose is straightforward: when police legally seize a cellphone as evidence, the technology can help them get past a locked screen and recover information stored inside.

That can include messages, photographs, videos, application data and other information that could become evidence in a criminal case. The technology is particularly important as organized crime becomes more dependent on smartphones, encrypted messaging services and other digital tools. Drug trafficking groups, fraud networks, kidnapping cases and other investigations can all involve phones containing information that investigators otherwise may struggle to access.

Cellebrite says its Inseyets software can work with both Android and Apple devices and can extract information from encrypted phones. The company markets the technology specifically for digital forensic investigations. However, OIJ’s system is different from spyware that can secretly infect someone’s cellphone from a distance.

That distinction is worth noting because Cellebrite is an Israeli company, and Israel is also home to NSO Group, maker of the controversial Pegasus spyware that has been used in several countries to secretly monitor journalists, political opponents and other targets. Pegasus can be installed remotely and used to collect information from a phone without physically possessing the device.

The Cellebrite system purchased by the OIJ works differently. Investigators must already have the cellphone in their possession. According to information reviewed about the OIJ purchases, the extraction takes place locally at Judicial Branch facilities. Access to the information also requires judicial authorization.

That means the technology is intended to operate as part of a criminal investigation rather than as a system for remotely monitoring people’s phones. Once police seize a phone, it also becomes part of the formal chain of custody used for criminal evidence. Investigators must document how the device and the information extracted from it are handled so prosecutors can later use that evidence in court.

The procurement documents show that the system includes computers with 128 gigabytes of memory and a central server capable of storing 264 terabytes of information. That computing power can help investigators try different methods of getting through passwords and process the large amounts of information now routinely found on smartphones.

Costa Rica’s Ministry of Public Security has used other Cellebrite technology for years. The ministry purchased its first UFED forensic equipment in 2018 and has since paid for licenses and updates. The newer OIJ investment significantly expands the Judicial Police’s own ability to examine seized devices.

The spending also comes at a time when the OIJ has warned repeatedly that budget limitations are affecting its ability to fight organized crime. The Judicial Branch said in July that government budget reductions could affect investigations, technology upgrades and other police operations.

That makes the investment notable as while investigators face pressure to stretch their resources, cellphones have become one of the most important sources of evidence in modern criminal cases. A suspect may delete a message, lock a device or refuse to provide a password, but investigators increasingly have technology designed to retrieve information that once might have remained inaccessible.

For the OIJ, the challenge is now to use those tools while maintaining the court oversight and evidence safeguards required under Costa Rican law.

World.title: Lagoon Operator Says German Consul Was Swimming When He Drowned
World.content:
The association that runs the recreation center where Germany’s consul in Costa Rica died on Saturday has disputed the account that circulated internationally in the hours afterward, saying Mario Genz was swimming in the lagoon rather than riding in a kayak. The Asociación de Desarrollo Integral de Río Cuarto, which administers the Centro Recreativo La Laguna, issued a statement to correct what it described as versions circulating in the media and on social networks.

It said Genz was engaged in a swimming activity in the lagoon at the moment the emergency occurred, and that he was a certified diver and a frequent visitor to the Laguna de Río Cuarto, where he regularly swam and dived. The association said that once staff became aware of the emergency, they acted immediately, removing him from the water and activating the site’s emergency response protocol.

It stressed that the medical causes and circumstances of the death must be determined exclusively by the competent authorities and asked for restraint regarding speculation circulating about the case. Out of respect for his family and for German diplomatic authorities in Costa Rica, it said it would not comment further. Much of the international coverage on Saturday and Sunday reported that Genz died after a kayak he was navigating overturned.

The Fire Department has not described a kayak. It said it received an alert to rescue a submerged 53-year-old adult at the site, and that Genz had been underwater for at least 30 minutes. Crews from the Fire Department and the Costa Rican Red Cross found him without vital signs and brought him out near the center’s dock, where they carried out basic and advanced resuscitation. He was declared dead at the scene.

Emergency services received the alert in the early afternoon. The Red Cross sent three ambulances and a first-response vehicle. Authorities have opened an investigation to establish the cause of death. No findings have been released. Costa Rica’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the death publicly on Saturday, offering condolences to Genz’s family and to his colleagues at the German Embassy and Consulate in San José, and saying it would provide the necessary support in coordination with Germany’s Federal Foreign Office and the embassy.

Genz was 53 and originally from Mannheim, in southwestern Germany. His diplomatic career took him to Florida, where he served as vice consul in the mid-2000s, and to Colombia, where he worked as cultural and press attaché before his posting to San José. He was a serious athlete. The German Embassy in Costa Rica noted publicly that he had won gold in the 5,000 meters in the 50-and-over category at Costa Rica’s national Masters track and field championship, and described him as someone who enjoyed diving, consular casework and time with his two children.

He posted footage of a diving expedition to Isla del Coco and images from a cycling competition on publicly accessible social media accounts. His wife, Isabell Genz, also serves as a consul at the German Embassy. The embassy has described the arrangement publicly as a job share, with each holding the post at 50 percent.

The Centro Recreativo La Laguna sits on the shore of the Laguna de Río Cuarto in the northern part of Alajuela province, roughly 75 kilometers (47 miles) north of San José. The lagoon draws families and day visitors for swimming, kayaking and diving, and is one of the better-known outdoor destinations in the region.

Costa Rica records a significant share of its drownings each year in open water without lifeguards on duty. Experience in the water is not a reliable protection against it, and the country’s water rescue services have long noted that strong swimmers and trained divers appear regularly among the dead.

World.title: Argentina’s Navone Hands Djokovic His Earliest Grand Slam Exit in 20 Years
World.content:
Novak Djokovic’s bid for a record 25th Grand Slam title ended almost as soon as it began Sunday night, with Argentina’s Mariano Navone pulling off the biggest win of his career in the first round of the US Open. Navone, ranked No. 49 in the world, defeated the fourth-seeded Djokovic 7-6(5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 in a four-hour, 36-minute battle inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The result was historic. Djokovic had never lost in the first round in 20 appearances at the US Open, and he had not been beaten in the opening round of any Grand Slam tournament since the 2006 Australian Open.For much of the night, it appeared the 39-year-old Serbian might escape.

Navone won a tight opening set in a tiebreak before Djokovic fought back to take the next two. Djokovic then broke serve early in the fourth set to take a 2-1 lead and appeared to be moving toward the second round. Instead, the match changed dramatically.

Djokovic had been struggling physically throughout the night and his condition worsened as the match stretched past three hours. He vomited during the match and later said he was dealing with cramping as well as pain in his back and shoulder. Navone immediately broke back in the fourth set and began taking control. The 25-year-old Argentine won five of the next six games to force a deciding set, while Djokovic’s movement and energy continued to fade.

The fifth set quickly became one-sided. Navone broke Djokovic repeatedly and closed out the biggest upset of the opening day with a 6-1 final set.Djokovic finished with 70 unforced errors and converted only four of his 12 break-point opportunities. Navone converted six of 17. Afterward, Djokovic acknowledged that the physical problems were not limited to Sunday night. He said he has been dealing with vomiting and other issues during matches throughout the year and that his body eventually begins to break down.

“I’m trying, man. I’m trying,” Djokovic said when asked whether the problem could be fixed.The defeat continued a troubling North American hard-court stretch for Djokovic. He also lost his opening match at the Cincinnati Open earlier in August, falling to another Argentine, Thiago Agustin Tirante.

New York appeared to offer Djokovic a chance to reset. He entered as the No. 4 seed and was chasing the one major milestone still hanging over his career: a 25th Grand Slam singles championship. Instead, his tournament lasted one match. Djokovic remains tied with Margaret Court at 24 major singles titles and will now have to wait until at least the 2027 Australian Open for another opportunity to reach 25. For Navone, the night represented the opposite end of the tennis spectrum.

The Argentine arrived in New York better known for his results on clay than hard courts. He entered the match with one ATP Tour title and only two previous US Open victories. Facing one of the most successful players in tennis history under the lights at Arthur Ashe Stadium, he refused to go away even after Djokovic took control in the middle of the match.

“It is a dream come true,” Navone said after the victory. Navone now moves into the second round, where he will face the winner of the match between three-time Grand Slam champion Stan Wawrinka and Matteo Berrettini. Djokovic, meanwhile, leaves New York after the earliest Grand Slam exit of his career in two decades and with renewed questions about whether his body can continue to withstand the demands of five-set tennis.

World.title: Flash Flood Sweeps Away Guide and Hiker in Pérez Zeledón
World.content:
Update, August 31: The excursion guide swept away in this incident was found dead Sunday evening. The Red Cross confirmed he was the only person reported missing, and everyone else in the group was brought out.

A sudden surge of water swept two people down a river in Barú de Pérez Zeledón on Sunday afternoon, and about 40 others who were crossing with them were brought out over the following hours. The Costa Rican Red Cross said the group was in the middle of a guided excursion when rain upstream sent a cabeza de agua — a wall of water that arrives without warning — down the channel. Two members of the group were carried away. One of them was the excursion’s guide.

The rest of the group was split by the surge. Some were stranded on the far bank with no safe way back across. “The group is divided and several people remain on the other side of the river, unable to leave the site given current conditions,” the Red Cross said.

Two basic life support units are working the scene. The Red Cross has also sent a first-response unit from its National Emergency Response Directorate, along with specialists from its urban search and rescue team and its water rescue team. As of mid-afternoon, neither the condition of the two people swept away nor the status of those still stranded had been confirmed.

What a cabeza de agua actually does

If you are near a river anywhere on the South Pacific slope this afternoon, this is the thing to understand: the water that kills you falls somewhere you cannot see. A cabeza de agua forms when heavy rain lands high in a watershed and funnels into a narrow channel. It travels downstream as a single front.

The sky above you can be bright and the river can be ankle-deep, and the surge still arrives — often in under a minute, and often carrying rock and timber. That is why river levels are the wrong thing to check. What matters is what the clouds are doing in the mountains behind you, and Costa Rica’s terrain means those mountains are frequently out of sight.

Do not cross a river that is rising, or that has turned brown, or that has started to carry debris. If you hear a low rumble from upstream, move away from the channel and uphill immediately rather than trying to finish the crossing. Once a surge is visible it is already too late to outrun it.

The involvement of a professional guide here matters. Guides in this corridor cross these rivers routinely and know the conditions better than any visitor will. When a surge takes the guide, it is a signal that the water moved beyond what experience could read.

Today’s forecast pointed straight at this

The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) forecast strong afternoon downpours with thunderstorms across the Central and South Pacific on Sunday, with the possibility of those conditions running into the early evening. Tropical wave 38 left the country on Saturday, but the instability behind it did not. Morning trade winds kept pushing moisture toward the Caribbean and the Northern Zone, and the IMN warned the atmosphere over the country remained unsettled.

The National Emergency Commission (CNE) has kept its alerts in force. Soils across the Northern Zone and the Caribbean are still saturated after weeks of rain, which means smaller amounts of rainfall now run straight off the ground instead of soaking in. Nine cantons remain under the national emergency decree signed on August 20.

Not the first time

Barú is a district of about 2,400 residents spread across 191 square kilometers (74 square miles) on the Pacific side of Pérez Zeledón. It is also the district that contains Nauyaca Falls, one of the most visited waterfalls in the southern zone. In June, a 30-year-old American visitor, Ashley Phillips, was swept away by a cabeza de agua at Nauyaca. The Red Cross recovered her body 11 days later, roughly 600 meters (1,970 feet) from where she disappeared.

The corridor between Dominical, Uvita and Barú draws heavy visitor traffic during the green season, and its rivers drain steep ground that receives far more rain than the coast below. Anyone booked on a river hike, canyoning trip or waterfall tour in the southern Pacific over the coming days should confirm with the operator that conditions have been checked that morning and should treat a cancellation as the system working rather than as an inconvenience.

This story is developing and will be updated.

World.title: Woman accuses Minister Gilroy Usher of cutting down fence in land dispute; Home Affairs issues warning on land disputes
World.content:
Woman accuses Minister Gilroy Usher of cutting down fence in land dispute; Home Affairs issues warning on land disputes

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City woman is accusing Minister of State in the Ministry of Public Utilities, Energy and Logistics, Gilroy Usher, of entering property she claims belongs to her and cutting down a portion of her chain-link fence amid an ongoing land dispute.

The woman, identified on Facebook as, Jamie Maximo documented the incident during a Facebook Live on Saturday, August 29, repeatedly identifying Usher as she filmed what was unfolding at the property. Maximo said she has documents for the land and has lived and developed the property for approximately 17 years.

In the video, Maximo accused Usher of trespassing and damaging her property and called for police and the media to respond to the scene.

Maximo further alleges that an attempt is being made to divide her lot and transfer a portion of the land to another individual whom she claims is associated with the Usher family. BBN has not independently verified the ownership documents, survey boundaries or the alleged intended transfer of the parcel as yet.

In a subsequent Facebook Live, Maximo also filmed Usher’s son, former police officer Darrel “Tutsi” Usher, visiting the property as the dispute continued. Maximo again maintained that the land belonged to her and questioned why the area she had developed was being targeted for subdivision.

The Ministry of Home Affairs has since released a public service message on the proper legal procedure for dealing with land disputes, fence boundaries and alleged encroachments. While the message did not specifically name Maximo or Usher, it comes in the immediate aftermath of the highly publicized incident.

The Ministry said parties alleging encroachment should first hire a licensed surveyor and, where the findings are disputed, make an application to the Land Registry for the Registrar of Lands to formally determine the legal boundary. If a party subsequently refuses to comply, the property owner may seek a court order regarding trespass, removal of the fence and possible damages.

The message concludes: “Belize is a country of order and discipline. Know the Law. Follow the Law. Nobody is above the law.”

World.title: International News: US-Iran attacks send oil prices higher as conflict escalates
World.content:
International News: US-Iran attacks send oil prices higher as conflict escalates

By Zoila Palma: The United States and Iran have exchanged attacks for the first time in more than a month, raising fears that the conflict could intensify after weeks of relative military calm.

The US said it struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island after observing Iranian forces preparing to deploy sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz, a key global shipping route.

Iran said it responded by launching missiles toward US military targets in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, CNN reports.

The attacks pushed global oil prices nearly 3% higher as tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz intensified. Jordan said its air defenses intercepted eight missiles, while the UAE reported detecting a drone over its territorial waters and condemned the developments as a dangerous escalation.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country was not seeking war but would respond to aggression. Iran’s military also warned neighboring countries against allowing their territory or airspace to be used for US military operations.

The latest exchange comes as diplomatic efforts remain stalled, although Iran and Oman continue discussions on restoring maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Toledo Institute for Development and Environment participates in Belize’s Climate Change and Carbon Market Policy workshop
World.content:
Toledo Institute for Development and Environment participates in Belize’s Climate Change and Carbon Market Policy workshop

By Zoila Palma: Recently, Toledo Institute for Development and Environment (TIDE) participated in the ongoing development and refinement of Belize’s Climate Change and Carbon Market Policy, in Belmopan.

The workshop brought together key stakeholders to review and validate the draft policy and its six annexes.

TIDE contributed to important discussions on blue carbon, environmental safeguards, sustainable development, and benefit-sharing, helping to keep conservation, communities, and biodiversity at the forefront of Belize’s evolving climate and carbon market framework.

TIDE says that it remains committed to sharing its conservation and community-based experience to support the development of effective and inclusive climate solutions in Belize.

“Through continued collaboration, we support solutions that strengthen climate resilience, safeguard Belize’s natural resources, and deliver meaningful benefits for communities and biodiversity,” TIDE expressed.

World.title: Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry celebrates 30 years of Expo Belize Marketplace
World.content:
Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry celebrates 30 years of Expo Belize Marketplace

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI) is celebrating 30 years of Expo Belize Marketplace, Belize’s premier business and trade exposition.

The 2026 edition will bring businesses from across the country together for two days of shopping, networking, product showcases, food, entertainment and family-friendly activities.

Expo Belize Marketplace 2026 will be held on September 12 and 13 at the Marion Jones Sports Complex in Belize City, from 10:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.

The BCCI is inviting the public to join in celebrating three decades of promoting Belizean businesses and entrepreneurship.

World.title: Belize advances Electronic Single window for trade initiative
World.content:
Belize advances Electronic Single window for trade initiative

Belize has achieved a significant milestone in the implementation of its Electronic Single Window for Trade (ESW) with the successful completion of an intensive four-day Knowledge Exchange Mission with the Jamaica Customs Agency (JCA). This initiative, undertaken under the Trade and Investment Facilitation Program, a loan program for the Government of Belize financed by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and executed through the Central Executing Unit of the Ministry of Finance, focused on acquiring practical, first-hand insights from Jamaica’s established Single Window for Trade (JSWIFT) system to inform and accelerate Belize’s own digital trade transformation.

The Belize delegation comprised members of the Electronic Single Window (ESW) Project Technical Team, representing the Directorate General for Foreign Trade (DGFT), the Belize Customs and Excise Department, the Belize Agricultural Health Authority (BAHA), the Central Information Technology Office (CITO), and the Ministry of Finance. Belize’s ESW Technical Team serves as the inter-agency working body responsible for reviewing and validating business processes and requirements and supporting business process re-engineering, testing, and implementation.

The Belize ESW for Trade forms part of the Government’s broader efforts to modernize and digitalize trade and border processes, improve government efficiency, facilitate legitimate trade, and strengthen Belize’s competitiveness through greater coordination among agencies involved in import, export, and other trade-related procedures. This coordinated effort also involves the Belize Fisheries Department, the Ministry of Health (Pharmaceutical Division), and the Supplies Control Unit, all of which are working to improve processes and advance a seamless trade facilitation agenda.

World.title: Allan Pollard: “Regular Belizeans gave what they could to support me”
World.content:
Allan Pollard: “Regular Belizeans gave what they could to support me”

By Zoila Palma: Allan Pollard has expressed gratitude to the hundreds of delegates and supporters who stood behind his candidacy in the People’s United Party’s (PUP) Belize City mayoral race, saying the support he received from ordinary Belizeans made the campaign particularly meaningful.

Pollard thanked the 341 delegates who voted for him, describing the contest as “the hardest” campaign he has faced. He said the support he received from across the country helped him remain committed despite the challenges he encountered along the way.

Pollard placed particular emphasis on the backing he received from everyday Belizeans, stating, “ordinary people stood up for me.”

He said that despite the significant resources involved in the campaign, supporters contributed what they could because they believed in his leadership and the cause behind his candidacy.

“Some made personal sacrifices because they believed in me and believed in what we were trying to accomplish,” he said.

He also thanked the three of the party’s ten Area Representatives who supported his candidacy, praising their courage and saying, “Your courage will not be forgotten.”

“I believe I have contributed greatly to the success of this Party over the years,” while acknowledging that recent decisions he made would have consequences.

Pollard said he remains at peace with the choices he made during what he described as a difficult period.

World.title: Allan Pollard to PUP: “Message received”
World.content:
Allan Pollard to PUP: “Message received”

By Zoila Palma: Today, Allan Pollard conceded defeat in the People’s United Party’s (PUP) Belize City mayoral race, thanking the 341 delegates who supported his candidacy and saying the experience was among the most difficult campaigns he has faced.

Pollard said, “Firstly, I would like to thank the 341 delegates who, despite all the odds, believed in my leadership and came out to vote for me.”

He also thanked those who supported him throughout the campaign, saying, “That love kept me going when things became increasingly difficult by the day.”

Pollard said he faced significant challenges during the campaign, alleging that he was “defamed, degraded and attacked in ways that only God knows how I managed to endure.”

Despite those challenges, he said he was encouraged by ordinary Belizeans who stood behind his campaign, noting, “ordinary people stood up for me.”

He added, “Some made personal sacrifices because they believed in me and believed in what we were trying to accomplish.”

Pollard said he believes he made difficult decisions based on what he considered best for the country and would make those choices again.

“I believe I have contributed greatly to the success of this Party over the years. But I also knew that some of the decisions I made recently would come with repercussions.

The good thing is that I can sit here today and live with myself, knowing that when the difficult decisions came, I did what I believed was best for the people of this country,” Pollard said.

He thanked the PUP for the opportunity to serve and called for reflection within the party, delivering a pointed message: “To the party, I say: message received.”

Pollard ended by thanking his family, friends and campaign team and said that, for now, his family, business and the remainder of his term will be his primary focus, while “the development of my country will always remain my greatest purpose.”

World.title: Rental vehicle taken and never returned!
World.content:
Rental vehicle taken and never returned!

By Zoila Palma: Police are seeking the public’s assistance in locating a red 2015 Chevrolet Equinox, license plate CYC-50188, which was rented in Camalote Village, Cayo District, but has not been returned.

The vehicle was reportedly due to be returned on August 28, 2026.

According to reports, the person who rented it allegedly used a stolen identification card to obtain the vehicle and has since failed to return it.

Anyone who sees the vehicle or has information about its whereabouts is asked to contact Crime Stoppers at 922, use the P3 Tips app, report to the nearest police station, or call 624-7776.

World.title: Crackdown on care
World.content:
TUFTON...people must play their part...or they make way for someone else to do itPhoto: Garfield Robinson

SPURRED by more than 1,000 patient complaints in the Ministry of Health and Wellness’s Client Care Connect report, portfolio Minister Dr Christopher Tufton says efforts to expose system failures and hold negligent medical professionals accountable will intensify.

The move comes as the ministry prepares to publish its accountability data in September, which Tufton says highlighted various client complaints of poor communication, professional conduct, and overall patient experience.

“We’re looking to transform the health workforce. We are taking an inward look, recognising that a highly qualified health system cannot exist without sound governance, and that transformation requires effective leadership, which will be essential to managing the critical components of health.

“So when we speak about an accountability framework, it’s about delivering service with compassion, with empathy and, of course, ensuring that every patient is treated with dignity, respect, and fairness at every point of care,” said the minister as he delivered the keynote address at the Barry Wint Memorial Scholarship Awards Ceremony at S Hotel Kingston in St Andrew last Friday.

According to him, the report’s data aims to isolate departments and individuals responsible for poor patient experiences rather than allowing the failures of some to tarnish the reputation of the wider health-care system.

“Where there is a problem, we need to identify the institution, the department, and who is in charge. You have to start with all the names, because you can’t allow one bad apple to spoil the whole lot…Tell me where the worst experience takes place, the bad experience; tell me which department, and tell me who is in charge.

“And what leadership ought now to do is to address the specifics of a problem. Stop generalising the problem, because we’re letting down people who make sacrifices every day to do the work, and that’s a new modus operandi…People must play their part, and we must emphasise and insist on it, or they make way for someone else to do it,” charged Tufton.

The minister’s push for greater accountability comes amid heightened public scrutiny of the health-care system after the death of 33-year-old Kenise Dunn gained widespread media traction. The eight-month pregnant mother of three passed away at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital five days post-delivery.

When asked if his call for accountability extended to the contentious incident, Tufton told the Jamaica Observer that he cannot comment conclusively while the investigation is ongoing. Still, he emphasised that health-care professionals are always bound by a duty of care. “What I’ve heard, preliminary, is that, clinically, there was a diagnosis of the problem, but it appears, based on some of the feedback — including from persons who are on the ward — that maybe the management of the customer care and the empathy to the patient may have been less than desired. Now, I don’t have the final report, so I prefer not to conclude on that,” he said. “But the truth is drawn from what I said about the complaints report, the 1,000, which I spoke to, it’s quite clear that while we have excellent health workers, we have to work harder at delivering service with compassion and with empathy. And it’s not good enough to just have technical competence. If you treat people badly, if you don’t listen to them, if you don’t respond to them, if you don’t give them a sense of comfort when they’re in distress, then it hampers the healing process,” said the minister. In the meantime, Tufton urged the 141 recipients of the Barry Wint medical grant, valued at over $190 million, to be the difference once they enter their respective fields of practice. “I say this at the risk of offending some, that money is not the primary issue in health care, currently public health; the primary issue is how we conduct ourselves within the system. People who are in the system only for a pay cheque are not sufficiently willing to give the commitment and show care. You cannot afford to be like that. You have to show a better way, and that’s what Barry Wint is investing in. Not just in your capacity as a technical and competent person, but in moving the process forward,” the minister said. Pointing to what he identified as the major weaknesses of the system, Tufton noted that health care in Jamaica lacks a sufficient number of practitioners — specifically specialised individuals — and professionals with the capacity to show empathy to patients. He reiterated that that was not the type of behaviour that he expected from recipients of the Barry Wint scholarship, and challenged them to become “a catalyst for change”. “If you just want to be a nurse, a doctor, a biotech engineer because at the end of the month you’re going to get a fat pay cheque, and that’s the only driving motivation to apply and to pretty up the application for this money, do not accept it. There are too many people in the profession who see the profession only in financial terms, and not enough as a passion and commitment to enhance service delivery for those who need it, Jamaicans who are in distress,” he said firmly.

World.title: Jamaicans loud and proud!
World.content:
Trinidad and Tobago’s High Commissioner to Jamaica Deborah Thomas-Felix shares her admiration for the manner in which Jamaicans display pride in their country while speaking at the Jamaica Observer Press Club last Friday. Photo: Naphtali Junior

FROM schoolchildren in the country’s colours to packed cultural events, Trinidad and Tobago’s new High Commissioner Deborah Thomas-Felix says the unapologetic pride Jamaicans display in their identity is one of the things that has impressed her most since taking up her post.

Having lived in several Caribbean countries, Thomas-Felix said Jamaica’s expression of national pride stands out to her because of how openly it is displayed in everyday life, from the workplace to sporting and cultural events.

She was particularly struck by the way Jamaicans embrace national occasions, including Jamaica Day, when people turn out in the country’s colours, adding that the celebration of national identity extends beyond the traditional observances of Independence and Emancipation.

“You all have a national day — schoolchildren, big people going to work in Jamaica colours. I was so struck by that when I experienced it… Don’t get me wrong, because Trinidad and Tobago has a deep sense of pride and love, but it’s the way, the open way in which it’s displayed in Jamaica,” she expressed during the a Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s Beechwood Avenue, St Andrew, headquarters last Friday.

For Thomas-Felix, the pride is also visible in how Jamaica celebrates its culture, with Reggae Month — commemorated in February — providing an entire month of activities centred on one of the country’s most recognisable cultural exports.

She said that visible enthusiasm has helped her better understand Jamaicans in the Diaspora.

“Everywhere you go within the country, they say, ‘Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica,’ and I think that is so encouraging, and it gives me a better understanding of the Jamaicans I know who don’t live in Jamaica,” she said.

Thomas-Felix, whose parents are Grenadians and who has lived in St Vincent, Barbados, and Trinidad and Tobago, stressed that she was not suggesting that Trinbagonians lack national pride, but said she was particularly impressed by how visibly Jamaicans express theirs.

“There’s this open display of pride, and I think you all should keep that. I think that is just an excellent way to let [future] generations inherit that and continue with that, because I really, really like that,” she said.

Her comments come as Thomas-Felix seeks to strengthen ties between Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago across areas including trade, culture, and people-to-people relations.

She said the relationship between the two countries extends well beyond governments, pointing to Trinidadians who have built lives and careers in Jamaica and Jamaicans who have done the same in Trinidad and Tobago.

For Thomas-Felix, those personal connections are part of the Caribbean relationship that she wants to strengthen during her tenure.

“So the relationship is way beyond government to government, it’s really about people, and we interact through music, we interact in terms of culture, and so I want to really strengthen those bonds,” she said.

World.title: Slow movement on Spring Mount road repairs
World.content:
Residents of Spring Mount listen keenly as manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw (left) provides an update on plans to rehabilitate collapsed roads in the area.

SPRING MOUNT, St James — A soil test is among the items to be done before the State-run National Works Agency (NWA) can finalise a design to rebuild Spring Mount road in south St James. Last October’s Hurricane Melissa caused two major breakaways on the heavily trafficked route, leaving commuters with the choice of engaging in risky road use or a much longer, more costly journey.

With schools about to reopen, residents of Spring Mount and neighbouring areas have become increasingly anxious for an update on what is being done to fix the road. They were given the clearest signal, Thursday evening, that the road will likely be rebuilt in the same location; but there was no timeline on when work will start.

“We are looking to build back the road. We have looked at different possibilities and I can tell you straight up, one of the things that we are looking at is to take down the hillside and acquire [those] two houses on top of the hill,” manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw told residents during a meeting held at Spring Mount Basic School.

He said the goal is to rehabilitate the roadway as soon as possible, restoring the vital connection between the north and south of the parish. The damage has made safe passage by vehicular traffic impossible just beyond Spring Mount Police Station. Residents have established a pedestrian path which is sometimes utilised by motorcyclists.

Shaw made it clear that there will be challenges in executing the project, given its scope and magnitude.

“It is not the normal run of the mill [approach of] looking at it as a breakaway, put up a wall, backfill it, and move on. No. We are going to have to do what are called bore hole tests,” he warned, adding that this falls outside the technical capabilities of the NWA and a private sector firm would have to be engaged.

These tests, he explained, will provide laboratory-based information on the soil in the area that will guide the designs on which work has already started.

“That testing of the material beneath there will inform us as to what else, if required, needs to be done to ensure that… when we build up that road, you have it longer than all of us inside here will live,” Shaw told the audience.

“Based on the survey that was executed, a design is being worked on but that design will not be finalised until the boreholes are done,” he added.

He explained the importance of the soil tests.

“A crucial factor in this area is the springs. It’s called Spring Mount for a reason. We have to design with that in mind to ensure that we don’t see a situation where we build a big wall, costing a lot of money… and then, [as seen in other locations] rain came, and the entire retaining wall just moved like… it was plastic,” Shaw outlined.

“We have that kind of experience and historical knowledge on which to build or not to build. We are not taking anything lightly in ensuring that the design solutions that we come up with, they are adequate, they are appropriate, are sufficient, and necessary for the particular areas that we are going to be working,” he added.

Responding to residents’ questions about timelines, the NWA representative said he was unable to provide one as it depends on the soil testing which is being done outside of the agency. He did, however, promise to explore ways in which alternate routes — such as the journey through Kempshot, up the treacherous Charlie Mount — may be improved.

Councillor Uvel Graham (Jamaica Labour Party, Spring Mount Division) was at the meeting and while he acknowledged that the project is complex he expressed frustration that it is moving too slowly.

“To be honest, I was looking for more of a timeline and that these tests would be done already and people would be hearing that the next two to three months, the work would start,” he told the

Jamaica Observer after the meeting.

World.title: ‘I’ve run my leg’
World.content:
GREENE...I’m filled with mixed emotions because this is my last time serving within the context as permanent secretary here at the Ministry of Health and Wellness (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

AFTER a brief but impactful two-year term as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Health and Wellness, Errol Greene is ready to pass the baton, proud of his legacy but acknowledging that critical work remains.

“As we gather to award students pursuing courses in public health, I am filled with mixed emotions. I’m filled with mixed emotions because this is my last time serving within the context as permanent secretary here at the Ministry of Health and Wellness,” said Greene, as he formally announced his retirement from the role — which takes effect Monday, August 31 — while delivering greetings at the Dr Barry Wint Memorial Scholarship Awards Ceremony at S Hotel Kingston last Friday.

Under the scholarship, named in honour of the former chief medical officer, recipients are awarded up to $1 million annually for health care-related studies in priority fields such as nursing, biomedical engineering, and medicine.

For this year’s staging, 141 awardees were selected from more than 700 applicants to benefit from over $190 million in scholarships, with the Government having spent approximately $900 million towards the initiative to date.

“While there’s a sense of nostalgia, there’s also a sense of tremendous pride and optimism as I look out at this room filled with talented, ambitious, enthusiastic, and determined persons who represent the future of health care in Jamaica,” said Greene, who noted that he would continue to watch their progress as professionals in the health field from the sidelines.

When asked by the Jamaica Observer if his retirement signalled a complete departure from public service, Greene offered a cryptic, “We’ll see how it goes.” However, he maintained that he is ready to hand over the reins to a capable professional who can drive the remaining work forward.

“We have done well, and we can do better. I certainly want to be a part of the journey because I know my minister is passionate about health, he’s passionate about service delivery, and I would have run my leg of the race and I have handed over the baton, so I’ll just go in the pavilion and watch the race finish,” he said.

Before his two-year stint as permanent secretary, Greene led a career spanning decades. His life as a public servant began when he assumed the role of town clerk of the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) and also served at the St Thomas Municipal Corporation.

He then pivoted to begin service in the health sector, serving as regional director of the South East Regional Health Authority (SERHA), which oversees health services in Kingston and St Andrew, St Thomas, and St Catherine.

He was also a former regional director of Western Regional Health Authority and a former chief executive officer of the Kingston Public Hospital.

Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton, who delivered the keynote address at the scholarship event, used the opportunity to acknowledge Greene’s contributions and bid him farewell.

“Our permanent secretary, who is not riding off in the sunset, but is closing one chapter to start another, Mr Errol Greene…give him a round of applause, please. I believe he has done 50 years, thereabout. I don’t want to tell his age, because he is still young,” joked Tufton. “But he has done a whole heap of years, whole heap of decades to public service, and I just want to recognise him and thank him for his services.”

World.title: UWI Freshers’ Series delivers a hit, energises campus
World.content:
DJ Breeze in full flight at Freshers’ Fete.

Jermaine Francis, vice-president of properties and special initiatives at The University of the West Indies, Mona Guild of Students, has described this year’s Freshers’ Series as one of the most successful in the past five years, attracting one of the largest turnouts seen during that period.

The Freshers’ Series took place from August 26-28.

According to Francis, the strong participation and vibrant atmosphere throughout the week signals that “the vibes on campus are back.” He noted that the enthusiasm and engagement displayed by students demonstrates the immense value and potential of the university market.

“UWI, Mona provides corporate entities with a unique opportunity to connect with the next generation of leaders and consumers. The energy is back, the students are engaged, and the platform is growing. I am urging corporate Jamaica to tap in and become part of these experiences,” Francis told the Jamaica Observer on the weekend.

Francis is therefore encouraging corporate Jamaica to take greater interest in and tap into this unique and dynamic student market. With major events such as UWI Integration Thursday and UWI Carnival on the horizon, he believes there are significant opportunities for brands to engage directly with thousands of young, influential, and emerging consumers.

The first event in the Freshers’ Series was the Freshers’ Concert, which took place inside Students’ Union on the campus. Representatives from the various halls performed talented pieces including singing, drama and poetry.

“The idea behind the Freshers’ Concert is really to give our new students a proper welcome to UWI and allow them to experience the university beyond the classroom. We wanted each hall to come together, showcase their creativity and talents, and give the freshers an opportunity to build friendships and create memories from the very start of their university journey. We also ensured that the freshers got the opportunity to interact with their guild councillors.

The George Alleyne Hall emerged winner, with Mary Seacole Hall, Elsa Rynie Towers, Irvine Hall, and Taylor Hall finishing in second, third, fourth and fifth places, respectively.

“The halls showcased a range of talents, including singing, dancing, drama and other creative performances. What stood out to me was how each hall found its own way to tell a story and represent their identity through their performance.
