World.title: How China buried Tibet flood images after Nepal disaster
World.content:
In Tibet, a digital crackdown followed the deadly flood that has devastated communities along the China-Nepal border. Censors erased viral footage while Chinese state media flooded platforms with official content.

When a catastrophic flash flood swept through the rugged China-Nepal border on August 26, the physical devastation was immediate.

In Nepal, a black torrent of mud and rock tore through communities, leaving hundreds dead and thousands more missing along the borderlands.

But across the frontier in Tibet, an autonomous region of China, the physical disaster was almost instantly followed by a digital one: the rapid, high-tech erasure of the catastrophe's visual evidence.

As survivors tried to upload raw footage of the deluge, China's state-backed information control apparatus swung into action, executing a sophisticated, precision operation to shape the public narrative and bury inconvenient truths.

The contrasting realities — a tragic humanitarian crisis in Nepal and a tightly sanitized, triumphant rescue narrative in China — reveal the evolving mechanics of Beijing's modern censorship machine.

Rather than imposing a blunt, blanket blackout, authorities deployed advanced image-recognition technology and "saturated information" tactics to drown out domestic scrutiny while deflecting diplomatic friction abroad.

Collapse of the border gate

In the immediate aftermath of the flood-triggered mudslide, local residents captured dramatic footage of the torrent engulfing Gyirong Port, a critical overland trade hub between China and Nepal.

The most striking video showed a black wall of water and debris crashing into and destroying the "national" border gate.

In an article titled "An Unrecorded Mudslide Rushes into Gyirong Port" on China's WeChat, a universal app that combines messaging with payment options and social media functions, local blogger "Matou Qingnian" described the chaotic scene.

"The most terrifying moment happened at the Gyirong Port," the author wrote, describing video footage of crowds, including children, fleeing in panic before a pitch-black torrent swallowed the camera's view.

Within hours, both the article and the raw video footage had vanished from Chinese social media.

According to China Digital Times (CDT) , an independent watchdog that tracks Chinese internet censorship, the video of the collapsing border gate was systematically blocked from being shared on WeChat, even in private messages.

"The footage itself contained no graphic violence, no protests, and no political slogans," explained Mira, a CDT editor who specializes in tracking sensitive keywords and media. "The target of the censorship was the symbol itself: the National Gate."

Digital analysts note that this censorship highlights a significant upgrade in China's internet policing tools. Instead of merely filtering text-based keywords, platforms now rely heavily on video fingerprinting, image hashing and machine-learning models to recognize specific visual scenes.

Once a visual sequence is blacklisted, it is intercepted before it can ever be posted.

Satiety as a shield: The art of 'saturated' censorship

The suppression of the Gyirong Port disaster reflects a broader shift in Beijing's strategy: from mass deletion to "precision surgery" and narrative flooding.

A search for "Tibet mudslide" on Xiaohongshu — China's popular lifestyle and search platform — reveals the mechanics of this "saturated information environment."

Rather than showing an empty search page, the platform's algorithm feeds users a carefully curated stream of state-media reports from China's state broadcaster CCTV and news agency Xinhua.

The visual landscape is dominated by high-resolution, sterile graphics: "before-and-after" comparisons, maps of high-altitude glacial collapses — the official scientific cause of the disaster — and state-approved aerial drone footage.

The raw, chaotic cellphone videos recorded by eyewitnesses at the border are entirely absent.

By filling the digital space with a high volume of "safe" and visually appealing official content, the state satisfies the public's immediate curiosity while preemptively suffocating independent reporting or organic discussions, analysts note.

Rescuers have been carrying out search-and-rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port since last Wednesday Image: Lhasa Fire and Rescue Mobile Detachment/Handout/Xinhua/picture alliance

On Weibo, China's microblogging giant, the narrative arc was similarly managed. While "Tibet mudslide" briefly trended on August 26, the domestic casualty figures were quickly frozen the next morning at three dead and 558 missing.

Almost immediately, the platform's trending topics were redirected toward the government's swift response.

Two heavily publicized, lengthy official reports dominated the news cycle: Chinese President Xi Jinping convening a Central Politburo meeting to coordinate rescue and relief efforts, and Premier Li Qiang arriving in Gyirong to personally direct operations on the ground.

These headlines effectively turned a major human tragedy into a highly orchestrated exhibition of state competence.

Dangerous 'half-year' question

Beneath the veneer of efficient state rescue efforts lies a deeper, systemic vulnerability that Beijing was desperate to hide: a history of structural negligence.

On August 27, a hashtag briefly slipped through the censors and trended on Weibo: "Gyirong Port Reopened Only Half a Year Ago." It amassed over 347,000 views in less than an hour before it was abruptly deleted. The hashtag pointed to a damning timeline of infrastructure failures.

In July 2025, Gyirong Port was completely shut down after being devastated by another severe flash flood. It took nearly six months to rebuild and reopen the port on January 1 of this year. Eight months later, the port has been destroyed again.

As the deleted "Matou Qingnian" article noted, Gyirong Port has now suffered mudslides during the flood seasons of 2024, 2025 and now 2026. In 2025, several Chinese personnel went missing or were killed.

By erasing the "half-year" trend, censors blocked an inevitable and dangerous train of public inquiry.

If the state-of-the-art border facility was destroyed twice in 14 months, it raises critical questions about site selection, shoddy infrastructure construction, and the complete failure of glacial lake monitoring and early-warning systems in Tibet.

These questions are especially sensitive in Tibet, a region under intense security and political control since the 1950s. Foreign journalists are strictly barred from entering the region outside of highly choreographed government-led tours.

According to human rights groups, local Tibetans who attempt to speak with foreign journalists or share independent accounts online face immediate detention or arrest.

High-altitude friction

The informational firewall does not stop at China's borders; it has also created a diplomatic rift with neighboring Nepal, which has borne the brunt of the disaster's human toll.

In Nepal, families cling to hope as thousands still missing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Parshuram Kaphle, a prominent Nepalese foreign policy journalist, publicly accused Beijing on X (formerly Twitter) of failing to share critical trans-boundary data.

"Nepal has been addressing the legitimate security concerns of our neighbors," Kaphle wrote in a post that has since been deleted. "However, it must be said with sadness that our northern neighbor has significantly undermined us. By failing to provide early warning of such a massive disaster, we suffered immense loss of human life."

He further wrote : "We have continually faced crises originating from their territory, while we continue to address all their concerns, necessary or unnecessary. Why must Nepal alone pay the price of one-sided love?"

The Chinese government has rejected any accountability. On August 27, the Chinese Embassy in Nepal issued a statement on Facebook, dismissing accusations of failing to issue warnings or causing the disaster through upstream dam failures as "fake news."

"Accusation helps nothing," the embassy statement read. "Cooperation saves lives."

But for families searching for the thousands of missing loved ones along the muddy banks of the Himalayan border, cooperation remains as obscured as the truth behind the digital firewall.

This article was originally written in Chinese.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: At Venice Film Festival, politics take center stage
World.content:
With works about Gaza, Ukraine and Elon Musk, political cinema is in the spotlight at the 2026 Venice Film Festival.

The Venice Film Festival used to be the place where the awards season put on its best tuxedo. This year, it looks more like a war room, with politics and political cinema set to dominate the red carpet.

The 83rd Venice International Film Festival kicks off on September 2 with Danny Boyle's "Ink," a drama about Rupert Murdoch's 1969 takeover of Britain's The Sun tabloid — the origin story of the Murdoch right-wing media empire.

Over 11 days on the Lido, audiences will also get films about Israel and Gaza, Russia's war on Ukraine, the CIA-backed coup in Pinochet's Chile, ICE raids in Minneapolis and a tell-all documentary on the world's richest man.

Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera has called it Venice's "most political" edition ever.

'Naza,' a documentary by 'No Other Land' directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, runs in the official competition Image: Venice Film Festival/AP Photo/picture alliance

Venice goes political

This year's competition includes "Naza," a documentary from "No Other Land" Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, examining Israeli military killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.

US-Russian director Julia Loktev chronicles Russian President Vladimir Putin's crackdown on independent journalism in "My Undesirable Friends Part II — Exile," a sequel to her 2024 doc.

DW co-production 'Letters From the Silenced Country' portrays life under repression in Belarus Image: DW/ZDF/Arte

Andrei Kutsila's "Letters From the Silenced Country" a DW, ZDF/Arte and TVP co-production about repression in Kutsila's native Belarus, will have its world premiere in Venice.

As will Alex Gibney's four-hour Elon Musk documentary "Musk," a film the richest man in the world has already denounced, sight unseen, as a "hit piece."

And Laura Poitras, the Oscar-winning director of "Citizenfour," will screen what she describes as a "short horror film," the documentary "They're Here," co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller and built from previously undisclosed footage of ICE's deportation surge in Minneapolis last January.

Laura Poitras also won the Golden Lion award in 2022 for best film for 'All the Beauty and the Bloodshed' Image: Domenico Stinellis/AP Photo/picture alliance

This is a new look for Venice.

Under artistic director Barbera, the festival had until recently cultivated a reputation as a place for movie stars and Oscar campaigns. You go to Venice to watch Timothee Chalamet on the red carpet, or George Clooney and Brad Pitt yucking it up at a press conference.

Venice let the other big European festivals — Berlin, and to a lesser degree Cannes — be the homes of political movies and the polemical debates that accompany them.

Berlin's political backlash

But Berlin's reputation as a festival for activist cinema has taken a major hit. The past three years have seen political debate, primarily over the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, overwhelm discussions of cinema at the Berlinale, to the point where the future of the festival looks in doubt.

At this year's Berlinale, jury president Wim Wenders was lambasted online for saying filmmakers "have to stay out of politics." Later, when Syrian-Palestinian director Abdallah Al-Khatib called out the German government at the awards ceremony for being "partners in the genocide in Gaza by Israel," the backlash nearly cost Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle her job.

Venice, by contrast, has spent the past two years leaning into political cinema.

How will she react to political questions? Actor Maggie Gyllenhaal is the president of the international jury this year Image: Federico Vespignani/AA/picture alliance

Venice leans into controversy

Last year saw the world premiere of Kaouther Ben Hania's "The Voice of Hind Rajab." The harrowing docudrama, which recreates the killing, by Israeli forces, of a 5-year-old Palestinian girl and her family in Gaza City, received a 22-minute standing ovation, a Lido record. The Israeli military has recently announced an official investigation into Hind Rajab's death.

Just days before, thousands marched on the Lido in protest of the war in Gaza. Filmmakers called on Barbera to label Israel's campaign "a genocide." He didn't go that far, speaking instead of his "huge sadness" over the suffering in Gaza and Palestine.

But the Venice boss didn't flinch, then or now, from programming films that address, head-on, the most controversial topics of the day.

Danny Boyle's Rupert Murdoch drama 'Ink' opens the festival Image: StudioCanal/AP Photo/picture alliance

Ukraine objects to 'DAU'

Russian films selected by the festival are also sparking protest.

Ukraine's Foreign Ministry, Culture Ministry and its embassy in Italy have issued a formal complaint over Barbera's decision to include Ilya Khrzhanovsky's "DAU," an art house drama about life under Soviet rule in Ukraine, in official competition. Ukraine objects to the film's Russian connections.

Khrzhanovsky is Russian-born, though he renounced his Russian citizenship and now lives in exile in Berlin. The film's lead, Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, still lives and works in Russia and has never publicly condemned Russia's war on Ukraine.

Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, who stars in 'DAU,' has remained silent on Putin's invasion of Ukraine Image: Getty Images/AFP/S. de Sakutin

In a statement, the Ukrainian ministries said programming the film "sends a deeply worrying signal" given the war.

Barbera is not backing down. He called the criticism a "smear campaign" from people who haven't seen the film.

Khrzhanovsky took to social media on August 20 with his rebuttal: "'DAU' is not an instrument of Russian state cultural policy," he wrote on Facebook. "It is an artistic statement about the nature of totalitarian evil."

Stars are still coming

Venice hasn't completely abandoned its Hollywood stars.

Robert Pattinson, of "Batman" and "Twilight" fame, will hit the Lido this year with "Primetime," playing a controversial US reality TV producer.

Robert Pattinson is among the stars expected on the red carpet Image: Luca Carlino/NurPhoto/picture alliance

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play CIA agents in Chile on the eve of the Pinochet coup in "Wild Horse Nine" from director Martin McDonagh ("Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri").

Real-life couple Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz star as husband and wife in Florian Zeller's "Bunker," about an architect commissioned to build a nuclear shelter for a billionaire.

George Clooney and 93-year-old acting legend Ellen Burstyn will swing by to collect Golden Lion awards for lifetime achievement.

George Clooney, a Venice regular, will attend this year to receive an honorary Golden Lion Image: Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

Venice also hasn't abandoned its role as a gathering place for cinema's elder statesmen — several of them German.

Wim Wenders, fresh off the Berlinale storm, brings an altogether gentler work to the Lido, a 3D documentary on the work of Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.

Werner Herzog, the last wild man of '70s German cinema, returns to narrative filmmaking for the first time in seven years in Venice with "Bucking Fastard," starring real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara.

And for those who want to forget about the world for a moment and just kick back and sing, pop stars Liam and Noel Gallagher are expected on the Lido for the premiere of the Oasis reunion documentary "Don't Look Back in Anger."

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

World.title: Deceived and deployed: How young Cameroonians end up fighting in Russia's war in Ukraine
World.content:
Analysts say economic desperation and fraudulent recruitment schemes are funneling Cameroonian youth into the Russian military — with deadly consequences.

Cameroon has emerged as one of the leading sources of African recruits for the Russian military, with young men lured to Europe by false promises of jobs and fast-tracked Russian citizenship, only to find themselves on the front lines of the war in Ukraine.

As of May this year, Ukrainian officials say that nearly 3,000 citizens from various African countries were known to have fought — or to still be fighting — for Russia : Cameroon, Ghana, Egypt, Kenya and Uganda were identified as significant.

In April, the Cameroonian government confirmed that Russia had reported the deaths of 16 Cameroonian nationals, seven of whom had died in military action in Ukraine.

Charles Ojiambo Mutoka, 72, shows a picture of his son Oscar, who he learned was killed while fighting for Russia in Ukraine Image: Tony Karumba/AFP

Poverty driving youths into Russia's duplicitous schemes

The actual death toll is likely higher according to DW correspondent Dorcas Ekupe, reporting from Bamenda in northwestern Cameroon.

"When you look at other publications and see what is happening — even seeing families who are grieving their loved ones — the number is really much higher than what the government had earlier said," Ekupe told DW's AfricaLink program.

She described two forces causing this worrying phenomenon: economic desperation and deliberate deception.

Many recruits, she said, travelled to Russia believing they had secured jobs in construction or as security guards, or that they were participating in study programs.

"Once in Russia, they then end up on the battlefield," Ekupe said.

African recruits fighting in Ukraine: Where's the AU? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia's perceived appeal meanwhile is also being amplified by well-organized campaigns.

Banjo Herman, a lecturer and political analyst at the University of Bamenda, pointed to the key role of the the Russian paramilitary Wagner Group as well as its successor, the Africa Corps, as Moscow's primary instrument for expanding its presence and reputation across Africa.

Military recruitment dressed up as 'cultural' outreach

Herman also cited Russian government programs such as the African Initiative and Alabuga, which present themselves as cultural or educational exchange schemes but have been linked to military recruitment.

"On the surface, sometimes it looks like cultural outreach," he said. "Sometimes Cameroonians are lured, thinking it is for work, not necessarily knowing what is beneath the surfac.," He added that offers of Russian nationality within six months were a particularly powerful draw.

France has previously described the African Initiative as a front administered by Russian intelligence services, designed to spread propaganda.

Why young men continue to risk their lives

Herman stressed, however, that the economic situation of the men was typically the main motivator.

"Imagine that you are a carpenter in Cameroon who cannot even earn 100,000 CFA francs (€150; $175) a month, but somebody is promising you 3 million CFA francs to come and work," he explained. "It is very attractive."

He also highlighted the fact that not all Cameroonians in Russia were the victims of deception: Some had lived there for years, had been absorbed into the military over time and were doing reasonably well.

But he pointed out that it was the promise of financial reward combined with the prospect of gaining Russian citizenship that explained why even people aware of the risks continued to accept recruitment offers to fight in Ukraine.

Ekupe corroborated this, noting a prevailing attitude of fatalism among some youth: "Sometimes people say, 'If I die, I die.'"

Africans pay high human cost fighting for Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Those left behind often suffer the most

Families left behind, meanwhile, are forced to bear the cost in silence: Ekupe described cases in which mothers only learned of their sons' deaths years after the fact — in one instance, when a fellow soldier called home to report that a 35-year-old Cameroonian had been killed in combat.

She added that many families had received no financial compensation from the Cameroonian government and that some of the men who died had left behind pregnant wives as well as children.

Contact between recruits and their families is often severed abruptly, Ekupe said.

"When they get there and discover it was not as promised, it is really difficult to inform their family," she added. "Sometimes they have to take time to adjust to the new environment and the situation, in which they find themselves."

According to the Kenyan Ministry of Foreign Affairs, more than 200 Kenyan nationals had crossed into Russia by January 2026, but only 18 had returned Image: Minako Sasako/AP Photo/picture alliance

Russia ducking from responsibilty

On the question of legal responsibility, Herman noted that international law does not, in principle, prohibit a foreign national from voluntarily enlisting in another state's armed forces.

Legal liability arises, however, when recruitment involves fraud, coercion, trafficking or mercenary activity.

Herman cited Article 47 of the Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, which defines a mercenary as someone who agrees to take direct part in hostilities with private financial gain as their main motivation.

Under current frameworks, the responsibility for the death of a foreign fighter in another country's war rests largely with the individual and their family, not the recruiting state.

Cameroon: insufficient campaigns to fight recruitement

Cameroon's government has stated publicly that it does not deploy troops abroad outside international mandates, and has warned citizens against joining foreign conflicts.

Analysts have nevertheless called on the Cameroonian government, and African governments more broadly, to pursue a three-pronged response to stop more people from risking their lives in Russia.

This approach would include economic reforms to create opportunities and reduce the conditions that make deceptive recruitment attractive; direct diplomatic engagement with Russia to hold recruitment networks accountable; and a public awareness campaign that issues clear, proactive public warnings to citizens about the dangers of following such schemes.

Relatives of Kenyan nationals conscripted by the Russian army have demanded government action to repatriate their kin Image: Tony Karumba/AFP

Ghana has also formally raised the issue with Russia, demanding an end to the recruitment of its nationals.

However, in Cameroon's case, the country's longstanding military ties with Russia, which President Paul Biya moved to renew in 2014 and 2015, could prevent a similar move.

Herman said that the absence of an official Cameroonian policy response to date reflected, at least in part, the government's awareness that the recruitment is carried out by private actors — limiting the state's formal grounds and opportunities for intervention.

"For the government to stop this," he said, "it has to go back to its governance policy and have a policy that is inclusive, transparent, and in which people can find opportunities within the system."

This article contains material generated by artificial intelligence (AI) from the AfricaLink podcast.

World.title: Tariffs spat: Carney bets Canada can defy Trump
World.content:
Canada is facing new US import penalties after Prime Minister Mark Carney refused to match US tariffs on China. Other countries are watching as the Trump trade clash turns into a fight over economic sovereignty.

Canada has been quietly praised for refusing to fold under pressure from US President Donald Trump in the long-running fight over trade tariffs.

The latest talks between the North American neighbors collapsed on August 21. Until the 11th hour, both sides were talking as if a deal was within reach.

The United States then put 50% tariffs on about $20 billion (€17.2 billion) worth of Canadian goods, while Ottawa pledged to match those duties on US imports.

Until the talks folded, Canada's approach was to cut a deal that would reduce the tariffs and keep cross-border supply chains functioning, particularly in the automotive and steel sectors.

Threat of all-out trade war between US, Canada looms To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US negotiators were, however, accused of changing the terms at the last minute, which the Canadian side said would have forced them to match US tariffs on China.

According to Ottawa, Washington wanted a say on future trade deals with other nations and to prevent Chinese goods being routed through Canada to evade US duties.

Trade spat becomes sovereignty issue

Dan Ciuriak, a senior fellow at the Waterloo, Canada-based Center for International Governance Innovation, described Trump's tariff-matching plan as "fortress North America," which he said was now a sovereignty issue for Ottawa.

"Canada is a trading nation," Ciuriak told DW. "If we align perfectly with the Americans — primarily about China — we then end up sacrificing our trade policy."

There is a recent precedent. When the US imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles last year, Canada followed suit. Beijing retaliated with 100% tariffs against one of Canada's biggest exports — canola.

Canada's $4.9 billion exports of canola oil, meal and seed to China were cut in half last year, according to data from the Canada China Business Council.

Why Canada rejected Trump's terms despite economic risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The smaller country is the one that bears the brunt in this kind of game. So that's one very good reason for Canada to have an independent trade policy," said Ciuriak.

As the US-Canada talks collapsed, Ottawa also complained that Washington had sought relief from rules on French-language movies and shows. Canada said this amounted to interference in its language and culture.

Canadians back walk away from US

Despite the uncertainty and higher cost to business from walking away, the Canadian prime minister's approach to negotiations with the US has broad public support.

A survey conducted by the Angus Reid Institute found that three-in-four Canadians backed the more hard-line move, despite concerns over the impact on the domestic economy.

Ciuriak noted how Trump's barbs of turning Canada into the 51st US state and threats to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America have emboldened ordinary Canadians to boycott US travel and products.

"Travel by Canadians to the United States has plummeted," he said. "There has been a popular consumer backlash against buying American products."

New government data show Canadians made nearly 500,000 fewer trips to the US in the first three months of 2026 and spent about $800 million less on those visits.

A survey last month by the Angus Reid Institute found that 40% of Canadian grocery shoppers were checking product origins, and that most of those shoppers avoided US goods when they could.

Trump has ordered US officials to rename Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' Image: Al Drago/UPI Photo/IMAGO

Although the two economies are tightly bound together, the new US duties apply to only about 5% of the $382 billion in goods that Canada exports to its southern neighbor.

The Royal Bank of Canada has warned that a no-deal would impact 0.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) and jobs, while University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimated it could cost as many as 90,000 jobs.

Canada's stance closely watched globally

Other governments are also watching to see how standing up to Trump plays out.

During their own negotiations, the European Union, United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea and dozens of smaller partners all agreed to lower tariffs in return for market access, investment pledges or alignment with US policy.

Only China has so far met Trump's tariff threat head-on, matching tariffs with tariffs and negotiating as a fellow superpower, rather than taking the first deal on offer.

Speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney said middle powers must act together, warning that if they were "not at the table," they would be "on the menu."

Trump has threatened higher tariffs on Canadian automakers from January Image: Dax Melmer/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

But for now, Carney is holding the line largely on his own. New Canadian tariffs on $20 billion worth of US goods — including steel, aluminum, dairy, electronics and farm equipment — take effect on September 8. They are likely to be met with US retaliation.

While matching US tariffs dollar-for-dollar sounds aggressive, Ciuriak thinks they need not "punish" the Canadian economy.

"Canada's tariffs ... apply to products Canada both buys from and sells to the US. As American tariffs cut off Canadian sales south of the border, the Canadian measures create space at home for that production."

New Trump pressure on Canadian autos

From January, Trump has threatened to raise duties on Canadian autos, trucks, parts and steel unless production moves to the US.

He also refused to extend the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) for another 16 years. Instead, the North American free-trade pact, which still covers most cross-border goods, will be reviewed year by year.

Will Canada cancel its order for US-made F-35 jets? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With no new talks planned with the US, Canadian lawmakers are talking up trade opportunities in other markets and weighing other retaliatory measures, including backing away from an order for US fighter jets.

Canada had planned to buy 88 Lockheed Martin F-35s, with 16 already on order. The rest are now on hold.

"When your friend kicks you in the back, one of the first rules is you don't then go and buy $12 billion of fighter jets from that person," British Columbia Premier David Eby said last week.

World.title: Sánchez exculpa a Marruecos por la crisis de Ceuta y avanza que el Rey la visitará por primera vez con este Gobierno
World.content:
Pedro Sánchez exculpa completamente a Marruecos de la crisis de Ceuta, aunque insiste en que lo hace porque no tiene datos que indiquen lo contrario, y no por miedo a su reacción. De hecho, Sánchez ha anunciado en una larga entrevista en la Cadena SER que el rey Felipe VI visitará por primera vez la ciudad autónoma “en cuanto se den las condiciones”, esto es, bajo el mandato del Gobierno de coalición. La visita supondría una tensión fuerte con Marruecos, como se demostró la única vez que Juan Carlos I estuvo allí, durante el mandato de José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero. Por eso, el anuncio de Sánchez de ese viaje, aún sin fecha, pretende ser una prueba de que él no es blando con Marruecos, porque está dispuesto a hacer algo que no hicieron ni José María Aznar ni Mariano Rajoy, autorizar un viaje a Ceuta y Melilla del jefe del Estado, pero a la vez Sánchez insiste en que detrás de esta crisis no está Marruecos, sino las redes sociales que, según él, han sido manejadas por Rusia e Israel para debilitar a España.

Sánchez ha insistido en que Marruecos ofreció una “cooperación instantánea, inmediata” tras la entrada a nado masiva de decenas de miles de migrantes. Los Gobiernos de ambos países “estuvieron al habla constantemente el 30 y el 31 de julio, y el 31 de julio se empezó un despliegue operativo por parte de las autoridades marroquíes”, ha detallado. El presidente ha defendido en todo momento la gestión del Gobierno en Ceuta, sin autocrítica, y ha cerrado cualquier posibilidad de crítica sobre Marruecos porque insiste en que la cooperación con este país es la clave para resolver esta crisis y todas las que puedan venir. Sánchez ha sostenido que, de no existir tal sintonía entre ambos países, “la crisis se agravaría” y ha explicado que se coordina con Rabat la “devolución de migrantes una vez que se haya hecho toda la gestión que nos marca la ley”.

Frente a las críticas en Ceuta que indican que Sánchez ha “abandonado” la ciudad, el presidente ha detallado todas las ayudas económicas que su Gobierno ha desplegado y ha recordado que él ha visitado la ciudad cuatro veces de forma oficial, mientras Aznar y Rajoy no lo hicieron nunca ―el primero fue solo una vez como candidato en las elecciones de 2000 para dar un mitin y el segundo fue en 2016 cuando estaba en funciones―. “He sido el presidente del Gobierno en ejercicio que más ha ido a Ceuta y a Melilla”, ha defendido.

El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, durante la entrevista dirigida por Aimar Bretos en el programa ‘Hoy por hoy’ de la Cadena SER.

“Creo que hay argumentos y razones suficientes para que el jefe del Estado visite por fin, después de 20 años, Ceuta y Melilla; eso es lo que he compartido con el jefe del Estado y es lo que se va a hacer, pero también le digo que se va a hacer cuando se den las condiciones para ello”, ha asegurado el presidente. Sánchez se ha referido a “20 años de reinado” de Felipe VI cuando en realidad suma 12, desde su proclamación en 2014. Tras la entrevista, este lunes por la tarde, el presidente y el rey se han reunido “en uno de los despachos habituales que mantienen varias veces al mes”, según fuentes de la Monclo, que aclaran que la reunión estaba prevista desde antes de verano. Ha transcurrido, explican, “con la normalidad habitual”.

“Hay discursos políticos peligrosos, cada vez más comunes, en los que parece que hubiera una contradicción entre la fortaleza del Estado y el respeto a la dignidad humana. Las grandes democracias eso lo hacen compatible. Se puede ser fuerte en el respeto al Estado de derecho y, en segundo lugar, ser consciente de que son seres humanos que tienen derechos”, ha defendido el presidente, que ha insistido en dar una visión humanitaria a la crisis.

El papel del CNI

Sánchez ha querido subrayar que “ningún centro de inteligencia con los que habitualmente el Gobierno de España colabora alumbra ninguna duda sobre la participación de una u otra forma por parte de las autoridades marroquíes”. A lo que ha añadido que “el CNI compartió informes de situación, como también lo hizo la Policía Nacional”, pero en ninguno de ellos anticipó las dimensiones de lo que venía. Con esto se coloca más cerca de la posición que mantuvo el ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, frente a la de la ministra de Defensa, Margarita Robles, aunque ha querido minimizar la polémica diciendo que ambas son “compatibles”.

¿Y qué pasó para que entraran más de 70.000 personas en la ciudad autónoma en dos días? Sánchez dice que “se tergiversó una sentencia del Tribunal Supremo que fue expandida por las redes sociales a través de bulos de desinformación también de organizaciones criminales” y ha asociado esa ola de desinformación a Rusia, a Israel y a “una internacional ultraderechista que utiliza siempre la migración no solamente para atacar a España, sino también a Europa y dividirla”. El presidente exculpa así a Marruecos y apunta a otros gobiernos.

“Hubo redes rusas e israelíes que difundieron esos bulos y atacaron al Gobierno de España y los europeos en un tema corrosivo como la migración irregular que divide y polariza a muchas sociedades europeas”, ha dicho. Sánchez ha explicado que en esos mensajes en redes se tergiversaba la sentencia del Supremo dando a entender que “si se entraba a nado, por ejemplo, en la ciudad autónoma de Ceuta, era imposible la devolución en frontera, cosa que no es cierto”. “En todo caso —ha apuntado el presidente—, se utilizó y se expandió a través de las redes sociales este tipo de bulo. Esto es lo que sabemos”.

El ministro de Exteriores israelí, Gideon Saar, ha acusado a Sánchez de “mentir descaradamente” al señalar “asombrosamente a Israel difundir información engañosa respecto a los eventos en Ceuta. Y le ha lanzado un ataque político. “Seguir difundiendo mentiras difamatorias no distraerá del fracaso vergonzoso de Sánchez para gestionar los asuntos de su país”, ha afirmado, informa Antonio Pita.

El Kremlin también ha negado las acusaciones de Sánchez. “No, no lo está”, ha respondido lacónicamente el portavoz de Putin, Dmitri Peskov, al ser preguntado este lunes si Rusia ha estado vinculada con la crisis migratoria desatada en Ceuta. La acusación de Sánchez contra Moscú y su exculpación de Marruecos ha sorprendido tanto a los medios de propaganda del Kremlin como, incluso, a parte de los medios independientes rusos. “Aparentemente, la culpa es de todos menos de él”, decía el canal Nexta, informa Javier G. Cuesta.

El ‘aticazo’, las elecciones y Zapatero

La crisis de Ceuta ha dominado la mayor parte de la entrevista, pero el presidente ha cambiado el tono y ha estado mucho más cómodo cuando las preguntas han saltado a la polémica por el ático que la Comunidad de Madrid ha comprado por 6,3 millones de euros, y que según él era para la presidenta Isabel Díaz Ayuso. “Lo que parece es que esta señora ha querido comprarse un aticazo con la pasta de los madrileños para vivir en él y se le ha pillado”. “Un aticazo con el dinero de los madrileños y sin aplicar la ley de vivienda, porque la señora lo que necesita es un piso grande de 400 metros cuadrados y 200 de terraza”, se ha burlado.

El presidente ha jugado con la idea de la fecha de las elecciones, y no ha querido dejar claro si serán antes o después de las autonómicas y municipales de mayo de 2027. Lo único seguro es que serán en 2027. “Mi intención es agotar la legislatura”, ha insistido. “Los Presupuestos van a sustanciar su debate en 2026, van a ser presentados en 2026, y va a haber elecciones en 2027″, ha avanzado para confirmar que él se presentará como candidato “con las mismas ganas que en el año 2019″. Sánchez cree que su proyecto es imprescindible “para frenar una ola reaccionaria” que solo trae involución. En su opinión, con la alianza del PP y Vox y el escoramiento a la derecha de los populares, “no estamos hablando de alternancia en este caso, estamos hablando de una involución que se ha visto en otras partes del mundo y que yo, desde luego, voy a pelear con uñas y dientes para que no se dé en nuestro país”.

Sánchez ha jugado con la fecha electoral. “Si me pregunta ‘¿van a ser en julio tal día?’, pues ya entramos en un territorio en el que, efectivamente, pues puede haber adelantos técnicos o no”. El presidente ha mostrado su enfado con los que dicen en su partido que las elecciones generales tienen que ser antes de las municipales, para evitar un golpe como el de 2023. “Lo que pasa es que esas voces, que por cierto son bastante minoritarias, obvian algo importante. Y es que en las elecciones generales, el PSOE sacó un mejor resultado que en las elecciones municipales y autonómicas”, se ha defendido Sánchez. “Esto pone en cuestión alguno de estos argumentos que se utilizan por parte de estos queridos compañeros”, ha rematado de forma irónica.

Ya cerca del final de la entrevista, el presidente ha defendido a Zapatero de las acusaciones por las que permanece investigado en la Audiencia Nacional por presunto tráfico de influencias: “Hay un legado, una trayectoria, que hace que tengamos que defender más que nunca su presunción de inocencia”. Ha sostenido su respaldo en el argumento de que hay “una amplísima mayoría” de expresidentes de Gobierno que se dedican al lobby. Al mismo tiempo, ha cerrado filas ante una posible imputación del PSOE en la causa en la que se investigan las cuentas del partido: “La imputación no es una condena”.

World.title: Asombrosas experiencias en San Cristóbal de La Laguna: practicar el salto del pastor, comer en una cueva o viajar en el tiempo en Bajamar
World.content:
La primera capital de la isla de Tenerife es ciudad patrimonio de la Unesco, uno de los Pueblos Gastronómicos de España y la puerta del selvático y abrupto macizo de Anaga. Además, en verano hace fresco

En la Península hay pocas localidades donde no haga un calor preocupante en verano. Y en Canarias, que están 1.400 kilómetros más al sur, menos aún. Eso es lo que piensan muchos viajeros al hacer la maleta, y cuando llegan a San Cristóbal de La Laguna descubren tiritando que deberían haber leído algo más de historia y geografía tinerfeñas, que la primera capital de la isla se fundó en 1496 a buena altura, a 550 metros sobre el mar, en un valle del noreste rodeado de montañas, ideal para defenderse de los guanches alzados, pero también para quedarse pajarito, porque los alisios amontonan nubes y humedad que da gusto. Es la eterna panza de burro, les advierten a los turistas los muy pacientes y abrigados laguneros, ya demasiado tarde.

Así que lo primero extraordinario que hay que hacer si se viaja allí en verano es incluir algo de ropa de abrigo en el equipaje. Algo para arriba y para los pies, porque la laguna que dio nombre a la ciudad sigue estando ahí, enterrada bajo las calles en damero que sirvieron de modelo para trazar muchas urbes de América. Cómo era la laguna de La Laguna —valga la redundancia— puede verse en el plano que dibujó en 1588 el ingeniero italiano Leonardo Torriani y que está reproducido en el suelo de la plaza de la Junta Suprema. Aquí traen los guías a los muchos ingleses que suben al atardecer desde la soleada costa sur de Tenerife y visitan esta alta y nublada ciudad maldiciendo la hora en que decidieron venir en chanclas y manga corta.

Más información Las mejores terrazas de los cafés históricos de Viena

Un ciclista por la calle San Agustín, en el centro histórico de La Laguna. Andrés Campos

Tan importante como hacer bien la maleta, es dar en el clavo con la compañía aérea, que sea económica pero formal. Por unos 45 euros se puede volar en agosto con Iberia Express de la Península al aeropuerto de Tenerife Norte, que está a 10 minutos de La Laguna, y hacerlo con absoluta puntualidad: en 2025 fue la aerolínea de Europa más cumplidora en esto por tercer año consecutivo. Si se coge el vuelo de las 6.35, se estará desayunando a las 9.00 un canelé de Burdeos o cualquiera de las dulces maravillas que obra Pablo Fernández del Castillo en Makika, en el casco histórico de La Laguna.

Desayunar frutas ecológicas

Tampoco se desayuna mal en el bufé del céntrico y señorial hotel Laguna Nivaria, sobre todo si se explora su sección de frutas ecológicas: plátanos, papayas, mangos, aguacates, acerolas, piñas… Todo esto lo cosechan en La Vizcaína, una finca certificada de 50.000 metros cuadrados que hay en Valle de Guerra, a 15 kilómetros al noroeste de La Laguna. Si tenemos mucho interés, se puede visitar solicitándolo en el mismo alojamiento. Allí descubriremos frutas insólitas en España —como los canisteles mesoamericanos que, en el árbol, parecen limones, pero saben a dulce de leche y tienen una textura harinosa, como de yema de huevo duro— y también animales de granja autóctonos, como el cochino negro canario o la oveja pelibuey.

Visitantes observando los papayos en la finca ecológica la Vizcaína. Andrés Campos

De paso, podemos parar a curiosear y desayunar (¡otra vez!) en Frutas y Verduras Nito, un mercado con cafetería del vecino municipio de Tegueste propiedad de Sergio Rodríguez, Nito, un agricultor que vende sin intermediaros lo que cultiva y que arrasa en Instagram —tiene 161.000 seguidores— con sus reels francos y combativos.

Moverse como una torre de ajedrez por el tablero urbano

Después de desayunar, los forasteros en Canarias suelen bajar a la playa o a la piscina. En La Laguna no hay playa —en el municipio, sí, como luego veremos— y pocos hoteles tienen piscina descubierta, por motivos obvios. Además, aquí lo que apetece es entrar en calor y, para ello, nada como moverse adelante y atrás, a izquierda y derecha, cual torre de ajedrez, por el tablero de San Cristóbal de La Laguna, primer ejemplo de ciudad colonial no amurallada trazada en cuadrícula, y patrimonio mundial de la Unesco desde 1999.

Si tomamos como casilla de partida la plaza del Adelantado, donde se alza desde el siglo XVI la mansión que hoy ocupa el Laguna Nivaria, saldremos por la calle Obispo Rey Redondo y nos plantaremos enseguida delante de la Casa de los Capitanes Generales, palacio de toba volcánica roja y amplio patio donde entre 1705 y 1723 vivieron seis mandamases de Canarias. Admiraremos luego los dragos de la plaza de los Remedios, frente a la catedral, que son talluditos, pero unos jovenzuelos de 60 años comparados con otros varias veces centenarios de la ciudad. Y subiremos 99 escalones para otear La Laguna desde lo alto del campanario de la iglesia de la Concepción.

El antiguo convento de San Agustín, en La Laguna (Tenerife). Andrés Campos

Al pie del campanario, en el patio de la Casa Museo Cayetano López Felipe, hay una terraza perfecta para un descanso. Bajando después por la calle San Agustín, veremos el mapa de Torriani, el formidable claustro renacentista del antiguo convento de San Agustín y la no menos imponente Casa Lercaro, sede del Museo de Historia y Antropología de Tenerife. Los forofos de la historia se arrimarán finalmente al convento de Santa Catalina de Siena para recordar a la monja milagrosa Sor María de Jesús, La Siervita, y a la parroquia de Santo Domingo de Guzmán, donde yace bajo una losa decorada con una calavera pirata su devoto amigo Amaro Pargo (1678-1747), el corsario más famoso de España, un lagunero que ha inspirado leyendas, novelas e incluso un juego para buscar un tesoro suyo oculto en la ciudad siguiendo las pistas con el móvil.

La tumba del corsario Amaro Pargo, en la parroquia de Santo Domingo de Guzmán. Andrés Campos

Quienes prefieran la ruidosa multitud, concluirán el recorrido urbano paseando con un montón de vecinos y con cien palmeras canarias seculares a cada lado por el llamado Camino Largo, la Avenida de la Universidad, o acercándose al mercado municipal para cotillear en los puestos de papas —Tenerife cuenta con ¡18 variedades— y en las pescaderías donde las viejas, los chernes, los pejeperros y las morenas compiten por ver quién es el pez más feo y colorido.

Viajar 50 años atrás en el tiempo, a Bajamar

En los años sesenta y primeros de los setenta del siglo XX, antes de que se inaugurara el aeropuerto de Tenerife Sur y el litoral meridional de la isla se masificara, uno de los mayores reclamos turísticos de la misma era Bajamar, a 15 kilómetros al norte de la ciudad de La Laguna. Como en el resto del municipio y del norte de Tenerife, aquí no lucía mucho el sol. Tampoco había playas excelentes en esta empinada y abrupta orilla: solo una pequeña protegida por una escollera y otra de arena negra volcánica y cantos rodados donde rompían, y rompen, olas de susto. Por ello, el turismo en Tenerife tomó otros derroteros más soleados y Bajamar se fue quedando traspapelada, con el hotel Neptuno —el mejor de los años dorados— en ruinas, y con una fecha escrita debajo, “diciembre de 1971”, cuando Camilo Sesto inauguró la discoteca Tívoli, muy cerca del anterior.

La asociación Cervantear invita a viajar al Bajamar de hace medio siglo con guías locales, recordando las paellas multitudinarias que aquí se hacían —hubo una en 1973 para 10.000 personas— y la riada de 1977 que convirtió este rincón de la costa lagunera en una escombrera, en un lugar que ya no levantaría cabeza. Invitan porque la ruta es gratis. Tres lugares que hay que visitar, con guías o sin ellos, son la cancha de fútbol donde el hijo más famoso de Bajamar, Pedri, dio sus primeros pases; el mural en homenaje al cantante Quevedo que alegra las ruinas del hotel Neptuno y las piscinas naturales de dimensiones olímpicas que hay junto al faro, al borde del océano, y en las que, a falta de buenas playas, uno se puede bañar como hace medio siglo, con permiso de las olas, que son tremendas.

Bañistas en las piscinas naturales de Bajamar. Andrés Campos

Caminar hasta un observatorio guanche y practicar el salto del pastor

Un poco más al norte, donde la costa urbanizada y/o urbanizable se acaba y empiezan los acantilados y barrancos del macizo de Anaga, se encuentra Punta del Hidalgo, que, al igual que Bajamar, tiene un aire demodé, de lugar de vacaciones de los setenta metido en una bola de cristal.

El plan extraordinario aquí es seguir el sendero litoral que lleva en menos de una hora hasta la ermita de San Juanito, pasando al pie de un altísimo y futurista faro blanco. Junto a la ermita, en la rasa intermareal basáltica, hay un yacimiento de cazoletas y canales guanches. Era un observatorio donde los aborígenes del achimenceyato de Addar veían cómo el sol naciente asomaba una vez al año a través de la cima hendida del cercano Roque de los Dos Hermanos —Aramuygo, para ellos— y sabían que era el solsticio de invierno. Así lo cuentan los profesores laguneros José Farrujia y Miguel Ángel Martín en su libro Cuando el cielo nos habló. Y así lo creen muchas personas que se acercan el 21 de diciembre a este punto para ver amanecer.

Un senderista en la laurisilva del macizo de Anaga, cerca de Cruz del Carmen. Andrés Campos

Cualquier otro día, lo que se ve en los altos roques de Punta del Hidalgo es a gente que practica el salto del pastor canario, deporte que consiste en descender por las escarpadísimas laderas apoyándose en una larga lanza o astia de madera con un picudo regatón de hierro. Al llegar abajo, los saltadores invitan amablemente a los curiosos a iniciarse dando unos pequeños brincos en la orilla rocosa, delante de la ermita. Solo unos saltitos. Más no, porque es peligroso y hay que estar federado. En Tenerife hay 161 apasionados de esto federados. Y hay demostraciones y cursos de los que se informa en la web saltodelpastorcanario.org.

Comer pescado del día

En Cofradía de La Punta, en Punta del Hidalgo, se cena viendo los barcos arribar al puertito con lo que llevará la parrillada. Abundan en el municipio de La Laguna los restaurantes como este, donde hacen bien lo de cerca y lo de siempre, y también los que le dan una vuelta imaginativa, sin pasarse. Por eso La Laguna forma parte de la Red de Pueblos Gastronómicos de España. ¿Sugerencias? Tomen nota.

En el centro ajedrezado de la ciudad, merece la pena reservar en El Guadyl, en Bejeque y en Sorimba. El primer restaurante, moderno y desenfadado, está siempre a tope, y el almogrote y las cervezas artesanas Chutney no deben faltar en la mesa. En el segundo, el venezolano de raíces lusas Adrián Oliveira elabora lo canario con técnicas japonesas. Usa carbón Binchotan, el más puro y caro del mundo. Y el tercero es ideal para cenar: todo lo sirven en platos de cerámica artística y atienden con susurros.

Fuera del casco histórico, pero a solo 10 minutos de paseo, se encuentra Mallar, un restaurante que engaña, porque parece un tosco mesón y es un no parar de platillos deliciosos: taco de vieira, lomo de salmón fileteado con aceite de sésamo y picadillo, chorizo picante de El Hierro con huevo frito... El joven chef Rubén Pérez también engaña: tiene más experiencia de la que aparenta. Por último, en un promontorio sobre la cala del Roncador, en la costa norte, está Agrocardón, con mucho comedor al aire libre rodeado de huertos y frutales y con animales por doquier: cabras, burros, caballos, ponis, gallinas, pavos reales… En la zona chill-out, los bípedos implumes liban cócteles y las mariposas monarca, el néctar de las asclepias.

A la Reserva de Anaga en guagua

Cuesta creer que, a solo seis kilómetros de la ciudad histórica de La Laguna, una urbe trazada a escuadra y cartabón, bastante llana y sin apenas nada verde a la vista, se encuentre la Reserva de la Biosfera de Anaga, un territorio primitivo, montañoso y selvático a más no poder que alberga la mayor extensión de laurisilva que hay en Tenerife y un número de endemismos sin igual en Europa. Es como si el Renacimiento y y la era Terciaria —cuando se formaron la ciudad y la laurisilva­— fueran dos páginas seguidas de un mismo libro.

Si vamos a Anaga en coche, pararemos de camino en Las Mercedes para conocer el venerable molino de gofio La Fuerza de La Voluntad, que lleva en marcha desde el 2 de febrero de 1942. Si subimos en guagua —en la número 275, desde el intercambiador de La Laguna—, llegaremos directamente, en una media hora, a Cruz del Carmen, donde está el Centro de Visitantes y arrancan dos senderos sencillos, perfectos para empezar a explorar a esta jungla primigenia: el de los Sentidos y el el de Hija Cambada. Para ver bien Anaga, necesitaríamos un mes. Habrá que volver.

Comer en La Cueva y bajar 500 escalones para catar vinos

Javier González, en su Bodega 500 Escalones. Andrés Campos

Aunque poca, en Anaga vive gente: hay unas 2.500 personas repartidas por 30 aldeas y caseríos, seis de los cuales pertenecen al municipio de La Laguna. En uno de ellos, Chinamada, se siguen usando casas-cueva, como en tiempos de los guanches, y se debe comer en el restaurante La Cueva (922 69 00 76), que está excavado en la roca volcánica. Hay escaldón, papas, ropa vieja, más papas, carne de cabra, carne con papas, queso frito de cabra… Todo muy sencillo, muy guanche, muy rico. Aquí no hay sumiller, ni vinos extraordinarios. Para esto último, hay que ir a la Bodega 500 Escalones, que, como su nombre avisa, está medio millar de peldaños más abajo que el caserío Los Batanes, en el fondo de un barranco aparentemente inhóspito. No hay carretera. Hay un viejo guinche, un montacargas suspendido de un cable en el que los enoturistas podrían bajar y subir cómodamente antes y después de alucinar visitando los viñedos que alguien plantó allá abajo y que recuperó en 1999 Félix González, el padre de Javier, que es el enólogo y la cara visible y sonriente de esta increíble bodega. Pero no está preparado para que lo usen personas. Lástima. Toca bajar por la escalera labrada en la toba volcánica, catar un par de vinos y subir los 500 escalones con varias botellas a cuestas. Se habla mucho de la viticultura heroica y poco del enoturismo heroico.

World.title: Former CDA leader Elco Brinkman dies aged 78
World.content:
Elco Brinkman, the Christian Democrat minister and party leader whose 1994 election defeat pushed the CDA into opposition for the first time in decades, has died aged 78. He died on Monday in Leiden after a short illness, his family said.

Brinkman became minister of welfare, health and culture in 1982, aged 34, serving seven years under Ruud Lubbers.

As minister he coined the phrase “caring society”, arguing that people had grown too dependent on the welfare state. He pushed through cuts to welfare and the arts and steered a new media law that opened the Netherlands to commercial television.

He took over as CDA leader in parliament in 1989 and was earmarked as Lubbers’s successor, but his 1994 campaign collapsed after Lubbers publicly withdrew his backing. The CDA fell from 54 seats to 34, and Brinkman left national politics in 1995.

He later chaired the construction federation Bouwend Nederland and returned as the CDA’s senate leader from 2011 to 2019.

World.title: From Sting to the beach: 12 great things to do in September
World.content:
The heat has receded and autumn is almost upon us. Hanneke Sanou has a round up of ideas to keep you busy in September.

Go once more unto the beach

Scheveningen is saying goodbye to a torrid summer with Live on the Beach. Whether sodden sand or glorious sunshine, the line-up will cheer up fans of Guus Meeuwis, Suzan and Freek, Acda en De Munnik, among many others. There are four live events on four consecutive days. September 3-6. Website

Get the picture

The Fotomuseum Den Haag is mounting a retrospective of 300 photographs by Eva Besnyö (1910-2003) from its own extensive collection. It follows Besnyö’s career, from Budapest to Berlin and Amsterdam, where she arrived in 1931 and where she became part of the New Photography movement which favoured dynamism and immediacy in photography.

Besnyö, who was Jewish, had to go into hiding during the war years and was active in resistance work. Her social commitment never flagged; in the 1970s she documented the Dutch feminist movement Dolle Mina. Eva Besnyö – The Liberated Camera is on from September 5. Website

Connect the dots

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam presents a retrospective of the work of Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, who, it emerged last week, died on August 14 aged 97. Kusama turned her hand to everything during her long career, from painting and sculpture to performances, fashion, and literature. The show includes a new version of one of her installations executed in a characteristic black and yellow pattern, so tactile and organic, to wander round in. From September 11. Website

Drop by the Voorlinden birthday party

The Voorlinden Museum in Wassenaar is celebrating its 10th anniversary with an exhibition which combines the museum’s favourites with equally well-loved work pilfered from other collections.

The impressive line-up of Celebrating the Icons of Art includes artists Francis Bacon, Louise Bourgeois, Alexander Calder, Nick Cave, Félix González-Torres, Damien Hirst, David Hockney, Martha Jungwirth, Mike Kelley, Yayoi Kusama, Fernand Léger, Roy Lichtenstein, Henri Matisse, Annette Messager, Joan Miró, Claude Monet, Bruce Nauman, Louise Nevelson, Lygia Pape, Gerhard Richter and Bridget Riley. From September 12. Website

Catch a monument

It’s visit-a-listed-building day, or Open Monumentendag, on September 12 and 13, when the public are invited to take a peek at special buildings, some of which are off-limits for the rest of the year.

This year’s theme is Resilient heritage in turbulent times, which puts the focus on threats such as climate change and the more pedestrian, but no less urgent, lack of finances and volunteers. Some 6,000 buildings are opening their doors, including some weird and wonderful ones like riding schools and the smallest house in Groningen. September 12 and 13. Website

Play the game

How has video game technology evolved over the years, and do video games turn people into isolated weirdos, creative problem solvers, or both? Those are the questions Game On, at the NEMO Science Museum in Amsterdam is trying to answer. For those who cannot be without their consoles, Super Nintendo, Atari 2600 and PlayStation 5 are on standby. Until October 26. Website

Get a load of Van Gogh(s)

Van Gogh lovers should head for the Kröller-Müller museum in Otterlo which has dusted off all 88 of its Van Goghs and put them all together in an exhibition for the first time in over 40 years. Built around faith, hope and charity, extolled in a sermon before he switched from preacher to painter as a profession, Van Gogh – All Our Paintings seeks to discover these virtues in the artist’s work. From September 15. Website

Don’t touch the art at Sonsbeek

“I don’t need a garden, I’m sharing a park” is the title of this year’s edition of the open-air art event in Arnhem’s Park Sonsbeek. The event features site-specific art, performances, film, and workshops by Dutch and international artists, including British-Ghanaian artist Larry Achiampong, whose work, wrapped in a pan-African flag, was recently vandalised. The torn flag will remain part of the work. Until October 11. Website

Climb the stairway to heaven

Soaring temperatures in June prevented Willem-Alexander from attempting the inaugural climb but now the spruced-up Kijk uit Attention, by Krijn Giezen (1939-2011), is open to the public once more. The attraction in the sculpture park of the Kröller-Müller museum consists of a path leading to stairs going up 87 metres, affording a view of the national Veluwe park. Website

Don’t miss

You still have a chance to catch the Rijksmuseum’s in-depth look at Dutch photographer Ed van der Elsken. The museum turned his private archive upside down in search of his methods and motivation, resulting in nine rooms covering 40 years of work, including the iconic Woman on a bike sticking out her tongue, which graces the Rijksmuseum, much to the surprise of the subject. Ed van der Elsken Up Close is on until September 13. Website

The run of Sting’s musical The Last Ship, fronted by the man himself, has been extended at Carré theatre in Amsterdam. Best be quick if you want to make it on board. Until September 13. Website

There is still time to catch the impressive but strangely titled exhibition Gerard van Honthorst – Different to Rembrandt at the Centraal Museum in Utrecht. Some 60 paintings and 30 drawings show the 17th-century master for who he was. Until September 13. Website

World.title: Beyond profit: Why Dutch firms want impact-driven leaders
World.content:
The Netherlands is fast becoming a testing ground for business that treats social and environmental impact as a measure of success. Its universities are adapting too: Nyenrode Business University runs an English-language Impact MBA, taught in Amsterdam and Breukelen, that builds sustainability into leadership training rather than setting it apart as a separate subject.

On April 8, 2026, the Netherlands’ National Coordinator for Sustainable Development Goals, Anna Pot, was handed a copy of the recently hashed out Impact Agenda 2030 at the Social Enterprise Government Congress in Nijmegen.

Described by the collaborative coalition of social entrepreneurs, foundations, municipal leaders, knowledge institutions and civil society initiatives that participated in its making as a “national framework for a future-proof and resilient economy”, the Impact Agenda aims to move the Dutch economy towards a system that has social and environmental metrics embedded in its core – not merely as an afterthought after profits are tallied.

“Impact is not a niche, it is a necessity,” is the message the Dutch Impact Ecosystem says it’s sending to national leaders. “And it has real economic value – for impact-driven organisations and traditional businesses alike.”

The agenda – which focusses on such themes as impact governance, procurement and finance, social and digital innovation and education and is in line with the European Commission’s Social Economy Action Plan – is just the latest national accomplishment that cements the Netherlands’ standing as a world leader in the move to sustainability and societal impact in its business sectors.

A recent report looking at how firms balance profit with impact found that of the 77 large companies the private-public consortium surveyed doing business in the Netherlands, the majority believe the initial regulatory hassles of the EU’s CSRD [Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive] are overshadowed by its long-term benefits, all while helping their businesses.

The report found that “Dutch companies are leading the way in integrating impact governance into their strategies.”

Learning laboratory

The country’s strong collaborations between businesses, government and knowledge institutions create an environment of innovation and entrepreneurship that has led professionals worldwide to increasingly choose the Netherlands to learn how businesses can create both commercial success and positive societal change.

In the Netherlands’ dynamic Dutch business ecosystem, leaders have the opportunity to put theory into practice.

New leaders

Driven by European sustainability regulations, evolving investor expectations, rapid technological developments such as AI and growing stakeholder expectations, companies today are looking for leaders who can navigate complexity rather than optimize a single bottom line.

And the country’s universities and knowledge institutions are keeping pace. Nyenrode Business University, with locations in Amsterdam and Breukelen, offers an English-language MBA program focused on creating the future leaders of this brave new business world.

Its Impact MBA was designed as a response to changing employer needs rather than as a traditional MBA program. Instead of teaching sustainability as a standalone subject, the curriculum integrates leadership, digital transformation and sustainability throughout the learning experience.

“Sustainability transitions involve long-term developments with significant short-term implications for organizations,” says Prof. Dr. Nicolas Chevrollier, Professor of Sustainability Transitions and designer of the Impact MBA. “This requires new competences, new collaborations and sometimes entirely new business models.”

Chevrollier emphasises that organizations cannot solve today’s challenges independently. Businesses increasingly operate within ecosystems involving governments, knowledge institutions, investors and civil society, meaning effective leadership depends on building partnerships rather than optimising organisations in isolation.

“Many organisations suffer from tunnel vision,” he says. “To truly innovate, leaders need to broaden their perspective.”

The Impact MBA gives tomorrow’s leaders a chance to do just that: innovation and a systems-thinking approach are embedded in its curriculum, creating business trailblazers who can balance financial and societal objectives while thinking across entire systems instead of just individual organizations.

Are you looking to develop the new capabilities needed for the profound transformations taking place in today’s business world? Then check out Nyenrode ‘s Impact MBA, available both part-time and full-time, or join one of their on-campus and online events to discover more.

World.title: Large explosion at restaurant in Utrecht
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A major explosion occurred early Monday morning at a barbecue restaurant in Utrecht, according to local broadcaster RTV Utrecht.

The blast went off at 1am at the Topkapi restaurant, shattering windows and destroying the front of the building.

No one was injured but nearby residents were evacuated as a precaution.

The restaurant was the target of another bombing in 2023. A 19-year-old from Utrecht was later convicted of the crime. According to the court, he had attempted to extort money from the restaurant’s owner.

The police would not comment on a motivation and are investigating.

World.title: Coalition budget talks still deadlocked with hours to go
World.content:
Plans to cut more than €6 billion from social security and to change the way savings and investments are taxed are in the balance, as the three coalition parties struggle to agree next year’s budget among themselves with only hours to go before it is due for review.

D66, the VVD and the CDA negotiated through the whole of Sunday and into the early hours of Monday without reaching a deal, and are still talking on Monday afternoon. The meeting at which the full cabinet has to sign off the budget, first scheduled for 11am, has been put back twice and is now set for 6pm.

Until last week, the main question was whether the minority coalition could win enough opposition votes to pass the budget. Prime minister Rob Jetten ended those talks on Friday, saying the plans would go to parliament without a majority.

That has left the coalition parties to settle the budget between themselves, and they remain divided. Jetten acknowledged on Friday that the three parties still disagree fundamentally on some key points.

What they are arguing over

Broadcaster NOS reported that two issues are holding up a deal: the box 3 tax and the planned social security cuts.

Box 3 is the tax on income from savings and investments, which the government has been trying to reform for years. The coalition’s spending plans also include cutting more than €6 billion from social security – the benefits paid to people who are unemployed, older or too ill to work.

The largest opposition party, the left-wing PRO, has made scrapping that cut a condition of its support and wants wealthy households taxed more instead. Led by Jesse Klaver, PRO already won a concession from the government this year, when it dropped a plan to raise the retirement age more quickly.

D66 and the CDA want to avoid tilting the budget too far to the right, so as to keep PRO within reach. The VVD is wary of concessions to the left that could sour its relations with the far-right JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.

The coalition could pass the budget through the lower house with JA21 and SGP support, but that combination would leave it well short in the senate, where PRO’s backing offers the more realistic route to a majority.

The draft is due at the Council of State, which reviews the plans before they are presented on Prinsjesdag on September 15.

World.title: The number of English-language bookstores is on the rise
World.content:
Thanks in part to social media, the number of English-language books read in the Netherlands is increasing, and with it, the number of shops catering to those bookworms.

One in five books sold in the Netherlands is in English, according to industry monitor KVB Boekwerk. Broadcaster NOS reported that over the past four years, at least ten new English-language bookshops have opened their doors in the country, including in Tilburg, Utrecht and Amersfoort.

The increase is attributed in large part to social media, particularly the popularity of BookTok, a community of content creators making videos primarily about books.

Many bookstores now stock books popular on BookTok and have entire displays of what’s currently going viral online.

These new shops are often operated by people who came from outside of the publishing world. Daan Severijns changed course after a career in IT. He runs Books and Beans in Tilburg together with his partner Ana Maria Vallejo Perez .

“We used to philosophise about what we would like to do after retirement: run a small bookstore in a beautiful location. Then I lost my job, and the wish quickly grew into what it is today,” he told NOS.

World.title: Big cities buckling under homelessness and drugs, says Halsema
World.content:
Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema has called on the government to take national action on rising homelessness, crack addiction and public disorder, warning that they are eroding quality of life in the country’s biggest cities and cannot be tackled by city authorities alone.

Speaking in an interview with Het Parool and on current-affairs programme Buitenhof, Halsema said the same pressures were affecting all four big cities – Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht – and that the government was partly responsible.

“The problems in the big cities are gradually overwhelming us,” she said, calling for “major measures” from The Hague.

Amsterdam has 3,644 recorded people who cause public disorder, Halsema said, though she stressed the number of homeless people is far higher. The most recent count, in 2024, recorded more than 15,000 people in the Amsterdam region as homeless or at risk of losing their home, though the city says the true figure is higher.

“Public poverty”

The most visible problems come from a combination of homelessness and crack use, particularly in the city’s parks, which Halsema said was distressing residents and traumatising for the addicts themselves.

She said that debates in The Hague ahead of the budget focus on income and taxation, while cities are left dealing with “public poverty”: the visible result of underfunded services, the housing shortage and a strain on the mental health care system.

She wants the government to structurally improve mental health provision and overhaul rules governing foreign workers.

Foreign workers

About 1,500 of the people causing nuisance come from eastern Europe, according to Halsema, many of them foreign workers who end up losing their housing and their jobs because the two are tied together. Amsterdam organisations have previously helped hundreds return home, a significant number of them crack users.

Employers in the Netherlands are allowed to house foreign workers while deducting the cost from their wages, currently up to a quarter of the minimum wage. Former social affairs minister Mariëlle Paul ended a planned phase-out of that rule last year, a decision Halsema branded “disastrous”.

She wants the rule reversed, faster action against rogue employment agencies, and more money for shelter: of the €13 million she said was made available last year for housing foreign workers, Amsterdam received €2 million, which she said is far too little.

Sleeping outdoors

Amsterdam stopped fining people for sleeping outdoors in June last year and, like Utrecht, now wants to decriminalise it entirely. Halsema says fines only push homeless people further into debt and further from help.

Police have raised concerns about that approach. In a review by the local health service in April, officers said people were coming to Amsterdam because they were allowed to sleep outdoors there, and that police and other enforcement teams had fewer tools to steer them towards help.

With annual budget talks ongoing, Halsema said the government must act: “Enable us to make sure our city is in order and liveable.”

World.title: Psychiatrist apologises to parents over euthanasia letter
World.content:

A psychiatrist who co-signed a letter calling for an investigation into the parents of a 17-year-old who died by euthanasia in 2023 has said he apologised to them in 2024, telling the TV programme Zomergasten the letter must have been “incredibly painful” for them to read.

Psychiatrist Jim van Os was one of 14 prominent doctors who signed a letter urging the public prosecution office to take action in the case of Milou, a teen suffering from depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts.

“For the parents, it can be incredibly painful to read something like this, and I have also apologized for that,” van Os said on Sunday.

The letter asked prosecutors to investigate the extent to which Milou’s parents and treating physicians had influenced her choice for voluntary euthanasia.

The psychiatrists had never spoken to the girl or her parents and doctors. The federation of doctors KNMG has called the letter “indecent and unacceptable”.

Milou had suffered from mental health problems from the age of 11 following sexual abuse. She was again sexually abused in an institution by another patient.

After years of treatment and various suicide attempts, she chose euthanasia at the age of 17 on the grounds of unbearable mental suffering.

The psychiatrist who approved her decision acted in accordance with the guidelines, the regional euthanasia review committee RTE found.

The committee reviews all euthanasia procedures to make sure the correct procedures have been followed and reports back to the prosecution service.

The girl’s parents have sued the Public Prosecution Service to disclose the names of all doctors behind the controversial letter. A court in The Hague will give its verdict on Thursday.
