A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000). The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city. To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏 Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala. Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn — Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026 On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents. The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków. According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B., has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison. “The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention. An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”. “We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.” At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far. Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child. As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps. “Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw. Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous. Godzina ciszy w Krakowie. Mieszkańcy upamiętniają parę, która zginęła w sobotniej tragedii przy ulicy Solnej. Na miejsce przybyły tłumy. „Nie chcemy bać się chodzić po chodnikach” – apelują.@RadioKrakow pic.twitter.com/DlOn5GvyL5 — Elżbieta Raczyńska (@_eraczynska) August 25, 2026 Acting mayor Stanisław Kracik said that an inspection of the street carried out after the accident had not shown any problems with the existing signage or need for traffic-calming measures. He added, however, that the city would be installing a speed bump. “I believe that this is simply what we should do…as a kind of expression of solidarity with the victims of this tragedy,” he said, quoted by broadcaster TVN. City police said they had been monitoring and taking action about road safety issues in the district for years, but that the street in question had not previously been reported as a particularly dangerous place, with just one incident causing one injury in the five years before the fatal accident. MPs from The Left have called for tougher rules on illegal street racing, saying police currently do not have sufficient legal tools. It comes after a crash on Saturday in which four men died after their car was filmed driving at dangerously high speeds https://t.co/OSRvyPAtVA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2023 The police also claimed that Kraków is “one of the safest cities” in Poland, with 768 road accidents per 100,000 residents this year, compared to over 1,000 in some other cities. However, TVN points out that the same statistics show that, this year, Kraków has had 71 accidents per 100,000 inhabitants in which someone was injured or killed, compared to 28 in Katowice and 27 in Warsaw. Road safety in Poland has improved dramatically, with the country recording the EU’s largest decline in road deaths between 2019 and 2024. However, its overall number of road deaths in relation to population is still above the EU average. Road deaths have fallen by 35% in Poland since 2019, which is the largest decline in the EU. World.title: Polish student accused of planning Islamist terrorist attack on Christmas market to stand trial
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish student is to stand trial accused of planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market in Poland as an act of support for Islamic State. On Monday, prosecutors announced that they have filed an indictment against the 20-year-old suspect, a student at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) who can be named only as Mateusz W. under Polish privacy law. Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesman for Poland’s security services, confirmed that Mateusz W. had been “preparing a mass attack at a Christmas market, which he planned to carry out using explosive materials”. Wracamy do sprawy 20-letniego Mateusza W. – studenta Katolickiego Uniwersytetu Lubelskiego podejrzewanego o przygotowywanie masowego zamachu na jednym z jarmarków świątecznych, którego planował dokonać z wykorzystaniem materiałów wybuchowych. Do Sądu Okręgowego w Koszalinie… https://t.co/6vGPcjiDnc pic.twitter.com/seFGV8nHMz — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026 The suspect was detained late last year, when details of his alleged plot and plans to establish contact with Islamic State were first revealed. He has remained in custody since then. Though the authorities have confirmed that Mateusz W. was a first-year student at KUL, a leading Catholic university that counts the late Pope John Paul II among its former students and lecturers, and that they have also searched premises in the province of Łódź, they have not revealed where his alleged attack was planned. However, prosecutors reported today that the suspect had established contacts through which he could gain access to explosive materials and devices, had looked for bomb-making instructions, and had tried to recruit others to his terrorist cause. “Mateusz W.’s actions were intended to further the policies of the terrorist organisation known as Islamic State and to seriously intimidate people with views contrary to the ideology espoused by the suspect,” wrote Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska, a spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office. In a separate statement, the Internal Security Agency (ABW) revealed that the suspect had “intended to join a terrorist organisation affiliated with the so-called Islamic State and sought people who could help him carry out this plan”. Neither the security services nor prosecutors have indicated whether Mateusz W. denied or admitted to his alleged crimes or has offered any explanation for his actions. If convicted of preparing a mass attack, he could face up to ten years in prison. Last year, after Mateusz W. was detained, Dobrzyński said that he came from a devoutly Catholic family but had become “deeply infatuated with Islam” and had “fallen in love with terrorism”. In an appeal to parents, Dobrzyński said that, “if you see your children interested in Islam, communism, or fascism, and collecting all sorts of information and items on the subject, that’s the first sign. Take care of your own children, because things can only get worse from there”. Poland has detained a man who was allegedly planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market as an act of support for Islamic State. The suspect, a 19-year-old Pole, had become "infatuated with Islam", say the security services https://t.co/N4WDVZdlai — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 After news of Mateusz W.’s detention emerged, KUL suspended his student status. The university’s spokesman, Wojciech Andrusiewicz, said that neither fellow students nor lecturers had noticed any unusual behaviour by the suspect. World.title: Polish WWII massacre victims reburied in Ukraine at ceremony attended by officials from both countries
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of 55 Poles – around half of them children – massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, many of whose bones show signs of brutal deaths, were exhumed this summer after Ukraine recently ended a moratorium on searches for tens of thousands of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres who are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. “This is an important moment for [the victims’] families, but also the Polish state, because this funeral follows decades of waiting,” said Polish culture minister Marta Cienkowska at the ceremony in Ostrówki (Ostrovky in Ukrainian), a depopulated former village that, before the war, was part of Poland and now lies in Ukraine. “Poland has the right and obligation to speak about the crimes committed against its citizens. It has the obligation to commemorate the victims, search for their remains, and provide them with a dignified burial…We will continue this work…everywhere that the graves of the victims of the Volhynian crimes still remain.” Pogrzeb ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej Na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach na terytorium Ukrainy odbyła się uroczystość pogrzebowa 55 ofiar zbrodni dokonanej 30 sierpnia 1943 roku. W uroczystości, zorganizowanej w 83. rocznicę tragicznych wydarzeń,… pic.twitter.com/4dXPOj4m7y — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) August 30, 2026 Others to attend the reburial included deputy Ukrainian culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi; Vitaly Skomarovsky, the bishop of Lutsk and president of Ukraine’s Roman Catholic episcopate; Piotr Zgorzelski, the deputy speaker of the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament; and former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. Karol Polejowski, the deputy head of Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which led the exhumation work, said that the presence of Ukrainian representatives “fills me with optimism for the future”. While Polish President Karol Nawrocki did not attend, one of his advisors, Jakub Banaszek, read a letter on his behalf, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will never forget those who died in agony simply because they were Poles,” wrote Nawrocki. “We will not cease our efforts to ensure that all our compatriots murdered by members of the OUN-UPA are properly buried and commemorated.” ✝️ W 8⃣3⃣. rocznicę zbrodni dokonanej przez ukraińskich szowinistów, na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach pochowaliśmy ofiary ludobójstwa na Wołyniu. 🔻🔻🔻 pic.twitter.com/5oh3uiCKX4 — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 30, 2026 The Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Poles were killed, were led by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was a partisan group founded by a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) faithful to nationalist leader Stepan Bandera. They sought to ethnically cleanse areas that they saw as Ukrainian territory by wiping out other ethnic groups, in particular the large Polish population. Massacres took place in dozens of villages, including Ostrówki and the neighbouring Wola Ostrowiecka (Volya Ostrovetska in Ukrainian), where on 30 August 1943 the UPA killed over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Exhumations previously took place on the site of the two villages in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Earlier this month, the IPN announced the results of that work. They uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres by Ukrainian nationalists during WWII have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools https://t.co/LbLPzJcG1b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 8, 2026 The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit. Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where Zelensky’s counterpart Karol Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest honour. In his letter read at Sunday’s ceremony, Nawrocki warned those who “continue the tradition of Banderite ideology” that they “place themselves outside the community of citizens of the free, civilised world” and are sending “a clear sign of hostility towards Poland and Poles”. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Since the crisis broke out in May, there have been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Earlier this month, Zelensky signed a law establishing a new national pantheon of Ukrainian heroes. Poland has warned that the inclusion of figures associated with the massacres could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. A survey conducted this month by Rating Group, a Ukrainian research agency, which asked Ukrainians to name their country’s greatest hero found that Bandera was the fourth most popular choice, having been chosen by 11% of respondents. World.title: Poland is terrible at promoting itself – but has never had better press
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Two incidents this month have highlighted how state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad often disappoint. Yet, at the same time, the country has never had better international press. Politicians should let Poland’s successes speak for themselves, and support those already telling its story. Poles care a lot about what the world thinks of their country. Major Polish media outlets regularly devote entire articles to what Western journalists, commentators and influencers are saying about Poland. “A German showed what he saw on the streets of Poland,” read one typical recent headline by Onet, Poland’s biggest news website, which devoted an entire report to one video by a German-speaking TikToker with around 7,000 followers. One rarely sees such reports in more self-confident Western countries. Given Poland’s history, such sensitivity regarding the country’s status is not surprising. Poland was, up until the 18th century, a major European country. But, for most of the last 250 years, it has been under foreign subjugation. Only since 1989 has it been able to develop independently, and Poles are understandably keen for the world to take note of their return to the top table. Poland has emerged as Europe’s undisputed growth champion over the past 35 years. In the first part of a new series of articles and podcasts, @AlicjaPtak4 explores the reasons behind Poland's rapid economic development, and the dangers that may lie ahead https://t.co/bW3bnV7Ozn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2025 Polish politicians are also inevitably eager to capitalise on such sentiment by showing voters that they are making an effort to promote Poland abroad. The problem is that such efforts are often poorly conceived and executed – as two examples this month have shown. In mid-August, the sport and tourism ministry launched a new advertising campaign intended to attract visitors from western Europe and the United States. However, the first advert – featuring Polish football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, and actor Nikodem Rozbicki playing Fryderyk Chopin – was widely panned in Poland. Res Futura, an organisation that monitors social media sentiment, found that 85% of comments about the advert were negative. The campaign’s slogan – “Poland. More than you expected” – is negative and lacking confidence. The Polish Tourism Organisation says it is based on research showing that visitors to Poland are often positively surprised by how nice it is. Yet, while that is undoubtedly true, it does not mean it is a good idea to try to attract potential tourists by focusing on their low expectations. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The video also has no narrative, with the creators seeming to think that showing famous faces will be enough. Rubik does not speak a single word, while Eisenberg says only “Poland” and Lewandowski “More than you expected”. The film itself does nothing to show that Poland is more than anyone expects. In fact, its depressingly colourless palette and focus on Warsaw’s Stalinist Palace of Science and Culture actually reinforce (false) stereotypes of Poland as grey, dull and post-communist. The country has so many interesting and colourful places that could have been showcased instead. The advert is also a wasted opportunity to tell a story about the film’s stars, especially Eisenberg, who has reconnected with his family’s Polish roots, produced a critically acclaimed movie set in Poland, and last year obtained citizenship. Instead, Chopin dominates the film, but his dialogue is incoherent. When he says, “Warsaw is where my heart is”, almost no potential visitors would understand that this is a reference to the real Chopin’s heart being transported from Paris, where he died, to Warsaw, where it is now entombed in a church. Not long after that advert launched, another controversy emerged around a state official, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, who had been appointed only weeks earlier by the government to lead the promotion of Poland. It quickly transpired that a report she had authored last year on creating a national brand – and which appeared to have played a big part in her getting the new job – contained significant errors, questionable methodology, and bizarre language. Many parts showed signs of being AI-generated. Mróz-Gorgoń, who has now resigned, insists that the report was the genuine product of work by her and her team at Marka Polska (Brand Poland), a think tank she leads. However, that is not particularly reassuring given the report’s content. Many parts are simply obvious: at the end of the 26-page text, the three recommendations for the government are to “develop a coherent, long-term national branding strategy”, “invest in promotional campaigns in key markets”, and “coordinate between ministries and other entities”. Other sections are very strange, such as noting that “Germany does not build its brand on the Holocaust”. But perhaps the most telling aspect is that, although the introduction claims it is “a comprehensive report on building…a coherent, long-term branding strategy in the international arena”, the document focuses entirely on how Poles themselves view their own country (its title is even A Self-Portrait of the Poles). It includes no research into what foreigners know or think about Poland and what could interest or attract them. While any national branding exercise should of course take account of the views of the native population, it is clearly incomplete without research into the target of such a campaign, the outside world. Yet that is sadly typical of many state-led efforts to promote Poland, which focus more on pleasing a domestic audience – the voters that politicians want to keep happy – than on being truly outward looking. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland's brand abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing major errors, bizarre language, and signs of being generated by AI https://t.co/9fpfzFCFuI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 It should be noted that such failings are nothing new. Successive governments have been responsible for botched efforts to promote Poland. The uninspiring slogan “Poland. More than you expected” has been used since 2021. A previous one, “Polska. Spring Into”, launched in 2014, was simply bizarre and quickly disappeared. In 2016, the former Law and Justice (PiS) government established the Polish National Foundation (PFN), which was pumped full of money from state-owned companies and tasked with promoting Poland abroad. Instead, it focused much of its efforts on domestic activity, often intended to support PiS’s political agenda. The work it did do internationally was often of questionable efficacy, such as spending millions on buying a yacht, naming it “I Love Poland”, then attempting to sail it around the world (before it ended up breaking down and getting stuck in port). A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds. The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026 Yet, despite woeful state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad, the country has in recent times been enjoying a soaring international reputation. Western media have been full of articles about the country’s economic success; about how not only are Polish emigrants returning from the UK, but many Brits are moving to Poland too; about how Poles are becoming major buyers of property in Spain; about how companies with roots in Poland, such as InPost and ElevenLabs, are pioneering their industries. Social media feeds are full of influencers extolling Polish cities, with their safe, clean streets; the beauty of Polish nature, with its mountains, lakes and beaches; and the sense of dynamic development that you can feel as soon as you set foot in the country. Last weekend,@thetimes reported on how Brits are moving to Poland. This weekend, on how Poles are replacing Brits as property owners in Spain. pic.twitter.com/IDDdDlluTE — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) June 21, 2026 This positive publicity is largely organic – it is the product of Poland’s own actual successes, not of artificial efforts to create an image of success. It is generated from the bottom up, not from the top down. While the state can play a role – for example, by arranging visits for foreign journalists and influencers and supporting media and institutions that are already telling Poland’s story – it would be better for politicians to focus on creating the conditions for those successes, rather than concocting cockeyed schemes to promote them. World.title: Polish government sets out draft 2027 budget with deficit remaining at 7.1% of GDP
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing. The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024. Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok. Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków 🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026 The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year. Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year. Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty. The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level. Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year. Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates. Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising. What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025 The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules. In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. “The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.” Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Efforts to reduce the deficit have also been complicated by political stalemate between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed several fiscal measures, including tax increases. Nawrocki did, however, approve a new levy on banks that came into force this year. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. However, speaking today, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the 2027 budget reflects Poland’s position at a time when war is being waged across its eastern border and other conflicts are weighing on the country’s finances. Meanwhile, 2027 will also see pivotal parliamentary elections, at which Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, will seek a second term while the right-wing opposition, supported by Nawrocki, will attempt to win power. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead. The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger. In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine. The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered. Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later. “It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN. The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning. “In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living. However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element. Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin. “The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023 Poliński believes that the woman may have been ill or had a physical or mental disability, leading her neighbours to treat her badly while she was alive and fear that she would haunt them after her death. However, the researchers found no skeletal evidence of trauma, violence or disease that might explain her treatment, and her cause of death remains unknown. The Pień cemetery, which has not been marked on maps, contains several other unusual burials, including a child buried face down with a padlock beneath the foot and skeletons weighed down with rocks. This has led researchers to suggest that the cemetery may have been located on unconsecrated ground, away from a church or chapel, and used for people who were poor, disgraced, feared, or otherwise excluded from the community. Zosia’s burial, however, appears to have been unusual in another respect. Analysis suggests she was of relatively high social status. Traces of silk and gold-and-silver thread near her skull suggest she wore an expensive cap, a luxury item generally associated with nobility or wealth. Two years ago, sculptor and artist Oscar D. Nilsson unveiled a 3D facial reconstruction of Zosia, based on measurements of her skull and skeletal clues about her age, weight and health. The reconstruction shows a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose. “It’s really ironic, in a way,” Nilsson told Reuters at the time. “These people burying her, they did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead…We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life.” A team of scientists has reconstructed the face of a 400-year-old woman, once believed by her neighbors to be a vampire, revealing the human story buried by supernatural beliefs https://t.co/Q6sipo7h4O pic.twitter.com/0gLVIEfaZi — Reuters (@Reuters) October 30, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. A dispute has emerged between Poland’s government and the office of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over whether Poland would be willing to host allied nuclear weapons. Deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski announced on Thursday that Poland wants to participate in the US-led NATO nuclear sharing programme, but without actually hosting warheads. That prompted criticism from Nawrocki’s senior foreign policy aide, Marcin Przydacz, who says Poland should host such weapons. Jedno zdanie wiceszefa MON wystarczyło, by wywołać polityczną burzę wokół kwestii broni jądrowej w Polsce. Paweł Zalewski stwierdził w Kwaterze Głównej NATO w Brukseli, że Polska nie chce głowic nuklearnych na swoim terytorium. Kilka godzin później zareagował szef MON Władysław… pic.twitter.com/EqjTPKqidg — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) August 28, 2026 Zalewski met on Thursday with Elbridge Colby, US under secretary of defence for policy, at NATO’s headquarters in Brussels. Afterwards, he was asked by reporters if an expanded future US military presence in Poland might include nuclear weapons. “No. I would like to say this very clearly and openly: Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory,” replied Zalewski, quoted by broadcaster TVN. The minister added that Poland still wants to be part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme. However, he said that this could be achieved without hosting the weapons themselves. Those remarks triggered criticism from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. Former PiS defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak said that refusing to host warheads “in practice means renouncing participation in nuclear sharing”. “Poland should strive for full participation in nuclear sharing,” added Błaszczak. “This is not a matter of Poland possessing its own nuclear weapons, but of strengthening NATO’s nuclear deterrence on the eastern flank.” Criticism also came from other sources, including retired Brigadier General Stanisław Koziej, who served as head of the National Security Bureau (BBN) of former President Bronisław Komorowski, who is an ally of the current government. Koziej called Zalewski’s announcement “an incomprehensible strategic mistake in the field of deterrence”. He said that, to deter Russia, Vladimir Putin must know that there is the possibility Poland could host nuclear weapons. Chęci nie odstraszają. Odstraszają realne zdolności – własne i sojusznicze. A przede wszystkim takie, o jakich użyciu sami decydujemy. To elementarz, który warto przypomnieć https://t.co/Nc3xXnA7bU — Paweł Zalewski (@ZalewskiPawel) August 27, 2026 Late on Thursday, Zalewski commented on the controversy. He rejected Błaszczak’s claim that refusing to host warheads would effectively exclude Poland from nuclear sharing. “We want to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme without wanting the stationing of nuclear weapons in Poland,” he wrote. “Thanks to our efforts, NATO has opened up precisely such a possibility.” In response to Koziej, Zalewski argued that “intentions do not deter, real capabilities do…above all, those whose use we ourselves decide upon”. Meanwhile, defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also weighed in, declaring that “Poland remains strongly interested in participating in the NATO nuclear sharing programme” and is also “conducting talks regarding the proposal for participation in a European nuclear protective umbrella”. Kosiniak-Kamysz did not, however, comment on the issue of Poland potentially hosting warheads. Rozwiewając wszelkie wątpliwości: Polska jest niezmiennie zainteresowana udziałem w programie NATO Nuclear Sharing. Prowadzimy także rozmowy na temat propozycji uczestnictwa w europejskim nuklearnym parasolu ochronnym. Stanowisko naszego rządu jest w tych kwestiach… — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) August 27, 2026 On Friday morning, Przydacz, who is the head of President Nawrocki’s International Policy Bureau (BPM), joined the criticism of Zalewski, calling his comments “bizarre, absurd and completely inconsistent with what Poland has been saying so far and what the policy of the Polish state is”. “Both the presidential palace and the executive branch of the government have so far supported Poland joining the nuclear sharing programme as part of its deterrence policy,” he continued. Przydacz added that “it is not true” the country wants to participate without actually hosting warheads. “Poland also wants to have warheads on its territory,” he said. Nawrocki, who is a close ally of President Donald Trump, has made clear his support for Poland seeking a nuclear sharing arrangement with the United States. But it remains unclear exactly what the government’s plans are. Earlier this year, Poland entered discussions with France over the extension of the French “nuclear umbrella” over Europe. Later, however, Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated that Poland would not want to actually host French nuclear-armed aircraft. Both last year and this year, Tusk has also hinted that Poland could seek to develop its own independent nuclear deterrent. However, Colby made clear that the US would “strenuously oppose” European countries such as Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian states seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has regularly clashed with the government, including vetoing a record number of laws. However, the two sides have sought to present a more united front on issues of national security. The United States would “strenuously oppose” Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian countries seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons, says a senior Pentagon official. His comments come amid discussions in Poland and Europe over nuclear deterrence https://t.co/e9J8tNxcc9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Prague Philharmonic Could Begin Construction in 2028. New Visuals Reveal Design
World.content:
Prague has taken another step toward building the long-planned Vltava Philharmonic.

The Prague Development Company (PDS) submitting an application for planning permission and new visualizations revealing the project in greater detail.

The application covers not only the Philharmonic building but also the surrounding public spaces, transport infrastructure and connections to the existing metro, tram, road, cycling and pedestrian networks.



If the permitting process stays on schedule, the city expects to receive the necessary approval in the first quarter of 2027. A tender for the construction company would then follow, with building work potentially starting in the first quarter of 2028.

The project is planned for the Bubny-Zátory district, near the existing Vltavská metro station. The new cultural complex is expected to be completed in 2033, when trial operations could begin.

The building was designed by Danish architecture studio BIG – Bjarke Ingels Group, which won an international competition in May 2022. Preparation of the detailed permit documentation began in 2025.

The complex will have three underground levels and six floors above ground. It will contain five music halls, creative spaces, restaurants and other facilities.

The project is also intended to provide new premises for the Prague Symphony Orchestra FOK and music collections belonging to the Municipal Library of Prague. The Czech Philharmonic is also expected to gain additional facilities, addressing the limitations of its current premises.

Construction could start in early 2028

The current estimated cost of the Philharmonic building is around CZK 12.33 billion, including equipment but excluding VAT. The surrounding infrastructure and public spaces are expected to cost an additional CZK 5 billion, also excluding VAT.

World.title: Tiny Steps, Big Milestones: What Really Matters When Toddlers Start Preschool
World.content:
For a one-year-old, starting preschool is not about learning letters or sitting through lessons.

It is about feeling safe without Mum or Dad nearby, discovering the joy of playing alongside other children, and slowly gaining the confidence to explore the world independently. At Tiny Tots in Prague, these small everyday moments are at the heart of the programme.

A favourite toy clutched tightly in one hand. A cautious look back at Mum or Dad from the classroom door. Perhaps a few tears (from either side).

For families with children aged one or two, the first experience of leaving a little one in someone else’s care can feel like a very big step.

And for the child, it is one too.



At this age, development happens through moments that can look almost insignificant to adults: reaching for a spoon without help, joining another child in play, recognising a familiar song, saying a new word, or feeling comfortable enough to wander a little further away from a trusted adult.

These are precisely the moments that Tiny Tots, a programme for children aged 1–2 at Nessie English Preschool, part of Park Lane International School, is designed to encourage.

Before learning comes feeling safe

For very young children, a good first preschool experience begins with something much more fundamental than an academic curriculum: trust.

“Parents often want to know how their child will cope with separation, whether we can follow the rhythm they are used to at home and, above all, whether their child will really be seen as an individual,” says Catalina Gonzalez-Got, who leads the Tiny Tots programme.

Catalina knows the feeling from both sides. An early-years educator with international experience, she is also a mother herself. Becoming a parent, she says, gave her a much deeper understanding of how emotional it can be to entrust a young child to somebody else for the first time.

That is why settling in is treated as a process rather than a test that a toddler is expected to pass on day one.

Some children may quickly become curious about their new surroundings. Others need more time, reassurance and proximity to a familiar adult before they are ready to explore.

Both are perfectly normal. The goal is to allow each child to find that confidence at their own pace.

For toddlers, play is serious business

Adults sometimes separate “playing” and “learning”. Toddlers do not.

When a child squishes playdough between their fingers, listens to a story, sings along to a familiar song, explores the garden or watches another toddler build something, they are constantly learning.

They are practising movement and coordination. They are discovering cause and effect. They are learning how to communicate, negotiate space with other children, manage emotions and make choices.

Tiny Tots therefore follows a play-based approach inspired by the English Early Years Foundation Stage framework, with activities designed around the developmental needs of one- and two-year-olds.

There are no miniature school desks or pressure to perform.

Instead, children encounter language, movement, music, creative activities, sensory experiences, stories and outdoor play as a natural part of their day.

The programme keeps the class to a maximum of eight children, allowing teachers to pay close attention to individual personalities, routines and developmental stages.

English without the flashcards

The same philosophy applies to language.

At one or two years old, learning English does not mean memorising vocabulary lists. Children absorb language through relationships and repetition: hearing the same words during snack time, listening to songs, following simple instructions, sharing a picture book or hearing an adult describe what is happening during play.

Tiny Tots provides an English-language environment, giving children regular, natural exposure to the language throughout their day.

Catalina, who raises her own child in a multilingual family, sees communication as something that should grow out of connection rather than performance.

Toddlers often understand far more than they can say, she explains. What matters is creating a positive environment in which language is associated with people, experiences and emotions that make sense to the child.

Learning to do things “all by myself”

Anyone who lives with a toddler knows how powerful those words can be.

Between one and two, children increasingly want to try things independently — even when the result is a spoon on the floor, mismatched shoes or a task that takes considerably longer than if an adult simply did it for them.

Tiny Tots gives children safe opportunities to practise that emerging independence while knowing that an adult is close by when they need help.

The milestone may be eating more independently, choosing an activity, joining a group song, approaching another child or simply becoming comfortable enough to explore a new corner of the room.

For a toddler, these are significant achievements.

And independence does not mean pushing children away from adults. In fact, the opposite is often true: children are more willing to explore when they know they have a trusted person to return to.

A small community for Prague’s smallest residents

For international families in particular, early-years programmes can provide something else that is easy to overlook: a sense of community.

Many parents raising children in Prague live far from grandparents, siblings and the wider family network that might otherwise form part of everyday life.

A nurturing preschool environment can therefore become more than somewhere a child spends part of the day. Familiar teachers, other children and their families can gradually become part of the support network that makes a new city feel more like home.

Tiny Tots is based at Nessie English Preschool in Prague 5, in a quiet residential setting with its own garden. The programme combines experienced early-years teachers, personalised attention and structured routines with plenty of room for children simply to play, discover and be little.

Because at one or two years old, success does not need to look impressive.

Sometimes it is a child who cried at the door last week walking in happily today.

Sometimes it is making a first little friend.

Sometimes it is a new word, a messy painting, a favourite song or the confidence to let go of a teacher’s hand and go exploring alone.

Those tiny steps are exactly where the big journey begins.

Tiny Tots at Nessie English Preschool is designed for children aged 1–2 years. Families interested in the programme can arrange a visit to the Prague 5 campus to see the environment and meet the team.

Enrolment for the 2026/27 school year is now open.

World.title: Wine Harvest Festivals in Prague in September: The Full Guide
World.content:
Every September, Prague celebrates vinobraní, the traditional wine harvest festival marking the end of the grape season.

Visitors can look forward to concerts, dance and theatre performances, food stalls, and tastings of young wine and the seasonal favorite burčák (partially fermented grape juice). The festivals are family-friendly, offering children’s theatre, horse rides, folk craft demonstrations, competitions, and workshops.



Here is an overview of the main wine festivals in Prague in 2026:

Vinohrady Wine Harvest Festival

September 11–12, 2026, 10:00–21:00

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad

Facebook

Winemakers from across Europe — Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Romania, Serbia, Ukraine, and Poland — will join Czech and Moravian producers.

Alongside wine, expect a wide range of food: sausages, cheeses, potato spirals, langoše (fried dough with toppings), and traditional Wallachian cakes (frgály). The festival also offers live music and a children’s zone with a playground, carousel, and creative workshops. Admission is free.

Wine Harvest at Prague Castle

September 5–6, 2026, 11:00–18:00

Royal Garden & Ball Game Hall, Prague Castle, Hradčany

hrad.cz

Set in the historic Royal Garden of Prague Castle, this festival features tastings of Czech and Moravian wines, sparkling wines, fresh grape juice, burčák, and high-quality local produce. The program includes folk ensembles, historical fencing, and family activities.

Entry to the garden is free; a tasting glass costs 120 CZK.

Grébovka Wine Festival

September 18, 2026 (14:00–20:00) at náměstí Míru

September 19, 2026 (13:00–20:00) at Havlíčkovy sady (Grébovka Park)

Facebook

Organized by Prague 2, the Grébovka Festival is one of the city’s largest and most popular wine events. Set in Havlíčkovy sady (often described as a hidden gem of Vinohrady), the festival offers wine tastings, culinary specialties, live music, dance performances, and a cultural program celebrating wine traditions. Families can enjoy workshops, theatre, competitions, and children’s activities.

St. Clare’s Vineyard Harvest Festival

September 12–13, 2026

Prague Botanical Garden, Fata Morgana greenhouse, Troja

botanicka.cz

Hosted at the St. Clare’s Vineyard in the Prague Botanical Garden, this festival is renowned for its carefully made burčák, produced from handpicked grapes. Guests can sample varietal wines, cuvées, and brandies from this rare Prague vineyard, along with wines from leading Czech and Moravian producers. Guided cellar tours, food stalls, live music, and terrace dancing complete the program.

Troja Wine Harvest Festival

September 13, 2026, 11:00–20:00

Gardens of Troja Chateau, Prague 7

Facebook

Held in the baroque Troja Chateau, this festival combines wine tastings from Czech, Moravian, and international producers with burčák, traditional food, and live music. Children’s activities include games, workshops, and a kids’ zone. Admission is free.

St. Wenceslas Wine Festival

September 28, 2026, 12:00–18:00

Villa Richter & St. Wenceslas Vineyard, Prague Castle

Facebook

World.title: Czechia Spent CZK 19 Billion on COVID Vaccines and Used Less Than Half
World.content:
The Czech Republic has spent roughly CZK 19 billion on COVID-19 vaccines since 2020, but fewer than half of the 41 million doses supplied under its pandemic-era procurement agreement were ultimately used in the country.

More than 18 million doses expired and had to be destroyed, representing a value of about CZK 8 billion.

A further four million doses were donated to other countries, according to information provided by the Czech Ministry of Health in response to a request from the Czech Technical Committee.



For the 2026-27 vaccination season, around 900,000 doses will be available in the country. By comparison, fewer than one-third of that number was administered during the previous season. The vaccination season runs from September through the end of August the following year.

Demand for COVID-19 vaccination has fallen sharply since the initial rollout. More than 15 million doses were administered during the first year vaccines were widely available. A year later, demand had fallen to roughly one-fifth of that level. Between 2022 and 2023, interest dropped by more than 80 percent, followed by further declines of about one-third in subsequent years.

Only about 1,500 doses had been administered by July 26 this year. Most vaccinations, however, take place during the autumn months.

The low demand has contributed to substantial vaccine waste. When the original purchases were made, authorities faced considerable uncertainty over how the pandemic would develop, how many booster doses would be required and how many people would seek vaccination.

Maintaining sufficient supplies was considered necessary in case the epidemiological situation deteriorated.

The Czech Republic is now considering a different approach to future procurement. The Ministry of Health is negotiating with vaccine manufacturers, health insurance companies and medical organisations over supplies and financing for the 2027-28 season. The talks are taking into account both the expected demand and the cost-effectiveness of vaccination.

World.title: Foreign Pupils on the Rise in Czech Schools — Nearly One in Five in Prague
World.content:
Of the nearly one million pupils attending Czech primary schools last academic year, almost 8% were foreign nationals, most commonly from Ukraine.

According to the Czech Statistical Office (CSO), Prague recorded the highest proportion, with foreign pupils making up 18% of all children in its primary schools.

Compulsory education is mandatory for Czech citizens as well as citizens of other European Union member states who reside in the Czech Republic for more than 90 days. The requirement also applies to foreign nationals with long-term residence permits.

Their children therefore have the same rights as Czech children, including access to free education, school meals and extracurricular activities.



The number of foreign pupils increased significantly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, nearly doubling that year. Their numbers have continued to rise ever since. Today, children from Ukraine account for 5% of all pupils in the Czech Republic.

The trend is similar in secondary schools, where the proportion of foreign pupils reached its highest level in the past 10 years, at almost 5% of the total.

Although the number of children in primary schools has remained relatively stable at just over one million in recent years, a sharp decline is expected in the coming years due to the falling birth rate, according to Vendula Kašparová of the CSO’s Social Development Statistics Department. The office said the birth rate has been falling continuously for the fifth consecutive year.

The decline is already visible at the kindergarten level. The number of children enrolled in kindergartens fell below 350,000 in the 2025/2026 academic year, the first time this has happened since 2013. Over the past three years, enrolment has dropped by more than 21,000 children, or around 5.8%.

Fewer Children Receiving Deferrals From Starting School

Kašparová identifies another clear trend: fewer children are being granted deferrals from starting compulsory school. Since the 2021/2022 academic year, the proportion of six-year-olds whose school entry was deferred has fallen from 24.1% in September 2021 to 17.7% in September 2025, representing just under 21,000 pupils.

Furthermore, an amendment to the Education Act is expected to reduce the number of deferrals even further. Under the new rules, deferrals will only be granted when justified by a medical condition that prevents a child from attending school.

This could include a serious medical condition following surgery, cancer treatment or a moderate intellectual disability.

World.title: Czechia, the Land of Burgers. More Fast Food Chains Enter the Market
World.content:
The Czech fast food market is expanding beyond its established players, with new international brands entering the country and existing chains opening restaurants in smaller cities.

McDonald’s and KFC continue to build their networks, while brands from Germany, the United States and Poland are looking for opportunities in the Czech Republic.

The expansion is increasingly moving beyond Prague and other major cities, with retail parks becoming an important location for new restaurants.



Burgermeister prepares Czech debut

One of the newest international brands preparing to enter the Czech market is Germany’s Burgermeister. The Berlin-based burger chain plans to open its first restaurant on Wenceslas Square at the beginning of next year.

The company already sees its Prague location as more than a single restaurant. It is also considering further locations across the country.

Popeyes and Burger King continue expanding

Burger King entered the Czech market 18 years ago and now operates around 70 restaurants. Popeyes arrived much later but has expanded quickly, opening 19 locations during its first three years in the country.

The companies are building a network that stretches from smaller regional towns to central Prague. In Králův Dvůr, a town of around 11,000 people, both Burger King and Popeyes operate at the Litavka Retail Park.

Popeyes is preparing additional restaurants at the Eden shopping centre and in the Budějovická area of Prague. The chain is also expanding into regional cities, with planned locations in Klatovy and Písek.

Five Guys adds another international brand

The Czech burger market gained another major international name last December when U.S. chain Five Guys opened its first Prague restaurant.

The restaurant is located in the former Máj department store on Národní Street. Five Guys is known for burgers prepared to order and a wide range of toppings, allowing customers to customise their meals.

Its prices, however, are generally higher than those of traditional fast food chains.

Another U.S. brand, Dave’s Hot Chicken, is also expected to enter the Czech market this year, according to consulting firm Cushman & Wakefield.

The chain specialises in spicy fried chicken and will therefore compete directly with established players such as KFC and Popeyes.

Czech chains are looking beyond their home cities

The expansion is not limited to international companies.

Czech burger chain Mama’s Burger is also developing its network. Originally based in Ostrava, the company has expanded into several larger Czech cities and operates a restaurant at Prague’s Arkády Pankrác shopping centre.

The company is also seeking franchise partners as it looks to increase the number of locations.

World.title: Slavia Prague to Face Bayern Munich, Arsenal and Porto in Champions League
World.content:
Slavia Prague have learned their eight opponents for the 2026/27 UEFA Champions League league phase following Thursday’s draw in Monaco.

Slavia will play four matches at home at Eden Arena and four away.

At home, Slavia will welcome Arsenal, Aston Villa, Villarreal and Lens. Their away fixtures will take them to Bayern Munich, Porto, Fenerbahçe and Sabah Baku in Azerbaijan.



The most high-profile home fixture will be against Arsenal, the reigning Premier League champions. Slavia also faced the London club in last season’s Champions League campaign, making the return meeting at Eden Arena particularly notable.

The toughest away assignment is likely to come in Munich, where Slavia will face six-time European champions Bayern at the Allianz Arena. The team will also travel to Portugal to meet Porto and to Istanbul for a match against Fenerbahçe.

The longest trip of the league phase will be to Baku to face Azerbaijani champions Sabah, who are making their debut in the Champions League league phase.

How the Champions League league phase works

The 2026/27 competition is being played under UEFA’s new league-phase format for the third consecutive season. Instead of a traditional group stage, all 36 teams are placed in one league table.

Each club plays eight matches against eight different opponents, with two opponents drawn from each of the four seeding pots. Every team has four home and four away games.

The top eight teams in the final standings will advance directly to the round of 16. Teams finishing ninth to 24th will enter a knockout playoff for the remaining eight places, while clubs finishing from 25th to 36th will be eliminated.

The league phase begins on September 8–10, with six rounds taking place before the end of 2026. The final two matchdays will be played in January, with the league phase concluding on January 27. UEFA will announce the exact dates and kick-off times for each individual match later.

World.title: MINT Market Returns to Prague’s Náplavka with More Than 130 Local Brands
World.content:
MINT Market returns to Prague’s Rašín Embankment on Sunday, September 6, bringing more than 130 independent brands and makers to the Vltava riverbank.

From 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., visitors can browse a wide selection of independent fashion, jewellery, ceramics, natural cosmetics, illustrations and original accessories, with many of the products made by small Czech and Prague-based businesses.



The popular design market is also known for its relaxed atmosphere, food stalls and chill-out area. Admission is free, and the riverside venue is fully accessible. The event is suitable for visitors of all ages.

MINT Market has been supporting independent and local creators since 2010.

Over the past 16 years, the project has grown from a small market into a nationwide platform, hosting more than 450 events in over 20 Czech cities and bringing together a community of more than 1,500 designers and makers.

For visitors, the September event offers a chance to discover products that are often made locally and in small quantities, while meeting the people behind the brands directly.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The best design markets in CZ (@mintmarket.cz)

“Supporting small and local brands has been one of the core ideas of our project from the very beginning,” says MINT Market organizer Lenka Šašková.

“We provide creators with a place where they can showcase their products and meet their customers, because nothing can replace a personal meeting.”

The full list of vendors and further information about the September market can be found on the MINT Market website. Updates are also available through the Facebook event and Instagram.

World.title: PM Magyar: Hungary has met all conditions to access frozen EU funds
World.content:
Hungary has met all the European Union’s requirements to access “thousands of billions” of forints in EU funding, “in line with its commitments and by today’s deadline”, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Facebook on Monday.

“Now the funds from Brussels are welcome to arrive,” Magyar said, thanking everyone who had contributed to the Government’s efforts. Hungary has reportedly completed the measures required to unlock around €10 billion from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility, while a total of €16.4 billion in previously frozen EU funds is at stake.

Magyar talks about a more constructive role

Hungary had become a more constructive player within the European Union under the new Government, Magyar said at the Bled Strategic Forum. “But that does not mean that we would not defend Hungarian interests every minute of every day,” he added.

PM Péter Magyar and FM Anita Orbán in Bled, Slovenia. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Magyar also spoke of the need to strengthen the EU’s political leadership, improve its competitiveness and harness the potential of Central European co-operation. He said Hungary was ready to play a more constructive role in the European Union than it had in the past.

‘We have come for our money’

“It is not a great challenge to be more constructive than we were before,” he remarked.

Magyar stressed that the Prime Minister’s duty was to represent the interests of the Hungarian people, just as every EU member state was required to defend its own interests.

If you missed: Hungarian Parliament clears fiscal reforms to unlock additional EU funds

Recalling his first meeting with Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, in Brussels, Magyar said he had made Hungary’s position clear: “We have come for our money.”

Photo: Anadolu/Dursun Aydemir

He described negotiations over €16.4 billion in Hungarian EU funds, which had been frozen for three or four years, as smooth. According to Magyar, Hungary gained access to the money within a single day, although the European Commission is expected to assess the country’s compliance with the agreed milestones before funds are disbursed.

Hungary set to launch EUR 5.5 billion railway upgrade as development plan gets green light

World.title: Péter Magyar in Bled about crisis management, budget deficit, EU affairs, illegal migration, regional cooperation
World.content:
Hungary’s government has already solved several crisis situations since coming to power in May, Prime Minister Péter Magyar told the Bled Strategy Forum in Slovenia on Monday, adding: “I am proud of my government.”

He cited the energy supply crisis due to extreme weather conditions as an example, saying that the solution was provided by “a huge, unprecedented cooperation.” He also said that while his government had inherited a significant deficit, they have managed to shrink it by 2.5 billion euros.

PM Péter Magyar and FM Anita Orbán in Bled, Slovenia. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Straightforward dialogue

A straightforward dialogue is crucial when it comes to resolving problems facing the European Union, Magyar said. Concerning the fight against illegal migration, Magyar said “it is hard to explain to Hungarians why Hungary receives unfair treatment in Brussels.”

Under a European court ruling, Hungary has to pay a significant amount a day “just because we protect the common EU borders … this is not fair,” he said, adding that border control was “one of the most important tasks” of EU member states.

Tisza government ‘more constructive’ than predecessor

The Tisza government is “more constructive than its predecessor in the EU, but it does not mean that we would not promote the Hungarian interest day and night,” the prime minister said at the Bled Strategy Forum on Monday.

The European Union needs to focus on such issues as economic cooperation and competitiveness, he said. “It is not too late for change … we need to decide if the EU just wants to survive or win,” he said, adding that the two ways required two different approaches.

He said “the latter is still not the goal” in Brussels, but added that central Europe “must work to become a winner” and highlighted the importance of regional cooperation.

Regional cooperation important for Hungary, FM Anita Orbán highlighted

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán underscored the importance of regional cooperation ahead of the Bled Strategic Forum, which begins on Monday. Hungary’s security, competitiveness, transport and energy connections, and the European integration of the Western Balkans all depend on how well the country can cooperate in the region, Orbán said in a post on Facebook.

If you missed – Péter Magyar’s government promises a new era for Hungarian schools: should pupils and teachers be celebrating?

The minister is attending the forum in Slovenia, which she described as “one of the most important foreign policy meetings in central and south-eastern Europe”, where political and diplomatic leaders gather to discuss the region’s most pressing issues.

She said the Bled Strategic Forum had “tangible stakes” for Hungary. Orbán said she would discuss regional cooperation with her counterparts on Monday and hold several bilateral meetings.

The 21st Bled Strategic Forum, which begins on Monday, will focus on Europe’s future, European Union enlargement, European security, and the Western Balkans. The two-day event will bring together heads of state and government as well as foreign ministers from central and south-eastern Europe, EU commissioners and economic and policy experts.

New home-building programme in Hungary may reshape property market

World.title: Another Budapest city centre district may ban Airbnb – referendum on the horizon
World.content:
Buda Castle District council is launching a poll on short-term rentals (Airbnbs), allowing residents’ views to inform decisions on future regulation, the council told Hungarian news agency MTI.

Mayor wants a vibrant and attractive residential district

The issue is particularly timely because the statutory moratorium on registering new short-term accommodation will expire at the end of the year. The council must therefore decide what rules should apply in District I, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

Short-term rentals are a particularly significant issue in District I, one of Budapest’s main tourist destinations, especially in and around Buda Castle. Short-term rentals generates tourism revenue, but residents’ associations and property owners have also raised a number of concerns about such rentals.

Buda Castle District: operating short-term rental(s) here can be a gold mine for families, companies. Photo: PrtScr/Youtube

“There are markedly different arguments and interests at stake in the debate, and all of them deserve consideration. As mayor, I believe it is right that we should not make decisions over the heads of the people who live here,” László Böröcz said, according to the statement.

The Fidesz mayor added that the council wanted to preserve Buda Castle as a vibrant and attractive residential district, while recognising that tourism and short-term rentals are important to many people and local businesses.

Buda Castle district may ban Airbnb

Residents aged 18 or over who have a permanent address in District I will be eligible to take part in the poll. They will be asked two questions.

The first will ask whether they support a complete ban on Airbnb. The second will ask whether, if Airbnb were not banned, they would support the council imposing conditions on the provision of short-term accommodation.

Airbnb restrictions in Budapest could deter tourists

In response to a question from MTI, the council said that District I currently has more than 400 licensed private accommodations and other properties, typically operated as commercial businesses.

The first Budapest district to ban Airbnb rentals was the capital’s 6th district following a referendum, which had a very low turnout.

Locals against the ban of new short-term rentals in Budapest’s 6th district. Photo: Facebook/Magyar ApartmanKiadók Egyesülete

World.title: Man in life-threatening condition after huge fall near Budapest’s Chain Bridge
World.content:
A man is in a life-threatening condition after plunging on to the paved embankment beside the Danube in central Budapest, near the Pontoon entertainment venue.

Accident near popular Budapest riverside venue

The serious accident took place in the early hours of Sunday near the Pest end of the Chain Bridge. The man, believed to be aged about 40, fell on to the embankment paving and was taken to hospital by ambulance with severe injuries, Telex wrote.

Both Pontoon and the police issued statements about the incident. The venue stressed that the accident had not occurred on its premises.

Pontoon said the accident occured in a public space. Photo: Facebook/PONTOON

“The incident did not take place within the area of Pontoon’s open-air hospitality venue, but further away, in a public space,” it said.

According to Pontoon, the man’s fall was preceded by a fight. The venue said members of the group involved had also used pepper spray. It did not, however, provide further details of what happened during the fight or the circumstances in which the man fell on to the embankment.

Photo: Facebook/PONTOON

Police opened an investigation

The venue said it had offered immediate assistance after the accident, helped secure the scene and co-operated with the authorities. It added that, to its knowledge, the responding authorities had not linked the incident to Pontoon’s operations.

The Budapest Police Headquarters confirmed that it had received several reports at about 1.23am on August 30 that a man had fallen on to the paved embankment near the Pest end of the Chain Bridge. Officers who arrived at the scene gathered information, while paramedics took the injured man to hospital.

Photo: Facebook/PONTOON

If you missed: Bus and car crash at Budapest’s Astoria leaves nine injured, woman in life-threatening condition

Police have opened an investigation on suspicion of the criminal offence of disorderly conduct committed by a group, in an effort to establish the full circumstances of the incident. Investigators have questioned witnesses and seized CCTV footage.

Pontoon said that the investigating authorities were best placed to provide an authoritative account of the precise details, adding that the venue fully supported efforts to establish what had happened.

The venue is in the heart of Budapest’s city centre, so the police will probably be able to find out what happened exactly. Photo: Facebook/PONTOON
