World.title: Domestic mosquitoes spread African virus linked to serious illness as first Hungarian case diagnosed
World.content:
The case was diagnosed in the 33rd epidemiological week of 2026, with laboratory tests by the National Public Health and Pharmacy Centre confirming the infection. An epidemiological investigation found that the patient had not travelled abroad before falling ill, meaning the infection is considered to have been acquired in Hungary.

Virus behind exotic disease is active in Hungary

The case is particularly noteworthy because last year’s first locally acquired infection in Hungary was identified as early as the 31st epidemiological week. The latest infection therefore once again indicates that the virus is present in the country’s mosquito population, Szúnyogmonitor wrote.

The West Nile virus’s natural cycle takes place primarily between birds and the native and widespread Culex mosquito. Humans and horses are known as ‘dead-end hosts’: they can become infected but generally do not pass the virus on.

The infection often goes unnoticed. Most human cases are asymptomatic. When symptoms do develop, they may include fever, headache, muscle pain, malaise and other flu-like symptoms. In rarer cases, however, the virus can attack the nervous system, causing encephalitis or meningitis, severe neurological symptoms and, in extreme cases, death.

It can be fatal: these groups face the greatest risk

Fatal cases are not unknown in Europe. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), 1,112 locally acquired infections and 97 deaths were recorded across 14 European countries in 2025. The situation was particularly serious in Italy, where 72 of 779 cases proved fatal – a mortality rate of almost 10 per cent.

The greatest risk is faced by older people and those whose immune defences are weakened by an underlying medical condition. Most infected people, however, recover from the illness without serious consequences.

The Hungarian case should therefore prompt heightened vigilance rather than panic. Mosquitoes play a key role in the virus’s emergence in Hungary, making the continuous monitoring of mosquito populations and the pathogens they carry particularly important. There are no vaccines or specific treatments for the virus.

Multiple deaths in Europe

In the Netherlands, an infection causing West Nile fever was detected in August for the first time in seven years. The country’s public health institute said at the time that about 80 per cent of people infected with the virus showed no symptoms. However, roughly 1 per cent developed neurological complications, chiefly people over 50 and those with weakened immune systems. In rare cases, the infection can prove fatal.

The agency advised people to wear long-sleeved clothing, use insect repellent and keep mosquitoes at bay with bed nets and window screens.

If you missed: A curious experiment reveals why Hungary is fighting a losing battle against a mosquito invasion

But on August 26, the Hungarian news agency MTI reported that the first person in the Netherlands had died from West Nile fever, in the province of Utrecht. The only detail released about the victim was that they were elderly. At the time, two further cases were known to have been acquired within the country. Another patient being treated in hospital for West Nile virus was also reportedly elderly, according to the Dutch newspaper De Volkskrant. Earlier, a woman had died after contracting the infection while travelling in south-eastern Europe.

This is hardly surprising: reports last week said that further West Nile virus infections had been recorded in Serbia and Croatia, while North Macedonia was facing the most serious outbreak in the region.

According to figures released last week by the ECDC, Albania, Austria, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Kosovo, the Netherlands, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia and Spain have reported cases this year.

ECDC: Hungary, among other countries, facing a growing threat from mosquito-borne diseases

World.title: Documents revealed: how former Economic Minister Márton Nagy splashed public money on luxury and private jets abroad
World.content:
While not a single hope, plan or promise Márton Nagy made as economic minister concerning economic growth appears to have materialised, the minister seems to have been more than willing to spend public money – both at the time and in retrospect, inexplicably – on luxury accommodation and private jets. All the while, Hungary was enduring one of the most severe bouts of inflation in its history.

Ministry releases inexplicable figures

Documents released in response to a freedom-of-information request by the Ministry for National Economy and its legal successor show that tens of millions of forints in public money were spent on the minister’s travel and accommodation between 2023 and 2026. The figures suggest that these were not merely expensive trips: in several cases, both the choice of hotel and the mode of transport are difficult to justify.

Márton Nagy speaking as Hungary’s Economy Minister at the CPAC 2024 conference in Budapest. Photo: Facebook/Alapjogokért Központ

The documents reveal that Márton Nagy travelled on official business to 51 cities in 32 countries between 2023 and 2026, spending a total of 115 nights abroad. Accommodation cost 51.9 million forints in total, amounting to an average of 451,000 forints per night, according to 24.hu.

That figure is striking enough in its own right. According to figures from Hungary’s Central Statistical Office, the country’s net median salary was 438,000 forints in July 2026. In other words, an average night abroad for Márton Nagy cost more than a Hungarian employee took home in an entire month, hvg.hu reports.

The most extravagant spending

The detailed expenses include even more eye-catching items. In September 2025, two nights at The Stafford in London cost 1.8 million forints, while three nights at Copenhagen’s Hotel Sanders came to 3.8 million forints – approximately 1.2 million forints per night. Two nights at the Botanic Hotel in Antwerp were charged at 980,000 forints.

Illustration. It seems that Márton Nagy loved to spend public money on luxury accommodations…

The choice of hotel does not appear particularly restrained, either. According to the figures, the delegation regularly stayed at hotels belonging to international luxury chains such as Four Seasons, Mandarin Oriental, Ritz-Carlton and Waldorf Astoria. In Antwerp, Márton Nagy stayed several times at the same luxury hotel, despite having an official programme in Brussels. He did the same in Zagreb, where he stayed in accommodation on the Adriatic coast, and in the Far East.

Public money for private jets

The use of private aircraft substantially inflated the cost of the trips. A journey from Paris to Davos in January 2024 cost 39.7 million forints, of which the private jet alone accounted for 30 million. According to HVG, private aircraft were also used for destinations that could easily have been reached by commercial flights.

… and private jets. Photo: depositphotos.com

The 2024 trip to South Korea is particularly noteworthy. Márton Nagy and his seven-member delegation also visited Jeju Island, one of South Korea’s most popular resorts, often described as the Hawaii of Korea. The official purpose of the visit was listed as “strategic partner consultations”, yet the documents provided do not make clear how many days the minister spent on the island or what his specific programme there involved. The delegation’s accommodation, however, cost slightly more than 1 million forints for five days.

How Márton Nagy grew wealthy under the Orbán government

An investigative series by Válasz Online, published in three parts (HERE, HERE and HERE), suggests that Márton Nagy has accumulated considerable wealth in recent years through economic interests linked to his family and its business network. According to the publication, his brother, Szilárd Nagy, has played a particularly important role, as has the circle of lawyers he operates, which over the years has received a lot of public money through commissions from numerous state-owned and state-backed companies.

Válasz Online’s analysis found that contracts awarded by at least 80 state-linked entities were connected to this network. In the case of 34 companies, it identified specific contracts worth at least 8.2 billion forints. According to Márton Nagy’s own asset declaration, he has owned a 89-square-metre flat in Budapest’s District II since 2014. He bought it while serving as a central-bank executive, with the National Bank of Hungary providing financial assistance towards the purchase.

Luxury property and asset managers

The family’s property holdings are considerably more substantial, however. His wife owns a stake in a 168-square-metre luxury flat in District II, estimated to be worth roughly half a billion forints, the larger share of which belongs to Szilárd Nagy. She also has an interest in a property in Vászoly worth approximately 150 million forints. A bank mortgage of 447 million forints was registered against the luxury property in Buda, but according to Válasz Online, it was repaid within just four or five months.

If you missed: Was a EUR 275 million fraud uncovered in connection with Gondosóra emergency alert device for the elderly?

Another important figure in the family’s business network is Péter Fenyvesi, who was previously involved in managing Szilárd Nagy’s property assets and later became head of Trustify Investment Fund Management. The private-equity funds managed by Trustify received substantial amounts of state capital, Válasz Online reports. Trustify Impact I, for example, was allocated 35 billion forints through a state capital programme, while a bank loan backed by a state guarantee was also used to finance the fund’s contribution.

The funds have acquired interests in a range of ventures, including property developments around Lake Balaton, an office building in Buda, energy and technology companies, and solar and wind farms. Their investments include a property project in Zánka that was previously state-owned.

Taken together, the three Válasz Online investigations point to a network linking state positions, family business connections, legal commissions, property holdings and private-equity funds operating with substantial public money. Through this network, Márton Nagy appears to be connected – directly or through his family – to assets and business interests of considerable value.

Horror over Paks II NPP overpricing: did Orbán-linked and Tisza-affiliated businessmen and politicians pocket the cash?

World.title: Video, photos: Hungarian man who evaded FBI for years and wanted for crimes against kids tracked down
World.content:
A 48-year-old Hungarian man arrested in Győr and wanted by the authorities over child pornography has been extradited to the United States, the National Bureau of Investigation of Hungary’s Rapid Response Police told police.hu on Monday.

Hungarian man handed over to the FBI

According to the statement, US authorities had been pursuing multiple proceedings against the man for several years over the possession of child pornography, after videos of that nature were found on electronic devices seized from him.

The Hungarian had been on the run for four years, prompting speculation that he may have sought refuge in Hungary. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) asked the Hungarian authorities for help in tracking him down at the beginning of this year.

He was eventually arrested in Győr on March 17, when it emerged that he had lived in the city for two years.

Photo: police.hu

The Budapest-Capital Regional Court ordered his extradition detention on March 18, after which the Hungarian justice authorities ordered his extradition.

Photo: police.hu

In the early hours of August 28, Hungarian police officers handed him over to representatives of the US authorities at Budapest’s Liszt Ferenc International Airport. The defendant is being taken to Florida before being transferred to a correctional facility. The US proceedings against him can therefore continue while he remains in custody, the statement said.

Photo: police.hu

World.title: Péter Magyar’s government promises a new era for Hungarian schools: should pupils and teachers be celebrating?
World.content:
Péter Magyar, the prime minister, and Judit Lannert, the education minister, made a series of long-awaited and reassuring promises to pupils and teachers at the start of the new school year, setting out their vision for the future of Hungary’s schools, education system and its objectives.

Photo: MTI

Péter Magyar: schools must teach critical thinking, with pay rises on the way

“The most important task of a school is to teach pupils to think as well as possible — and to think critically,” the prime minister said on Monday at the national school-year opening ceremony at the Dr Mező Ferenc Grammar School in Nagykanizsa.

Alongside critical thinking, pupils should learn at school how to stand up for one another, work as a team and remain decent human beings in all circumstances, Magyar Péter said, according to MTI.

In his speech, the prime minister also stressed the priority that must be given to education and healthcare.

“We know exactly what our task is,” Péter Magyar said, listing the renovation of school buildings, the creation of new places in boarding schools, decent school meals, and support for teachers, teaching assistants and other education workers.

He added that the government had heard and understood the call for action, and had not forgotten its commitments. Pay rises in the sector would therefore be announced shortly, he said.

Photo: MTI

A genuine, predictable career path is needed

Péter Magyar also spoke specifically about the tens of thousands of teaching assistants who help classroom staff, saying that they could count on the Tisza government.

The timetable for the pay rises would be announced shortly, the prime minister indicated. He stressed, however, that the country needed a genuine career path rather than one-off increases — and conditions capable of attracting more young people and new recruits to both education and healthcare.

Péter Magyar also said that the government could not allow wages to be eroded by inflation again.

The government wants schools to provide a calm environment for development, give pupils room to express their creativity and become better places for everyone, Judit Lannert, the minister for education and children’s affairs, said on Monday, also in Nagykanizsa.

Graduated at the Franciscan School in Esztergom. Source: Facebook/Szent Antal Esztergomi Ferences Gimnázium és Kollégium – Franka

The government wants schools to become spaces for creativity for pupils and teachers alike, where steady development is possible and where children can discover the subjects and activities that interest them and bring them joy, the minister added.

Knowledge was important, she said, but perhaps even more important was sparking and sustaining curiosity and motivation. She identified the following objectives:

strengthening professional and managerial autonomy;

reducing administrative duties;

introducing a more varied range of teaching materials;

reducing the number of compulsory assessments.

According to Lannert, the school of the future must guarantee equal opportunities. While factual knowledge remained important, she said, so too were problem-solving skills and the ability to adapt to different situations.

Emphasising the role of schools in helping, including and supporting children, the minister said that attention must also be paid to what happens in everyday school life — particularly in the case of children facing difficulties or struggling to fit in.

Starting school remains hugely expensive for Hungarian families

The start of the school year remains one of the largest household expenses of the year. A typical Hungarian household spends 107,539 forints on the new school year, while the average cost per child is 66,928 forints, according to fresh research by PwC.

Total school-start spending per child averages 70,055 forints for primary-school pupils in the lower years, 69,282 for those in the upper years, 62,532 for secondary-school pupils and 80,795 for students in higher education.

Some 75.5 per cent of school-age children and higher-education students have a mobile phone, while 61.9 per cent have a laptop and 45.1 per cent a tablet. Desktop computers are owned by 31.5 per cent, printers by 33.6 per cent and smartwatches by 18.4 per cent.

How pupils use AI

Fifteen per cent of households use a paid AI service, while a further 48.6 per cent use solutions available free of charge. In 31.4 per cent of respondents’ households, AI tools are not used at all.

Children primarily use artificial intelligence to search for information, cited by 74.2 per cent of families that use AI. Some 52.2 per cent use it to explain school material, 46.6 per cent for brainstorming and 39.4 per cent to help with homework.

World.title: Romanian Language Day celebrated simultaneously in Romania, Moldova and Ukraine
World.content:
Romanian Language Day was celebrated for the first time simultaneously in Romania, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine, according to a message posted by Romanian president Nicușor Dan on Facebook on Monday, August 31.

The president said that “protecting the rights of Romanians everywhere and promoting our language and culture remain essential objectives of the Romanian state beyond its borders.” He also highlighted the importance of the Romanian language. “We are united by this valuable bond of the Romanian language, which anchors us in history and opens our future,” the head of state said.

Nicușor Dan ended the message with a greeting addressed to those who speak, write and keep the Romanian language alive: “Happy Romanian Language Day and happy Romanian Language Day to all those who speak it, write it and keep it alive!”

In the Republic of Moldova, Romanian Language Day has been marked on August 31 since 1990. In Romania, Romanian Language Day has been officially celebrated since 2013, following the adoption of the law establishing August 31 as a day of celebration. Ukraine is officially marking Romanian Language Day for the first time in 2026. The decision was made through a decree signed by Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy on March 12.

Celebrations in Romania

Aside from the Romanian head of state, numerous public bodies, officials, and personalities mentioned the event within the country. Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted in a message that “promoting the Romanian language abroad is a mission with a permanent mandate.”

The institution noted that “August 31 is therefore also the symbol of the defeat of artificially fabricated formulas such as the ‘Moldovan language’, which does not exist de jure,” the message posted on the MFA’s Facebook page says.

According to the cited source, “today, Romania, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine are more cohesive, demonstrating that we bring unity through a vector of communication, language and culture, in a period marked by an unjust and illegal war that should never have taken place on the European continent.”

The US embassy in Romania marked the day in a video posted on Facebook.

Events and celebrations were moreover organized throughout the country for Romanian Language Day. To mark the event, president Nicușor Dan decorated the National Institute for Oriental Languages and Civilizations in Paris and university professor Alexandru-Daniel Mardale, head of the institute’s Romanian Language Department, on the occasion of Romanian Language Day. The decorations were in appreciation of the outstanding merits in promoting the Romanian language in the French Republic, and for the contribution to deepening bilateral relations and strengthening the Romanian-French dialogue.

Romanian Language Day in Moldova

In Moldova, the Romanian Language Day has a special significance, as the country was long subjected to a process of Russification before the fall of the USSR, of which it was a part. In 1989, following pressure exerted by tens of thousands of people gathered at the first Great National Assembly, Romanian was proclaimed the state language of the Moldavian SSR and the Latin script was restored. In 2023, Moldova recognized Romanian as its national language.

Romanian Language Day was marked in Chisinau, Moldova’s capital, throught the fourth edition of the Great National Dictation and other cultural events. The former brought together more than 3,500 participants from across the country. This year, participants had to transcribe a fragment from the work of the late Gheorghe Urschi, the beloved actor, director, playwright and humorist, nicknamed the “king of humor” in the Republic of Moldova.

Present at the Dictation, Moldovan prime minister Vasile Tofan spoke about the importance of the Romanian language, as well as the sacrifices of those who fought for the return to the Latin script and the recognition of the Romanian language in the Republic of Moldova. He paid tribute to those who fought for the Romanian language and national identity and paid a price for this.

“The Romanian language survived here despite the Soviet occupation, the foreign alphabet that was imposed on it and the enormous pressure of the Russian language in education, administration and public life. It survived because it could not be removed from people. It was the language spoken at home, the language of grandparents, the language of songs, the language in which people shared their joys and sorrows. It was in the marrow of this nation,” the Moldovan prime minister said, cited by Agerpres.

“The Romanian language should not be a barrier; it should be a bridge. Knowing the Romanian language means the possibility of fully participating in the life of this country; it means access to education, work, culture, institutions, the possibility of speaking to one another and building the same society together,” he added.

Moldovan president Maia Sandu also sent a congratulatory message on the occasion of Romanian Language Day, highlighting the role of the Romanian language in preserving the identity and memory of generations.

“The Romanian language is part of our being. [...] Today we can speak it freely, without fear. All the more, we have a duty to take care of it. And, above all, to pass on to our children the love for the Romanian language, just as we received it from those who came before us. Let us leave them this precious heritage: a living language, beautifully spoken, in which they can tell their stories, sing their doinas and express their longing. Happy Romanian Language Day!” Maia Sandu said.

Romanian Language Day in Ukraine

Romanian Language Day was marked for the first time in Ukraine on Saturday, August 29, in Chernivtsi, in the southern part of the country.

Representatives of the Romanian authorities, the Romanian diplomacy in Ukraine, as well as the Romanian community in the Chernivtsi region laid wreaths at the statue of Taras Shevchenko and the statue of Mihai Eminescu in the city center. Candles were also lit at the Heroes’ Memorial in Chernivtsi’s Central Square, according to Digi24.

The event was attended by Romania’s ambassador to Kyiv, Victor Micula, Romania’s consul general in Chernivtsi, Irina Loredana Stănculescu, State Secretary at the Ministry of Culture Diana Băciuna, president of the Iași County Council Costel Alexe, as well as the military governor of the Chernivtsi region, Ruslan Osipenko, and president of the Chernivtsi District Council, Mykola Guitor.

Later, the Romanian officials held a meeting with the leaders of the Romanian community at the National Palace.

Back in March, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky signed a decree establishing Romanian Language Day in Ukraine. “To develop mutual understanding, mutual respect and cooperation in Ukrainian-Romanian relations, encouraging intercultural dialogue, taking into account the preservation of identity and developing the linguistic and cultural identity of Ukrainian citizens, I decree: Romanian Language Day is hereby established in Ukraine, to be celebrated annually on August 31,” the decree said.

World.title: Social Democrat leader Sorin Grindeanu says party ready to form Romania’s next government
World.content:
The Social Democratic Party (PSD) is ready to form a new government around itself, including a minority administration, party leader Sorin Grindeanu announced on Monday, August 31. However, the party will not support any governing formula in which it does not participate, he said following a meeting of the PSD National Political Council in Sinaia.

“PSD is ready to support a functional government and assume the formation of a government around itself, including a minority government, but only on the basis of a clear program with precise objectives, deadlines, financing, and assigned responsibilities,” Sorin Grindeanu said, as quoted by News.ro.

“To be unequivocal, PSD will not support any governing formula of which it is not part,” he added.

Romania has been governed by a caretaker administration since the Liberal-led government of interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan was dismissed in a no-confidence vote in early May.

The Social Democrats had withdrawn from the previous governing alliance before joining the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) in passing the motion. Forming a new majority remains difficult, as the National Liberal Party (PNL) and Save Romania Union (USR) have repeatedly ruled out joining another government that includes PSD.

PSD, meanwhile, has said it would not accept PNL leader Ilie Bolojan as a member of a future cabinet.

On Monday, Sorin Grindeanu said PSD would first negotiate the objectives of a future administration and discuss its political structure, government positions, and allocation of responsibilities only if those priorities are accepted.

“Romania must restart its economy. Our goal is to protect purchasing power, stop fiscal experiments, and relaunch production in Romania,” he said.

PSD has proposed a two-year political agreement built around ten priorities to parties willing to help form a parliamentary majority. These include energy and natural resources, the national defence industry, reindustrialization, improved tax collection before the introduction of new taxes, reforming state costs, wages linked to productivity, education and healthcare, irrigation and rural development, strategic investments, and defending Romania’s interests within the EU and NATO.

Grindeanu said each measure included in the agreement should have identified financing, a deadline, a responsible institution, and a publicly available performance indicator. Progress would be assessed after the government’s first 100 days and again by a final evaluation deadline.

Any breaches of the agreement would be formally reported, technically assessed, and subjected to a 15-day mediation period.

Romania’s constitutional, European, and transatlantic orientation would remain non-negotiable, the PSD leader added.

Last week, interim prime minister and PNL leader Ilie Bolojan confirmed that his party will not vote for a government with PSD ministers and warned that if negotiations on a new government remain deadlocked, Romania may head towards early elections. However, he added that the odds of early elections are rather slim.

World.title: Romanian billionaire Daniel Dines publishes book about AI written with help of AI
World.content:
Daniel Dines, founder of Romanian-American software robots and artificial intelligence company UiPath (NYSE: PATH), has launched a book about AI, which he wrote with the help of AI chatbots ChatGPT from OpenAI and Claude from Anthropic.

Daniel Dines is the founder and Chief Executive Officer of UiPath, a global leader in business orchestration and automation. In the early 2000s, Dines spent five years at Microsoft in Seattle, working on SQL Server Agent. In 2005, he returned to Romania, his home country, and from his apartment started the company that would become UiPath. The company is now a leader in business orchestration and automation.

In his book, Dines, 54, draws on his experience to “outline a new operating model for the company of the future.” He examines one of the most important questions facing business leaders: “As AI becomes capable of taking over more and more intellectual work, how should companies rethink the way they work without giving up responsibility, control and human judgment?”

The Romanian self-made billionaire sets out to “offer business and technology leaders a practical framework for exploring the role that responsibility, control and human judgment will play in the company of the future, built by orchestrating AI agents, automation and people,” according to a UiPath statement sent to Romania Insider.

Dines describes the book as an accessible guide for leaders trying to understand a rapidly changing AI landscape. “You will learn more about AI in four hours than you have learned in the past year,” Daniel Dines promised.

Dines' book, The Work That Remains/What Remains to Be Done When Machines Do the Rest, can be downloaded for free in PDF format from the UiPath website.

The book is available in English and Japanese in digital format starting August 27, followed by a limited print edition on September 22.

World.title: Romanian authorities inaugurate new PNRR-funded medical centers in Cluj-Napoca, Târgu Mureș
World.content:
Interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan and other officials attended the inauguration of the new cerebrovascular pathology and neurosurgery center within the Cluj County Emergency Hospital on Saturday, August 29. Another medical center was inaugurated on Monday, August 31, in Târgu Mureș, central Romania. Both projects were completed with EU-backed PNRR funds.

The new center is able to provide modern services in the field of neurosurgical pathologies, has an area dedicated to imaging investigations, and is equipped with equipment for neurosurgical and neurovascular investigations and treatment. The center, built in Cluj, has six operating rooms for neurosurgical procedures, 105 beds, of which 26 are intensive care beds, the Romanian government said in a press release.

The facility was financed from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, which ended on August 31, and from national funds and was badly needed, according to the head of the executive, since most serious cases in the Transylvania region are treated in Cluj-Napoca.

“I am here for this great city, Cluj-Napoca, a locomotive of Romania's development, for the people here,” the interim prime minister also said at the inauguration of the Cerebrovascular Pathology and Neurosurgery Center in Cluj-Napoca.

Bolojan thanked the doctors and medical students in the city. “I am grateful to them for what they do in our medical system, Cluj being one of the strongest centers from this point of view,” he said.

Cluj County Council president Alin Tișe avoided delivering any message at the inauguration event of the new medical center, amid a spat with the prime minister. Instead, Cluj-Napoca mayor Emil Boc was alongside Bolojan, delivering an extensive message about the PNRR-funded investment carried out in Cluj-Napoca with the government's support.

“The new hospital, the Cerebrovascular Pathology and Neurosurgery Center, was built from scratch,” Boc said, emphasizing that the investment secured through the PNRR amounts to more than EUR 50 million. “Cluj's medical sector is richer as of today. Richer with a new hospital, with more than 100 beds and state-of-the-art technology for doctors and patients,” he added.

The new facility has 79 beds for neurosurgery and neurology patients, 26 intensive care beds for neurosurgical and neurovascular pathologies, 6 operating rooms for neurosurgical procedures, and a 70-square-meter hybrid room, a modern imaging area equipped with a 3 Tesla MRI, multislice CT and angiograph, among others.

The Cluj mayor further emphasized that the hospital will become “a new landmark of Romanian medicine.”

The Cluj-Napoca County Emergency Clinical Hospital is one of the first six Class I medical units in Romania, alongside the county hospitals in Constanța, Iași, Târgu Mureș, Timișoara and the Central Military Hospital, the government also said.

New medical facility in Târgu Mureș

Alongside the Cerebrovascular Pathology and Neurosurgery Center in Cluj-Napoca, Romanian authorities also inaugurated the Emergency Institute for Cardiovascular Diseases and Transplant (IUBCvT) in Târgu Mureș on Monday, August 31. The facility was valued at over RON 770 million, out of which roughly RON 500 million came from the EU-backed National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

The facility has 214 beds for inpatients and five beds for day hospitalization, surgery rooms equipped to a top technological level, as well as modern spaces dedicated exclusively to investigation, treatment and intensive care (ICU) activities.

The new institute is equipped with state-of-the-art equipment, while the structure and equipment of the new rooms were specifically designed to reduce the risk of nosocomial infections.

Also present at this inauguration, the Romanian prime minister highlighted that Romania was unable to fully take advantage of the PNRR funds.

“In healthcare, we started with a PNRR budget of more than EUR 2 billion and, through successive cuts, we reached just over EUR 1 billion, which means that the money was not lost, but went to other areas where it could be spent. And this means that from 19 hospitals, after the PNRR was rearranged in 2023, we ended up completing eight,” Bolojan said, cited by Agerpres.

At the same time, the interim prime minister spoke about the need to simplify procurement procedures and partnerships with local authorities.

World.title: Romania’s budget deficit nearly halves to 2.34% of GDP in January-July 2026
World.content:
Romania managed to halve its budget deficit to RON 48.08 billion in 2026, from RON 76.44 billion in the same period of 2025, according to a government press release published on Monday, August 31. As a share of GDP, the deficit fell from 3.99% to 2.34%.

Revenues increased by 11.2%, to RON 412.31 billion, while expenditures advanced by only 2.9%, to RON 460.39 billion. Significantly, VAT collections increased by more than 25% in the first 7 months of 2026 compared with 2025, and investments increased by nearly 24% to RON 76.51 billion.

“The 1.65% reduction in the deficit is proof of balanced management, in which fiscal responsibility is combined with direct support for the economy,” Romanian finance minister Alexandru Nazare said, also mentioning VAT refunds to companies of more than RON 20.4 billion, and the more than 60% increase in payments from European funds and the PNRR.

State revenues up

During the first 7 months of 2026, tax revenues increased by 15.4%, to RON 214.32 billion, with their share of GDP rising from 9.69% to 10.42%.

The largest contribution came from VAT: net collections reached RON 88.55 billion, up 26.5%, amid the new rates in late 2025 and the 21.7% increase in gross collection, even as refunds to the private sector continued to rise, reaching RON 20.48 billion.

Social security contributions brought in RON 129.14 billion (+6.7%), the largest revenue line in the execution, supported by the expansion of the tax base. Wage and income tax increased by 8.6%, to RON 38.34 billion, partly due to dividends distributed heavily in December 2025 before the tax changes, while corporate income tax increased by 8.3%, to RON 28.35 billion. These were joined by reimbursed European funds of RON 37.28 billion, up 30.3%.

Lower personnel expenses

While the state’s revenues increased, some expenditures decreased. The most significant decrease was in personnel, which totaled RON 95.67 billion, 4.1% lower than the previous year. As a share, personnel expenses fell from 22.3% to 20.8% of total public expenditure, a notable move, given that this is one of the most rigid components of the budget.

Social assistance expenditures, the largest expenditure category in the budget, fell slightly, by 0.6%, to RON 146.59 billion, while spending on goods and services increased by 11.2%, to RON 59.6 billion, driven particularly by the healthcare system.

One category of the Romanian state’s expenses that increased sharply compared to last year concerned debt-servicing. Interest expenses reached RON 40.12 billion, 26.5% more than in the same period last year, and now account for 2% of GDP, partially eroding the savings made on wages.

Investments still strong

Unlike previous episodes of fiscal consolidation in Romania, this time the reduction in the deficit was not based on cutting investments. Capital expenditure increased by RON 14.83 billion compared with last year, while 71% of this volume comes from projects financed through European funds and the PNRR, where payments increased by 60% to more than RON 20 billion.

The Romanian finance minister nevertheless drew attention to a technical element that will complicate the reading of future budget executions: starting in August, the effects of the fiscal measures adopted in July 2025 are annualized, which changes the comparison base.

“The differences compared with last year will naturally narrow,” Nazare said on Facebook, adding that the next stage targets “the structural and sustainable consolidation of the fiscal adjustment,” through wage discipline, faster absorption of European funds and prioritization of investments.

World.title: BCR, Erste provide EUR 132 mln financing for Scatec wind farm in Romania
World.content:
Banca Comercială Română (BCR) and Erste Group said they are providing EUR 132 million to finance Scatec’s 77 MW Urleasca onshore wind farm in Romania. BCR is contributing EUR 76 million of the total financing, the bank announced.

Located in Brăila county, approximately 150 kilometers northeast of Bucharest, the wind farm will feature 11 Nordex N175/6.X turbines. Commercial operations are scheduled to begin in the second half of 2028.

With financing now secured, the project is entering the construction phase. OX2 will manage construction through to commissioning under a Construction and Asset Transfer Agreement.

Scatec holds a 100% stake in Urleasca and will provide operations, maintenance, and asset management services after commissioning.

The project is backed by a Contract for Difference (CfD) covering around 57% of its expected output. The remainder of the electricity generated will be sold on Romania’s wholesale power market.

“Urleasca is an important milestone for our growth in Romania,” said Alex Patrascu, Scatec’s country manager for Romania. “With multiple renewable projects now under construction, we are building scale in a market with strong fundamentals and significant potential.”

Urleasca is Scatec’s first onshore wind project in Europe. It complements the company’s 190 MW solar portfolio currently under construction in Romania.

This is the second financing BCR has provided for a Scatec project in the country, following EUR 42.5 million for the 190 MW Dobrun and Sadova solar portfolio in Dolj and Olt counties.

“Energy has become a competitiveness standard, and investors increasingly look at its availability, cost, and predictability when assessing a market,” said Manuela Trisnevschi, BCR’s head of energy and utilities.

BCR provided EUR 450 million in financing to Romania’s energy sector in the first half of 2026. More than EUR 362 million went to renewable energy projects, including EUR 288 million for wind farms, EUR 41 million for solar projects, and EUR 33 million for battery storage investments.

World.title: Cluj-Napoca mayor decorated with highest distinction given by Moldovan Parliament
World.content:
The mayor of Cluj-Napoca, Emil Boc, was decorated on Saturday, August 29, by the president of the Parliament of the Republic of Moldova, Igor Grosu, with the “Medal of Democracy,” the highest distinction handed by the legislature in Chisinau.

The medal was awarded in recognition of Boc’s constant support and investments carried out in the infrastructure of the Moldovan city of Ungheni, according to Igor Grosu. The support has already enabled several major urban infrastructure projects in the city, including the renovation of two municipal parks and the modernization of public transport.

Cluj-Napoca and Ungheni were twinned in 2016, and over the past ten years, Cluj-Napoca City Hall has allocated more than RON 17 million to support urban development initiatives in Ungheni, according to Mediafax.

The partnership between the two cities is ongoing through the works to arrange and modernize, for the first time, the promenade along Lake Delia, according to the same source.

"For me, this medal bears a name that says it all: Democracy. Democracy means the freedom to choose your own path. It means respect for people, for their dignity and for the right of each generation to build its own future. And the Republic of Moldova has demonstrated that, no matter how difficult the path may be, freedom and democracy are worth defending every day," mayor Boc said upon receiving the medal.

Since 2023, Emil Boc has also been an honorary citizen of the municipality of Ungheni, a title awarded for his “impressive contribution to the development of the municipality of Ungheni and to the development of truly friendly relations between Ungheni and Cluj-Napoca.”

World.title: Romania deploys new team of firefighters to Greece
World.content:
Romania sent a third contingent of firefighters specializing in tackling forest fires to Greece on Sunday, August 30. The team will continue the monitoring and firefighting missions carried out by the previous Romanian contingent over the past two weeks, the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (IGSU) announced.

The firefighters are traveling by road from the Special Emergency Intervention Unit in Ciolpani to Nea Makri in Greece’s Attica region, around 25 kilometers northeast of Athens.

The new team will use the equipment already deployed in Greece, including three forest fire engines with capacities ranging from 3,000 to 5,000 liters, a 10,000-liter high-capacity vehicle, and a 30,000-liter water tanker. The equipment also includes a first-response and command vehicle fitted with an unmanned aircraft system, a shortwave radio communications vehicle, a minibus, a container truck, and a utility terrain vehicle equipped for firefighting.

Romania is participating in Greece between August 1 and September 15 with a national module specializing in forest fire response. The mission is part of a pre-positioning program organized by the European Commission’s Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (DG ECHO).

The EU-funded program was designed to support European communities severely affected by major wildfires in previous years. It is part of the bloc’s efforts to prevent and limit forest fires in southern Europe.

Operational teams from Romania, the Czech Republic, France, and Moldova are participating in this year’s program in Greece.

Romania has taken part in the pre-positioning initiative each year since 2022. Greek authorities formally requested the deployment of another Romanian forest firefighting module in 2026 through the European Commission’s Emergency Response Coordination Centre.

World.title: Montenegro Opposition Seeks Parliament Speaker’s Dismissal Over Mladic Condolences
World.content:
Parliament speaker Andrija Mandic addresses parliament in Podgorica, October 2023. Photo: EPA/BORIS PEJOVIC.

Montenegro’s main opposition party, the Democratic Party of Socialists, said on Monday it will seek the dismissal of parliamentary speaker Andrija Mandic over his decision to express condolences to the family of Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb wartime commander convicted of genocide and other war crimes.

Danijel Zivkovic, the leader of the Democratic Party of Socialists, DPS, said the party would send an initiative to all parliamentary groups and independent lawmakers before formally submitting it to parliament.

Zivkovic said Mandic “had crossed a line that could no longer be ignored by expressing condolences following Mladic’s death”.

“For a long time we have been told that a distinction should be made between his personal political views and the office he holds, that we should show understanding for the stability of the government and that difficult issues should not be raised because of the European path,” Zivkovic told reporters in parliament.

“But there are moments when silence ceases to be political wisdom and becomes acquiescence. This is one of those moments,” he said.

Zivkovic said the initiative was not simply about Mandic, but a test for the other lawmakers in the ruling majority.

“We are not asking them to support the DPS, change the government or change their political relationship with Andrija Mandic,” he said.

“We are asking only one question – can a man who, from the position of parliament speaker, expresses such an attitude toward a legally convicted war criminal and a man responsible for genocide have their confidence to represent the parliament of a country that wants to become the next member of the EU?”

The initiative comes amid renewed controversy and divisions in Montenegro following Mladic’s death.

Mandic, the leader of the ruling pro-Serb New Serb Democracy party, said last week that he had sent condolences to Mladic’s son, Darko, “in his own name and in the name of New Serb Democracy”.

President Jakov Milatovic sharply criticised the move, saying that respect for Mladic’s family could not be used to play down war crimes.

His office said Mladic had been convicted of genocide in Srebrenica and other serious crimes by an international court and that this “must not be subject to political relativisation”.

Several other pro-Serb politicians also praised Mladic. Milan Knezevic, leader of the opposition Democratic People’s Party, posted a photograph of Mladic saying that “every Serbian household has one Ratko.”

The Serbian Orthodox Church’s Metropolitan Metodije of the Budimlje-Niksic Eparchy also praised Mladic, saying that Serbs had recognised in him “not only a great Serb and a man worthy of respect, but all the beautiful and holy qualities of the holy Serbian warriors and knights”.

Metodije said Mladic had “stoically” borne his conviction and that his death should serve as a lesson to Serbs not to abandon the path of their “holy ancestors”.

Montenegro’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic, who leads the Bosniak Party, another coalition member, took a sharply different position, saying a convicted war criminal, “both alive and dead, deserves only contempt”.

The Bosniak Party later said Ibrahimovic had received death threats and calls for his expulsion from Montenegro, torture and violence on social media. It urged the police and National Security Agency to assess and strengthen security for Ibrahimovic and his family.

Islamic Community leader Rifat Fejzic said Montenegro “cannot move forward while some officials glorify Mladic”, urging the government to “decisively put its house in order”.

Human Rights Action, a prominent Montenegrin rights group, meanwhile warned that there was no “military or human honour” in war crimes, and recalled that Montenegro’s criminal code punishes certain forms of public approval, denial or minimisation of genocide and war crimes established by final court judgments when they can incite violence or hatred.

Zivkovic said the DPS would proceed with the initiative regardless of whether it secures enough votes to remove Mandic, arguing that the vote itself would show where each lawmaker stands on the issue.

The positions of the Europe Now Movement and the Democrats, allies of Mandic’s party in the governing majority, are not yet known, but the motion is unlikely to pass in the 81-member parliament, as the three groups hold a majority even without the Bosniak Party.

“If there are 41 votes for his dismissal, Montenegro will say that, regardless of political differences, there are lines that must not be crossed,” he said. “If there are not, citizens will at least receive a clear answer about who considers preserving the majority more important than those lines.”

Political analyst Stefan Djukic told BIRN that a similar initiative had previously been launched over similar actions by the parliament’s speaker in 2014, but failed to result in his dismissal.

“I do not expect that to happen this time either,” Djukic said briefly.

The European Commission last Friday told Vijesti, responding to Mandic’s condolences to Mladic’s son, that “glorification of war criminals was contrary to fundamental European values and had no place either in the European Union or in candidate countries seeking membership.”

The Commission also recalled that Mladic was serving a life sentence for crimes against humanity and genocide in Srebrenica. “He was a war criminal,” the Commission said.

World.title: Kosovo’s Vetevendosje, LDK Agree on Ex-Judge as Joint Presidential Candidate
World.content:
Kosovo presidential candidate Bekim Sejdiu (C) at a joint press conference with (L-R) former President Vjosa Osmani, LDK leader Lumir Adbixhiku, LDK MP Lutfi Haziri, and Vetevendosje leader Albin Kurti in Pristina on August 31, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Vetevendosje and the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK party agreed on Monday on a joint presidential candidate – a move that could end the country’s long-running political crisis.

Following a meeting between the respective party leaders, Albin Kurti and Lumir Abdixhiku, the latter announced Bekim Sejdiu, a former judge at the Constitutional Court and a former diplomat, as their pick for the vacant post.

“The talks were not easy, but they were exhaustive; we held long meetings and engaged in continuous, quite intense discussions. Both sides were committed to finding a consensus candidate for the president of Kosovo,” LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku told media at a joint press conference with acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti and MPs from the LDK and Vetevendosje.

“Various names were considered during the discussions. Ultimately, we agreed on one name: Professor Doctor Bekim Sejdiu,” Abdixhiku said.

“It is a great mark of trust and a great honour,” 51-year-old Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court and ambassador, who currently lectures in law, told the press conference.

“Although my ambitions have always leaned more towards the academic and professional spheres, I have – fully aware of the burden and responsibility entailed by the office of the president, and mindful of the current political context in the Republic of Kosovo – placed myself at the service of the republic, its citizens, and our state,” he added.

The agreement is a move towards ending the political deadlock that has paralysed Kosovo since parliamentary elections in June. Parliament has yet to be inaugurated since then, as political parties disagreed over who should be the next president – a position whose incumbent is elected by MPs. Without an agreement, new elections seemed inevitable.

Amid the institutional logjam, the provisional parliament speaker, Avni Dehari from election-winning party Vetevendosje, refused to resume the inaugural session that started on August 6. Vetevendosje also refused to submit a name for the new parliament’s speaker, as it first demanded an agreement with other parties on the election of a new president.

When announcing the deal on Monday, Abdixhiku called for the inauguration of parliament “without delays” and a vote for a new government before the vote for the new president.

In elections in June, Albin Kurti’s Vetevendosje won 53 of the 120 seats in the Assembly, putting it well ahead of the PDK, which won 22. The Democratic League of Kosovo (LDK) won 18 seats.

Kurti is likely to obtain a simple majority in the assembly to form a new government by again relying on the support of MPs from ethnic minority communities – Roma, Ashkali, Egyptian, Turk and Bosniak – plus one of the Serb MPs.

In the presidential election, Sejdiu must receive at least 80 MPs’ votes in the first two rounds of voting to be confirmed in the role. In a potential third round, he would need a simple majority of 61 votes.

Sejdiu is a former judge of the Kosovo Constitutional Court and served as as ambassador to Turkey from 2008 to 2012, and as Kosovo’s consul general in New York from 2012 to 2014.

Since 2002, he has worked as an assistant professor in the Department of International Law at the University of Pristina’s Faculty of Law.

Sejdiu was also the rapporteur judge in the December 2020 Constitutional Court ruling that the government led by the LDK’s Avdullah Hoti was illegitimate because it was voted in with an invalid vote from a MP who had been convicted of a crime.

Most recently, he served as an adviser to then President Vjosa Osmani. Osmani returned to political activity with the LDK after her presidential mandate ended.

World.title: Two Kosovo Serbs Plead Guilty to Participating in 2022 Unrest
World.content:
Dusan Dobrac (R) and Milos Radosavlevic (L) at the Pristina Basic Court on August 31, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Dusan Dobrac and Milos Radosavlevic were given prison sentences of one year and nine months respectively at Pristina Basic Court on Monday after pleading guilty to violating the constitutional order by participating in setting up roadblocks in the north of Kosovo in December 2022.

Dobrac was convicted of activity that breaches the constitutional order and obstruction of an official in the performance of their duties, and Radosavlevic of violating the constitutional order.

The indictment charged six Kosovo Serb men – Dusan Maksimovic, Dusan Drobac, Milos Radosavljevic, Nemanja Jolovic, Nenad Orlovic and Srdjan Vucinic – with staging organised, coordinated and violent activity to subvert the constitutional order by blocking public roads to two border crossings with Serbia: Jarinje and Bernjak.

While Dobrac and Radosavlevic have been sentenced, the trial of Maksimovic, Jolovic, and Vucinic will continue, as they have not pleaded guilty. The sixth defendant, Orlovic has not been arrested yet and the judge announced that Kosovo will seek his arrest internationally as he has failed to appear in court for two hearings in a row.

The charges relate to unrest in December 2022, when Serbs in northern Kosovo were setting up barricades at the two border crossings with Serbia, parking trucks, ambulances, diggers and other vehicles across access roads in what was cast as a ‘spontaneous’ outpouring of popular anger. It began after the arrest of a Kosovo Serb on suspicion of attacking election facilities.

The prosecution file, seen by BIRN, claims the unrest endangered the lives of police and customs officers. Those involved also allegedly participated in creating “a tense security situation through the opening of fortified positions and the presence of uniformed and armed persons”, according to the prosecution.

During questioning, Maksimovic, Jolovic, and Vucinic denied any role in organising the barricades, saying they were only part of a protest by local residents. Orlovic refused to answer the prosecutors during questioning.

However, the police discovered a Viber group named ‘Barricades December 2022’ on Maksimovic’s phone, suggesting the incidents were organised and coordinated.

They acquired the phone in September 2023, after Maksimovic was arrested over his involvement in an armed attack on Kosovo police in the northern village of Banjska, in which one Kosovo Albanian officer was killed and a cache of military-grade weaponry was seized. He was sentenced in the first instance to 30 years in prison over the Banjska incident,

The contents of his phone helped prosecutors investigating the unrest in Serb-majority municipalities and the setting up of the barricades of December 2022. The messages it contained included “Today we’ll all receive ammunition” and “In the afternoon we could try the weapons in Suvi Dol [local village] with two or three bullets each.”

Prosecutors stated that the phone evidence undermined claims that local Serbs had spontaneously set up the barricades and sparked the unrest.

World.title: Warsaw’s Political Fight with Kyiv Is Being Settled on Polish Streets
World.content:
Anti-Ukrainian card

In June, Polish-Ukrainian relations made international headlines after President Volodymyr Zelensky was stripped of Poland’s highest order, and returned it by post. But the hostility did not begin with a single political dispute.

Last year, BIRN documented how during Poland’s presidential race candidates across the political spectrum reached for the “anti-Ukrainian card”, pushing the boundaries of what is acceptable to say in public.

“The campaign was the real turning point, because that was when Ukrainians living in Poland – and, more broadly, Ukraine and support for it – became a domestic political issue,” says Iwaniuk.

It was much easier to blame “failing public services” on Ukrainian ‘privileges’ than to fix the system itself, she says: “Populists need an enemy, and after other groups, including the LGBTQ community, it became the Ukrainians’ turn – because there were enough of them to turn resentment into political capital.”

Ideas that had once largely been confined to the political right moved into the mainstream. After taking office, President Karol Nawrocki vetoed an extension of the Ukrainian assistance law, arguing that the 800+ child benefit should be reserved for Ukrainians working in Poland. Revised legislation tied access to some benefits more closely to employment and school attendance. In March, Poland also began winding down much of the exceptional system created after the invasion.

For Bartlomiej Pejo, an MP from the right-wing Confederation party, measures limiting exceptional treatment are not evidence of hostility but a correction to policies he believes privileged Ukrainians over other foreigners. “The Polish state should treat all foreigners equally, without granting special privileges,” he tells BIRN.

Pejo condemns attacks against Ukrainians but rejects the idea that Poland is experiencing an extraordinary wave of hostility. He argues that crimes by Ukrainian citizens against Poles receive less attention, and that Polish anger over Ukrainian attitudes to the massacres committed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, or UPA, during World War II is too readily dismissed as prejudice.

That historical dispute has become impossible to separate from the deterioration in relations.

The latest escalation began in May, when President Zelensky granted a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title of “Heroes of the UPA”. The UPA tis celebrated by many Ukrainians for fighting for Ukrainian independence during World War II, but its members were also responsible for wartime massacres of tens of thousands of Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia. Responding to Zelensky’s decision, President Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest state decoration in June, which Zelensky famously returned by courier.

By July, for the first time since this question was asked in polling, 52 per cent of Poles opposed accepting Ukrainian refugees, against 42 per cent who supported it.

“In Poland, the feeling was roughly: ‘We helped them so much, we opened our homes to them, and in return they honour people responsible for the genocide of Poles’,” Dr Adamski explains. “In Ukraine, it was: ‘For four and a half years we’ve been fighting, suffering and, in doing so, defending Poland too from Russian aggression – and now they’re trying to tell us who we can and cannot regard as our national heroes.’

Russia has inevitably sought to amplify those tensions. An analysis by the Polish Institute of International Affairs found that between May 26 and July 13 the number of Polish-language social-media posts containing extreme anti-Ukrainian hate speech rose by 171 per cent, while engagement with them increased by 345 per cent. Russian fingerprints were visible throughout the surge: VKontakte (VK), Russia’s largest social network, was the most prominent forum, while coordinated pro-Kremlin networks such as Operation Pravda also featured prominently. The institute concluded that, while Moscow did not create the crisis, Russia has become its main beneficiary.

The deeper problem, Adamski argues, is cumulative. Older prejudices met Russian disinformation, social media and a coarsening political debate, while journalists and intellectuals lost some of their traditional role as gatekeepers. Resentments that might once have been moderated increasingly reach voters directly – and can be rewarded politically.

But carelessness has not been one-sided.

History itself is understood very differently in the two societies. Growing up in Kyiv, Iwaniuk says she was barely taught about Volhynia: “Poles are immersed in history. They talk about history in magazines, on television, at the dinner table.” In Soviet and post-Soviet Ukraine, by contrast, people were taught not to ask too many questions about the past. She remembers asking her father about the UPA and Volhynia when she was still a schoolgirl. He answered: “I don’t know – I think they were the ones who fought against everyone.”

That gap, she argues, helped produce remarkably hapless political gestures. For example, the former Ukrainian president Petro Poroshenko knelt at a memorial to Polish victims of Volhynia a day after Kyiv renamed Moscow Avenue after UPA leader Stepan Bandera; Ukraine’s parliament recognised UPA members as independence fighters on the same day that former Polish president Bronislaw Komorowski was visiting Kyiv.

“President Zelensky certainly knew that Poland had a different view of the UPA than Ukraine, but I doubt the decision to name one of the units after the ‘Heroes of the UPA’ was meant as a deliberate provocation,” Adamski says. “My impression is that no one in Kyiv fully anticipated the fallout.”

There is also an economic asymmetry.

“Poland’s post-Communist transformation succeeded, while Ukraine is still fighting for survival as a state,” Iwaniuk argues. “While Poles have the luxury of looking back and debating the past, for Ukrainians the reaction is often: ‘Are you kidding? You want to talk about this now, when we don’t even know if our country will exist?’”

That does not make anti-Ukrainian violence an inevitable or legitimate consequence. But it helps explain how a relationship built on extraordinary solidarity became politically combustible.

The distinction is visible in another paradox that Iwaniuk points to: Ukrainians are becoming more integrated into Polish society just as the imagined collective “Ukrainian” is becoming more threatening in political discourse.

“They are your neighbour, the father of your child’s classmate, a colleague, the woman working in the local shop, someone running a business down the street,” she says. Yet the abstract Ukrainian is increasingly portrayed as a criminal, competitor or security threat.

Vladimir Medvedev, a Belarusian-born Polish citizen who founded the Glos Migranta (The Migrant’s Voice) initiative this summer, encountered another consequence when organising a recent migrants’ rights demonstration: people with legal status worried about far-right activists, provocations and deportation. Even a German acquaintance of his, married to a Polish woman and fluent in Polish, had been told to “fuck off to Ukraine” after somebody heard his accent.

Both governments now appear to understand the danger. Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk has publicly urged Warsaw and Kyiv to de-escalate, and recent bilateral talks have stressed the importance of “responsible communication” and a balanced tone in public debate.

On August 24, Warsaw hosted an event marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s declaration of independence at Castle Square, where blue and yellow flags flew next to the white and red ones.

But the political temperature does not fall on command. On August 14, a 14-year-old Ukrainian girl and her 12-year-old brother were allegedly abused and physically attacked near the railway station in Bydgoszcz after speaking Ukrainian. A woman was later charged with insulting them and violating their bodily integrity because of their nationality. She has denied the allegations.

World.title: Author Lea Ypi Explores Albanians’ Struggles for Dignity Under Communism
World.content:
Throughout her childhood, Lea Ypi knew her parents were “talking in secret”.

“My childhood was full of mysteries about my family,” she recalled.

Ypi, author of the acclaimed 2021 memoir Free: Coming of Age at the End of History and, more recently, Indignity: A Life Reimagined, was 11 when communism in Albania crumbled and only later came to learn of the suffering her grandparents endured under the Stalinist regime of Enver Hoxha.

“I grew up as a girl in a communist system, a child who believed in the truths of that system, while I understood that there was something in my family that was not exactly the way I saw it,” Ypi said in an interview with BIRN during a visit to Pristina as a guest lecturer at the annual International Seminar on Albanian Language, Literature, and Culture.

World.title: From Zvornik to Visegrad, Bosnian Serbs Keep Cult of Mladic Alive
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Hundreds of people marched through the streets of the eastern Bosnian city of Zvornik on Thursday night, clapping and chanting the name of the man convicted of some of the worst atrocities in Europe since World War II, glorifying his name as they paid tribute after his death in custody.

“Ratko Mladic!” they shouted in unison. “Ratko Mladic!”

In the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity, the cult of Mladic lives on. Significantly, many of the participants in the Zvornik march were young men who may not have even been born when the Bosnian Serb Army chief waged his bloody campaigns during the 1992-95 war.

“This is Zvornik, the city of the mass graves of my people,” Bosniak politician Camil Durakovic, vice president of Republika Srpska, wrote in a shocked reaction to the video footage.

World.title: Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said on Friday that “The Hague wanted [Ratko] Mladic to die behind bars, not in a hospital” because the UN court declined to release the former Bosnian Serb military chief for palliative care in Belgrade ahead of his death.

“We have seen that they did not want to allow the general to die in Serbia, where he wanted to die. That is uncivilised behaviour, behaviour without precedent and without justification,” Vucic said in his first public statement after the death of Mladic on Thursday.

He added that he had been in close contact with Mladic’s family, and that Serbia would ensure that the former Bosnian Serb military leader’s funeral would be “done in a dignified and proper manner”.

On Thursday, Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic said that Mladic would be buried with state honours in Serbia. Vucic introduced a note of doubt, however, saying that everything published in the press had been inaccurate.

Vucic also claimed that “the West” had only found Serbs guilty of war crimes from the 1990s.

“Do I believe in justice from The Hague? I never have, and I still do not,” he said.

“All those who took part in crimes against Serbs in the former Yugoslavia were always either acquitted or given token sentences, only for those decisions to later be changed on appeal and the defendants ultimately released,” he added.

Vucic’s statement, slamming the Hague court, echoes Thursday’s reactions to Mladic’s death in pro-government media, among members of the governing Serbian Progressive Party, from hardline nationalist politicians Vojislav Seselj and Aleksandar Vulin and from Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik.

Serbia is an EU candidate state, and on Friday, the European Commission told Radio Free Europe that it was up to the Belgrade authorities to decide what role they would play in the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.

However, the Commission warned: “The European Commission considers any glorification of war criminals to be contrary to the most fundamental European values and to have no place either in the EU or in countries that are candidates for EU membership.”

World.title: Rijeka Becomes a Key Regional Hub as Rijeka Gateway Welcomes 100th Vessel
World.content:
August the 31st, 2026 – Rijeka has become a key regional hub as the Rijeka Gateway facility welcomes its 100th vessel.

Rijeka Gateway successfully tested parallel ship operations for the first time back in April, as this operating model enables better utilisation of the operational quay, shorter waiting times for ships and greater efficiency of terminal operations. Poslovni reports that Rijeka Gateway is currently the technologically most advanced container terminal in this part of Europe, marked the arrival of its 99th and 100th ships just a few days before the first anniversary of the start of commercial operations at the terminal. The feeder ships Moraga and Conship Luv berthed at the terminal almost simultaneously, after which terminal operations of unloading and loading cargo began.

The ships Moraga and Conship Luv, which have been calling at Rijeka in a regular weekly rotation since the end of July, have further strengthened the role of Rijeka Gateway and cooperation with the global shipping companies Hapag-Lloyd and Maersk. After the successfully established cooperation model with Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd has also started using the terminal as a transhipment hub for import and export cargo from neighbouring Italy, just across the Adriatic.

In this way, Rijeka Gateway has further confirmed its role as a regional logistics hub for container traffic within the Adriatic and is currently the only terminal on the Adriatic that performs this type of operations within the Gemini network. The Gemini network is an operational cooperation between the companies Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd, which covers seven main global trade routes and serves to accelerate and optimise traffic, and Rijeka Gateway is a key port of call within the Gemini cooperation on the AE12/SE1 line that connects major Asian ports with the Mediterranean. Rijeka is now further connected with Trieste, Venice, Ravenna and Ancona over in neighbouring Italy, and the terminal has expanded its accessibility and connectivity with regional markets.

“It’s a particular pleasure for us that we welcomed the 100th ship before marking the first anniversary of commercial operations. In just one year, as a newly built terminal, Rijeka Gateway has received 100 ships, of which 47 large container ships, so-called mother vessels, on intercontinental services between Asia and Europe, and 53 feeder ships that connect Rijeka with regional Italian ports. But behind each of these numbers stand people. I am extremely proud of our team, which in a very short time has built organisational and operational capabilities comparable to the best terminals in the network. Today Rijeka Gateway employs more than 420 people, and it is precisely their expertise, dedication and professionalism that have enabled the achievement of such a significant success already in the first year of operations,” stated Peter Corfitsen, Chief Executive Officer of Rijeka Gateway.

World.title: Kucel – The Sandy Oasis Less Than an Hour from Zagreb
World.content:
August the 31st, 2026 – You’ll likely have never heard of it, but Kucel is a sandy oasis less than an hour from the heart of Zagreb, but it seems as if it couldn’t possibly be further away.

There’s a rather unknown touch of the tropics in a completely unexpected place not far from Zagreb, more specifically Lijevi Dubrovčak near Ivanić-Grad. Putni kofer writes that the beach is called Kucel Beach, and it’s worth discovering.

a surprise on the sava’s banks

Kucel Beach is nothing like a small accumulation of sand mixed with gravel. Instead, it’s an expansive stretch of shoreline made of the finest sand, which is quite a surprise compared to the gravel banks most are used to seeing. Almost perfect sand, together with the beautiful nature, are its main assets. The beauty of this beach also lies in its peace. You’re likely to have Kucel Beach entirely to yourself. Navigation will easily take you to this area, and it’s no more than an hour’s drive from Zagreb at most. There is no infrastructure on this beach, meaning that wild and natural is precisely what you’ll get. Nevertheless, various events are sometimes held on the beach. Kucel Beach isn’t an organised bathing area, nor is swimming actually intended on the beach. Because of the currents of the Sava, it’s safe only in the shallows, so it’s recommended only to dip your feet in and paddle. Dogs are also freely allowed on the beach.

an area for walks, bike rides and unwinding

Kucel Beach, if you don’t mind the sand, can indeed be an excellent option for a picnic and a starting point for exploring the rest of the area. In the latter case, it is enough simply to stay in the embrace of the Sava and follow its course. As you follow it you will notice that a number of places there have a left and a right version, depending on which bank of the Sava they are on. Lijevi Dubrovčak, home to the Posavina Corn Maze which we also visited that day, is just one such example. There is also Desni Dubrovčak.

The wider area is made for a relaxed road trip, cycling or walks. The region is peaceful, the fields are expansive, and although the road is quite narrow there is still room for two cars to pass. On one side of the fence there is often the steep bank of the Sava, hidden behind dense bushes and trees; on the other side it drops a few metres towards the fields. You can also “switch” sides of the Sava: you can cross the river by ferry or via the 160-metre-long bridge in Martinska Ves.
