World.title: Green-blue infrastructure and heritage: building a resilient and timeless Delhi
World.content:
A city’s greatness is measured as much by what it safeguards as by what it builds. On that count, Delhi has few equals. Its ecological wealth spans the Yamuna and its floodplains, the Ridge, urban forests and biodiversity parks, while its cultural wealth lives on in monuments, historic precincts, and archaeological sites that span centuries.

With the country working towards the Prime Minister’s vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, Delhi carries the responsibility of showing how a fast-growing metropolis can pursue development alongside environmental restoration and heritage conservation. The Master Plan for Delhi (MPD) 2047 gives the national capital a framework to put both at the centre of its future.

Nature as core infrastructure

Urban planning today operates under rules that climate change has rewritten. Higher temperatures, extreme rainfall, water stress, worsening air quality, and shrinking biodiversity all bear directly on residents’ health and daily lives. Rivers, forests, wetlands, lakes, and parks have moved beyond the status of amenities: they now function as core urban infrastructure.

At the heart of MPD-2047 is a connected green-blue network that draws the Yamuna, the Ridge, forests, biodiversity parks, water bodies, drains, and neighbourhood parks into one ecological system.

Urban forests and green corridors filter the air, cool heat-trapped neighbourhoods, and give native species a place to thrive. Revived water bodies, wetlands, and floodplains recharge groundwater and help the city cope with intense rainfall. Parks, trails, and cycling routes support active living and give communities spaces they can reach. The aim is straightforward: nature should run through daily urban life, not sit apart from it in scattered green patches.

Reviving the Yamuna and the Ridge

Any picture of Delhi’s future is incomplete without the Yamuna. The river has shaped the city’s geography and civilisation for centuries, though rapid urbanisation has left its floodplains under unprecedented strain. MPD-2047 puts the Yamuna at the heart of this ecological renewal, proposing to protect, conserve, and ecologically restore close to 1,700 hectares of floodplain.

Pollution is to be addressed where it starts: drains emptying into the river will be intercepted and treated through upgraded sewage infrastructure, constructed wetlands and bioremediation, restoring the river’s ecological health, and the floodplain’s natural functions.

The ambition extends further than restoration: Delhi has to rebuild its relationship with the river. A planned 52-kilometre cycling corridor, with walking trails, green stretches and organised recreational areas, will bring citizens back to the waterfront, turning revived sections into lively public spaces without compromising their ecology. A restored Yamuna could serve as both an ecological lifeline and a landmark public space.

Standing alongside it is Delhi’s other ecological pillar, the Ridge, an extension of the ancient Aravali range. MPD-2047 plans to restore roughly 7,784 hectares of it, guided by native species and scientific ecosystem management. The point is not simply to plant more trees but to build healthier ecosystems that sustain local biodiversity and secure the national capital’s environmental balance over the long run.

A living heritage

Delhi’s heritage has few rivals among cities. Its forts, monuments, stepwells, archaeological remains, and historic precincts each carry the story of an era that helped shape the city. Modernisation makes protecting this inheritance more urgent, not less. Yet conservation cannot mean preserving buildings and neighbourhoods as if frozen in time. Heritage has to stay a living part of the city, tied to the lives and ambitions of the people who inhabit it.

Under MPD-2047, close to 1,500 heritage assets are to come under Cultural Resource Management Plans, moving conservation from scattered efforts towards a structured, long-term system. Adaptive reuse is central to this: heritage buildings, carefully repurposed as museums, libraries, hotels, offices or cultural venues, stay useful to the city while their historic character remains intact.

A mix of planning and financial incentives, including Transferable Development Rights, façade retention and reasonable relaxation of space standards by the competent authority, subject to fire and life-safety norms, is meant to make conservation economically viable. It should be seen as an opportunity rather than a burden.

Heritage carries economic weight too: well-maintained historic areas draw tourism, create jobs, and open opportunities for local businesses. MPD-2047 proposes heritage, cultural and festival circuits linking monuments, precincts and public spaces, so visitors take in Delhi as a living historical landscape rather than a checklist of monuments. Precincts active around the clock, supported by better public spaces and walkable streets, can sustain local crafts, hospitality, and cultural enterprise.

Real strength

What gives MPD-2047 its real strength is bringing ecological and cultural planning together. Many historic sites sit within or beside forests, water bodies, the Ridge, and the Yamuna landscape. Linking them through greenways, cycling paths, and revived water systems builds a complete urban experience: water bodies as community spaces, green corridors joining neighbourhoods to biodiversity parks, residents cycling beside a restored river, and historic precincts humming with culture and commerce. As India works towards Viksit Bharat 2047, Delhi has to show that development and conservation reinforce rather than oppose each other. A Viksit Dilli cannot measure itself by growth alone. It must breathe easier, live healthier, and honour the heritage that gives it a soul.

Taranjit Singh Sandhu, Lieutenant-Governor, Delhi

World.title: Delhi SIR documents differ on categorisation of voters left out
World.content:
Among the documents published by the office of the Delhi Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) on Monday, two — the minutes of a meeting between Booth Level Officers (BLOs) and booth-level agents (BLAs), and a media statement — placed voters whose names had been left out of the draft roll in five categories: ‘absent’, ‘shifted’, ‘dead’, ‘duplicate’ and ‘others’.

A third document, also published on Monday and containing details of the voters left out, however, classified them under only four categories: ‘permanently shifted’, ‘untraceable/absent’, ‘dead’ and ‘already enrolled’.

The mismatch assumes significance because official documents and an earlier press statement from the CEO’s office identify ‘others’ as a category comprising electors who did not submit or refused to submit their enumeration forms (EFs) and who were marked as ‘EF refused’.

An analysis by The Hindu of the list of names removed across 14,947 polling booths found no separate category for ‘EF refused’.

In Tughlaqabad Extension, 15 electors were recorded as ‘EF refused’ in the minutes of the meeting dated August 17, the last day of the enumeration phase, beyond which no changes were allowed. The minutes were signed by BLOs and BLAs of the BJP and AAP.

In Monday’s list, however, one of these 15 electors was categorised as ‘shifted’, while the remaining 14 were shown as ‘untraceable/absent’. Similar instances were found in other records.

When reached for comment on the issue, the CEO’s office did not respond.

World.title: Delhi SIR draft roll out; 47.56 lakh names deleted
World.content:
The names of 47.56 lakh (32.78%) voters in Delhi were removed from the draft electoral roll published on Monday. The deletion of names, carried out during the 49-day enumeration phase of the ongoing special intensive revision (SIR) drive, is based on forms that were not returned, said poll officials.

War of words

Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convener Arvind Kejriwal took a swipe at the Election Commission (EC) over the deletion of names.

In a post on X, he wrote: “The names of 47 lakh voters are missing. The Government of India is unnecessarily worried about the population. Through SIR, the Election Commission will reduce our country’s population from 140 crore to 50 crore.”

Delhi Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) chief Harsh Malhotra said, “If Kejriwal believes that any genuine and eligible voter has been left out despite submitting the form, he should present such cases before the EC instead of levelling allegations.”

Meanwhile, the Congress’s Delhi unit alleged that despite repeated requests, Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) Ashok Kumar’s office has refused to share data on unmapped electors and those identified under ‘absent’, ‘shifted’, ‘dead’, ‘duplicate’ and ‘others’ categories.

Of the 97.53 lakh voters in the draft roll, over 33 lakh will receive notices because their forms could not be mapped to previous SIR or because they were flagged for various anomalies, including multiple children linked to the same parent; an age gap of under 15 years between parent and child; mismatched names between rolls; and differences in surnames.

The highest number of notices is set to be issued to voters in the North East district (3 lakh), which includes the constituencies of Karawal Nagar, Mustafabad, Gokalpur, and Babarpur, as per data accessed by The Hindu.

BLOs to serve notices

A senior official said that from the date of the issuance of the notice, which will carry details such as the reason, time and location of the hearing, the voter will have seven days to reply and seek an extension.

The notices will be delivered by Booth Level Officers (BLOs) while hearings will be conducted by Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) or Assistant Electoral Registration Officers.

Appearance for hearing

The BLOs will go house to house to serve notices, the official said, adding that it is not mandatory for an elector to physically appear for the hearing.

“The notices will carry a QR code where voters can upload the document or send it through the BLO,” the official said.

Appeal process

In cases where a person does not appear for a hearing, fails to provide any of the 11 prescribed documents or if their eligibility is in doubt, the ERO will issue an order removing the name and specifying the reasons for it.

Those whose names have been removed can approach the District Election Officer (the first appellate authority), followed by the CEO (the second and final appellate authority).

In a release, the CEO stated that those excluded could apply for re-inclusion in the final roll by enrolling as new voters through Form 6 along with a declaration – format of which is similar to the enumeration form – and documents till September 30.

World.title: CJP march: police step up security, to look out for participants at July 20 stir
World.content:
The Delhi Police have drawn up a multi-layered security plan involving online monitoring, drone surveillance, call records’ analysis at sensitive locations ahead of the proposed Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest on September 5, stressing that no permission has been granted for a gathering at India Gate, Police Headquarters (PHQ) or the approach routes.

Days before the BRICS Summit on September 12 and 13, the CJP has decided to hit the streets again over Centre’s failure to live up to its assurances after July protests, including the immediate withdrawal of FIRs against student protesters. The Supreme Court on Monday declined to pass any order against the protest in central Delhi.

CJP co-convenor Saurav Das said, “Delhi Police can continue with their routine work. But, as we have done in the past, our protest marches have always been peaceful. There should be no apprehension that this protest will not be peaceful.”

Multi-layered deployment

Security personnel will be deployed at Delhi’s inter-state borders, the periphery of New Delhi district, India Gate, PHQ and routes leading to these locations. Officials said the focus would be on preventing large gatherings and filtering out protesters before they reach the proposed sites.

A dedicated control room will coordinate inputs from field locations. Additional forces will be deployed in coordination with CAPFs, while detention teams and buses will be kept ready.

The Law and Order units across districts have been tasked with identifying Jantar Mantar participants who were flagged through facial-recognition systems (FRS) during the July 20 protest. Police officials have been asked to visit the residences of those who participated in the earlier protest, issue advisories against participation and document compliance.

Police have also stepped up online monitoring, tracking posts containing specific keywords and using algorithms to flag videos and other content considered suspicious, sources said.

Preventive action under Sections 107 and 116 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) is planned against identified organisers, an official said. Prohibitory orders under Section 163 BNSS are also likely. Security will additionally be strengthened around high-security areas.

Multi-level coordination

Police will coordinate with the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) and other transport authorities to regulate movement around the protest sites. App-based services, including food and delivery platforms, are also likely to be suspended within a five-kilometre radius on September 5. Internet suspension has not been confirmed and would require approval from competent authorities, an official said.

Officials will also use Aman Committee and Nagrik Suraksha Committee meetings to communicate the no-permission position and attempt to de-escalate mobilisation.

Delhi Police will coordinate with forces in Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab and Rajasthan for mirror picketing and restrictions on Delhi-bound movement of identified groups. Barricades will be erected at inter-state borders, including arterial and link roads. The Special Cell will provide technical surveillance support, including analysis of call-detail records and tower dumps at sensitive locations, where legally sanctioned. CCTV feeds from across the city will be monitored and preserved for post-event investigation, while drones may supplement surveillance.

The Intelligence and Special Branches have been asked to assess mobilisation trends, logistics providers, leaders, their movements and possible political backing.

Ambulances will be positioned and hospitals, including AIIMS, Ram Manohar Lohia and Lok Nayak Jai Prakash hospital, will be kept coordinated. An uninterrupted emergency corridor will be maintained through the sealed zone, officials said.

CJP response

Mr. Das said barricading protest sites like Jantar Mantar or India Gate would not prevent young people from demonstrating, adding that the larger issue is the violation of rights.

He said the party had communicated with police through multiple channels and assured them of cooperation, while questioning the requirement for permission to protest. “The very concept of requiring permission from the State to protest against the State is absurd and not acceptable,” Mr. Das said.

He also said a high-level government delegation had contacted him while he was in Puducherry, which he said indicated that the Centre was aware of the seriousness of the issue.

World.title: Govt. school student dies; teacher made her stand in sun, alleges kin
World.content:
A 10-year-old girl student at a government school in east Delhi’s Vinod Nagar died during treatment after suffering a seizure, with her family alleging days later that she had fallen ill after a teacher made her stand in the sun as punishment for not bringing a book. The teacher has been transferred. However, the police said a preliminary inquiry found no evidence to support the allegation.

According to the police, the girl died on August 27 at the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences (IHBAS) in east Delhi, where she had been undergoing treatment for nearly a month after suffering a seizure at school on July 22.

“After she suffered a seizure during school hours, the authorities called her parents and asked them to take her home. She was admitted to IHBAS, where she remained until her death. The family subsequently performed her final rites,” a senior police officer said.

On Monday, the family approached the school, alleging that the girl had died because of the punishment meted out to her. The school subsequently made a PCR call, following which the police conducted a preliminary inquiry.

“Preliminary verification of the medical and school records indicated that the cause of death was a seizure. We also questioned students and school staff and found no evidence that the girl had been made to stand in the sun. She had a history of epilepsy,” the officer said.

The inquiry also found that the parents had neither lodged a complaint nor raised any grievance with the school or the police regarding the incident when it occurred, more than a month before the girl’s death, the officer said.

“No case has been registered at this stage since the family is yet to submit a written complaint,” he added.

Teacher transferred

In a statement, Education Minister Ashish Sood said the accused teacher had been transferred with immediate effect to ensure that the “investigation was conducted fairly and without interference”.

“An inquiry is currently under way into the death of the student. The government is treating this matter with the utmost seriousness and sensitivity. If the inquiry establishes any negligence, dereliction of duty or irregularity at any level, strict and decisive action will be taken against those found responsible, in accordance with the law,” the Minister said.
