World.title: Azerbaijan slams ‘untrue’ reports by The Independent, The Guardian, and BBC
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 31. In recent days, articles containing untrue information aimed at misleading public opinion regarding the Republic of Azerbaijan have been published in the UK-based newspapers The Independent and The Guardian, as well as by the Russian service of the BBC.

This was stated in a statement by the Media Development Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

The Media Development Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan states that these publications, based on an overtly biased approach and subjective claims, create the impression of being part of a targeted information campaign aimed at damaging Azerbaijan's international image.

“The authors of the articles took no steps to investigate the subject in a balanced and objective manner or to seek the official position of the opposing side, preferring instead to present arguments based solely on their subjective assertions. This raises serious suspicions that the materials in question may be politically motivated and stem from the interests of certain lobby groups, which is deeply regrettable. Relevant measures will be taken to investigate such cases, which are aimed at casting a shadow over Azerbaijan's sovereignty, domestic and foreign policy, as well as its international prestige, and to take the necessary steps accordingly.

We once again call on the media organizations — The Independent, The Guardian, and the BBC — to remain committed to their declared professional principles, refrain from publishing biased, prejudiced, and inaccurate materials about Azerbaijan, and restore impartial information coverage in accordance with journalistic ethics,” the statement reads.

World.title: Hundreds feared stuck in hydropower tunnels since Nepal-Tibet floods
World.content:
Rescuers are racing to free hundreds of workers believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites that were buried in mud by catastrophic flooding on the Nepal-China border, with the death toll climbing and increasingly desperate families searching for missing loved ones.

The combined deaths in Nepal and China have surpassed 950, with more than 4,400 people missing, including 43 Australians.

A private-sector association representing power companies said at least 900 workers were unaccounted-for at 12 hydropower projects damaged by the flash floods in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

Nepal army personnel work during a search and rescue operation near the Trishuli Hydropower Project site in Nepal's Rasuwa district. (Reuters: Nepal Army/Handout)

About 500 of those workers were believed to be trapped in tunnels. At least one expert said that some workers could have access to oxygen, but others warned that the chances of finding survivors were diminishing. As the rescue efforts intensified, four bodies were recovered from three mud-filled tunnels, Nepal's army said.

Nepali survivors return to unrecognisable villages entombed in mud The ABC sees firsthand the devastation and rescue operation underway in the worst-hit areas of Nepal.

Some workers managed to call for help when the disaster struck last Wednesday and others who managed to flee told authorities and relatives that many of their colleagues were still in the tunnels, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of the Independent Power Producers' Association, Nepal.

It was unclear whether rescuers have had any contact with the trapped workers since the initial calls for help.

Six days after the disaster, fears were growing that some might have suffocated, Mr Dangi said.

Giant tunnels are built to control water flow

Rescue efforts were focused on people trapped in the gigantic tunnels built for controlling the flow of water.

"These tunnels are big enough to drive trucks through," said Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria based in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

"And from what we understand, they have managed to get oxygen to some of those stuck inside and are trying to rescue them now.

" It's a race for time, though, as people need food and water. "

In the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project, in the hard-hit Rasuwa district, at least 576 people were missing, Mr Dangi said, adding that about 300 of them were believed to be trapped inside the project's tunnel.

Nepal's paramilitary force personnel carry the body of a flash flood victim for burial at a mass burial site in Chitwan, Nepal. (AP: Dar Yasin)

At the Trishuli-3 Hydropower Project, crews were working to descend about 15 metres into a tunnel in an effort to reach those believed trapped inside, according to Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal's army spokesman.

Workers shovelling mud from a flood-ravaged power station in Dhading, Nepal, told The Associated Press that the station is a key connection for providing power to more than 20,000 people in the region.

Families desperate for information about missing loved ones

Nepal's disaster agency said on Monday that 939 deaths had been counted in that country, with 3,925 people missing, including 592 foreigners. As of Sunday, Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing. Chinese state media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including over 100 Nepalis.

Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said there were great fears for the safety of 43 Australians still missing.

"We are urgently seeking to ascertain their whereabouts … we do hold grave fears, grave concerns for their safety," she told 7.30.

Ms Wong said the department was able to confirm nine of the missing 43 Australians had crossed the border into China at the time of the disaster.

"What we don't have as yet, confirmed from any of the authorities, is any information about the 43 in total," she said.

"This is such a difficult time. It's incredibly distressing.

"We are working to do whatever we can and to provide any information we obtain."

An Australian Air Force C-17A carrying humanitarian supplies, equipment and personnel is set to travel to Nepal on Tuesday, as part of $8 million in humanitarian support announced by the federal government.

People stand on remnants of a bridge that spanned across Trishuli river in Nepal's Dhading District. (AP: Niranjan Shrestha)

Chinese media highlight government efforts to rebuild roads

On the Chinese side, rescue and recovery efforts included rebuilding the road leading to the Gyirong Port border crossing that regulated travel between China and Nepal.

Trucks carried giant rocks as workers tried to repave a portion of the road, state broadcaster CCTV showed on Monday, next to rapidly rushing waters, which have been made more powerful by days of rain.

The road is now under 2 to 3 metres of water. The repaving effort was just a little over a kilometre from the border, CCTV said.

Although some rescue teams have managed to reach the border, that represented only a portion of the force.

Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People's Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side.

Scientists who studied satellite images said Wednesday's flash floods started after bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region collapsed on Wednesday, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as a magnitude-5.2 seismic event.

The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

AP/ABC

World.title: Live: Voters sent Labor message in WA by-election loss, Wong says
World.content:
Australia will miss the economic benefits of the artificial intelligence boom unless businesses actually use the technology to make bigger changes, Treasury has warned.

New advice provided to Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Australia's current AI uptake was widespread but shallow, with less than 10 per cent of businesses reporting "significant" adoption.

The Treasury note said much-feared job losses had not yet materialised, but officials were watching young and entry-level workers overseas for early signs.

Officials described AI as the first "credible" accelerant of global economic growth in almost two decades, but found Australia was at risk of failing to capture the benefits of the technology.

Chalmers said AI was shaping up to be the "biggest economic transformation in our lifetime" and he was confident Australia could "maximise the economic upside and minimise the risks".

Read more of this story at the link below.

World.title: New Sydney women's refuge thanks entirely to philanthropic donations
World.content:
The charity behind an in-demand women's refuge will open a second Sydney location thanks to philanthropic donations, after being unsuccessful in securing federal government funding.

For over a decade, Mary's House Services has provided accommodation and services in Sydney's north for women and children escaping domestic violence.

The site of their first refuge, a leased property, has provided more than 20,000 safe room nights.

Mary's House Services is almost entirely philanthropically funded. (Supplied)

Mary's House Services recorded a 63 per cent increase in client referrals in 2025 compared with the previous year.

"We receive referrals from all parts of Sydney as well as from rural and regional areas in New South Wales and even interstate, because often families need to relocate for safety, financial, employment and other practical reasons," Mary's House Services CEO Yvette Vignando said.

In the 2024-25 financial year, 118 women (and their children) were declined refuge accommodation because of no vacancy, with 38 referrals for social worker support also declined due to no capacity, their annual report states.

In the 2025-26 financial year, Ms Vignando said they had to decline 176 refuge accommodation referrals due to no vacancy.

Yvette Vignando says the refuge receives referrals from all parts of NSW. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Government knocked back funding for refuge purchase

Amid a peak in demand, the organisation pursued funding through Housing Australia's National Housing Infrastructure Facility Crisis and Transitional Housing program (now known as the Housing Australia Future Fund – Crisis and Transitional program) to purchase and upgrade an existing building in Sydney for use as their second refuge.

In the 2024-25 federal budget, the Australian government committed $1 billion to fund crisis and transitional accommodation for women and children.

Mary's House Services had consulted with Homes NSW and Housing Australia about their proposed application.

"We were devastated to be informed that our application was unsuccessful," Ms Vignando said.

The charity's application for federal government funding was unsuccessful. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

The not-for-profit organisation is a registered charity that is almost entirely philanthropically funded, though it has received some NSW government funding to add three caseworkers to its team.

Independent MP for Warringah Zali Steggall made representations on Mary's House Services' behalf, but that was also unsuccessful.

Ms Steggall told the ABC she felt "very disappointed".

"Domestic violence is a national crisis. A suite of urgent action is needed, and that has to include proper support to the frontline organisations that are there when people are at their most vulnerable," she said.

" It's simply not acceptable that families in my electorate, or anywhere in Australia, might be turned away in their hour of need due to a lack of crisis accommodation. "

Zali Steggall says urgent action is needed to better fund frontline services. (ABC: Ian Cutmore)

Two factors noted in Housing Australia's rejection correspondence were that the project did not provide an uplift in housing supply and that the organisation had not demonstrated sufficient or secure funding.

The rejection also said the NSW government assessed the project's "overall priority as low".

Homes NSW declined to comment to the ABC.

A Housing Australia spokesperson said applicants were assessed against eligibility criteria.

"We recognise that funding outcomes may be disappointing for unsuccessful applicants and acknowledge the effort involved in developing and submitting proposals for consideration," they said.

"Housing Australia previously advised Mary's House Services of the outcome of its application and identified the areas where the proposal did not meet the program requirements."

Do you know more? If you have any information about the story, contact Isabella Ross.

Mary's House Services instead reached out to its philanthropic networks and secured the money to purchase the property through donations.

"If it was not for the incredible generosity of a small number of philanthropic individuals, we would not be where we are today," Ms Vignando said.

New safe haven a win for Sydney's north

The new refuge will consist of self-contained apartments for women and children.

This second site will primarily provide temporary crisis housing for women and children of all ages, including families with pets.

The second refuge will provide temporary crisis housing for women and children of all ages, including families with pets. (Supplied/Unsplash: Vasu Pendyala)

Between both refuges and its accompanying services such as specialist social workers, housing coordination and trauma-informed counselling, Mary's House Services will support hundreds of victim-survivors annually.

"Ten years ago, a group of caring community members on Sydney's lower north shore decided that more women and children experiencing domestic and family violence should be provided with safety, critical care and hope," the organisation's chair Helen Conway said.

"They recognised a gap in services … the founders say that their vision has now grown beyond anything they imagined."

Ms Steggall said she was pleased the organisation had found the necessary financial backing: "It's an important project that I'm very proud to support."

Helen Conway praised the work of the Mary's House Services's team. (Supplied)

Now, the focus is planning for the future.

The purchase of the property will be complete in October, then upgrades to security and renovations will take place so that it is ready to offer refuge accommodation from 2027.

Women sleeping in cars after escaping violence not a 'solution', say experts Domestic violence services in NSW are at 150 per cent capacity, with short-term refuge solutions like car parks being viewed as a response to the immediate crisis.

To operate the refuge, the charity will need to employ more specialist social workers.

But at this stage it was entirely reliant on philanthropic generosity, Ms Vignando said, with no government funding committed to service delivery at the second refuge.

"We're always cheering for our friends in the sector when they become the recipient of funding.

"But my observation is that there is not enough federal or state government investment in crisis and transitional housing across Sydney's northern suburbs," Ms Vignando said.

World.title: Breaking: Man shot dead in Sydney home invasion
World.content:
A man believed to be in his 20s has been shot dead during a home invasion in Sydney's south-west, police say.

Emergency services were called to the Glen Alpine home about 3:45am.

Police said Campbelltown City Police Area Command officers found the man with a gunshot injury inside the house.

The man, who is yet to be formally identified, died at the scene.

Emergency services were called at about 3:45am on Tuesday. (ABC News)

Police said they were told the unknown offenders left the scene a short time before officers arrived.

A crime scene has been established and an investigation is underway with assistance from the State Crime Command's Homicide Squad.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Fracked gas from Beetaloo Basin will flow to NT power grid from today
World.content:
Gas fracked from the Beetaloo Basin will this week begin feeding into the grid to power Northern Territory homes and businesses — a milestone that has been met with both celebration and concern.

Eight years after the NT's moratorium on fracking was lifted, the tap is officially being turned on at the remote and expansive onshore gas development hundreds of kilometres south of Darwin today.

In a statement, NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said gas from the Beetaloo Basin would "drive new investment in the Territory across a range of sectors, creating employment and growing the economy".

Gas, gold mining key in plan to reversing NT's $11b debt Northern Territory Treasurer Bill Yan says the government is turning the tide on the Territory's $11 billion debt, supported by progress on major projects including Beetaloo Basin gas and a number of gold and lithium mines.

"This is a pivotal moment in the Territory's history, and a turning point in our bright future as a decade of potential becomes production," she said.

Government officials, gas company heads, native title holders and the Northern Land Council (NLC) are expected to be in attendance for the moment.

NLC chair Matthew Ryan said in a statement the NLC believed the new agreement would lead to jobs and benefits for native title holders in the Barkly region, the remote town of Elliott and surrounding communities and outstations.

"Today is an example of what can be achieved when native title holders have a seat at the table with industry," Mr Ryan said.

" Working with traditional owners is key for economic growth for the whole territory. "

The Sturt Plateau Pipeline connects Tamboran Resources' gas development in the Beetaloo Basin to the Amadeus Gas Pipeline. (Supplied: APA Group)

Gas company Tamboran Resources' chief executive Todd Abbott said the company was "committed to ensuring this development creates meaningful and lasting opportunities".

The Country Liberal Party (CLP) government has long claimed the Beetaloo Basin would be a key economic driver for the NT, and said "more than 40 terajoules a day will flow straight into the Territory grid" from today.

"Development of the basin is forecast to generate more than $17 billion in economic value over the next two decades and support more than 13,000 jobs by 2040," the statement said.

Orange flags promoting mining in the Beetaloo have recently popped up around Darwin. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

'Bit of hype' around economic benefits

However, there is some disagreement about exactly how much revenue and employment the Beetaloo will generate.

Independent economist Saul Eslake described the milestone as "significant" but said it would not offer a silver-bullet solution for the NT.

Saul Eslake says there is a variety of estimates regarding how much revenue Beetaloo will generate. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

"I think there's a bit of hype in saying it will change the Northern Territory economy forever, but it is a very significant development," he told ABC Radio Darwin yesterday.

Mr Eslake said annual estimates on the amount of royalties the project would generate varied from $36 million to "in excess of $220 million a year".

Over the weekend, concerned Territorians gathered in Darwin's northern suburbs for an anti-fracking rally organised by the Environment Centre Northern Territory (ECNT).

The anti-fracking protest took place in Nightcliff. (ABC News: Oliver Chaseling)

"This is a PR stunt from an industry with bleak economic prospects and no social license to operate in the Territory," ECNT acting co-chief executive Bree Ahrens said.

Part of their concern was an NT government plan to make the territory the data centre capital of the world, powered by gas fracked from the Beetaloo.

"We are calling for a ban on fracking and AI data centres before it's too late," Ms Ahrens said.

Environment Centre NT says more than 500 Darwin residents have signed up for the Ban Fracking placards. (ABC News: Oliver Chaseling)

While the NT government has rolled out pro-Beetaloo Basin flags across Darwin, Ms Ahrens said new anti-fracking signage was going up simultaneously.

"More than 500 Darwin residents have already signed up to put a new 'Ban Fracking' sign on their home or business," she said.

World.title: Former grand slam semifinalist smashes racquet after early US Open exit
World.content:
Frenchwoman Lois Boisson has provided the first big blow-up of the US Open, smashing her racquet in disgust after going down in three sets to American 26th seed Emma Navarro.

A semifinalist at the French Open in 2025 and a winner on the WTA Tour, Boisson has had a tough 12 months, with injuries forcing a long lay-off and a comeback that has not yielded many good results.

The 23-year-old has a career-high ranking of 34, which she achieved in February despite not playing a professional match between September 2025 and April.

Since her career-high ranking, Boisson has tumbled to 237th in the world with many early exits from tournaments as she tries to regain the stunning form she showed last year.

But another first round exit at a grand slam, a third consecutive this year, was too much for Boisson to take on the court.

With an attempted backhand slice falling well short, Navarro was handed a 7-6(6), 6-7(1), 6-3 win and Boisson threw her racquet to the ground.

The two met at the net for the handshake, but as Navarro waved to the crowd, Boisson grabbed a second racquet and proceeded to demolish it with three powerful slams on the hard court, followed by another throw.

While Boisson will try to regroup to finish the year on a more positive note, Navarro will either face fellow countrywoman Caty McNally or Anouk Koevermans of the Netherlands.

Sabalenka begins US Open defence, men's draw blown open with second big exit

Aryna Sabalenka is attempting to win the US Open for a third consecutive year. (Reuters: Imagn Images/Robert Deutsch)

Aryna Sabalenka got off to a winning start in her quest for a third successive US Open title on Monday and men's 10th seed Arthur Fils exited as the second day of the tournament kicked off after Novak Djokovic's shock defeat left another major hole in the men's field.

Sabalenka has been trying to regain her usual dominance after a frustrating stretch, having failed to reach a final since March, and looked well on her way with an easy 6-2, 6-4 win over Colombia's Camila Osorio.

The world number one launched 32 winners in the first match of the day at Arthur Ashe Stadium to set up a meeting with Russian Polina Iatcenko in the second round.

"I'm happy with my performance. She's a tough opponent, makes you work really hard to get every point," Sabalenka said.

"So I'm happy that I was able to close the match in straight sets."

Greek Stefanos Tsitsipas stunned the Cincinnati winner Fils 4-6, 7-6(3), 6-1, 6-4 in the early match at Louis Armstrong Stadium, setting up a second-round meeting with South African Lloyd Harris.

Fils's upset marked the latest surprise exit in the men's draw after the 24-time major winner Djokovic crashed out the previous evening.

Seven matches were suspended on the outer courts on Sunday night due to rain and resumed on Monday local time, with organisers benefiting from the extended three-day first-round schedule after expanding the main draw to 15 days in 2025.

The Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova got the day underway on the Grandstand with a routine 6-3, 6-0 win over Austrian Sinja Kraus. The Czech seventh seed plays Briton Katie Boulter in the second round.

The Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen, who was forced to go through qualifying only two years after reaching the quarterfinals in New York, beat Kristina Liutova 4-6, 6-3, 6-1.

American Anisimova cruises to birthday win at US Open

Amanda Anisimova breezed past Ashlyn Krueger 6-1, 6-3 in the first round of the US Open in a strong start for last year's runner-up as she looks to challenge for the title again.

Playing on her 25th birthday, Anisimova fought off three break points early for a 2-1 lead before running away with the opening set in the all-American match-up at Louis Armstrong Stadium.

The players traded breaks to open the second set but Anisimova, the world number 10, never let her grip on the match slip, breaking Krueger's serve in the final game to win the match in one hour and 12 minutes.

"Ashlyn's a great player so I knew it was going to be a tough match," Anisimova said in a post-match on-court interview, shortly before the crowd sang Happy Birthday to her.

Anisimova will face Austrian Lilli Tagger in the second round.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Birrell saves match point as Aussies advance to US Open second rounds
World.content:
Gritty Kim Birrell has overcome a match point and a restless night's sleep to break her first-round jinx with a maiden US Open victory in New York.

Birrell wore down Croatian Petra Marcinko 3-6, 7-6 (7-4), 6-3 to finally reach the Open's second round after losing all three of her previous tournament openers at Flushing Meadows in 2023, 2024 and 2025.

Resurgent veteran James Duckworth also advanced with a mighty four-set upset win over 2026 French Open semifinalist Matteo Arnaldi, the men's 30th seed.

After climbing to Australian number two this year behind only world number seven Alex de Minaur, Duckworth continued his hot run with a 5-7, 6-3, 6-2, 7-6 (8) comeback victory.

The 34-year-old has now reached round two at all four grand slams and next faces China's Yibing Wu for a place in the last 32.

Birrell and Duckworth follow WA rising star Taylah Preston in progressing, with three more Australians in action later on Monday (Tuesday AEST).

Birrell was forced to return to court 7 following a nervy 14-hour rain delay.

After surviving a match point in the 12th game of the second set on Sunday night, Birrell was still trailing by a set and a mini break in the second-set tiebreaker before rallying to post one of the most satisfying wins of her career.

The Gold Coaster had lost in straight sets to Marcinko on grass at Eastbourne two months ago, having dropped the opening set 6-0 to the Croat in their first meeting, which Birrell won in Texas in February.

The reward for Birrell's resistance is a showdown with Russian world No.19 Ekaterina Alexandrova and a guaranteed $US190,000 ($265,000) payday — or more if she wins again on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

While Birrell and Duckworth marched on, Aleksandar Vukic was unable to win his own weather-delayed epic against Rei Sakamoto.

Sakamoto was up a break deep in the deciding set when their battle resumed, and the Japanese quickly won six more points on serve, without dropping any, to close out a 6-4, 6-7 (5-7), 6-4, 3-6, 6-4 victory.

Alexei Popyrin, Rinky Hijikata and Maya Joint are also playing for second-round berths on day two at Flushing Meadow.

Popyrin takes on former semifinalist Grigor Dimitrov, who had to qualify this year after being out injured. Rinky Hijikata also has a tough one against third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime.

Duckworth faces Italian Matteo Arnaldi and Joint is up against the much-fancied Liudmila Samsonova.

Sixth seed Alex de Minaur opens his title quest on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST) against Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.

AAP

World.title: Politics of the parklands on show at Labor's big MotoGP reveal
World.content:
The backdrop of the Malinauskas government's carefully planned unveiling of Adelaide's new MotoGP circuit on Sunday was not a noisy motorsport track.

In February, when the government revealed it had snatched MotoGP hosting rights from Victoria, rider Jack Miller was drafted in to roar across the River Torrens footbridge.

But on Sunday, Premier Peter Malinauskas spoke in an immersive arts centre that looked more like the setting for a TED Talk about climate change.

He was flanked by two large trees as he ran through a slide show outlining the government's highly anticipated, and feared, $96 million street circuit.

More than half a dozen of those slides were dedicated to the environment, trees and the eastern parklands.

"This is the area that, of course, has got the most attention given the understandable angst and concern that exists in some elements of the community, which I sympathise with, on tree loss," the premier said on Sunday.

Peter Malinauskas unveils the design for the MotoGP circuit. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

The green optics of the day would suggest Labor has grappled with a fair bit of its own angst about the parklands.

But beyond that, its policies appear to have shifted in response to public pressure, so much so that it left one environmentalist "floored".

A stark warning

To briefly recap, the Malinauskas government has faced significant resistance to its plans to build a new street circuit for MotoGP in Adelaide's eastern parklands.

A petition calling for a halt to works has been signed by more than 43,000 people.

Thousands of people have turned out to protest the project, calling on the state government to "stop the chop".

The rallies come after the government's similarly controversial upgrade of the North Adelaide Golf Course which required the felling of 585 trees in the northern parklands.

Kirsty Bevan says she is surprised the government agreed to her suggestions. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Conservation Council SA chief executive Kirsty Bevan, who leads the state's peak environment body, was among those firmly against MotoGP in the city, writing to the government repeatedly to outline her position.

"The conversations from there just kept coming back, 'We're going to go ahead with it'," she told the ABC.

The impasse put her in an "uncomfortable position", but she said there was room to push for an "investment commensurate with the amount of damage they were proposing".

"There was a moment in one of the conversations I had direct with the premier where I talked about the long-term impacts on nature and the parklands," Ms Bevan said.

"And [I said] this government could be known as the government that destroyed the parklands for the future, or they could be a government that develops in a way that is very positive for nature.

"And he was very interested in what that actually meant."

Design for MotoGP street circuit released Nearly 400 trees will be removed in Adelaide's eastern parklands to make way for a new MotoGP street circuit costing $96 million, the South Australian government has revealed.

That interest was on show on Sunday when Mr Malinauskas spruiked the Conservation Council's view that the overall street circuit project would be "net nature positive".

That was partly due to a new $15 million parklands package that will go towards things like butterfly habitat restoration and new water infrastructure for platypuses in the River Torrens.

"If you care about the environment, and if you care about the parklands, you should care about this project because it improves them," Mr Malinauskas said.

That's not to mention a host of other upgrades to the eastern parklands, including new infrastructure for the Adelaide Fringe; all arguably sweeteners for some sceptical stakeholders, particularly in Town Hall.

Ms Bevan said she was surprised the government agreed to the $15 million parklands package she had put forward, adding: "It really floors me every time I think about it."

"I thought for sure they were going to come with around three or four [million]."

The government has proposed a host of other upgrades as part of the transition. (Supplied: SA government)

She was similarly surprised to see the government agree to her suggestion that for every tree felled, 10 must replace it.

That's up from the three-to-one replacement ratio for the North Adelaide Golf Course.

As a result, there will be 3,770 trees planted for the circuit project, according to government figures.

A green movement divided

The Conservation Council has already copped a backlash from other environmental campaigners for its "net nature positive" view, revealing a split in the green movement.

Councillor Keiran Snape, one of the figureheads of the stop-the-chop campaign, claimed the Conservation Council had "sold out our parklands to the corporate Malinauskas government".

"It's become clear that Conservation SA has been well and truly played by the state government, allowing themselves to be used as part of the government's greenwashing of the MotoGP announcement," he posted on Facebook.

The premier says 42 significant trees will be cut down for the MotoGP track. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

In response, Ms Bevan said "I don't react to that because we're non-political, we're non-partisan, and I don't play into politics".

"I know for a fact I didn't sellout," she said, adding she had "lost count" of the number of signatures she had raised for the stop-the-chop campaign.

Another campaigner against the project, Adelaide Park Lands Association president Mat Monti, has vowed to keep up the fight.

"We'd encourage the government to invest in the environment, we'd encourage them to plant these trees, we'd encourage them to continue with revegetation, and we'd encourage them to invest $15 million in the parklands," they said.

"But we don't want them to do it just to excuse the destruction of the eastern parklands for MotoGP."

Mat Monti says the government should invest in the environment, but not as an excuse to fell trees for the MotoGP. (ABC News: Sarah Maunder)

But, as this column explored over the weekend, the future of the street circuit appears set, despite the growing push against the incursion on the heritage listed parklands.

Questions now have turned to Mr Malinauskas's comment in February, a month before the state election, that 45 trees would be lost for the circuit, not 377.

"He's been saying that he's got a mandate to deliver this and that people voted for it, and in some respects that's true," Opposition Leader Ashton Hurn told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"But … it's worthwhile reflecting as to whether people would have changed their vote if they knew it was 400 trees.

"You can't just ignore the significant taxpayer cost as well."

Rider Jack Miller roared across the River Torrens footbridge at February's announcement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Malinauskas rejected suggestions he was being misleading in February, saying he "made very clear at the time that we released the plans that there was going to have to be tree loss".

"I put the numbers out there publicly that were available to us at the time and I've subsequently made clear that that 45 number was significant trees," he said.

He later added: "No government will have delivered more new trees in the parklands in net terms than this one."

But in the view of Kirsty Bevan from the Conservation Council, those improvements do not happen in a vacuum.

"I still think that the only reason I was able to get the outcomes I got, which are phenomenal, are because the public pressure was really strong," she said.

"That has to continue."

World.title: Man killed in violent home invasion in Sydney
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

A man has been killed in a violent home invasion in Sydney’s south-west on Tuesday morning.

Police were called to the house on Mount Sugarloaf Drive in Glen Alpine about 3.40am following reports a group of home invaders had stormed into the two-storey property and fired shots at a resident, a man believed to be in his 20s.

The man was declared dead by emergency services shortly after their arrival.

The home invaders fled the scene before police arrived, and they remain at large hours after the violent attack.

An expansive crime scene has been established outside the home, as detectives search for evidence and speak to neighbours.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: NSW man first Australian declared dead in Nepal as death toll of flood exceeds 900; Trump vows to ‘hit Iran hard’ as tensions in the Middle East escalate
World.content:
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has again been forced to field questions about the government’s decision not to ban the import of smart glasses in reforms to privacy laws unveiled yesterday.

She said the government understood the need to balance the legal implications of an import ban with the real concerns that the wearable surveillance devices could be used to inflict harm.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said blocking smart glasses carried international legal risks. Alex Ellinghausen

“We look forward to people’s views, but also we need to balance that against the fact that Australians have always been early adopters. But we are very concerned about the rate and the propensity for which this can be misused by nefarious individuals,” Rowland told Sunrise this morning.

During a press conference yesterday, Rowland said that the government did not want to play “whack-a-mole” with emerging technologies by banning AI glasses, and that it would be incumbent on businesses to restrict the use of smart glasses on their premises.

World.title: ASX set to retreat as Wall Street slides; Oil prices climb after US strike on Iranian sites
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to retreat as Wall Street slides; Oil prices climb after US strike on Iranian sites Damian Troise and Alex Veiga Updated September 1, 2026 — 6:39am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street closed out August on a downbeat note as stocks fell and the price of oil rose after the US launched its first military action in a month against Iran. The S&P 500 index fell 0.3 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.7 per cent and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.1 per cent. Wall Street has started the week on the back foot. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures at 6.15am AEST pointing to a fall of 22 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.2 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.64¢. August had no shortage of turbulence for the market, but the S&P 500 and Nasdaq each posted a gain for the month after losing ground in July and June. The Dow, meanwhile, managed its fifth-straight monthly gain.



Related Article Earnings season Star bleeds $307 million as auditors raise further doubts about its survival Monday’s losses were broad, with nearly every sector within the benchmark S&P 500 finishing in the red. Energy stocks, though, notched gains. Exxon Mobil rose 2.7 per cent and Chevron rose 2.1 per cent. On the losing side, Edison International slumped 23.1 per cent and PG&E fell 20.1 per cent for the two steepest declines. That followed reports about potential California wildfire legislation that would allow insurers to sue utilities over related claims. Amazon fell 2.5 per cent after The Wall Street Journal reported that the Federal Trade Commission and more than 20 states are preparing to sue the online retail giant over claims the company manipulated prices on its platform. The US war with Iran remained a key focus for Wall Street. US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates said it intercepted an Iranian drone over its waters on Monday.



The aggressive actions follow a lull in activity in the US war with Iran, which has lasted more than six months. The war has curtailed traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s oil shipments. Oil prices remain high after an initial surge earlier in the war and that has made everything from gasoline to shipped goods more expensive. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 2.7 per cent to settle at $US90.49 per barrel on Monday. Brent fell below $US80 earlier in August but has since moved higher with no sign of an imminent end to the war. The national average for gasoline in August has been above $US4 per gallon every day of the month for the first time ever, according to the AAA. It has been the most expensive August at the pump on record, outpacing even the enormous supply chain crunch during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022. Higher energy prices have fuelled already stubbornly high inflation. That has been weighing on household spending and consumer confidence. It has also given the Federal Reserve a more complicated path ahead for its interest rate policy.



The rate of inflation remains well above 3 per cent, which is far beyond the Fed’s 2 per cent target. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise interest rates at least once before the year ends in an effort to cool inflation. On Friday, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that inflation is still too high and suggested a rate hike might be necessary in the coming months. The Fed gets its next inflation update on Sept. 11, just days ahead of its next meeting to determine interest rate policy. Wall Street is forecasting a 66 per cent chance that the Fed will raise its benchmark rate at that meeting, according to CME FedWatch. “While a September hike is not a foregone conclusion, we expect the Fed to have limited tolerance for meaningful upside inflation surprises,” wrote Brock Weimer, investment strategy analyst at Edward Jones, in a research note. The yield on the two-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations about Fed moves, held steady at 4.34 per cent, where it was late Friday. That’s up significantly from about 3.50 per cent at the beginning of 2026. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.75 per cent from 4.73 per cent late Friday. That’s back up around the level seen two weeks ago when the Trump administration took the unusual step of announcing it would intervene in the bond market.



Any increase to interest rates that could cool inflation also risks hurting the jobs market. Later this week, the US reports August jobs data. In July, the US job market stalled unexpectedly as employers cut 23,000 jobs. Labor Department revisions slashed another 103,000 jobs from May and June payrolls. Company updates helped move several stocks Monday. GameStop rose 2.9 per cent after the video game retailer provided a preliminary second-quarter earnings outlook above its year-ago results. Shares of Aon slid 9.5 per cent as the company announced that it was buying insurance broker USI Insurance Services from private equity firm KKR in a deal valued at $17 billion, including debt. Related Article Energy Danish giant steps in to help break Australia’s wind farm drought All told, the S&P 500 fell 25.62 points to 7,686.14. It rose 2.6 per cent in August and is up 12.3 per cent so far this year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 374.09 points to 53,185.90. The Nasdaq fell 31.53 points to 26,370.89. The index, which is heavily weighted with big tech stocks, posted a 3.9 per cent gain for the month and is up 13.5 per cent this year.



Markets were mixed in Europe and Asia. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘Hoaxes’: Migrant border rush sparked by Israeli, Russian misinformation, Spanish leader says
World.content:
WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Hoaxes’: Migrant border rush sparked by Israeli, Russian misinformation, Spanish leader says David Crowe September 1, 2026 — 5:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Spanish Prime Minster Pedro Sanchez has blamed networks in Israel and Russia for spreading online claims that led at least 72,000 migrants to cross from Morocco into the enclave of Ceuta in a border crisis four weeks ago. Sanchez dismissed online claims that Moroccan authorities had encouraged migrants to swim to the Spanish enclave in northern Africa, saying the crisis was triggered instead by online misinformation spread by others. Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain return to a beach after being expelled from the area in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta late last month. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere But his claims were denounced by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon ⁠Sa’ar, who said the Spanish leader was “lying shamelessly” to distract attention from his failures in government. The dispute highlights the political tension over the Ceuta crisis when Sanchez is under fire over his migration policies at the same time he criticises Israel over its wars in Gaza and Lebanon.



Claims and counter-claims have spread online about the crisis ever since thousands of people stormed through border checkpoints on July 30 to get to Ceuta, an autonomous Spanish city surrounded by Morocco. One factor appeared to be a belief among migrants that entering Ceuta would entitle them to asylum in mainland Spain under a Supreme Court ruling in June that said Spanish authorities could not summarily deport asylum seekers without due process. Loading Sanchez told broadcaster Cadena SER that false claims about the court ruling were spread online, and that the “far-right movement” used the crisis to attack Spain and divide European leaders. “There were Russian and Israeli networks that spread these hoaxes and attacked the Spanish government and Europeans on a corrosive issue like irregular migration, which divides and polarises many European societies,” he said.



Sanchez said the online posts distorted the court ruling and spread the false idea that it would be impossible for Spanish authorities to force people back to Morocco. “This type of hoax was used and spread through social media. This is what we know,” he said, in reporting of his remarks by Spanish daily newspaper El Pais. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez. Getty Images Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg Spanish police dealt with the crisis by forcing most of the migrants back to Morocco, although about 5000 remain in Ceuta despite the challenge of gaining food and water when many local people do not want them in their city.



While some media reports on July 30 said Moroccan border guards encouraged the migrants to cross into Ceuta, the Spanish leader rejected the theory that Morocco sparked the crisis because it seeks sovereignty over Ceuta. Sanchez said at “no intelligence agency with which the Spanish government regularly collaborates” raised any concern about the involvement of Moroccan authorities. This included Spain’s own National Intelligence Centre. European leaders are at odds over how to toughen border checks under the Schengen pact that allows free movement between 29 member states. Italy has chosen to continue its suspension of the Schengen rules with Spain for another 15 days, despite protests from Madrid, due to concerns about illegal migrants.





Spain was the first European Union member state to join a claim made by South Africa at the International Court of Justice against Israel, accusing it of genocide in Gaza. Israel rejects this claim and a final ruling is not expected until 2030. Related Article Updated

Immigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe Spain has also pushed for the European Union to revoke an association agreement with Israel. Given these disputes between Israel and Spain, the Israeli foreign minister bluntly rejected the latest claims against Israel, saying Sanchez was “shamelessly” lying. “In his interview on Cadena SER today, he lied again, surprisingly accusing Israel of spreading false information about the events in Ceuta,” Sa’ar said



“This is a blatant lie. “Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not divert attention from Sanchez’s shameful failure in managing his country’s affairs.” A migrant who crossed from Morocco into Spain gathers his belongings after being cleared from the beach last month. World.title: Gutsy Birrell, Duckworth prevail at US Open as day two starts well for Australia
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Gutsy Birrell, Duckworth prevail at US Open as day two starts well for Australia Marc McGowan September 1, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New milestone unlocked. Facing a fourth straight first-round defeat at the US Open, Australia’s Kim Birrell reversed her fortunes with a typically gutsy performance to overcome Croatia’s Petra Marcinko in three sets and win for the first time in New York. The 3-6, 7-6 (7-4), 6-3 triumph booked a second-round clash with 18th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova and propelled Birrell to a live ranking of No.55, which would be a career high if she maintains it. Australia’s Kim Birrell is into the second round at the US Open for the first time. Getty Images Birrell, who overcame two career-threatening elbow surgeries before she even threatened to be a top-100 player, has now won at least one match at all four grand slams, highlighted by her round-of-32 run at the 2019 Australian Open.



Related Article Updated

US Open Cramps, vomiting, pain: Ailing Djokovic suffers shock US Open loss James Duckworth took an even bigger scalp, outlasting Italy’s No.30 seed Matteo Arnaldi 5-7, 6-3, 6-2, 7-6 (10-8) in three-and-a-half hours for his first US Open victory in four years. Duckworth hit 16 aces and rallied from a 4-1 fourth-set deficit, including staving off Arnaldi’s six set points. Three of those came consecutively from 0-40 in the 12th game of the set. The 34-year-old unleashed a tirade of forehands at eight-all in the tiebreak to earn his second match point – this time on serve – before putting away an overhead, after which he let out a guttural roar as his latest resurgence continued. They join day-one winner Taylah Preston, who made the most of her wildcard to down American Alycia Parks in straight sets. Preston faces Taylor Townsend, who defeated Roland-Garros finalist Maja Chwalinska.



But Aleks Vukic could not replicate her feat, going down in five sets – 6-4, 6-7 (5-7), 6-4, 3-6, 6-4 – to new Japanese rising star Rei Sakamoto, who ended his great countryman Kei Nishikori’s grand slam career in qualifying and appears poised to become a tour force in the years ahead. Former junior world No.1 Sakamoto looked on the verge of collapsing physically when the fifth set started a day earlier, but re-energised his hopes with a series of big and bold shots to break Vukic in the opening game. The 20-year-old never let Vukic back in, not offering the Australian even a single break point in the decider, including returning to complete the match on Tuesday (AEST) after rain forced the fifth set to be held over with Sakamoto serving at 4-3. Aleks Vukic could not hold off his 20-year-old rival Rei Sakamoto. Getty Images Like Vukic, Birrell had plenty of time to think about her plight when her match was suspended overnight while she was a set down to Marcinko and locked at three-all in the tiebreak, having already saved a match point.



The 28-year-old lost the first point on resumption to edge closer to defeat, but that only sharpened her resolve against an opponent who boasted more power but arguably less willingness to fight. Birrell reeled off four consecutive points to level the match and set up a fierce battle. The key moments came early in the final set. Marcinko dragged a forehand wide to concede serve in the third game, but menacingly brought up a break-back point on three separate occasions, only for Birrell to have an answer each time. Related Article US Open Demon’s tough draw and Tiley’s $150 million US Open splash The Queenslander staved off the last two with rare aces before going 3-1 up when Marcinko dumped a forehand volley into the net. It was not the last time she would have to fend off a Marcinko rally.



Already 15-30 down trying to push 4-2 ahead, Birrell had to hang in as Marcinko aggressively ripped groundstrokes at her. The problem for the Croatian was she could not find a way through the dogged Australian, who absorbed her rival’s best then capitalised once she inevitably faltered. Birrell was spared from having to serve the contest out when Marcinko double-faulted to go match-point down before putting one last forehand into the net to send Team Birrell into raptures. The schedule is full of Australians again, with Rinky Hijikata, Alexei Popyrin and Maya Joint all still to come, while seven-time major quarter-finalist Alex de Minaur starts his campaign on Wednesday. Hijikata has enjoyed a solid American hardcourt swing, but faces a tough opener against third-seeded Canadian Felix Auger-Aliassime, while Popyrin and Joint meet Grigor Dimitrov – who had to qualify as his injury comeback continues – and Liudmila Samsonova, respectively. Top seed Aryna Sabalenka’s bid for a title three-peat began with a 6-2, 6-4 demolition of Camila Osorio, but her world No.1 ranking remains under serious threat from Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff.



Seven-time grand slam champion and 2025 winner Carlos Alcaraz beat Roman Safiullin 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 in his first match since April after an extended layoff with a wrist injury. The day’s biggest upset so far came courtesy of Greek former world No.3 Stefanos Tsitsipas, who defied his run of outs to shockingly oust Cincinnati Masters champion and title fancy Arthur Fils in four sets. World.title: ‘Contagion risk’: Top central banker warns AI could spark global economic downturn
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeAI ‘Contagion risk’: Top central banker warns AI could spark global economic downturn Luke Barr Updated September 1, 2026 — 5:41am ,first published 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Andrew Bailey, governor of the Bank of England, has warned of a severe downturn in global stock markets if the AI bubble bursts. In a letter to G20 finance ministers, Bailey raised concerns over the economic fallout if the debt-fuelled AI investment boom begins to unravel. He warned that the soaring levels of debt that have been used to fund AI “could amplify a future market correction”. Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey highlighted “stretched asset valuations” in AI as a key risk. AP If the valuation of AI companies starts to plummet, investors face the prospect of losing trillions of dollars overnight. This could trigger a dangerous chain reaction if they are then forced to sell other assets. Bailey said the risk was compounded by investors borrowing huge sums to invest in a small number of AI companies and data centre providers, pushing up their valuations to astronomical levels.



Nvidia, which is worth more than $US5.2 trillion ($7.3 trillion), recently raised $US500 billion from a consortium of US banks and investors to fund its AI investment spree. Its share price has risen by 850 per cent over the past five years. Related Article AI ‘There is no plan’: Bill Gates sends a 6000-word warning on the dangers of AI Bailey warned that “stretched asset valuations” in AI are one factor that could trigger a sharp economic slump. “Markets remain vulnerable to a potentially disorderly correction that could spread across borders,” he said. “The issue is not simply that investors are borrowing more but that leverage is interacting with high valuations and market concentration.” Bailey’s warning was issued as the UK government unveiled a £100 million ($189 million) fund to back British AI start-ups. It forms part of an attempt to boost the UK’s sovereign AI capabilities, which are well behind those of the US and China.



In Bailey’s letter – sent as chairman of the Financial Stability Board, which works with central banks and governments around the world – he also warned that AI risked unleashing a wave of cyberattacks that could cripple the global economy. He highlighted the threat posed by frontier AI, which covers the world’s most cutting-edge models, developed by tech giants such as OpenAI and Anthropic. If the valuation of AI companies starts to plummet, investors face the prospect of losing trillions of dollars overnight. AP “The risk landscape has been further complicated by the emergence of frontier AI models, which are showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy and problem-solving abilities, as well as threat capabilities,” he said. “For the financial system, the most immediate concern is the potential impact of frontier AI on cyber risk.



“Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber risk, which could undermine market confidence system-wide.” He warned that a cyberattack at a major institution could rapidly unleash chaos across the world’s financial markets. “The global financial system is highly interconnected and cyber disruption can spread across jurisdictions through common technology providers, shared infrastructure and cross-border financial activity,” he said. His warning comes after a number of tech giants have reported incidents of AI agents going rogue, deceiving internal systems to launch cyberattacks elsewhere. US tech giant Anthropic has previously said that its AI models hacked into three organisations on their own during a private experiment.



Bailey said examples such as this should serve as a wake-up call for governments around the world. The letter was sent before a meeting between G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in North Carolina. Related Article Exclusive

AI This ‘AI refuser’ quit her dream job, and hopes others follow He said: “Recent developments have also highlighted to me that many jurisdictions do not have the protocols to manage the development, release and deployment of advanced frontier AI models, heightening risks for the financial sector and beyond.” He also noted how current economic risks are higher based on “fragilities in sovereign debt markets”. This refers to a recent rise in global borrowing costs, led by the US after its debt pile crossed $US40 trillion for the first time. Bailey warned some hedge funds are not only exposed to AI investment but also own government debt.



“In addition, a growing footprint of leveraged entities, such as hedge funds in equity markets, which are also exposed to sovereign debt, increase the scope for contagion risk,” he said. World.title: Courtney alleges she was raped by a classmate when she was six years old. Now she’s taking action
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaEducation Courtney alleges she was raped by a classmate when she was six years old. Now she’s taking action Nicole Precel September 1, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 2600 reports of “concerning incidents” of a sexual nature between students have been reported at Victorian state schools in the past three years, as experts warn of a crisis in gender-based harmful behaviour. Figures obtained under freedom-of-information laws show there were 2645 incidents recorded by state schools between January 2023 and August last year. Courtney Livingston is suing the state government after she was allegedly sexually assaulted by another student when she was in grade 1 at a school near Ballarat. Ruby Alexander A rise in incidents was recorded in 2024 compared with 2023 in primary, secondary and prep-to-year-12 schools, and the figures continued to climb in the eight months of 2025 for which data was released. Over that 2025 period, there were 817 incidents reported, at least 368 of them in primary schools.



“Peer-to-peer incidents of a sexual nature” refers to student-to-student behaviour considered inappropriate, harmful or concerning and recorded by schools in line with department policy. The severity of each incident can depend on age. A problematic incident for five to nine-year-olds might be continually rubbing their genitals in the presence of others, while a harmful behaviour could be grooming other children or forcing them to play sexual games. “Sextortion”, often involving online blackmail, can be a problem among older students. More incidents have been recorded since 2022, when strengthened reporting systems were introduced, but that earlier data was not made available. Dr Gemma McKibbin, a senior research fellow in the University of Melbourne’s Department of Social Work, said the 2645 incidents reported were probably a vast under-representation of concerning sexual behaviour in schools.



She said researchers were seeing a crisis in gender-based harmful sexual behaviour, whereby adolescent boys were sexually harassing, assaulting and exploiting adolescent girls or non-binary young people. “I don’t think that schools have quite worked out how to manage the kind of group dynamics that fit into that form of harmful sexual behaviours, such as the manosphere and hypermasculinity, exposure to pornography,” McKibbin said. Courtney Livingston alleges she was raped by a classmate when in year 1. He had exposed himself in class before asking her and another girl to meet him and another boy at a basketball court, where she says the boys abused the girls. Now 24, she is suing the State of Victoria in the Supreme Court, claiming her school, Redan Primary, on the rural-urban fringe near Ballarat, failed to protect or supervise students in 2008, when she alleges the abuse occurred. A writ filed on July 8 states, “there was a not insignificant risk that students in primary school may be sexually abused by other students”.



According to the 2023 Australian Child Maltreatment Study, adolescent boys are the most likely to inflict child sexual abuse in Australia. Of the people surveyed, 18.2 per cent said they had experienced child sexual abuse perpetrated by an adolescent, compared with 11.7 per cent who said an adult had abused them. The release of the fresh data comes amid renewed concerns that boys are increasingly involved in sex crimes and under the influence of the manosphere. Three students – a 13-year-old and two 14-year-olds, from top Sydney private boys’ school Scots College have been charged with aggravated sexual assault after allegedly raping a 14-year-old girl in an alley on July 22. The teens have been granted bail on strict conditions, as the school faces concerns over a perceived culture of misogyny. McKibbin said that across the board there had been an increase in young people non-consensually sharing peers’ nudes, setting up “slut-shaming hubs” and creating nude deepfakes.



Last month, Dr Sara Meger, of the University of Melbourne’s School of Social and Political Sciences, published the report Misogyny, Online Radicalisation, and Youth Extremism in Australia, which found 13 to 17-year-olds were more likely to hold hostile views towards women than adults were, and that was reflected in classroom behaviour. Misogynistic attitudes were held by

34.8 per cent of boys in that group compared with 23.4 per cent of Boomer men.

An Australian Federal Police spokesperson said most sadistic online exploitation victims were girls aged between 11 and 17. Most offenders were boys and young men aged between 12 and 24. How to respond to a disclosure of a child experiencing sexual harm Thank you for telling me.

for telling me. I’m sorry this happened to you.

this happened to you. It’s not your fault.

I believe you.

you. I will help you Taking action could involve informing the school, speaking with Child Protection and specialist sexual assault police, and seeking support from the local sexual assault service – you can find your service here: https://sasvic.org.au/ Source and other useful phrases: https://www.esafekids.com.au/ “Limited public awareness of sadistic online exploitation, coupled with child and youth victims being reticent to report the true breadth of their online experience to strangers, means incidents are often not recognised as even being extortion-related,” the spokesperson said. “We believe this crime type is underreported as victims may not view themselves as victims.”



Associate Professor Matt Tyler of Monash University said violent pornography was playing a role in the growth of child-on-child harm, with young people able to access it despite age verification requirements. “Often young people are ashamed or fearful of seeking help,” he said. Related Article Opinion

Private schools Stop blaming the school for sexual assaults: the buck stops closer to home Louise Clegg Former lawyer A Department of Education spokesperson said every incident was taken extremely seriously and government schools had clear and strict processes to respond to problem incidents, including supporting students, working with families and calling in police when appropriate. McKibbin said it was important parents and carers understood the difference between normal, problematic and harmful sexual behaviour. Children who disclosed incidents needed to feel believed and supported and that action would be taken to make abuse stop.



Schools, she said, should prevent children’s harmful sexual behaviour through whole-of-school sexual safety education, identify it using a traffic light tool, look for red flags and respond using reporting protocols. “It is a balancing act – victims must be supported and young people who harm do best when they are responded to therapeutically rather than through punishment,” she said. “Severe perpetration may require police intervention, however.” Livingston says she feels she was unprotected when she was a six-year-old. Ruby Alexander Courtney Livingston described her primary school’s response as horrific, saying all four children involved were given timeouts at recess. “As a six-year-old who already felt ashamed, being punished after what had happened only kind of reinforced that shame, and I carried that feeling with me for so many years,” she said.



Arnold Thomas & Becker lawyer Madison Duffy said liability for peer-on-peer abuse shifted to the school if staff failed in their duty of care, including ignoring warning signs, lacking clear safeguarding rules or failing to supervise students properly. If your child has displayed problematic or harmful sexual behaviour Gemma McKibbin recommends parents or carers remain calm, be curious and don’t minimise. Getting therapeutic support from a specialist harmful sexual behaviour service is essential and can help children and young people understand why they have developed the behaviour and how they can stop it – you can find your local service here https://sasvic.org.au/.

Have a think about the social contexts that a child or young person is living in – are they hanging out with people who subscribe to hypermasculine views of gender?

Are they accessing a lot of violent pornography or child sexual abuse material?

Does their school have a culture that normalises violence?

Is there something you can do to intervene in the damaging contexts?

Paying attention to the contexts of the behaviour can help the child or young person feel less stigmatised and ashamed.

Get more advice here https://raisingchildren.net.au/school-age/safety/child-sexual-abuse/supporting-children-harmful-sexual-behaviour

https://www.childsafety.gov.au/about-child-sexual-abuse/responding-child-sexual-abuse-disclosures “We allege the [Redan Primary School] failed its duty of care through inadequate supervision, that the harm was foreseeable, and the lack of supervision directly resulted in the incident and the injury,” she said. Livingston said she felt she had been carrying the weight of what happened for nearly 20 years. “While others may have been quick to close that chapter in my life, I never could, and it never ended for me,” she said. “I feel like no one protected me when I was six, and as I’ve gotten older, I felt an obligation to stand up for my younger self.



“It’s about taking back some of the power that was stolen from me.” The trial is set for next year. The state government is yet to file a defence. If you or someone you know needs support, contact 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or kidshelpline on 1800 55 1800. That followed reports about potential California wildfire legislation that would allow insurers to sue utilities over related claims. Amazon fell 2.5 per cent after The Wall Street Journal reported that the Federal Trade Commission and more than 20 states are preparing to sue the online retail giant over claims the company manipulated prices on its platform. The US war with Iran remained a key focus for Wall Street. US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates said it intercepted an Iranian drone over its waters on Monday.



The aggressive actions follow a lull in activity in the US war with Iran, which has lasted more than six months. The war has curtailed traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s oil shipments. Oil prices remain high after an initial surge earlier in the war and that has made everything from gasoline to shipped goods more expensive. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 2.7 per cent to settle at $US90.49 per barrel on Monday. Brent fell below $US80 earlier in August but has since moved higher with no sign of an imminent end to the war. The national average for gasoline in August has been above $US4 per gallon every day of the month for the first time ever, according to the AAA. It has been the most expensive August at the pump on record, outpacing even the enormous supply chain crunch during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022. Higher energy prices have fuelled already stubbornly high inflation. That has been weighing on household spending and consumer confidence. It has also given the Federal Reserve a more complicated path ahead for its interest rate policy.



The rate of inflation remains well above 3 per cent, which is far beyond the Fed’s 2 per cent target. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise interest rates at least once before the year ends in an effort to cool inflation. On Friday, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that inflation is still too high and suggested a rate hike might be necessary in the coming months. The Fed gets its next inflation update on Sept. 11, just days ahead of its next meeting to determine interest rate policy. Wall Street is forecasting a 66 per cent chance that the Fed will raise its benchmark rate at that meeting, according to CME FedWatch. “While a September hike is not a foregone conclusion, we expect the Fed to have limited tolerance for meaningful upside inflation surprises,” wrote Brock Weimer, investment strategy analyst at Edward Jones, in a research note. The yield on the two-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations about Fed moves, held steady at 4.34 per cent, where it was late Friday. That’s up significantly from about 3.50 per cent at the beginning of 2026. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.75 per cent from 4.73 per cent late Friday. That’s back up around the level seen two weeks ago when the Trump administration took the unusual step of announcing it would intervene in the bond market.



Any increase to interest rates that could cool inflation also risks hurting the jobs market. Later this week, the US reports August jobs data. In July, the US job market stalled unexpectedly as employers cut 23,000 jobs. Labor Department revisions slashed another 103,000 jobs from May and June payrolls. Company updates helped move several stocks Monday. GameStop rose 2.9 per cent after the video game retailer provided a preliminary second-quarter earnings outlook above its year-ago results. Shares of Aon slid 9.5 per cent as the company announced that it was buying insurance broker USI Insurance Services from private equity firm KKR in a deal valued at $17 billion, including debt. Related Article Energy Danish giant steps in to help break Australia’s wind farm drought All told, the S&P 500 fell 25.62 points to 7,686.14. It rose 2.6 per cent in August and is up 12.3 per cent so far this year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 374.09 points to 53,185.90. The Nasdaq fell 31.53 points to 26,370.89. The index, which is heavily weighted with big tech stocks, posted a 3.9 per cent gain for the month and is up 13.5 per cent this year.



Markets were mixed in Europe and Asia. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
