World.title: ‘Hoaxes’: Migrant border rush sparked by Israeli, Russian misinformation, Spanish leader says
World.content:
WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Hoaxes’: Migrant border rush sparked by Israeli, Russian misinformation, Spanish leader says David Crowe September 1, 2026 — 5:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Spanish Prime Minster Pedro Sanchez has blamed networks in Israel and Russia for spreading online claims that led at least 72,000 migrants to cross from Morocco into the enclave of Ceuta in a border crisis four weeks ago. Sanchez dismissed online claims that Moroccan authorities had encouraged migrants to swim to the Spanish enclave in northern Africa, saying the crisis was triggered instead by online misinformation spread by others. Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain return to a beach after being expelled from the area in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta late last month. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere But his claims were denounced by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon ⁠Sa’ar, who said the Spanish leader was “lying shamelessly” to distract attention from his failures in government. The dispute highlights the political tension over the Ceuta crisis when Sanchez is under fire over his migration policies at the same time he criticises Israel over its wars in Gaza and Lebanon.



Claims and counter-claims have spread online about the crisis ever since thousands of people stormed through border checkpoints on July 30 to get to Ceuta, an autonomous Spanish city surrounded by Morocco. One factor appeared to be a belief among migrants that entering Ceuta would entitle them to asylum in mainland Spain under a Supreme Court ruling in June that said Spanish authorities could not summarily deport asylum seekers without due process. Loading Sanchez told broadcaster Cadena SER that false claims about the court ruling were spread online, and that the “far-right movement” used the crisis to attack Spain and divide European leaders. “There were Russian and Israeli networks that spread these hoaxes and attacked the Spanish government and Europeans on a corrosive issue like irregular migration, which divides and polarises many European societies,” he said.



Sanchez said the online posts distorted the court ruling and spread the false idea that it would be impossible for Spanish authorities to force people back to Morocco. “This type of hoax was used and spread through social media. This is what we know,” he said, in reporting of his remarks by Spanish daily newspaper El Pais. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez. Getty Images Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg Spanish police dealt with the crisis by forcing most of the migrants back to Morocco, although about 5000 remain in Ceuta despite the challenge of gaining food and water when many local people do not want them in their city.



While some media reports on July 30 said Moroccan border guards encouraged the migrants to cross into Ceuta, the Spanish leader rejected the theory that Morocco sparked the crisis because it seeks sovereignty over Ceuta. Sanchez said at “no intelligence agency with which the Spanish government regularly collaborates” raised any concern about the involvement of Moroccan authorities. This included Spain’s own National Intelligence Centre. European leaders are at odds over how to toughen border checks under the Schengen pact that allows free movement between 29 member states. Italy has chosen to continue its suspension of the Schengen rules with Spain for another 15 days, despite protests from Madrid, due to concerns about illegal migrants.





Spain was the first European Union member state to join a claim made by South Africa at the International Court of Justice against Israel, accusing it of genocide in Gaza. Israel rejects this claim and a final ruling is not expected until 2030. Related Article Updated

Immigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe Spain has also pushed for the European Union to revoke an association agreement with Israel. Given these disputes between Israel and Spain, the Israeli foreign minister bluntly rejected the latest claims against Israel, saying Sanchez was “shamelessly” lying. “In his interview on Cadena SER today, he lied again, surprisingly accusing Israel of spreading false information about the events in Ceuta,” Sa’ar said



“This is a blatant lie. “Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not divert attention from Sanchez’s shameful failure in managing his country’s affairs.” A migrant who crossed from Morocco into Spain gathers his belongings after being cleared from the beach last month. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Gutsy Birrell, Duckworth prevail at US Open as day two starts well for Australia
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Gutsy Birrell, Duckworth prevail at US Open as day two starts well for Australia Marc McGowan September 1, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New milestone unlocked. Facing a fourth straight first-round defeat at the US Open, Australia’s Kim Birrell reversed her fortunes with a typically gutsy performance to overcome Croatia’s Petra Marcinko in three sets and win for the first time in New York. The 3-6, 7-6 (7-4), 6-3 triumph booked a second-round clash with 18th seed Ekaterina Alexandrova and propelled Birrell to a live ranking of No.55, which would be a career high if she maintains it. Australia’s Kim Birrell is into the second round at the US Open for the first time. Getty Images Birrell, who overcame two career-threatening elbow surgeries before she even threatened to be a top-100 player, has now won at least one match at all four grand slams, highlighted by her round-of-32 run at the 2019 Australian Open.



Related Article Updated

US Open Cramps, vomiting, pain: Ailing Djokovic suffers shock US Open loss James Duckworth took an even bigger scalp, outlasting Italy’s No.30 seed Matteo Arnaldi 5-7, 6-3, 6-2, 7-6 (10-8) in three-and-a-half hours for his first US Open victory in four years. Duckworth hit 16 aces and rallied from a 4-1 fourth-set deficit, including staving off Arnaldi’s six set points. Three of those came consecutively from 0-40 in the 12th game of the set. The 34-year-old unleashed a tirade of forehands at eight-all in the tiebreak to earn his second match point – this time on serve – before putting away an overhead, after which he let out a guttural roar as his latest resurgence continued. They join day-one winner Taylah Preston, who made the most of her wildcard to down American Alycia Parks in straight sets. Preston faces Taylor Townsend, who defeated Roland-Garros finalist Maja Chwalinska.



But Aleks Vukic could not replicate her feat, going down in five sets – 6-4, 6-7 (5-7), 6-4, 3-6, 6-4 – to new Japanese rising star Rei Sakamoto, who ended his great countryman Kei Nishikori’s grand slam career in qualifying and appears poised to become a tour force in the years ahead. Former junior world No.1 Sakamoto looked on the verge of collapsing physically when the fifth set started a day earlier, but re-energised his hopes with a series of big and bold shots to break Vukic in the opening game. The 20-year-old never let Vukic back in, not offering the Australian even a single break point in the decider, including returning to complete the match on Tuesday (AEST) after rain forced the fifth set to be held over with Sakamoto serving at 4-3. Aleks Vukic could not hold off his 20-year-old rival Rei Sakamoto. Getty Images Like Vukic, Birrell had plenty of time to think about her plight when her match was suspended overnight while she was a set down to Marcinko and locked at three-all in the tiebreak, having already saved a match point.



The 28-year-old lost the first point on resumption to edge closer to defeat, but that only sharpened her resolve against an opponent who boasted more power but arguably less willingness to fight. Birrell reeled off four consecutive points to level the match and set up a fierce battle. The key moments came early in the final set. Marcinko dragged a forehand wide to concede serve in the third game, but menacingly brought up a break-back point on three separate occasions, only for Birrell to have an answer each time. Related Article US Open Demon’s tough draw and Tiley’s $150 million US Open splash The Queenslander staved off the last two with rare aces before going 3-1 up when Marcinko dumped a forehand volley into the net. It was not the last time she would have to fend off a Marcinko rally.



Already 15-30 down trying to push 4-2 ahead, Birrell had to hang in as Marcinko aggressively ripped groundstrokes at her. The problem for the Croatian was she could not find a way through the dogged Australian, who absorbed her rival’s best then capitalised once she inevitably faltered. Birrell was spared from having to serve the contest out when Marcinko double-faulted to go match-point down before putting one last forehand into the net to send Team Birrell into raptures. The schedule is full of Australians again, with Rinky Hijikata, Alexei Popyrin and Maya Joint all still to come, while seven-time major quarter-finalist Alex de Minaur starts his campaign on Wednesday. Hijikata has enjoyed a solid American hardcourt swing, but faces a tough opener against third-seeded Canadian Felix Auger-Aliassime, while Popyrin and Joint meet Grigor Dimitrov – who had to qualify as his injury comeback continues – and Liudmila Samsonova, respectively. Top seed Aryna Sabalenka’s bid for a title three-peat began with a 6-2, 6-4 demolition of Camila Osorio, but her world No.1 ranking remains under serious threat from Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff.



Seven-time grand slam champion and 2025 winner Carlos Alcaraz beat Roman Safiullin 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 in his first match since April after an extended layoff with a wrist injury. The day’s biggest upset so far came courtesy of Greek former world No.3 Stefanos Tsitsipas, who defied his run of outs to shockingly oust Cincinnati Masters champion and title fancy Arthur Fils in four sets. World.title: ‘Contagion risk’: Top central banker warns AI could spark global economic downturn
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeAI ‘Contagion risk’: Top central banker warns AI could spark global economic downturn Luke Barr Updated September 1, 2026 — 5:41am ,first published 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Andrew Bailey, governor of the Bank of England, has warned of a severe downturn in global stock markets if the AI bubble bursts. In a letter to G20 finance ministers, Bailey raised concerns over the economic fallout if the debt-fuelled AI investment boom begins to unravel. He warned that the soaring levels of debt that have been used to fund AI “could amplify a future market correction”. Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey highlighted “stretched asset valuations” in AI as a key risk. AP If the valuation of AI companies starts to plummet, investors face the prospect of losing trillions of dollars overnight. This could trigger a dangerous chain reaction if they are then forced to sell other assets. Bailey said the risk was compounded by investors borrowing huge sums to invest in a small number of AI companies and data centre providers, pushing up their valuations to astronomical levels.



Nvidia, which is worth more than $US5.2 trillion ($7.3 trillion), recently raised $US500 billion from a consortium of US banks and investors to fund its AI investment spree. Its share price has risen by 850 per cent over the past five years. Related Article AI ‘There is no plan’: Bill Gates sends a 6000-word warning on the dangers of AI Bailey warned that “stretched asset valuations” in AI are one factor that could trigger a sharp economic slump. “Markets remain vulnerable to a potentially disorderly correction that could spread across borders,” he said. “The issue is not simply that investors are borrowing more but that leverage is interacting with high valuations and market concentration.” Bailey’s warning was issued as the UK government unveiled a £100 million ($189 million) fund to back British AI start-ups. It forms part of an attempt to boost the UK’s sovereign AI capabilities, which are well behind those of the US and China.



In Bailey’s letter – sent as chairman of the Financial Stability Board, which works with central banks and governments around the world – he also warned that AI risked unleashing a wave of cyberattacks that could cripple the global economy. He highlighted the threat posed by frontier AI, which covers the world’s most cutting-edge models, developed by tech giants such as OpenAI and Anthropic. If the valuation of AI companies starts to plummet, investors face the prospect of losing trillions of dollars overnight. AP “The risk landscape has been further complicated by the emergence of frontier AI models, which are showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy and problem-solving abilities, as well as threat capabilities,” he said. “For the financial system, the most immediate concern is the potential impact of frontier AI on cyber risk.



“Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber risk, which could undermine market confidence system-wide.” He warned that a cyberattack at a major institution could rapidly unleash chaos across the world’s financial markets. “The global financial system is highly interconnected and cyber disruption can spread across jurisdictions through common technology providers, shared infrastructure and cross-border financial activity,” he said. His warning comes after a number of tech giants have reported incidents of AI agents going rogue, deceiving internal systems to launch cyberattacks elsewhere. US tech giant Anthropic has previously said that its AI models hacked into three organisations on their own during a private experiment.



Bailey said examples such as this should serve as a wake-up call for governments around the world. The letter was sent before a meeting between G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in North Carolina. Related Article Exclusive

AI This ‘AI refuser’ quit her dream job, and hopes others follow He said: “Recent developments have also highlighted to me that many jurisdictions do not have the protocols to manage the development, release and deployment of advanced frontier AI models, heightening risks for the financial sector and beyond.” He also noted how current economic risks are higher based on “fragilities in sovereign debt markets”. This refers to a recent rise in global borrowing costs, led by the US after its debt pile crossed $US40 trillion for the first time. Bailey warned some hedge funds are not only exposed to AI investment but also own government debt.



“In addition, a growing footprint of leveraged entities, such as hedge funds in equity markets, which are also exposed to sovereign debt, increase the scope for contagion risk,” he said. World.title: Courtney alleges she was raped by a classmate when she was six years old. Now she’s taking action
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaEducation Courtney alleges she was raped by a classmate when she was six years old. Now she’s taking action Nicole Precel September 1, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 2600 reports of “concerning incidents” of a sexual nature between students have been reported at Victorian state schools in the past three years, as experts warn of a crisis in gender-based harmful behaviour. Figures obtained under freedom-of-information laws show there were 2645 incidents recorded by state schools between January 2023 and August last year. Courtney Livingston is suing the state government after she was allegedly sexually assaulted by another student when she was in grade 1 at a school near Ballarat. Ruby Alexander A rise in incidents was recorded in 2024 compared with 2023 in primary, secondary and prep-to-year-12 schools, and the figures continued to climb in the eight months of 2025 for which data was released. Over that 2025 period, there were 817 incidents reported, at least 368 of them in primary schools.



“Peer-to-peer incidents of a sexual nature” refers to student-to-student behaviour considered inappropriate, harmful or concerning and recorded by schools in line with department policy. The severity of each incident can depend on age. A problematic incident for five to nine-year-olds might be continually rubbing their genitals in the presence of others, while a harmful behaviour could be grooming other children or forcing them to play sexual games. “Sextortion”, often involving online blackmail, can be a problem among older students. More incidents have been recorded since 2022, when strengthened reporting systems were introduced, but that earlier data was not made available. Dr Gemma McKibbin, a senior research fellow in the University of Melbourne’s Department of Social Work, said the 2645 incidents reported were probably a vast under-representation of concerning sexual behaviour in schools.



She said researchers were seeing a crisis in gender-based harmful sexual behaviour, whereby adolescent boys were sexually harassing, assaulting and exploiting adolescent girls or non-binary young people. “I don’t think that schools have quite worked out how to manage the kind of group dynamics that fit into that form of harmful sexual behaviours, such as the manosphere and hypermasculinity, exposure to pornography,” McKibbin said. Courtney Livingston alleges she was raped by a classmate when in year 1. He had exposed himself in class before asking her and another girl to meet him and another boy at a basketball court, where she says the boys abused the girls. Now 24, she is suing the State of Victoria in the Supreme Court, claiming her school, Redan Primary, on the rural-urban fringe near Ballarat, failed to protect or supervise students in 2008, when she alleges the abuse occurred. A writ filed on July 8 states, “there was a not insignificant risk that students in primary school may be sexually abused by other students”.



According to the 2023 Australian Child Maltreatment Study, adolescent boys are the most likely to inflict child sexual abuse in Australia. Of the people surveyed, 18.2 per cent said they had experienced child sexual abuse perpetrated by an adolescent, compared with 11.7 per cent who said an adult had abused them. The release of the fresh data comes amid renewed concerns that boys are increasingly involved in sex crimes and under the influence of the manosphere. Three students – a 13-year-old and two 14-year-olds, from top Sydney private boys’ school Scots College have been charged with aggravated sexual assault after allegedly raping a 14-year-old girl in an alley on July 22. The teens have been granted bail on strict conditions, as the school faces concerns over a perceived culture of misogyny. McKibbin said that across the board there had been an increase in young people non-consensually sharing peers’ nudes, setting up “slut-shaming hubs” and creating nude deepfakes.



Last month, Dr Sara Meger, of the University of Melbourne’s School of Social and Political Sciences, published the report Misogyny, Online Radicalisation, and Youth Extremism in Australia, which found 13 to 17-year-olds were more likely to hold hostile views towards women than adults were, and that was reflected in classroom behaviour. Misogynistic attitudes were held by

34.8 per cent of boys in that group compared with 23.4 per cent of Boomer men.

An Australian Federal Police spokesperson said most sadistic online exploitation victims were girls aged between 11 and 17. Most offenders were boys and young men aged between 12 and 24. How to respond to a disclosure of a child experiencing sexual harm Thank you for telling me.

for telling me. I’m sorry this happened to you.

this happened to you. It’s not your fault.

I believe you.

you. I will help you Taking action could involve informing the school, speaking with Child Protection and specialist sexual assault police, and seeking support from the local sexual assault service – you can find your service here: https://sasvic.org.au/ Source and other useful phrases: https://www.esafekids.com.au/ “Limited public awareness of sadistic online exploitation, coupled with child and youth victims being reticent to report the true breadth of their online experience to strangers, means incidents are often not recognised as even being extortion-related,” the spokesperson said. “We believe this crime type is underreported as victims may not view themselves as victims.”



Associate Professor Matt Tyler of Monash University said violent pornography was playing a role in the growth of child-on-child harm, with young people able to access it despite age verification requirements. “Often young people are ashamed or fearful of seeking help,” he said. Related Article Opinion

Private schools Stop blaming the school for sexual assaults: the buck stops closer to home Louise Clegg Former lawyer A Department of Education spokesperson said every incident was taken extremely seriously and government schools had clear and strict processes to respond to problem incidents, including supporting students, working with families and calling in police when appropriate. McKibbin said it was important parents and carers understood the difference between normal, problematic and harmful sexual behaviour. Children who disclosed incidents needed to feel believed and supported and that action would be taken to make abuse stop.



Schools, she said, should prevent children’s harmful sexual behaviour through whole-of-school sexual safety education, identify it using a traffic light tool, look for red flags and respond using reporting protocols. “It is a balancing act – victims must be supported and young people who harm do best when they are responded to therapeutically rather than through punishment,” she said. “Severe perpetration may require police intervention, however.” Livingston says she feels she was unprotected when she was a six-year-old. Ruby Alexander Courtney Livingston described her primary school’s response as horrific, saying all four children involved were given timeouts at recess. “As a six-year-old who already felt ashamed, being punished after what had happened only kind of reinforced that shame, and I carried that feeling with me for so many years,” she said.



Arnold Thomas & Becker lawyer Madison Duffy said liability for peer-on-peer abuse shifted to the school if staff failed in their duty of care, including ignoring warning signs, lacking clear safeguarding rules or failing to supervise students properly. If your child has displayed problematic or harmful sexual behaviour Gemma McKibbin recommends parents or carers remain calm, be curious and don’t minimise. Getting therapeutic support from a specialist harmful sexual behaviour service is essential and can help children and young people understand why they have developed the behaviour and how they can stop it – you can find your local service here https://sasvic.org.au/.

Have a think about the social contexts that a child or young person is living in – are they hanging out with people who subscribe to hypermasculine views of gender?

Are they accessing a lot of violent pornography or child sexual abuse material?

Does their school have a culture that normalises violence?

Is there something you can do to intervene in the damaging contexts?

Paying attention to the contexts of the behaviour can help the child or young person feel less stigmatised and ashamed.

Get more advice here https://raisingchildren.net.au/school-age/safety/child-sexual-abuse/supporting-children-harmful-sexual-behaviour

https://www.childsafety.gov.au/about-child-sexual-abuse/responding-child-sexual-abuse-disclosures “We allege the [Redan Primary School] failed its duty of care through inadequate supervision, that the harm was foreseeable, and the lack of supervision directly resulted in the incident and the injury,” she said. Livingston said she felt she had been carrying the weight of what happened for nearly 20 years. “While others may have been quick to close that chapter in my life, I never could, and it never ended for me,” she said. “I feel like no one protected me when I was six, and as I’ve gotten older, I felt an obligation to stand up for my younger self.



“It’s about taking back some of the power that was stolen from me.” The trial is set for next year. The state government is yet to file a defence. If you or someone you know needs support, contact 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or kidshelpline on 1800 55 1800.
