World.title: Rotorua Marathon goes anti-clockwise for first time in over 50 years
World.content:
The Rotorua marathon has a radical course change - it's going anti-clockwise around Lake Rotorua.

For the past 50 years, runners have gone around the lake clockwise, but feedback from runners has led organisers to revert how it was run the first time, in 1965. It stayed that way until 1977 when runners went clockwise.

Event director Jason Cameron said the change to next year's route on May 1 would give athletes better lake views, while the journey would be quieter, away from busy main roads.

"We're always looking for ways to make this event better, and turning the course around is the boldest change we've made in a generation."

He said the reversal would mean runners would be beside the lake for longer.

"After 50 years the same way, we can't wait for runners to experience this new take on the lake."

The change to go clockwise in 1977 was made to keep road crossings manageable.

The race start would return to the redeveloped Rotorua lakefront, where there would be a single hub with the start and finish positioned around the event village outside the Novotel Rotorua Lakeside.

Cameron said a new half marathon course also stemmed from feedback, with runners wanting a more scenic and quieter event. The half-course would start at Hamurana Springs and run anti-clockwise into the city.

World.title: Kākāpō Population Soars to 325
World.content:
Biggest kakapo breeding season on record comes to an end Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The 2026 kākāpō breeding season, the biggest on record, has come to an end with a bumper number of kākāpō chicks produced. The youngest chick has just passed 150 days old, a milestone that marks its independence.

"We had 90 chicks reach that milestone," reports Deidre Vercoe, operations manager for the Department of Conservation's Kākāpō Recovery Programme, who is delighted with the success.

Kākāpō Files II 20 | Kākāpō Numbers Soar Wild Sounds: Kākāpō Files II S7 / E20 Season 7 / Episode 20 Download MP3 30m

Those 90 chicks are officially added to the kākāpō population on Monday, taking the critically endangered night parrot from 235 birds to 325.

Vercoe told RNZ's Kākāpō Files podcast that "to blow through that 300 population mark just knocks my socks off. Even as I say it now I think 'really? 325 - has that actually happened?' But it is true, it is fantastic."

When the Kākāpō Recovery Programme began in 1995 there were just 51 living kākāpō. Kākāpō only breed every two to four years, so it's taken a while to get to the point where the population can increase by a third in just a single breeding season.

"It took about 16 years to make 90 chicks in the early days of the recovery programme," Vercoe says. "And we've just done that in one season."

2026 Kākāpō breeding season by the numbers:

79 female kākāpō nested

258 eggs laid

106 chicks hatched

48 females produced living chicks

32 dads fathered chicks

90 chicks made it to 150 days

Kākāpō breeding is triggered by the intermittent mass, or mast, fruiting of forest trees such as rimu. In autumn, the ripening fruit is also a great food source for kākāpō mums to feed their hungry chicks, which grow from just 25 grams at hatching to about 1.5-2 kilos in weight at independence.

Intensive management, such as extra food for breeding mums in years when the fruit fails to ripen, has been a feature of kākāpō conservation. This year a very abundant rimu crop ripened on the kākāpō's two breeding islands in Fiordland, meaning mums on those islands did not require any extra food.

However, on Whenua Hou / Codfish Island, near Rakiura / Stewart Island, the rimu failed to ripen and the female kākāpō there still needed supplementary food to raise chicks.

In the past three decades, hand-rearing has also been an important tool, but this season only two chicks that had required medical treatment ended up being hand-reared. The rest were fully raised by kākāpō mums.

DOC Kākāpō Ranger Maddy Whittaker with 2026 chick Matilda-A1 Sarah Manktelow DOC

Stepping back from intensive management, like feeding and hand-rearing, has been a deliberate move. It is an important and necessary change, says Kākāpō Recovery science advisor Andrew Digby.

"It's been a really significant breeding season for us," Digby says. "Obviously it's the biggest one we've ever had, so that's very significant. But I think just as important are the methods that we've employed and some of the things that we've changed this breeding season. And in particular that's that real emphasis on trying to step back and do a little less of the intensive management that we've done in the past, and let kākāpō do things on their own."

Technology has been key to the evolving management regime for kākāpō. Every bird wears a smart transmitter and its activity can be remotely monitored.

Deidre Vercoe says "we were able to put a lot more faith in our remote technology data, and really carefully monitor that data, and make decisions about when we would step in and interfere at a nest, to move an egg or to help a chick, or when we were okay to stay hands off".

2026 kākāpō chick Hananui-A2 is living independently, but still gets regular ranger checks. Sarah Manktelow/DOC

All existing adult kākāpō have names, but Vercoe says this tradition is about to change.

"Not all the chicks will be named this year - some will remain unnamed. That's a bit of a symbol of heading towards a more natural state for kākāpō where they're not all individually managed and individually known."

The last two kākāpō breeding seasons were four years apart, but we won't have such a long wait until next time, Digby says. The key is a pattern of summer temperatures that triggers rimu fruiting.

"We look at temperature differences and that gives us a two-year heads-up. And there's an indication from those differences that 2028 will be another kākāpō breeding season."

While it's exciting news that there'll be more kākāpō chicks in two years time, the rapidly growing kākāpō population faces a challenge - the existing kākāpō islands are already full and we need more safe predator-free places for kākāpō to call home.

Pakiki-A1 is one of 90 chicks that successfully made it to independence in the record 2026 kākāpō breeding season. Sarah Manktelow/DOC

"After this next breeding season we desperately need another breeding site," Digby says. The search is on.

Among the highlights of the 2026 kākāpō breeding season were three four-year-old females that bred for the first time, the youngest females to ever breed.

Ten chicks were conceived through artificial insemination, a technique which is used to boost egg fertility and match-make good genetic matches. Ralph, an original male from Rakiura / Stewart, became a father for the first time as a result of artificial insemination.

The 'dad of the year' was ten-year-old Tūterangi. A first-time breeder, he mated with six females and fathered 10 living chicks.

World.title: Last call: 3000 hospitality businesses gone in a year as business feels the crunch
World.content:
How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

About 3000 hospitality businesses have closed their doors in the past 12 months, new data shows.

Credit bureau Centrix has released its latest update. which shows that while business defaults are down, company closures and liquidations are elevated.

In the hospitality sector alone, 422 companies, or 1.3 percent of the sector, entered liquidation in the past year. That was a 42 percent year-on-year increase. Restaurant liquidations were up 43 percent, takeaway food service liquidations 143 percent and cafe liquidations 27 percent.

There were 2900 hospitality businesses that ceased trading altogether, an increase of almost 40 percent.

Money with Susan Edmunds Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Retail trade liquidations were up 50 percent year-on-year.

In total, 3092 companies were liquidated in the past 12 months, up 14 percent year-on-year. There were 302 company insolvencies in July, compared to 276 a year earlier.

Construction accounted for 28 percent of them, property leasing and hiring at 13 percent and hospitality at 11 percent.

The 764 construction businesses liquidated in the past year was just under 0.1 percent of the sector.

Centrix said hospitality's insolvency rate was 3.3 times that of the average New Zealand business.

Centrix's chief operating officer Monika Lacey said slower consumer spending was a drag on the sector.

"If things get tough, you don't necessarily go out for dinner every week, you might go once a month so it's a hard part of the economic cycle, when people start hunkering down. The confidence isn't there."

Restaurant Association general manager Nicola Waldren said while 1.3 percent might seem a small proportion of the sector, every liquidation affected the owner, employees and the wider community.

"Liquidation figures are a lagging indicator. They reflect the cumulative effect of several difficult years rather than providing a complete picture of how every hospitality business is performing today. Many businesses have spent the years since Covid trying to rebuild their balance sheets and pay down debt accumulated during that period, while also managing rising food, wage, energy and compliance costs and constrained customer spending.

"The vast majority of hospitality businesses continue to trade and adapt, but unfortunately for some there has simply not been enough breathing room to recover."

She said July hospitality sales were up 7.8 percent year-on-year, the strongest monthly growth for some time. "However, one strong month does not yet amount to a sustained recovery, particularly for businesses still carrying debt accumulated through Covid and the difficult years that followed."

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said things would start looking up for the sector when unemployment started to fall.

Keaton Pronk, an insolvency practitioner at McDonald Vague, said winter was often the slowest time for the sector.

"Couple this with tough economic times where people start to cut their spending hospitality is a sector that will feel the immediate effects.

"We continue to see IRD pushing hard with recoveries against businesses that have fallen behind on tax debt. A business that may have tax debt and had an arrangement in place may suddenly find itself in default when it becomes strapped for cash and unable to meet its obligations."

The data showed mortgage arrears were up 1.22 percent and just under 20,000 home loans were past due.

That was 12 percent fewer than a year earlier.

Consumer arrears overall increased to 10.74 percent and 424,000 people were behind on repayments.

Lacey said overall the credit conditions were still improving. "There's definitely going to be a bit of a wobble through the winter months. It's been freezing lately... I just got my power bill, that was a bit of a shock so that's going to flow through into everyday households.

"Some will be able to manage that and others will need to potentially not pay something one month to pay the power bill.

"Overall, I think Kiwis are doing better than they were a year ago."

She said it would be interesting to see what happened if interest rates continued to push up. The official cash rate is expected to increase this week.

"If it continues to trend that way, things will start getting a bit tougher again because you don't have as much cash in your pocket."

Renters account for approximately 69,000 of consumers currently 90 or more days in arrears.

Overall new household lending declined 10.5 percent year-on-year during the July quarter, driven by weaker residential mortgage activity.

Approved new mortgage lending was down 11.6 percent compared with the same period last year, following stronger activity earlier in 2026.

Non-mortgage lending increased 4.9 percent year-on-year, supported primarily by continued growth in secured vehicle lending.

There are currently 14,000 accounts reported in financial hardship, up 450 from June but 1.3 percent lower than a year ago.

World.title: We don't think house prices will rise much, but 'it's a good time to buy'
World.content:
How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

New Zealanders don't expect house prices to rise so much any more, but they do think it's a good time to buy a house, ASB's latest housing confidence survey shows.

A net 9 percent now expect future price growth, down from 30 percent in summer. A reading of zero would indicate that people were evenly split on whether prices would rise or not.

Nationwide, a net 20 percent think it is a good time to buy a house. This sentiment is strongest in Auckland, although in Auckland only a net 4 percent expect prices to pick up.

Price growth expectations are stronger in Canterbury, at 23 percent, and 18 percent across the rest of the South Island.

More people expect interest rates will rise.

Money with Susan Edmunds Morning Report Download MP3 2m

"Fixed mortgage rates had started to tick up in the first half of the year, in anticipation of the OCR rising over 2026. Our survey suggests households are closely watching the Reserve Bank and anticipating what the impacts of the Middle East conflict could mean for borrowing costs," ASB acting chief economist Kim Mundy said.

"More than six in ten New Zealanders now expect interest rates to be higher in one year's time. This widespread expectation that borrowing costs will rise is likely to keep a lid on house prices and preserve buyers' bargaining power for the rest of the year."

She said there were "decent" buying opportunities, particularly for first-home buyers.

"The 20 percent who think it's a good time to buy, that's actually at some of the higher levels we've seen in a while.

"If anything, it's a reflection of the fact that there is plenty of choice out there, we know the inventory levels are high. We know it's a buyer's market.

"In Auckland in particular, prices are still well below the 2021 peaks so there is that affordability aspect at play as well.

"Buyers have more choice, more time to make decisions and more clout at the negotiation table than in recent years."

She said she expected the housing market to remain subdued through 2026 and pick up from next year.

"We can't rule out a small fall in house prices in the coming months, but we're expecting conditions to gradually improve through 2027, as fewer New Zealanders move to Australia, population growth strengthens and the broader economy gains momentum.

"Some of the current headwinds that we're facing will start to recede."

Buyer sentiment would depend on the future path of interest rates, she said.

"We're expecting that the OCR will lift to around 3.25 percent by the end of this year. If anything the risk is a more gradual hiking cycle given the weakness we've seen in some of the domestic economic data lately.

"Outside of that I think once respondents know that interest rates have got to where they're going to peak for now, that in itself can help to lift sentiment because that's one uncertainty taken out of the market."

World.title: Kainga Ora shuts down South Auckland community hub to use space for housing
World.content:
South Auckland community hub set to close Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A south Auckland community hub is being shut down by its landlord Kainga Ora, despite those involved in the hub saying it has helped make the neighbourhood a better place.

The Māngere Community Enviro-Hub had a four year lease from the state housing agency, which it has used to develop community gardens, clean up litter, and teach local young people about sustainability.

But Kāinga Ora said the lease was always temporary, and when it was up next March, the land would be needed for a new housing development.

The Community Enviro-hub was home to six different charities - including a stream clean-up team, and groups that sold cheap bags of fruit and veg.

Fifteen-year-old Jackson Davida had been working at the hub part-time for the past year and a half and said he was proud to try to make his neighbourhood a better place.

"Because some people mistake Māngere for a hood that's not really good, or some people shouldn't come here. But we want to give Māngere a good reputation.

"From what I've seen now, I've seen the streets cleaner, I've seen more positive people."

Davita Alofaki (L) and Jackson Davida at the enviro hub. RNZ / Luka Forman

Rangatahi from Māngere College, like Jackson, had been involved in setting up the hub and maintaining it, cleaning up their streets of litter and learning about growing their own food.

Jackson said it would be a big loss for the neighbourhood if the hub closed down.

"What the government is trying to do to us right now, I don't really support it. If they realise what we do in the community, I think they'll definitely be upset that they let go of us, if we were to get kicked off this land."

Kāinga Ora manager of urban development and delivery, Nick Howcroft, said in a statement that from the beginning of the lease, it was understood that the arrangement would be temporary, and the land was needed for future housing development.

But Rata Taiwhanga, who was the co-ordinator of the hub, said he always saw it as a long term project.

"You know, if we fulfill the metrics of Kāinga Ora , which we did, that they would extend and actually see the benefit that we've been doing within in our communities."

The enviro-hub had provided a positive place for local rangatahi to spend their time, Taiwhanga said.

"In the time of where we are in Tamaki Makaurau in Auckland here, and especially in Māngere, there are just so many environments that are set up for our rangatahi to be led down the wrong path. And I think having [places like] these are really crucial."

The were several other bare sites in the area, that could have been developed before theirs, he said.

Te Ararata Stream Team trustee Pragna Patel. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The Te Ararata Stream Team, which ran stream clean-ups and tree plantings, was one of the charities based at the hub.

Trustee Pragna Patel said it had a container full of equipment on the site that it would need to find a new home for.

"Moving a container is no simple undertaking. It's going to cost us X amount of money, which we could have saved and used in community engagement, but it's just the way the cookie crumbles."

Patel said it would raise the issue with the MP for Māngere, Lemauga Lydia Sosene, to try to keep the community hub where it was.

Nick Howcroft from Kainga Ora said the enviro-hub had made a valuable contribution to the community, and Kainga Ora had offered to help find alternative locations for it to continue.

World.title: Can we de-extinct the moa and more importantly, should we?
World.content:
Colossal Biosciences calls itself an advanced genetics company that's developing the science that will save us all.

But its claims of taking a novel approach to de-extinction that is "not copying or cloning" are disputed by a growing number of scientists around the world.

That is not stopping the company from pressing ahead with its moa project with the recent announcement that it hatched 26 artifical eggs in a "foundational step" toward its goal of resurrecting extinct bird species.

Colossal Biosciences is describing its artificial egg as a "major breakthrough" in its de-extinction moa project. Supplied / Christopher Klee (Colossal Biosciences)

Sharon Brettkelly spoke to Colossal Biosciences for Our Changing World about its moa de-extinction plans and the critics, including the Prime Minister's science communicator prize winner Associate Professor Nic Rawlence of the University of Otago.

He says Colossal Biosciences is wasting millions of dollars making a genetically modified emu, when the money should be spent on live, endangered species.

The two-part series also explores the ethics of bringing the moa back to life and who should be consulted on reviving what many in Aotearoa believe is a taonga.

Extinction is not the end of the story

Colossal Biosciences says it is working to bring back the woolly mammoth within five years, after engineering a woolly mouse. Also on its de-extinction list are the thylacine or Tasmanian tiger, a type of African antelope known as the bluebuck and the dodo.

It says it has already resurrected the dire wolf with the birth of pups Romulus, Remus and Khaleesi last year, after creating a genomic blueprint from a 13,000-year-old tooth and 72,000-year-old ear bone samples.

Of the moa it says it is "restoring the past for a better future" in a partnership that is as important for conservation as it is for bringing the moa back to life.

Colossal Biosciences Australia-based chief biology officer, Andrew Pask. Supplied / Colossal Biosciences

"We can learn all sorts of things about the biology of those birds from looking at their genome," says Colossal Biosciences chief biology officer Dr Andrew Pask.

"There's a huge amount that you can understand about what their population sizes would have been in New Zealand. You can really start to unpack a lot more about what that landscape looked like in New Zealand with moa in it and how abundant those species were. And then really that can give you a much deeper understanding of then the impact that that's had on your ecosystems that we have left today."

And he says the artificial egg they have created "really opens up the possibilities of ways that we can manipulate bird development for conservation outcomes".

A short video on its website features the New Zealand team behind the plans - Canterbury Museum's Paul Schofield, filmmaker Sir Peter Jackson, and Mike Davidson and Kyle Davis of Ngāi Tahu Research Centre at University of Canterbury.

Filmmaker Sir Peter Jackson is backing plans to de-extinct the moa. AFP / Getty

Sir Peter says it is estimated there were about 150,000 moa walking around Aotearoa before all nine species became extinct about 600 years ago.

"We're now at the point where being extinct isn't really the end of the story," he says in the video.

Colossal Biosciences chief executive Ben Lamm says to bring back the animal that "has a cultural heritage here, it's almost overwhelming".

It emphasises it is a Māori-led initiative.

"It's really their vision, really putting the Māori first," Lamm says in the video.

Two sides to the story

But Māori researchers Professor Amanda Black and Professor Phillip Wilcox told Our Changing World that Colossal Biosciences has not consulted properly with tangata whenua.

"We didn't ask to have the moa back, whose decision was that?" asks Professor Black.

"The access and benefit sharing again, that's our genome, why have you got it?"

Dr Andrew Pask explained the process of resurrecting the flightless bird after already taking DNA samples from moa bones.

"The plan is to do it across both Texas and New Zealand," Dr Pask says.

"We've only just announced the project, we're still sequencing the moa genome so there's still lots of stuff to figure out.

"Where the genome engineering side would happen potentially at Dallas and then a lot of the assisted reproductive technology on different bird species, artifical egg technologies and things would all happen in New Zealand."

The technology Colossal Biosciences develops from the moa de-extinction process has immediate conservation applications for native birds on the brink of extinction in Aotearoa, he says.

He believes the first moa eggs will be hatched in New Zealand but he doesn't know where.

"I think we've really got to figure out what our genomes are, which is the closest surrogate and then that will help us figure out timelines as well."

Dr Pask says it is difficult to put a timeline on the project because Colossal Biosciences has still not identified the closest living relative - South America's tinamou and Australia's emu are potential candidates.

The emu (pictured) and tinamou are potential candidates to be the moa's closest living relative. Be Funky

Sir Peter says the moa will not be released into the wild or put into zoos.

"We want to be able to give the moa a natural environment as big as we possibly can," he says.

The description conjures up a Jurassic Park-like setting, an image that thrills some people and disturbs others.

Director of the University of Otago's paleogenetics department Associate Professor Nic Rawlence says under New Zealand's biosecurity laws the first moa would have to be put into a strict quarantine enclosure, like Orana Wildlife Park in Christchurch.

Supplied / Te Ara

"Then apply for a soft release or a field trial, make sure all of the controls are in place and only then would you be able to release them into the 'wild', in quotation marks," Dr Rawlence says.

Lincoln University's Professor Amanda Black is skepetical about the de-extinction plans.

"It's not really the argument that you can de-extinct something or not that I am interested in, and for the record I don't think you can because once something's gone it's gone," says Professor Black, who is on the government's Māori advisory group on the Gene Technology Bill going through the parliamentary process and the director of government-funded Bioprotection Aotearoa.

She describes Colossal Biosciences as fascinating and concerning but believes its de-extinction plans are a "hearts and minds strategy to get the headlines".

"The business model for Colossal is not about conservation, it's really about intellectual property and patent technology and spinoff companies and they're using that with genomes they've collected around the world," she says.

"Ethically is that what people want to really support and let companies come into New Zealand and do?"

Professor Amanda Black Claire Concannon/RNZ

Our Changing World approached Sir Peter Jackson, Ngāi Tahu Research Centre, the iwi itself and Canterbury Museum for comment and did not get any response.

In a story in Science magazine by Veronika Meduna, the research centre's director Mike Stevens said the iwi has not mandated the research center to do this work.

He said the centre has the academic independence "to wade into difficult things," and help the iwi explore and develop a position on the technology.

Professor Black says there is no single Māori voice on the issue, but the lack of broad consultation on the touchy subject of genetic modification is concerning. The project raises numerous questions for mana whenua.

She calls it a "very new take on an extremely old theme which is colonial practices and sovereignty".

"Why have you got the data, do you have permission to have that data? It really speaks to the indigenous data sovereignty conversations that we're having globally about where genomic data gets deposited."

Professor Black says New Zealanders might want to take a leaf out of Sir Sam Neil's book and discuss it over a cup of tea at the table.

In a written response to further questions, Colossal Biosciences says it is not appropriate for it to comment on whether it has consulted widely enough, that is "a judgement for Māori to make" and it recognises consultation is "not a box to check once" situation.

World.title: John Galliano 2027 Met Gala cancelled amid outrage
World.content: The move comes after a growing outcry over the decision by the museum and Anna Wintour, global editorial director of Vogue , to honour the designer at the Met Gala. Galliano was fired from Dior in 2011 and found guilty of “public insults” based on origin, religion, race or ethnicity after videos emerged of the designer saying “I love Hitler” and ranting antisemitic abuse at a café in Paris. The Met Gala, which is held on the first Monday in May, would fall next year on Yom HaShoah, a day of Holocaust remembrance.

World.title: Power cuts remain for some in North Island after stormy weather
World.content:
Weather warnings are no longer in place, but Monday's strong winds in the Hawke's Bay left hundreds without electricity.

Powerco's website showed 136 power cuts across the Manawatū-Whanganui, Taranaki, Bay of Plenty, and Waikato regions.

Powerco said 44 properties in Ashhurst had been without power since 7.05pm on Monday due to a fault on the feeder.

The electricity company said a power cut affecting 13 properties in Ashhurst since Monday afternoon appeared to be wind-related, but was still under investigation.

It said a smaller power cut in Upokongaro, affecting six properties, was due to trees hitting lines on Monday afternoon.

Powerco crews were assessing affected sites and working to restore power, it said.

World.title: Football great Lionel Messi retires from Argentina team
World.content:
Football great Lionel Messi has announced he will retire from the Argentinian team.

The announcement comes less than a month after the death of his father Jorge.

Following his father's death on August 7, Messi expressed doubts about the future of his international career.

In a post on Instagram released on Monday, Messi said he had penned a resignation statement two days after this year's World Cup final, which Argentina lost to Spain, but made his final decision only after the passing of his father.

Referring to lines from the original note, a picture of which Messi also posted, he said stepping down was a "decision that hurt" but that the "time had come".

"There isn’t much time left, and chapters are coming to an end, and this is one that hurts me a lot. "I love, have loved, and will always love being part of the national team. I gave everything I had; I have nothing left to give. "And besides, there are some very talented young players coming through who deserve their chance."

Messi was the captain of Argentina's men's national football side, leading them to victory in the World Cup in Qatar in 2022.

He is considered by many to be the best footballer of his era.

Lionel Messi's dad dies aged 68 Jorge Messi, the father of Argentinian football superstar Lionel, is mourned after dying aged 68 following a short illness.

He first entered competitive football playing for Barcelona in 2004, made his debut for the Argentinian side a year later and became the national team's captain in 2011.

The record eight-times Ballon d'Or winner is his country's record appearance-maker and scorer with 125 goals in 207 games, having transformed a complicated relationship with the national team into a story of redemption and triumph.

Among his achievements is winning a gold medal at the 2008 Beijing Summer Olympic Games, then aged 21.

The former Barcelona and Paris St Germain forward who now plays for Inter Miami added another Copa America title in 2024 and arrived at his sixth World Cup hoping to complete an extraordinary final chapter.

Throughout his career, Messi's father Jorge has played a fundamental role in fostering his career.

His death in early August was mourned across Argentina.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Cats claim they are not distracted by concussion controversy
World.content:
Geelong midfielder Tom Atkins is adamant the club's concussion saga has not been a distraction for the players as they prepare for Friday night's elimination final against Carlton at the MCG.

The Cats were last week fined $140,000 for failing to officially inform the AFL about the concussion waiver in Jake Kolodjashnij's contract.

Geelong fined over concussion scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

The penalty is $100,000 plus a suspended sanction of $40,000, which stems from the league fining Geelong last October after an investigation into the club's third-party agreements.

Kolodjashnij, who came forward as the player involved shortly after the story broke and has not played at any level since, returned to the club last week ahead of the finals.

Asked on Monday whether he or another player had a discussion around a similar concussion agreement, Atkins said: "No."

"Our focus has been performing on the weekends and we just wanted to make sure Kola [Kolodjashnij] was all right as teammates and as friends," Atkins said.

Voss assesses Blues' finals hopes Michael Voss speaks about the Blues' chances in the finals following their stunning turnaround.

"That's probably the extent of the detail that we looked into it as players."

Atkins said it was "awesome" to have Kolodjashnij around the club, now the finals had arrived.

"Obviously we'd love him to be back playing and back in training, but hopefully that can get itself sorted soon," Atkins said.

"But just having him in the rooms and seeing him smiling again is good."

AAP

World.title: Ex-Carlton coach Voss gives assessment of Blues' finals hopes
World.content:
Michael Voss has stopped short of declaring Carlton a genuine premiership threat but sees no reason his former team cannot make a deep run in the finals.

The Blues are riding a wave of momentum under Josh Fraser, who has engineered a remarkable turnaround since taking the coaching reins when Voss stepped down in May.

Fraser has won 11 of 14 matches at the helm, capped off by the come-from-behind victory over Melbourne in last week's wildcard encounter.

The staggering run has optimistic Carlton fans daring to dream of a first premiership since 1995, ahead of an elimination final against Geelong at the MCG on Friday night.

But with another three wins required in sudden-death matches just to reach the grand final, Voss said a drought-breaking flag was most likely beyond the Blues this year.

"It's very hard, isn't it? Percentages say that's a tough gig," Voss said.

"But they're certainly playing a high level of football if you look over the course of the last 10 or 11 weeks.

"They're the equal-form team of the competition, so there should be no reason that they can't look at every game and say that it's winnable."

The Blues ended the Demons' season last Saturday night. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Voss fell on his sword at Carlton after a 1-8 (win-loss record) start to the season and is determined to look forward rather than back at what might have been.

He said Fraser was "doing a great job" as coach and results showed "the right decision has been made" in appointing the former Collingwood ruck as Blues coach.

Voss lauded captain Patrick Cripps and leaders of the playing group for their efforts in turning Carlton's season around.

"One of my last messages with the leaders was: 'It's over to you and how do you make this a really player-led group?'" Voss said.

"They've clearly done that and more numbers are coming with them, so the heavy lifting isn't just on a few.

"You've got a lot of people responding and there's some pretty incredible human beings amongst that group.

"I'm just really pleased that they're getting the rewards that they've obviously been working really hard for."

Voss says Carlton in a better place than when he took charge Michael Voss has struck a defiant tone after leaving Carlton, insistent the AFL club is in better shape than when he started as coach.

Carlton has won three of its past four meetings with Geelong, with Voss noting extra attention on key Cats duo Tom Stewart and Gryan Miers had served them well.

Voss said the Blues' work in the contested areas of the game would hold them in good stead.

"Where Geelong are underestimated quite a fair bit is their contested game," he said.

"They're not so much dominant when it comes to stoppages, but they are post-stoppage.

"Carlton can do that blindfolded and they showed that again on the weekend against Melbourne.

"When the whips were cracking they really ramped that part of the game up.

"Because they match up really well against that, they actually put themselves in a really good position to win games."

AAP

World.title: Knight's prop cops season-ending ban after send-off
World.content:
Jacob Saifiti's NRL season is all but over after the Newcastle prop was handed a four-game suspension for a high tackle on Warriors winger Luke Laulilii.

Saifiti was sent off in the first half of Sunday's 46-32 defeat in Auckland and was handed a grade two reckless high tackle charge by the NRL's match review committee on Monday morning.

The Knights have a bye for the final round of the regular season, meaning Saifiti's ban will only kick in for their first finals game.

Newcastle — currently sitting seventh — will play an elimination final in week one but even if they were to upset the odds and qualify for the grand final, the Fijian prop would still be on the sidelines.

Saifiti's only hope of playing in the NRL again this season hinges on the prop contesting the charge at the judiciary on Tuesday in a bid to reduce his punishment.

Should the front-rower fight the suspension and lose his appeal, he will have another week added to his four-game ban.

Elsewhere, Cronulla prop Tom Hazelton is set to miss Cronulla's final regular season game against Melbourne after being cited for a hip-drop tackle on Ronald Volkman.

Hazelton was sin-binned by referee Ashley Klein late in Sunday's loss to Parramatta but will serve a one-game ban with an early guilty plea and be free to return for week one of the finals series.

AAP

World.title: Indigenous numbers in the AFL are down, but there's talent in the Top End
World.content:
A couple of years ago Hawthorn's Kaitlyn Ashmore, a Dja Dja Wurrung woman, spent some time in Alice Springs.

She was immediately taken by the gift for footy so many kids had up there, but knew the pathways for development were limited.

"I've been out to the communities … the talent up there is incredible," Ashmore said on the eve of the AFLW's Indigenous Round.

"But it's just getting them down here, or getting them in a program, and then keeping them in there and making them feel culturally safe."

Loading Instagram content

She was in the Red Centre in support of the Dreamtime Academy, an initiative founded by AFLW player Lulu Pullar along with fellow First Nations players Courtney Hodder, a Badimaya and Whadjuk woman, and Ally Anderson, a Ghungalu and Wakka Wakka woman.

There are 22 Indigenous players listed across the AFLW competition, down from 26 in 2023. In the men's competition the number has dropped from 87 in 2020 to 62 this season.

Ashmore said that was why the Indigenous Round was so important.

"It's honestly representation," she said.

"If we keep doing that, and celebrating Indigenous people, culture and stories like that, then hopefully we can get some more girls that want to join us."

'Work to do': AFL targets Indigenous player boost The AFL is considering a range of measures to boost the number of Indigenous players in the league following a significant decline in recent seasons.

On Sunday night more than 4,000 people packed out the stands at Marrara Stadium to watch Richmond beat Essendon in the Dreamtime match.

Among the spectators were diehard Tigers and Bombers fans and some who had never seen an AFL game before.

Last year the marquee Indigenous Round match was on a Friday night in Darwin and attracted almost 6,000 people.

But the game was fixtured around the men's wildcard round on a day with six AFLW matches and many locals said Sunday's 6:50pm time slot may have led to lower attendance than last year.

Richmond beat Essendon in front of a 4,000-strong crowd in Darwin. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

Match gets young fans dreaming

The elite game in the Top End was one part of nurturing football in the Northern Territory and helping to grow grassroots participation.

Top End Youth Academy head coach Ben White said just a couple of years ago most kids did not have an answer when he asked who their favourite AFLW player was.

He said now they were naming players such as Richmond's Monique Conti and Sydney's Zippy Fish.

"We've got those figureheads of the AFLW that girls can look up to and see that pathway. It's amazing," White said, crediting the Dreamtime match for bringing the game closer to community.

The crowd in Darwin for the Dreamtime game was a mix of diehard footy fans and new supporters. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

This has also been helped by the recent Northern Territory inclusions to the AFLW of Annabel Kievit, who plays for the Gold Coast Suns, and Dom Carbone, who was elevated to Collingwood's senior list for this season after playing for the Darwin Buffettes.

Essendon captain Bonnie Toogood said one of the most pleasing parts of coming up to the Top End with the Bombers was seeing the next generation of Indigenous kids in the stands.

Essendon has a strong connection with the Tiwi Islands. In April this year, AFLW players Mia Busch and Amy Gaylor, alongside The Long Walk's Jack Peris, ran footy clinics across the Tiwi Islands and West Arnhem Land.

Bonnie Toogood (right) says the Dreamtime game in Darwin is special for the players and competition. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

The Essendon players and staff will visit schools in Darwin on Monday.

Toogood said it was important to the team to connect with the community.

"It's the main reason as to why we want to come up here and celebrate Dreamtime," she said.

The Top End Youth Academy is fostering young talent and aiming to improve the standard of the game in the NT. (AFLNT Media: Tymunna Clements)

AFLNT launched the Darwin-based Top End Youth Academy this year in response to years of community demand for development opportunities and to strengthen existing talent pathways.

In a matter of months more than 400 players attended academy trials and more than 270 participants were picked up.

Youth Academy manager Josh Kleine was not surprised by the interest.

"Where those numbers might be higher than we expected, it doesn't shock me because there is that love and passion for the game up here," he said.

The AFLW has shown young kids that there is a pathway to the elite level. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

Kleine said there were a few times during the trials when he and White looked at each other and thought "we've got a fair bit of work to do here'".

But within a matter of months the skills of the kids, aged 10-15, improved out of sight.

"We were actually sitting here in this room and watching them do their warm up and they're just kicking in lanes, getting ready for the game, and nearly every target was being hit," Kleine said.

"We've done some work on things like leg drives and different things. And to see someone who was struggling to get the concept, panicked a little bit, and sort of rushed handballs out, to see that then translate into a game where they're actually taking the tackler on and driving through the contest, it's amazing to see.

"They're the moments that really get you. When you've had that time with the kids and you're coaching them, and you see those things where it's a kid who might have been struggling in this area, you put in the time on the track and then you see it translate on the field.

"It's those little moments that you find really touching."

There are more than 270 players in the Top End Youth Academy. (AFLNT Media: Tymunna Clements)

Kleine said the Darwin kids had a bit more access to programs and competitions than those in other parts of the NT, but the plan was for the academy to expand to places such as Tiwi, Katherine and Alice Springs.

"One thing with our academy [that] we always talk about is, we've only got you for an hour and a half a week on the track with training … we're limited with the time we have," he said.

"So our encouragement is take the lessons we teach you and do the work away from on during the week as well.

"And the girls, the work they're putting in on the track, you're definitely seeing it. You can see when they come back the next week — they've gone away and they've worked on these things. They've done their extra 100 kicks or whatever it is."

Documentary follows young Indigenous women chasing AFLW dreams Arthurina Moreen's desire was so great to play footy, she'd practice kicking bottles with her bare foot. A new documentary has shone a light on her resilience, and that of three other Tiwi Islander women as they chase AFLW stardom.

Kleine said he hoped to see more local talent make it to the elite level, but the goal was also to strengthen the game in the NT.

"Ultimately, not everyone's going to make it, but we're creating stronger territory football off the back of it," he said.

"Half our kids, we hope they become the future captains, the future coaches, all those sorts of things, and that the local clubs are here in the next 15 years.

"It's a flow-and-effect to make Territory footy stronger in the long run … it is a tumbleweed-type thing, where it just flows on, and everyone's continually growing and improving.

"Hopefully it helps close those gaps."

World.title: Scheffler wins PGA Tour Championship, Min Woo Lee ties fourth
World.content:
Adam Scott has had to settle for yet another cool milestone as Scottie Scheffler surpassed Tiger Woods as the PGA Tour's all-time leading prize money earner with his second season-long FedEx Cup crown.

Scheffler once again underlined his undisputed status as the world number one with a decisive three-shot triumph at the $US40 million ($56 million) Tour Championship in Atlanta.

The 2024 champion fired a closing four-under-par 66 to reel in third-round leader Viktor Hovland and join grand slam greats Rory McIlroy (2016, 2019, 2022) and Woods (2007, 2009) as only the third player to win the showpiece finale multiple times.

In pocketing the monster $US10 million winner's cheque, Scheffler also surged past Woods ($US120,999,166) with a mind-blowing $US130,390,661 in career on-course earnings in only his seventh season on the PGA Tour.

After starting three shots behind Hovland and alongside Scott in joint third, Scheffler surged clear to finish at 16-under for the tournament.

Hovland, the 2023 winner, was the outright runner-up despite a Sunday slip-up, a 72 as the Norwegian fell short in his own bid to win a second FedEx Cup.

American Ryan Gerard was third at 12-under following his own faltering 72.

With a closing 68, Min Woo Lee wound up one shot ahead of Scott, finishing as Australia's top finisher in an impressive seven-way tie for fourth on his Tour Championship debut.

Lee finished at 11-under with England's Alex Fitzpatrick (66), Americans Jacob Bridgeman (68), Russell Henley (68) and Chris Gotterup (71), McIlroy (69) and Swede Ludvig Aberg (71).

At 46 years, one month and 14 days, Scott was striving to become the oldest FedEx Cup champion, with Vijay Singh more than a year younger when he won in 2008.

Alas, it was not the former world number one's day.

Scott was in third spot for much of the afternoon, even pulling to within two shots of the lead early on the back nine.

But, unable to buy a birdie putt, Scott's bold challenge ended with a bogey on the par-4 16th hole after he hooked his drive wildly off the tee and hit a sloppy drop shot on number 17.

He eventually signed for a 72 to finish at 10 under with England's 2025 champ Tommy Fleetwood (67) and American world number three Cameron Young (70).

Still, Scott's share of 11th, 20 years after winning the Tour Championship, earned the veteran a tidy $US660,000.

That was enough to push Australia's 2013 Masters champion one up to seventh, above Justin Thomas, on the PGA Tour's all-time money list with $US74,880,596 in prize money.

Only Scheffler, Woods, McIlroy, Phil Mickelson, Justin Rose and Dustin Johnson are now above Scott.

AAP

World.title: Tearful Djokovic makes shock US Open exit in first round
World.content:
An emotional Novak Djokovic has made his earliest exit at a major in 20 years following a shock five-set loss to Argentine Mariano Navone at the US Open.

Playing through tears in the final set, four-time champion Djokovic — who was in physical discomfort for much of the match — fell to 49th-ranked Navone in the first round, 7-6 (7/5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1.

The match lasted almost four hours and 36 minutes on Arthur Ashe Stadium and finished just before midnight, local time.

The last time Djokovic exited a major in the first round was at the 2006 Australian Open.

He had previously never lost in the opening round at Flushing Meadows.

Djokovic made 70 unforced errors during the match.

The 24-time major winner vomited at least once and later appeared to be cramping when he grabbed his left foot.

Novak Djokovic was in discomfort throughout the match. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

"I pretty much despised every moment ⁠I spent on the court for that," Djokovic told reporters.

"I didn't enjoy myself. I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling on the court for me."

Djokovic added: "It's something that I've been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year: vomiting, throwing up. [It's a] serious issue there.

"Then my whole body starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain. The back just gave up in the end and shoulder, and I couldn't close it out."

The 39-year-old swallowed pills brought to him by a doctor and had his lower back massaged during a medical timeout between the fourth and fifth sets.

He also grimaced after several shots.

Throughout his time on court, it was clear Djokovic was not himself, as sickness and soreness took a toll.

"Five sets, against ‌the GOAT (greatest of all time), it's not something you ​do every day. I'm ‌very happy," Navone said in his on-court interview.

"It means a lot to me. It's a dream come true. Now I have to recover. It's almost 12 am. We have to go to sleep."

Mariano Navone (left) shakes hands with Novak Djokovic after his upset victory. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

Djokovic arrived for his 20th US Open appearance with questions ​over ‌his form and fitness after losing to Thiago Agustin Tirante in Cincinnati two weeks ago.

The match began in humid conditions but the roof of the main show court was soon closed when rain fell at Flushing Meadows.

Earlier, former champion Daniil Medvedev made light work of France's Hugo Gaston 6-4, 6-2, 6-4, exorcising the demons of his ill-fated campaign a year ago with an aggressive performance at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

A frequent — and gleeful — villain at the tournament he won in 2021, Medvedev crashed out in the opening round in 2025 but was all business on Sunday (local time), with 34 winners against just 11 from his opponent.

"You need to play your game. I knew he was going to do some drop shots, some underarm serves," Medvedev said.

"I needed to make some winners, put some pressure on him."

Russia's Daniil Medvedev celebrates after winning his first round match against France's Hugo Gaston. (Reuters: Mike Segar)

Gaston's creative shot-making had little impact on the nimble-footed, six-foot-six-inch Medvedev, and the Frenchman did himself no favours as he handed his opponent the break with a misplaced backhand in the seventh game.

The seventh seed upped his level in the second set, where the Frenchman gifted him the break in the third game when he whacked a forehand into the net.

Medvedev held the momentum from there, leaping into the air to hit a superbly placed backhand shot out of Gaston's reach on break point in the seventh.

Only days after publicly pondering a career in pickleball after his opening-match defeat at Winston-Salem, the mercurial Russian converted another break-point chance in the opening game of the third when he whipped a forehand past the Frenchman.

He closed it out with an unreturnable serve and will play the winner of a match later on Sunday between American wildcard Sebastian Gorzny and Belgian Raphael Collignon.

Cilic, Ruud pull out injured

Former champion Marin Cilic and 2022 runner-up Casper Ruud pulled out of the tournament due to injuries shortly after the tournament got underway on Sunday (local time).

Croatian Marin Cilic has pulled out of the US Open, a grand slam he won in 2014. (Reuters: Imagn Images/David Kirouac)

Cilic won the only major title of his career at Flushing Meadows 12 years ago, and the Croat will be replaced in the draw by lucky loser Otto Virtanen, who faces 23rd seed Andrey Rublev in the opening round.

Virtanen pulled out of his third-round qualifying match against Grigor Dimitrov with an injury.

Organisers did not specify what injured the 37-year-old Cilic. The veteran joins a growing list of withdrawals with the likes of Jannik Sinner, Jack Draper, Joao Fonseca and Holger Rune skipping the tournament this year.

Ruud, the runner-up to Carlos Alcaraz four years ago, was another high-profile player to pull out earlier, and lucky loser Arthur Gea will take his place in the opening round. The Frenchman meets Juan Manuel Cerundolo first up.

Loading Instagram content

The 27-year-old Ruud had retired during the second set of his Cincinnati Open meeting with Christopher O'Connell this month and said his back injury had not recovered in time.

"Unfortunately, my back hasn't healed as quickly as we had hoped," Ruud said on Instagram.

"We've been optimistic that I would recover in time, but my team and I have decided that we need to think long-term and give my body the time it needs. I'm very sad to announce that I have to withdraw from this year's U.S. Open singles event.

"It's never easy to miss a Grand Slam, but I know this is the right decision. I'll take the time I need to recover properly and come back stronger."

Ruud competed in the revamped mixed doubles tournament last week, partnering Diana Shnaider and the pair were beaten in the quarterfinals by Rublev and Mirra Andreeva.

Pegula shakes off nerves to win

Third-ranked Jessica Pegula shook off nerves that contributed to a slow start against Elena-Gabriela Ruse, winning her opening match in straight sets.

Leading off at Arthur Ashe Stadium, the 32-year-old American missed her first nine opportunities to break Ruse but found a rhythm and began dominating. Coming off a trip to the final at the Cincinnati Open, which she lost to Coco Gauff, Pegula won 92 per cent of her first-serve points on the way to a 6-3, 6-2 victory in 83 minutes.

"I was so nervous," Pegula said. "I was like sending GIFs of what I felt like. It was GIFs of people freaking out and stuff. … The first round of a slam, there's always a ton of nerves."

Maybe a little more this time, given what's at stake.

Pegula leads the women's tour with 46 wins this season. She has two titles and has reached three other finals. Pegula can become number one in the women's rankings if she wins her first major title and number two Elena Rybakina loses before the semifinals.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Rain forces Aussies off with US Open matches in the balance, Preston wins
World.content:
Kim Birrell and Aleksandar Vukic have been forced off the court due to rain, with their first-round US Open matches hanging in the balance.

Taylah Preston was the only victorious Australian on the first day at Flushing Meadows, with Birell and Vukic needing to wait until tomorrow to finish their tense matches.

Birrell, who lost the opening set to Croatia's Petra Marčinko, was locked in a tiebreaker in the second set when play was suspended.

The tiebreaker was locked at 3-3 when play was called off for the outside courts just after 8pm, local time, with Birrell needing to win to send the first-round match into a third and deciding set.

In the men's singles, fellow Australian Vukic was nearing the end of a five-set thriller when rain halted play.

Vukic, the world number 96, came from behind twice in the match to force a deciding set in New York against Japan's Rei Sakamoto.

Vukic is down a break in the fifth set, with Sakamoto, the world number 157, walking off the court with a 3-4 lead.

Wildcard Preston gets first grand slam win outside Australia

Taylah Preston is the first Australian into the second round of the US Open, claiming a straight-sets win over American Alycia Parks.

Taylah Preston has advanced to the second round of the US Open for the first time. (Reuters: Imagn Images/Mike Frey)

The 20-year-old from Western Australia, whose only previous second-round appearance at a grand slam was this year's Australian Open, produced a terrific performance to secure a 6-3, 6-3 victory.

"It's really special," the 20-year-old said after the straight-sets demolition job vindicated Tennis Australia's decision to award the tyro entry to the final major of 2026 under a reciprocal arrangement with the United States Tennis Association.

"Glad that my first grand slam win was in Australia, but hopefully I can keep winning rounds at all the slams, not just at home."

The Australian faced three break points in the fourth game of the opening set but was able to rally and level at 2-2. Preston then applied pressure to Parks's serve in the very next game, getting a 15-40 lead before winning the game on her second break point.

Preston broke Parks's serve in the ninth game to win the opening set.

Parks responded immediately by breaking Preston in the opening game of the second set.

Down 0-2 and facing, Preston roared back to win five games on the bounce, on her way to another 6-3 set win to close out the match.

Preston, world number 100, will either face Polish 20th seed Maja Chwalinska or American Taylor Townsend in the second round at Flushing Meadows.

Gibson, Hunter and Walton out in first round

A dejected Talia Gibson is doing her best to extract the positives after Donna Vekic crashed the rising star's US Open party in a rough start for the Australian contingent.

Talia Gibson went down in three sets to Donna Vekic of Croatia. (AP: Andres Kudacki)

Storm Hunter and Adam Walton also made early exits on day one at Flushing Meadows as Gibson was unable to disguise her anguish at an opportunity lost.

The 22-year-old rallied from a set and a service break down to look poised to claim her maiden grand slam victory outside Australia before Vekic steadied to post a 6-2, 4-6, 6-3 in two hours and 33 minutes.

The veteran Croat and 2024 Wimbledon semifinalist seemed to be unravelling after blowing a set and 4-1 lead, cursing herself and berating her box as Gibson roared back into the contest.

But Gibson was unable to wrestle back control after failing to convert any of four break-point chances in the second game of the deciding set.

She had Vekic down 0-40 serving at 4-2, only to miss five straight returns to ruefully let the Paris Olympics silver medallist off the hook.

"It's a hard one to swallow," Gibson said.

"Most of the time it's who makes the most unforced errors on the court who comes away with the loss, and today that was me, so it's just something to learn from."

But after starting the year well outside the world's top 100, Gibson has slashed her ranking in half after racking up some 30 match wins, including over former No.1 and dual Australian and US Open champion Naomi Osaka.

"Days like these are really tough. It's hard not to be disappointed. When it comes to the slams, every player wants to do well," said the world No.63.

"But if I'm looking at my entire year so far, I've been able to achieve some things that probably at the start of the year I probably wouldn't have thought I'd be able to do.

"So to still be in the position ranking that I currently have and moving forward to these next tournaments, I don't really have any points to defend, so it's kind of just no pressure and more opportunities."

Aussie qualifier Storm Hunter was defeated by 11th seed Marta Kostyuk in straight sets.

Storm Hunter was knocked out in the first round of the US Open after qualifying for the grand slam last week. (AP: Andres Kudacki)

After stumbling at this year's Australian Open, Kostyuk has been in sublime form at the grand slams, making the semifinals of the French Open and Wimbledon to arrive at Flushing Meadows as a genuine contender in the women's draw.

The 11th seed got down to business quickly once the match began, and powered to a 4-1 lead before overcoming a wobble to close out the first set when Hunter produced a double fault on set point.

Kostyuk tightened her grip on the clash in the second set, breaking early and never allowing Hunter a route back as she wrapped up a 6-4, 6-1 victory in 67 minutes.

"I'm very happy to be back to this amazing place," Kostyuk said on court.

"It's not easy to play a qualifier; they've played a whole tournament [already]. I'm very happy with my performance today. I try to keep myself grounded. There's still a long way to go; I'm enjoying my tennis."

Walton also bowed out early, missing two set points in the third set of a tight 7-6 (7-2), 6-2, 7-5 loss to China's Yibing Wu.

World number seven and three-time US Open quarterfinalist Alex de Minaur opens his title quest on Tuesday against Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.

ABC/Reuters/AAP

Tech.title: Alienware’s budget-friendly QD-OLED is discounted for the first time
Tech.content:
While memory and storage prices are still high, there are still good discounts on other gaming-related hardware. Take Alienware’s AW2726DM, for example. Dell is selling it for $319.99, a $30 break from the usual price of $349.99. The 27-inch gaming monitor features an QD-OLED panel for deep, immersive black levels, and quantum dots for full and vivid colors. With a 240Hz refresh rate for super smooth gaming, and AMD FreeSync Premium Plus to keep your frames per second and refresh rate locked together, this monitor is a great, budget-friendly choice for PC gamers who don’t want to compromise on contrast and fast response times.

Connectivity is a bit limited, with a DisplayPort 1.4 port that supports up to 240Hz at 2560 x 1440, and two HDMI ports that support up to 120Hz at its peak resolution. While some other screens have USB hubs or audio connections, they aren’t necessary for PC gaming, and sometimes add to the cost. The included stand has adjustable swivel, height, pivot, and tilt, with a 100 x 100 VESA mount in case you want to mount it to a monitor arm or use a different stand. It also sports a lengthy three year warranty with coverage for burn-in.

Tech.title: Car owners want tech they can ignore
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Automakers keep shoving more tech into their cars, despite evidence that consumers are increasingly fed up with huge screens and glitchy software. In fact, the features that car owners appreciate the most happen to be the ones they barely notice, according to the latest tech survey from JD Power.

The consumer research firm surveyed 68,084 owners of new 2026 model-year vehicles after 90 days of ownership. The survey touched on 40 automotive technologies covering comfort and convenience; connected vehicles; driver assist; electric vehicles; and smart vehicles.

The features that scored the highest were the ones that were the most inconspicuous, like smart ignition, in which the vehicle automatically starts and turns off based on driver actions, or smart HVAC systems, which use AI to automatically adjust the cabin environment for maximum comfort and efficiency. These were the big winners in JD’s survey — mostly because they require the least attention from the driver. Smart ignition, in particular, delivered the highest overall satisfaction, with only 2.4 problems per 100 vehicles.

“For automakers, the opportunity is to prioritize technology that makes driving simpler, not more complicated,” Doron Hikry, director of customer success at JD Power, said in a press release. “The features that solve real problems without adding effort or stress for the driver are the ones resonating most with customers.”

Superfluous tech features like passenger screens, in which an extra screen is embedded in the dash in front of passengers, rated the lowest in satisfaction. These screens first began cropping up in premium brands, like Mercedes, BMW, and Porsche, but have yet to bleed over to more mass-market vehicles. Apparently, they’re just wasted space on the dash, with more than one-third of owners who have a passenger screen reporting they’ve never tried to use it. Only 6 percent admitted to using their passenger screens every time they drive. Yikes.

Another tech feature that has more work to do in winning over customers is hands-free driving, also known as Level 2 Plus automation. These are features like Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, Ford’s BlueCruise, GM’s Super Cruise, and Mercedes’ Drive Pilot.

Unlike Level 2 systems, which require drivers to keep their hands on the steering wheel, these L2 Plus systems allow for completely hands-free driving on certain roads. Car owners told JD Power they preferred L2 systems in terms of design and quality of experience, suggesting that more automation does not necessarily mean more customer satisfaction. Interestingly, Level 2 systems were recording slightly higher problems per 100 vehicles (14.3) as L2 Plus ones (13.8).

“The results indicate that owners may currently be more comfortable with systems that clearly assist the driver rather than those that introduce a greater degree of automation,” said Hikry.

What these results suggest is that car owners don’t necessarily mind more technology in their vehicles, just as long as they don’t make the task of driving more complicated. The individual awards underscore this point: The Cadillac Escalade and Toyota Tundra both won for camera mirrors, while other automakers notched wins for blind-spot cameras, digital keys, one-pedal driving, and EV charging schedulers.

Tech.title: Phil Schiller is leaving his biggest jobs at Apple
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Longtime Apple executive Phil Schiller is stepping down from his role as the head of the App Store and Apple events, according to a report from Bloomberg. Following the change, Schiller will keep his Apple Fellow title and continue “working on unspecified initiatives,” Bloomberg reports.

Schiller initially joined Apple in 1987 and became the company’s head of marketing in 1997. He helped launch the App Store alongside Steve Jobs in 2008, but only started heading up the store in 2015. Over the years, Schiller has played a role in the development of many of Apple’s products, including the iPhone, iPad, iPod, and Macs, and has presented several of them at the company’s launch events. In recent years, Schiller has started stepping away from some of these responsibilities, as he relinquished his role as senior vice president of marketing to Greg Joswiak in 2020.

The news comes just one day before hardware leader John Ternus is set to take over for Apple CEO Tim Cook, who is stepping down on September 1st. As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is moving the App Store division under services head Eddy Cue, while Carson Oliver will continue to lead the store with the help of Ann Thai, who is in charge of app distribution tools and third-party marketplaces.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Along with heading up the App Store, which facilitated more than $1.4 trillion in transactions last year, Schiller has had to contend with legal battles and government regulations that have forced Apple to change its stringent policies surrounding app distribution and payments.

Tech.title: Markiplier is now GoPro’s biggest shareholder
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

YouTuber Mark “Markiplier” Fischbach has invested enough in GoPro to become its single largest shareholder, with an 8.5 percent stake in the company, Bloomberg reports. Speaking to Bloomberg, Fischbach said he thought GoPro “seems undervalued” and sees his investment as “part of a larger mission to make filmmaking more accessible,” following the release of his first feature film, Iron Lung, earlier this year.

Fishbach posted a video last week praising GoPro’s new Mission 1 ILS camera and comparing it to the pricier Red Komodo-X, saying he plans to use the Mission 1 ILS in future movies. It includes an affiliate code for the new camera, but we didn’t spot any mention of his involvement in the company in the caption or the video itself.

Fellow YouTuber Marques Brownlee commented on the news of Fischbach’s investment in a post on Threads with a still from the video, saying, “This is not a line I see crossed very often, but to each their own.”

GoPro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Read Tim Cook’s final message to Apple staff as CEO
Tech.content:
Team,

Today is my last day as CEO of Apple. This is a moment I always knew would come one day, and yet it is still hard to believe it has arrived and I am writing these words. I love this company and the team behind it, and I couldn’t let this day pass without sending a note to you, to tell you how grateful I am for the outpouring of affection you’ve sent my way, for the way you’ve shown up each and every day, and most of all, for the privilege of a lifetime serving as your leader.

The truth is, whatever there is to say about my success, I know it is all because of you. You have brought out the best in me. In all my life, I have never seen or been with such an extraordinary team of people before, and every day I get to see more examples of that.

There is something truly special about Apple. I am most proud of what an annual report could never capture. This place is proof that culture triumphs over everything. We share a belief that what we build matters, and that we have both the opportunity and the responsibility to leave the world better than we found it. That purpose is part of what makes this place extraordinary. Apple helps nurture it, but I believe it lived within each of you long before you arrived here. It is what brought you to this company and what continues to drive the work you do every day. Together, we have created something far greater than any one of us could have imagined or accomplished alone. And that’s the secret to our success. We bring out the best in each other. We lift each other up. We have made it possible to leave our “dent in the universe,” as Steve once described it, because of who we are and what we believe, because of what we value and how we see the world. How fortunate we are. How fortunate I am.

As you know, I am not leaving Apple. But I am stepping away from a role that I have loved deeply. I will miss this work in ways I can only begin to imagine, even as I remain completely at peace with my decision. I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John. Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.

I hope you know how much I appreciate you and what an honor it has been to be your CEO. Most of all, I hope you will continue to be proud to be part of this remarkable place we call Apple and always give it your very best. When we bring our whole selves to this work, with care for one another and for the people we serve, there is no limit to the profound difference we can make.

I look forward to seeing you in my new role at Apple Park and around the world.

With all I have and all I am, I am always

Yours,

Tim

Tech.title: Debian won’t ban AI code from its Linux distribution
Tech.content: The Debian Project nevertheless expects that all contributions submitted to Debian, regardless of how and with which tools they were produced, satisfy the same standards of quality, correctness, maintainability, and legal compliance. The use of a generative AI tool does not diminish the contributor’s responsibility for the work they submit. Contributors are expected to understand, review, test, and, where appropriate, modify AI-assisted output before incorporating it into Debian. Blindly accepting or uploading AI-generated material without appropriate human review is inconsistent with Debian’s established development practices. We [encourage] our contributors to disclose whether a contribution was made with AI [assistance], but do not require them to do so.

Tech.title: FTC accuses Amazon of running a ‘secret ad surcharge scheme’ in new lawsuit
Tech.content:
Amazon is facing a new lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 22 states, which accuse the company of secretly charging businesses more for advertising on its platform.

The lawsuit, filed Monday, claims Amazon spent more than seven years quietly increasing the prices advertisers paid through its online ad auctions. According to the complaint, the alleged practice affected more than one million brands and sellers and may have generated tens of billions of dollars in additional revenue for Amazon.

The 22 states joining the FTC are Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Vermont, and Washington.

The lawsuit centers on Amazon’s Sponsored Products ads, Sponsored Brands ads, and Display ads that run alongside its search results. According to the FTC, Amazon told more than 500,000 small and medium-sized businesses that it ran a “second-price” auction where the winning advertiser would pay just one cent more than the next-highest bid, rather than the full amount of their own bid. Because businesses believed they’d only ever pay slightly more than the runner-up, they had an incentive to bid high, trusting the system would keep their actual costs in check.

But the FTC alleges that starting in 2019, Amazon made a “surreptitious” change without telling advertisers. It added a hidden surcharge that Amazon internally called a “soft reserve price,” and used what one internal document called an “invented auction participant” — a fake bidder, basically — to push prices higher than true competition would have produced. The complaint alleges this amounted to a shill bid: rather than the price coming from a real competing advertiser, Amazon itself was manufacturing a higher number for advertisers to beat. As a result, the FTC claims Amazon charged Sponsored Products advertisers their own full winning bid close to 80% of the time — effectively turning what was marketed as a second-price auction into a first-price one.

The FTC claims Amazon made this change because it wanted more advertising revenue, and kept it hidden because disclosing it could have led advertisers to lower their bids, which would have cut into that revenue.

The company generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year.

In a blog post, Amazon described the FTC’s lawsuit as “misguided,” arguing that the complaint “fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate.”

The company added that its auctions evaluate billions of bids across different placements and formats, so prices naturally vary, and advertisers are “properly” informed about the pricing system.

Tech.title: The Pentagon now has its own version of ChatGPT and Grok
Tech.content:
The Pentagon has launched versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok, giving 3 million civilian and military personnel access to generative AI tools that have been tailored to “warfighter needs.”

ChatGPT Mil and Grok for Government — custom versions of the popular consumer generative AI tools — are now part of GenAI.mil, a centralized, secure portal launched last year.

GenAI.mil, which offered Google Gemini when it first launched, is designed to give Department of Defense employees access to commercial frontier AI models without sending sensitive government data through ordinary consumer channels. In particular, the official military version is exempt from the data collection that is difficult to avoid in consumer tech products.

And according to the Department of Defense, the generative AI portal has proven popular. GenAI.mil has already onboarded more than 1.7 million unique users out of the department’s 3 million personnel, according to the department.

These latest additions are part of the Pentagon’s broader effort to use AI tools to accelerate work and give the Department of Defense an edge without sacrificing security. They also highlight the absence of Anthropic’s Claude model and the Pentagon’s effort to work with other companies following its dispute with the frontier lab. Anthropic was labeled a supply-chain risk by the Trump administration — a designation that it is currently fighting in court — after it refused to give the Pentagon unrestricted use of its AI tools and instead insisted on certain safety guardrails.

ChatGPT Mil, which came out of the company’s OpenAI for Government program, will offer an experience familiar to commercial ChatGPT users. The tool will focus on chat, files, projects, and custom GPTs, according to the Defense Department. The tool will also support document-heavy, routine unclassified work such as administrative tasks, logistics, planning, and policy. Other features will be added over time.

The Pentagon positioned Grok’s capabilities and potential uses in much broader and more militaristic terms.

“Starshield AI’s Grok for Government will provide the warfighter with immediate productivity gains, stronger knowledge continuity and more secure and efficient collaboration,” according to the Defense Department’s press release. (SpaceX’s Starshield AI is a secure satellite network that uses the company’s existing Starlink tech)

The department added that Grok would allow its military “to execute missions faster and with greater precision across numerous operational contexts, ranging from market research analysis for acquisition professionals to supply chain management for logisticians.”

The Pentagon has struck deals with a number of other tech companies in a bid to boost its AI capabilities, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Reflection AI.
